The first: if it please the Sovereign to maintain the present form of Government.

The second: if it please the People to leave the administration to those at present charged with it.

I assume here what I believe I have demonstrated, viz. that in the State there is no fundamental law that cannot be revoked, not even the social pact. For if all the Citizens came together to break this pact by common accord, one cannot doubt but that it would be very legitimately broken. Grotius even thinks that anyone can renounce the State of which he is a member, and recover his natural liberty and his goods by leaving the country.* Now, it would be absurd if the Citizens united could not do what each of them can do separately.

End of the Third Book

Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

Book IV

Chapter 1

How the General Will Is Indestructible

So long as several men together consider themselves a single body, they have but a single will, which is directed towards their common preservation and general welfare. Then all the impulses of the State are vigorous and simple, its maxims are clear and luminous, it has no muddled or contradictory interests, and the common good is manifestly visible everywhere, requiring good sense alone in order to be discerned. Peace, unity and equality are enemies of political sophistication. Upright, simple men are hard to deceive because of their simplicity; sophisticated tricks and arguments do not impress them; they are not even subtle enough to be dupes. When, among the happiest people in the world, you see bands of peasants regulating affairs of State under an oak-tree, and always behaving wisely, can you prevent yourself from despising the subtleties of other nations, which make themselves illustrious and wretched with so much art and mystery?

A State thus governed has need of very few Laws, and as it becomes necessary to promulgate new ones, this necessity is universally seen. The first to propose them merely says what all have already felt, and there is no question of intrigues or eloquence in order to secure the passage into law of what each has already resolved to do, as soon as he is sure that the others will do likewise.

What misleads theorists is the fact that, seeing only States badly constituted from their inception, they are struck by the impossibility of maintaining such an administration in them. They imagine with delight all the idiocies of which a clever rascal or ingratiating talker could convince the people of Paris or London. They do not know that Cromwell1 would have been set to hard labour by the people of Berne, and the Duke of Beaufort2 clapped in a house of corrections by the Genevans.

But when the social knot begins to loosen and the State to grow weak, when particular interests begin to make themselves felt and lesser societies begin to influence the greater, the common interest becomes diluted and meets opposition. Unanimity no longer reigns in voting, the general will is no longer the will of all, contradictions and disputes arise, and the best opinion does not go unchallenged.

When at last the State, close to ruin, subsists only in a vain and illusory form, when the social bond is broken in every heart, when the basest interest shamelessly flaunts the sacred name of the public weal, then the general will falls silent. Prompted by secret motives, all no more speak as Citizens than as if the State had never existed; and iniquitous decrees directed only to particular interest are falsely passed in the guise of Laws.

Does it follow from this that the general will is annihilated or corrupted? No, it is always unchanging, incorruptible and pure. But it is subordinated to others that prevail over it. In detaching his own interest from the common interest, each sees clearly that he cannot separate it off entirely; but his share of the public evil seems as nothing to him, compared with the exclusive good that he means to appropriate. This particular good aside, he wills the general good in his own interest just as strongly as anyone else. Even in selling his suffrage for money, he does not extinguish the general will within himself, but evades it. The fault he commits is to change the state of the question, and to answer something other than what he has been asked, so that, instead of saying by his suffrage: it is beneficial to the State, he says: it is beneficial to some man or some party that such and such an opinion should prevail. Thus the law on public order in assemblies consists not so much in upholding the general will in them as in ensuring that it is always interrogated and always answers.

I would have many reflections to make here upon on the simple right to vote in every act of sovereignty: a right that no one can take away from Citizens. Also upon the right of voicing an opinion, proposing, dividing, and debating – which the Government always takes great care to confine to its own members.3 But this important subject would require a separate treatise, and I cannot say everything in this one.

Chapter 2

Of Suffrages

You can see from the preceding chapter that the way in which general affairs are conducted provides a clear enough indication of the present state of morals, and the health of the body politic. The more concord reigns in assemblies, i.e. the more opinions approach unanimity, the more the general will is dominant too. But long debates, dissension and tumult signal the ascendant of particular interests and the decline of the State.

This seems less obvious when two or more orders enter into its constitution, as in Rome with the Patricians and the Plebeians, whose disputes often disrupted the comitia even in the Republic’s best times. But this exception is more apparent than real. For the defect inherent in the body politic meant that you then, so to speak, had two States in one. What was not true for the two together was true for each separately. And indeed, even in the stormiest times, plebiscites of the People would always go through peacefully when the Senate did not interfere in them, and with a large majority of suffrages. Citizens having but one interest, the people had but a single will.

At the diametrically opposite extreme, unanimity recurs. This is when citizens, fallen into servitude, no longer have either liberty or will. Then fear and flattery change suffrages into acclamations; people no longer deliberate, they worship or they damn. Such was the Senate’s despicable way of voicing opinions under the Emperors. Sometimes this used to be done with ridiculous precautions. Tacitus observes that under Otho the Senators, while heaping curses on Vitellius, at the same time contrived to make a dreadful din, so that if by chance he became their master, he could not tell what each of them had said.4

These various considerations provide the maxims that should regulate the manner of counting votes and comparing opinions, depending on whether the general will is more or less easy to know, and the State more or less in decline.

There is but one law which by its nature demands unanimous consent. This is the social pact. For civil association is the most voluntary act in the world. Every man being born free and his own master, no one on any account whatsoever may subjugate him without his permission. To decide that the son of a slave is born a slave is to decide that he is not born a man.

So if at the time of the social pact there are opponents to it, their opposition does not invalidate the contract, it merely prevents their being included in it: they are foreigners among the Citizens. When the State is instituted, residence is consent; to dwell in the territory is to submit to the sovereignty.*

Outside of that original contract, the vote of the majority always binds all the others; it is a consequence of the contract itself. But one wonders how a man can be free, yet compelled to conform to wills that are not his own. How are opponents free, yet subjected to laws to which they have not consented.

I answer that the question is badly put. The Citizen consents to all laws, even those passed in spite of him, and even those that punish him when he dares to violate one of them. The constant will of all members of the State is the general will; it is through this that they are citizens and free.† When a law is proposed in the People’s assembly, what is asked of the members is not precisely whether they approve the proposal or reject it, but whether it is or is not in conformity with the general will which is their own. In giving his suffrage, each expresses his opinion on this, and from the reckoning of the votes the declaration of the general will is drawn. So when the opposite opinion to mine prevails, that proves nothing other than that I was mistaken, and that what I considered to be the general will was not. If my particular opinion had prevailed, I should have done something other than what I had willed, and it is then that I should not have been free.

This presupposes, to be sure, that all the qualities of the general will still reside in the majority; when they are there no longer, whichever side you take, there is no more liberty.

In showing above how particular wills were substituted for the general will in public deliberations, I indicated clearly enough the practicable means to forestall such abuse; I shall say more about that later. As for the proportional number of suffrages required to declare the general will, I likewise gave the principles according to which this can be determined. The difference of a single vote breaks a tie, a single opponent breaks unanimity; but between unanimity and a tied vote there are various unequal splits, to any one of which this number may be assigned, depending on the state and the needs of the body politic.

Two general maxims can serve to regulate these ratios; one: that the more important and serious the deliberations are, the closer the opinion that prevails must be to unanimity; the other: that the greater the urgency of the business under consideration, the narrower the allowable difference in the split of opinions must be. With deliberations that have to be resolved straight away, a single-vote majority should suffice. The first of these maxims seems more suitable for laws, the second for normal business. Be that as it may, it is by combining them that you can determine the best ratios to give to the majority in reaching a decision.

Chapter 3

Of Elections

With respect to elections of the Prince and the Magistrates, which, as I have said, are complex acts, there are two ways to proceed in them: viz. by choice and by lot. Both have been used in various Republics, and a very complicated mixture of the two can still be seen today in the election of the Doge of Venice.

Drawing lots, says Montesquieu, is natural to Democracy. I agree, but why so? Drawing lots, he continues, is a method of election that wounds no one. It leaves each Citizen a reasonable hope of serving the fatherland. These are not reasons.

If you keep in mind that the election of rulers is a function of Government and not of Sovereignty, you will see why recourse to lots is more natural to Democracy, where administration is all the better for its acts being fewer in number.

In every true Democracy, magistracy is not an advantage but an onerous responsibility, that cannot rightly be imposed upon one individual rather than another. The law alone can impose this responsibility on whomsoever is singled out by lot. For then, with the condition being equal for all and the choice depending on no human will, there is no particular application to dilute the universality of the law.

Under Aristocracy, the Prince chooses the Prince, the Government preserves itself by its own endeavours, and that is where suffrages are appropriate.

The example of the election of the Doge of Venice, far from undermining this distinction, confirms it. This combined form suits a mixed Government. For it is a mistake to see the Government of Venice as a true Aristocracy. If the People has no share in Government there, the nobility is itself the people. A host of poor Barnaboti5 never came close to any magistracy, and of their nobility had only the empty title of Excellency and the right to attend the Grand Council. This Grand Council being of equal number with our General Council in Geneva, its illustrious members have no more privileges than our mere Citizens. Setting aside the extreme disparity between the two Republics, it is certain that the bourgeoisie of Geneva accurately represents the Venetian Patriciate, our natives and residents represent the townsmen and the people of Venice, our peasants represent its mainland subjects. In short, however that Republic may be viewed, if its size is disregarded, its Government is no more aristocratic than ours. All the difference is that, having no ruler for life, we do not have the same need to draw lots.

Elections by lot would not have any great disadvantage in a true Democracy, where, everything being equal in terms of morals and talents, and also of maxims and fortunes, the choice would become almost immaterial. But I have already stated that no true Democracy has ever existed.

When choosing and drawing lots are combined, the former should fill positions that require specific talents, like military posts. The latter is suitable for those where good sense, justice and integrity are sufficient, like judicial posts; for in a well-constituted state, these qualities are common to all Citizens.

Neither drawing lots nor suffrages have any place in monarchical Government. The Monarch being by right alone the Prince and the sole Magistrate, the choice of his lieutenants belongs only to him. When the abbé de St Pierre proposed to multiply the Councils of the King of France and to elect their members by Ballot, he did not see that he was proposing to change the form of Government.6

I might still say something about the way of casting and counting votes in the people’s assembly, but perhaps a historical outline of the Roman polity in this respect will explain more vividly all the maxims I could establish. It is not beneath the dignity of a judicious reader to consider in some detail how public and private business was conducted in a Council of two hundred thousand men.

Chapter 4

Of the Roman Comitia

We have no well-attested records of the earliest days of Rome; it is even highly likely that most of the things retailed about those days are fables;* and in general the most instructive part of the annals of peoples, which is the story of their establishment, is the one that we most lack. Experience teaches us daily what causes engender the revolutions of empires. But since peoples are no longer formed, we scarcely have anything better than conjectures to explain how they were formed.

The customs we find established prove at least that those customs did have an origin. Among the traditions going back to such origins, those supported by the greatest authorities and that stronger reasons confirm must be taken as most reliable. Such are the maxims I have endeavoured to follow in inquiring how the freest and most powerful people on earth used to exercise its supreme power.

After the foundation of Rome the infant Republic, in other words the founder’s army, made up of Albans, Sabines and foreigners, was divided into three classes, which from this division took the name of Tribes. Each of these Tribes was subdivided into ten Curiae, and each Curia into Decuriae, at the head of which leaders were placed called Curions and Decurions.

In addition to this, a body of one hundred Equites or Horsemen called a Century was drawn from each Tribe. From this it is clear that those divisions, hardly necessary in a township, were at first only military. But it seems that an instinct of greatness led the little town of Rome to equip itself in advance with a polity fit for the capital of the world.

This first division soon produced a disadvantage. For since the Tribe of the Albans* and that of the Sabines† always remained in the same condition, while that of the foreigners‡ grew steadily through a constant influx, the latter did not take long to outstrip the two others. The remedy that Servius found for this dangerous fault was to change the division, replacing that by race – which he abolished – with a different one, derived from the areas of the town in which each Tribe dwelt. In place of three Tribes he made four of them, each of which dwelt on one of the hills of Rome and bore its name. Thus, remedying the present inequality, he further forestalled it for the future; and so that this division would be not just between places but between men, he forbade the residents of one neighbourhood to move into another, which prevented the races from merging.

He also doubled the three old Cavalry centuries and added twelve others to them, but still under the old names; a simple and judicious means by which he succeeded in distinguishing the body of Equites from that of the People, without causing the latter to grumble.

To these four urban Tribes Servius added fifteen more called rustic Tribes, because they were formed from residents in the countryside, split into as many cantons. Subsequently, as many more were created, the Roman People eventually became divided into thirty-five Tribes, a number that remained fixed until the end of the Republic.

This distinction between Town Tribes and country Tribes produced a noteworthy effect, because there is no other example of it, and because Rome was indebted to it for both the preservation of her mores and the growth of her empire. You might think that the urban Tribes soon appropriated power and honours, and lost no time in degrading the rustic Tribes. It was quite otherwise. The taste for rural life of the first Romans is well known. This taste came to them from the wise founder who united rustic and military toil with liberty, while to the town he so to speak relegated arts, crafts, intrigue, fortune and slavery.

Thus, with all the illustrious in Rome living in the country and cultivating the land, people grew accustomed to seek there alone the bulwarks of the Republic. This estate, being that of the most worthy Patricians, was honoured by everyone. The simple, hardworking life of Villagers was preferred to the easeful, lax life of the Townsmen of Rome; and, as a husbandman in the fields, one who would have been but a wretched proletarian in town became a respected Citizen. It was not for no reason, Varro used to say, that our magnanimous ancestors established in the Village the nursery for those sturdy, valiant men who defended them in time of war and fed them in time of peace. Pliny says positively that the country Tribes were honoured because of the men who made them up; whereas cowards whom people wished to degrade would be transferred ignominiously to the Town tribes. The Sabine Appius Claudius, having come to establish himself in Rome, was loaded with honours there and enrolled in a rustic Tribe that subsequently took the name of his family. Finally, all freedmen used to enter urban Tribes, never rural ones; and during the entire Republic there is not a single example of any of those freedmen, albeit having become a Citizen, attaining any magistracy.

This maxim was excellent; but it was pushed so far that it eventually gave rise to an alteration, and certainly a fault, in the polity.

First, the Censors, after having long appropriated the right to transfer arbitrarily the citizens of one Tribe to another, permitted most to have themselves enrolled in whichever they pleased: a permission that surely served no good purpose, and took away one of the great responsibilities of the censorship. Furthermore, with the Great and the powerful all having themselves enrolled in country Tribes, and with freedmen who had become Citizens remaining with the populace in the town ones, the Tribes in general no longer had any place or territory; but were all found so intermingled that it was no longer possible to discern the members of each except by the registers, so that the idea of the word Tribe shifted in this way from property to persons, or rather became almost a chimaera.

It happened also that the town Tribes, being closer at hand, often found themselves strongest in the comitia, and sold the State to any who deigned to buy the suffrages of the rabble who made them up.

As for the Curiae, the founder having made ten of them in each Tribe, the entire Roman people then enclosed within the walls of the town found itself made up of thirty Curiae, each of which had its temples, its Gods, its officers, its priests, and its festivals called compitalia, similar to the Paganalia that the rustic Tribes had subsequently.

When Servius made his new division, this number of thirty could not be shared equally among his four Tribes, and he did not want to touch these, so Curiae independent of Tribes became another division of Rome’s inhabitants. But there was no question of Curiae either in the rustic Tribes or in the people of which they were made up, because, the Tribes having become a purely civil institution and another system having been introduced for levying troops, the military divisions of Romulus proved superfluous. Thus, although each Citizen was enrolled in a Tribe, it was far from being the case that each was enrolled in a Curia.

Servius made also a third division that had no relation to the two preceding ones, and that through its effects became most important of all. He distributed the entire Roman people between six classes, which he distinguished neither by place nor by person but by property. So that the uppermost classes were filled by the rich, the lowest by the poor, and the middling by those who enjoyed a mediocre fortune. These six classes were sub-divided into 193 other bodies called centuries, and these bodies were so distributed that the uppermost Class alone included more than half of them, while the lowest formed but a single century. It thus transpired that the Class least numerous in men was most numerous in centuries, and the entire lowest class was reckoned only as a sub-division, although it contained more than half the inhabitants of Rome.

So that the people might perceive less clearly the consequences of this last arrangement, Servius took care to give it a military cast. Into the second class he inserted two centuries of armourers, and two centuries of instruments of war7 into the fourth. In each Class apart from the lowest he distinguished between young and old: in other words, between those who were obliged to bear arms and those whom by law their age exempted from doing so. A distinction which, more than that of property, resulted in the need frequently to initiate a new census or count. Finally, he wanted the assembly to take place on the Campus Martius, and all those who were of an age to serve to attend with their weapons.

The reason why he did not follow in the lowest class that same division into young and old is that the populace which made it up was not granted the honour of bearing arms for the fatherland. It was necessary to have homes in order to win the right to defend them; and there is perhaps not a single one out of those numberless hordes of beggars today adorning the armies of Kings who would not have been driven contemptuously from a Roman cohort, when soldiers were defenders of liberty.

A distinction was also made, however, in the lowest class between proletarians and those who were known as capite censi.8 The former, not wholly reduced to nothing, at least provided Citizens for the State, sometimes even soldiers at times of pressing need. As for those who had nothing at all and could be counted only by head, they were regarded as absolutely nothing, and Marius was the first who deigned to enlist them.9

Without deciding here if this third enumeration was good or bad in itself, I think I can assert that it was made practicable only by the simple mores of the first Romans, their disinterestedness, their taste for agriculture, and their disdain for commerce or pursuit of gain. Where is the modern people whose consuming greed, unsettled spirit, intrigue, constant movement, and perpetual reversals of fortune could allow such a system to last for twenty years without overturning the entire State? It must also be borne in mind that mores and censorship in Rome were stronger than this institution and corrected its flaws, so that certain rich men saw themselves relegated to the class of the poor for having made too great a display of their wealth.

From all this it can easily be understood why mention is almost never made of any but five classes, although there were really six of them. The sixth, providing neither soldiers for the army nor voters on the Campus Martius,* and being of almost no use in the Republic, was rarely counted for any purpose.

Such were the different divisions of the Roman people. Let us now see the effect that they produced in the assemblies. These legitimately convened assemblies were called comitia. They were held ordinarily in the Roman forum or on the Campus Martius, and were distinguished into Curiate comitia, Centuriate comitia, and Tribal comitia, depending on which of these forms was the basis of organization. The Curiate comitia had been instituted by Romulus, the Centuriate by Servius, and the Tribal by the people’s Tribunes. No law received sanction, no magistrate was elected, except in the comitia; and since there was no Citizen who was not enrolled in a Curia, a Century or a Tribe, it follows that no Citizen was excluded from the right of suffrage, and that the Roman People was truly Sovereign both de jure and de facto.

For the Comitia to be legitimately assembled, and for what they did to have force of law, three conditions had to be met: firstly, the body or Magistrate which convened them had to be vested with the requisite authority; secondly, the assembly had to be held on one of the days permitted by law; thirdly, the omens had to be favourable.

The reason for the first rule has no need of explanation. The second was an administrative matter: thus it was not permitted to hold comitia on holidays and market days, when the country people coming to Rome on business had no time to spend the day in the forum. By means of the third, the Senate would hold in check a proud and restless people, and when necessary temper the ardour of seditious Tribunes, though the latter found more than one means to rid themselves of this hindrance.

Laws and the election of leaders were not the only matters submitted to the judgement of the comitia. The Roman people having usurped the most important functions of Government, the fate of Europe may be said to have been settled in these assemblies. This variety of aims gave rise to the different forms these assemblies would take, according to the matters on which they had to pronounce.

To judge these different forms it suffices to compare them. In establishing the Curiae, Romulus had in mind to contain the Senate by the people and the People by the Senate, while dominating all equally. So by this form he gave the people all the authority of numbers, in order to balance the authority of power and wealth which he left to the Patricians. But in keeping with the spirit of Monarchy, he nevertheless left more advantage to the Patricians through the influence of their Clients on the majority of suffrages. This admirable institution of Patrons and Clients was a masterpiece of politics and of humanity, without which the Patriciate, so contrary to the spirit of the Republic, would not have been able to survive. Rome alone had the honour of giving the world this fine example, which never led to any abuse, yet which has never been followed.

The fact that this same form of Curiae survived under the Kings up until Servius, and that the reign of the last Tarquin was not counted as legitimate, led to the royal laws being generally distinguished by the name of leges curiatae.

Under the Republic the Curiae, still limited to the four urban Tribes, and no longer containing any but the populace of Rome, could not suit either the Senate, which was at the head of the Patricians, or the Tribunes, who, albeit plebeians, were at the head of the prosperous Citizens. So they fell into disrepute, and their degradation was such that their thirty Lictors in assembly used to do what the Curiate comitia should have done.

Division by Century was so favourable to the Aristocracy that at first you cannot see how the Senate did not always prevail in Comitia thus designated, which elected the Consuls, the Censors, and the other curule Magistrates. For of the one hundred and ninety-three centuries that constituted the six Classes of the whole Roman people, since the uppermost Class comprised ninety-eight of them and since votes were counted only by Century, this uppermost Class alone prevailed over the rest in number of votes. When all its Centuries were in agreement, the suffrages would no longer even be collected; what the smallest number had decided was taken as the decision of the multitude, and in the Centuriate Comitia business may be said to have been settled far more by majorities of cash than of votes.

But this excessive authority was tempered by two means. First, since the Tribunes ordinarily and a great number of Plebeians always were in the class of the wealthy, they balanced the influence of the Patricians in this uppermost class.

The second means consisted in this: that instead of first making the Centuries vote in order, which would have meant always starting with the foremost, one used to be drawn by lot, and this one* proceeded alone to the election; after which all the Centuries, summoned on another day according to their rank, would repeat the same election and ordinarily confirm it. The authority of example was thus removed from rank and given to chance, in keeping with the principle of Democracy.

This custom resulted in another advantage too. This is that Citizens from the countryside had time between the two elections to inform themselves of the merits of the Candidate provisionally nominated, in order to give their vote only with full knowledge. But, on the pretext of speed, this custom was successfully abolished, and the two elections took place on the same day.

The Tribal Comitia were properly the Council of the Roman people. They were convened by the Tribunes alone; they elected the Tribunes and passed their plebiscites. Not only did the Senate have no status there, it did not even have the right to attend them, and, forced to obey laws on which they had not been able to vote, the Senators in this respect were less free than the humblest Citizens. This injustice was wholly ill conceived, and alone sufficed to invalidate the decrees of a body to which all its members were not admitted. If all the Patricians had attended these Comitia in keeping with the right they possessed as Citizens, by becoming mere individuals they would scarcely have influenced a system where suffrages were collected by counting heads, and where the least proletarian had the same power as the Prince of the Senate.

So you can see that, apart from the order resulting from these various divisions for collecting the suffrages of so great a People, those divisions could not be reduced to forms indifferent in themselves, but each one had effects related to the purposes that led to its being chosen.

Without going into greater detail about this, the foregoing clarifications indicate that the Tribal Comitia were most favourable to popular Government, and the Centuriate Comitia to Aristocracy. As for the Curiate Comitia, where the populace of Rome alone formed the majority, as these served only to favour tyranny and evil designs they necessarily fell into disrepute, and even the seditious abstained from a means that too openly exposed their plans. It is certain that the entire majesty of the Roman People was to be found only in the Centuriate Comitia, which alone were complete, given that the rustic Tribes were missing from the Curiate Comitia, the Senate and the Patricians from the Tribal Comitia.

As for the manner of collecting suffrages, among the earliest Romans it was as simple as their mores, albeit still less simple than in Sparta. Each man would give his suffrage aloud, a Clerk would duly write them down. A majority of votes in each Tribe determined the suffrage of the Tribe, a majority of votes among the Tribes determined the suffrage of the people, and likewise with the Curiae and the Centuries. This custom was good so long as honesty reigned among the Citizens and each was ashamed to give his suffrage publicly for an unjust opinion or an unworthy subject. But when the people grew corrupt and votes were bought, it agreed that these should be cast in secret, so that buyers might be restrained through mistrust and scoundrels provided with means not to be traitors.

I know that Cicero10 condemns this change and holds it partly responsible for the ruin of the Republic. But although I am sensible of the weight that Cicero’s authority must have here, I cannot share his opinion. I think, on the contrary, that the downfall of the State was hastened because not enough changes of the kind were made. Just as the diet of healthy people is not fit for the sick, you should not seek to govern a corrupt people through the same Laws which suit a good people. Nothing proves this maxim better than the long life of the Republic of Venice, which still retains a simulacrum of existence solely because its laws are suited only to wicked men.

So tablets were distributed to the Citizens, by means of which each could vote without anyone knowing what his opinion was. New formalities were also established for collecting the tablets, counting the votes, comparing the numbers, etc. Which did not prevent the integrity of the Officers charged with these functions* from often coming under suspicion. To prevent intrigue and the buying and selling of votes Edicts were eventually passed, the large number of which proves their ineffectiveness.

Towards the final days, it was often necessary to have recourse to extraordinary expedients to compensate for the inadequacy of the laws. Sometimes miracles would be invoked; while this device might impress the people, however, it did not impress those who governed it. Sometimes an assembly would suddenly be convened before the Candidates had time to arrange their intrigues. Sometimes a whole session would be used up in talking, when the people was seen to be convinced and ready to make a wrong move. But finally ambition overcame everything. And what is unbelievable is that, amid so much abuse, that immense people, thanks to its ancient rules, did not fail to elect Magistrates, pass laws, try cases, expedite private and public business, with almost as much facility as the Senate itself could have done.

Chapter 5

Of the Tribunate

When an exact proportion cannot be established between the constituent parts of the State, or indestructible causes are forever altering the ratios between them, then one sets up a particular magistracy, not of the same kind as the rest, which places every term back into its true ratio, and which makes a bond or middle term either between Prince and People or between Prince and Sovereign or, if need be, vis-à-vis both at once.

This body, which I shall call Tribunate, is the preserver of the laws and of the legislative power. It sometimes serves to protect the Sovereign against the Government, as the Tribunes of the people did in Rome, sometimes to support the Government against the People, as the Council of Ten does today in Venice, and sometimes to hold the balance on both sides, as the Ephors used to do in Sparta.

The Tribunate is by no means a constituent part of the City, and should have no portion of the legislative or executive power. But it is just in this that its own power is the greater: for while being able to do nothing, it can prevent everything. It is more sacred and more revered as a defender of the Laws than the Prince which executes them and than the Sovereign which gives them. This is what was very clearly seen in Rome when those proud Patricians, who always disdained the entire people, were forced to bend before a mere officer of the people, who had neither auspices nor jurisdiction.

The Tribunate wisely tempered is the most solid support of a good constitution; but should ever its strength be too great, it overturns everything. As for weakness, this is not in its nature; and provided it is something, it is never less than what is necessary.

It degenerates into tyranny when it usurps the executive power of which it is only the moderator, and if it seeks to dispense laws that it should only protect. The enormous power of the Ephors, which held no danger so long as Sparta preserved her mores, accelerated her corruption once this set in. The blood of Agis,11 whose throat was cut by those tyrants, was avenged by his successor: the crime and the punishment of the Ephors alike hastened the downfall of the Republic, and after Cleomenes12 Sparta no longer amounted to anything. Rome too perished in the same way, and the excessive power of the Tribunes, usurped by degrees, with the help of laws made for liberty finally served to safeguard the Emperors who destroyed it. As for the Council of Ten in Venice, it is a Tribunal of blood, horrible alike to Patricians and People, and which, far from proudly protecting the laws, after their degradation serves only to deal in the shadows blows that no one dares to perceive.

The Tribunate, like Government, grows weaker through multiplication of its members. When the Tribunes of the Roman people, at first two in number, then five, sought to double this number, the Senate allowed them to do so in full confidence of being able to play them off against each other, which did not fail to happen.

The best means of preventing the usurpations of so redoubtable a body, a means that has not yet occurred to any Government, would be not to make the body permanent, but to set intervals during which it would remain suppressed. These intervals, which should not be long enough to give abuses time to assert themselves, can be fixed by law, in such a way that, if the need arises, they can easily be shortened by means of extraordinary commissions.

This method seems to me to have no disadvantage, because the Tribunate, as I have said, not being part of the constitution, can be removed without harm to the latter; and it seems to me to be effective, because a newly established magistrate starts off not from the power that his predecessor had, but from that which the law gives him.

Chapter 6

Of Dictatorship

The inflexibility of Laws, which prevents them from bending to events, can in certain cases render them harmful, so that they can bring about the downfall of the State at a time of crisis. The order and slow pace of legal forms require a span of time that circumstances sometimes preclude. A thousand cases may arise that the Legislator has not foreseen, and it is a very necessary kind of foresight to be aware that you cannot foresee everything.

So you should not seek to affirm political institutions to the point of forswearing the power to suspend their effect. Sparta itself allowed its laws to slumber.

But it is only the greatest dangers that can outweigh the danger of diluting public order, and the sacred power of the laws should never be stayed other than when it is a matter of saving the fatherland. In such rare and manifest cases, public safety is provided for by an individual act handing responsibility for it to the most worthy. This commission can be effected in two ways, depending on the type of danger.

If to find a remedy it is enough to increase the government’s activity, government is concentrated in one or two of its members. Hence, it is not the authority of the laws that is diluted, but merely the form of their administration. But if the danger is such that the apparatus of laws is an obstacle to being safeguarded against it, then a supreme ruler is named who for a while may silence all laws and suspend Sovereign authority. In such a case the general will is not called into doubt, and it is obvious that the primary intention of the people is that the State should not perish. In this way the suspension of legislative authority by no means abolishes it. The magistrate who silences it cannot make it speak; he dominates it without being able to represent it. He can do everything except make laws.

The former means was employed by the Roman Senate when, by an accepted formula, it would charge the Consuls with providing for the safety of the Republic. The second occurred when one of the two Consuls nominated a Dictator* – a custom Rome had taken from Alba.

In the early days of the Republic, Dictatorship would often be resorted to, because the State did not yet have a sufficiently stable grounding to be able to maintain itself by the strength of its constitution. Since its mores then made superfluous many of the precautions that would have been necessary at another time, people feared neither that a Dictator might abuse his authority, nor that he might attempt to retain it beyond its term. It seemed, on the contrary, that so great a power was a burden to the person vested with it, so hastily did he seek to rid himself of it, as if taking the place of the laws would have been too onerous and dangerous a responsibility!

So it is the risk not of abuse but of depreciation that in the earliest times causes injudicious use of this supreme magistracy to be condemned. For while the practice used to be lavished on Elections, Dedications and purely formal matters, it was to be feared that it might become less formidable when the need arose, and that people might become accustomed to look upon a title used only for empty ceremonies as an empty title.

Towards the end of the Republic the Romans, grown more circumspect, were as unreasonably sparing with Dictatorship as they had formerly been lavish with it. It was easy to see that their fear was ill-founded; that the weakness of the capital then ensured its safety against the Magistrates it harboured in its bosom; that a Dictator could in certain cases defend public liberty without ever being able to undermine it; and that Rome’s shackles would not be forged in Rome herself, but in her armies. The small resistance offered to Sulla by Marius, and to Caesar by Pompey,13 clearly showed what might be expected of internal authority against external force.

This error caused them to make big mistakes. One such, for example, was that of not nominating a Dictator during the Catiline affair.14 For as this involved only the interior of the town and at most a few provinces in Italy, a Dictator with the limitless authority that the Laws gave him would easily have dismantled the conspiracy, which was suppressed only by a combination of lucky chances that human prudence should never have expected.

Instead of that, the Senate contented itself with handing over all its power to the Consuls. Whence it happened that Cicero, in order to act effectively, was compelled to exceed that power at a critical juncture; and if the first transports of joy caused his conduct to be approved, it was with justice that he was subsequently called to account for the blood of Citizens shed against the laws – a reproach that would not have been made to a Dictator. But the Consul’s eloquence carried all before him. And since he himself, albeit a Roman, preferred his glory to his fatherland, he sought not so much the most legitimate and safest means to save the State as the means to have all the honour in this affair.* So he was rightly honoured as the liberator of Rome, and rightly punished as a violator of the laws. However brilliant his recall might have been, it was undoubtedly a pardon.

Furthermore, however this important commission is conferred, it is vital to fix its duration to one very brief term that can never be extended. In the crises that lead to its establishment, the State is soon destroyed or saved; and once the pressing need is over, Dictatorship becomes tyrannical or pointless. In Rome, where Dictators held office for only six months, most abdicated before this term. Had the term been longer, perhaps they would have been tempted to extend it further, as did the Decemvirs with their one-year term. The Dictator had time only to attend to the need that had prompted his election; he had no time to dream of other projects.

Chapter 7

Of the Censorship

Just as the general will is declared by the law, public judgement is declared by the censorship. Public opinion is the kind of law of which the Censor is the Minister, and which he merely applies to particular cases, following the example of the Prince.

Hence, far from the censorial tribunal being the arbiter of the people’s opinion, it is merely the body that declares the latter; and as soon as it distances itself from that opinion, its decisions are vain and ineffective.

It is useless to distinguish the mores of a nation from the objects of its esteem; for all this stems from the same principle and necessarily intermingles. Among all the peoples of the world, it is not nature at all but opinion that determines their choice of pleasures. Reform the opinions of men and their mores will purify themselves. You always love what is beautiful or what you find so, but it is in this judgement that you may err; so it is this judgement that must be regulated. Whosoever judges mores judges honour, and whosoever judges honour takes his law from opinion.

The opinions of a people spring from its constitution. Although the law does not regulate morals, it is legislation that engenders them; when legislation weakens, morals degenerate, but then the judgement of the Censors will not do what the force of the laws has not done.

It follows from this that the Censorship can be useful for preserving morals, never for re-establishing them. Establish Censors while the Laws are in vigour; as soon as they have lost their vigour, all is desperate. Nothing legitimate still has force, when the laws have force no longer.

The Censorship upholds morals by preventing opinions from becoming corrupted, by preserving their rectitude through wise applications, sometimes even by fixing them when they are still uncertain. The use of seconds in duels, carried to excess in the Kingdom of France, was abolished there by the following few words from an Edict of the King: as for those who are so cowardly as to call upon Seconds. This judgement, anticipating that of the public, at a stroke determined it. But when the same Edicts sought to declare that it was also an act of cowardice to fight a duel, which is quite true but contrary to the common opinion, the public took no heed of this decision, on which its judgement was already formed.

I have said elsewhere* that since public opinion is subject to no constraint, there should be no vestige of constraint in the tribunal established to represent it. The art with which this device, wholly lost among the moderns, was put into effect among the Romans and especially among the Lacedaemonians15 cannot be sufficiently admired.

When a man of bad morals offered a good suggestion in the council of Sparta, the Ephors paid no heed to it but had the same proposal made by a virtuous Citizen. What an honour for one, what shame for the other, without having given praise or blame to either of the two! Certain drunkards from Samos defiled the Tribunal of the Ephors.† The next day a public Edict gave Samians permission to be filthy. A real punishment would have been less severe than such impunity. When Sparta has pronounced on what is or is not decent, Greece does not appeal against its judgements.

Chapter 8

Of Civil Religion

Men at first had no other Kings than the Gods, nor any other than Theocratic Government. They reasoned like Caligula, and they were then reasoning correctly. It takes a long deterioration of feelings and ideas before you can bring yourself to take a fellow man as your master, and flatter yourself that you will do well by it.

From the mere fact that people used to place God at the head of every political society, it followed that there were as many Gods as peoples. Two peoples alien to one another and almost always hostile could not long acknowledge the same master. Two armies locked in battle would not be able to obey the same leader. So national divisions gave rise to polytheism, and thereafter to theological and civil intolerance, which are naturally the same, as will be stated below.

The fantasy harboured by the Greeks of finding their own Gods among barbarian peoples came from their other fantasy of regarding themselves as the natural Sovereigns of those peoples. But in our day the sort of erudition that turns upon the identity of Gods of different nations is quite ridiculous: as if Moloch, Saturn and Chronos could be the same God; as if the Baal of the Phoenicians,17 the Zeus of the Greeks and the Jupiter of the Latins could be the same; as if chimaerical Beings bearing different names could still have something in common!

And if you ask how it was that under paganism, when each State had its cult and its Gods, there were no wars of religion? I answer that it was precisely because every State, having its own cult as well as its Government, made no distinction at all between its Gods and its laws. Political war was also Theological: the provinces of the Gods were so to speak fixed by the boundaries of nations. The God of one people had no rights over other peoples. The Gods of the Pagans were by no means jealous Gods: they shared among them the empire of the world. Even Moses and the Hebrew People sometimes countenanced this idea, by speaking about the God of Israel. It is true that they regarded as naught the Gods of the Canaanites, proscribed peoples destined for destruction, whose place they were to occupy. But see how they used to speak about the divinities of the neighbouring peoples whom they were forbidden to attack! Is not the possession of what belongs to Chamos your God, Jephtha said to the Ammonites, lawfully due to you? We by the same token possess the lands that our victorious God has won.* It seems to me that there was a clearly acknowledged equivalence here between the rights of Chamos and those of the God of Israel.

But when the Jews, subject to the Kings of Babylon and later to the Kings of Syria, wished to insist on not acknowledging any other God than theirs, this refusal, viewed as a rebellion against the victor, brought down upon them the persecutions that can be read about in their history, and of which no other example is seen before Christianity.†

Since every religion was thus attached solely to the laws of the State that prescribed it, there was no other way of converting a people than to subjugate it, nor any other missionaries than conquerors. And since the obligation to change cult was the law for the vanquished, it was necessary to start by winning before talking about it. Far from men fighting for the Gods, as in Homer it was the Gods who would fight for men. Each man would ask his own for victory, and pay for it with new altars. Before taking a place, the Romans would call upon its Gods to abandon it; and when they left to the Tarentines their irate Gods, it was because they then regarded those Gods as subject to their own and obliged to do them homage. They let the vanquished keep their Gods as they let them keep their laws. A crown for the Capitoline Jupiter was often the only tribute they would impose.

Eventually, the Romans having extended their cult and their Gods with their empire, and having themselves adopted those of the vanquished by granting them and their Gods the rights of the City, the peoples of that vast empire imperceptibly found themselves with multitudinous Gods and cults, more or less the same everywhere. And this is how paganism in the known world was eventually just one single Religion.

It was in these circumstances that Jesus came to establish a Spiritual kingdom on earth, which, if the theological system is separated from the political system, resulted in the State ceasing to be one and caused the internecine divisions that have never ceased to trouble the Christian peoples. Now, since this new idea of an otherworldly kingdom had never succeeded in entering the heads of the pagans, they still regarded the Christians as true rebels who, cloaked in a hypocritical submission, were only waiting for the moment to make themselves independent and masters, and adroitly to usurp the authority that in their weakness they were feigning to respect. Such was the cause of the persecutions.

What the pagans had feared took place. Then everything began to look different, the humble Christians adopted a different language, and the supposed otherworldly kingdom was soon seen to become, under a visible ruler, the most violent despotism in this world.

However, since there was always a Prince and civil laws, the result of this twofold power was a perpetual conflict of jurisdiction that made any good polity impossible in the Christian States, and people never succeeded in knowing whom they were obliged to obey, the master or the priest.

Several peoples, however, even in Europe or its near neighbourhood, sought to preserve or to re-establish the old system, but without success. The spirit of Christianity was victorious everywhere. Holy worship still remained or again became independent of the Sovereign, and without any necessary connection with the body of the State. Mohammed had very sound views; he bound together his political system well and, so long as the form of his Government survived under the Caliphs who succeeded him, that Government was precisely single and in this respect good. But the Arabs, having become prosperous, learned, civilized, soft and weak, were subjugated by barbarians. Then division between the two powers began anew; although less apparent among Mohammedans than among Christians, it is nevertheless there, above all in the sect of Ali,18 and States exist such as Persia where it continually makes itself felt.

Among us, the Kings of England have installed themselves as rulers of the Church, the Tsars have done as much. But by this title they have made themselves less its masters than its Ministers. They have acquired not so much the right to change it as the power to preserve it. They are not its legislators, they are merely its Princes. Wherever the Clergy forms a body,* it is master and legislator in its domain. So there are two powers, two Sovereigns, in England and in Russia, just as elsewhere. Of all Christian Authors, the philosopher Hobbes is the only one to have seen clearly the malady and the cure; to have dared propose to join the two heads of the eagle and reduce everything to political unity, without which neither State nor Government will ever be well constituted. But he must have seen that the dominant spirit of Christianity was incompatible with his system, and that the interest of the Priest would always be stronger than that of the State. It is not so much what is horrible and false in his politics as what is right and true that has made it hateful.†

I think that by exploring historical facts from this angle it would be easy to refute the opposing sentiments of Bayle and Warburton,19 one of whom claims that no Religion is useful to the body politic, while the other maintains that on the contrary Christianity is the latter’s firmest prop. To the former I would prove that no State was ever founded without Religion serving as its basis, and to the second that Christian law is at bottom more harmful than useful to the strong constitution of the State. To make myself fully understood, it is necessary merely to give a little more precision to the overly vague notions of Religion that relate to my subject.

Religion considered in relation to society, which is either general or particular, can also be divided into two kinds, viz. the Religion of man and that of the Citizen. The former, without Temples, without altars, without rites, limited to the purely inward cult of the Supreme God and to the eternal duties of morality, is the pure and simple Religion of the Gospel, the true Theism, and what can be called natural divine right. The latter, inscribed in a single country, gives the latter its Gods, its own tutelary Patrons: it has its dogmas, its rites, its external cult prescribed by the laws; outside the single Nation that follows it, all is infidel for it, foreign, barbarous; it extends the duties and rights of man only as far as its altars. Such were all the Religions of the first peoples, which can be given the name of civil or positive divine right.

There is a third, more bizarre, form of Religion which, by giving men two legislations, two rulers, two fatherlands, subjects them to contradictory duties and prevents them from being at once devout men and Citizens. Such is the religion of the Lamas, such is that of the Japanese, such is Roman Christianity. It may be called the religion of the Priest and results in a sort of mixed and unsociable right that has no name.

Considering these three sorts of religion politically, they all have their defects. The third is so manifestly bad that to amuse oneself by proving it is a waste of time. All that breaks social unity is worthless. All institutions that place man in contradiction with himself are worthless.

The second is good in that it unites the divine cult with love of the laws, and by making the fatherland the object of the Citizens’ adoration teaches them that to serve the State is to serve its tutelary God. This is a kind of Theocracy, in which there should be no other pontiff than the Prince, nor other priests than the magistrates. To die for your country is then to seek martyrdom, to violate the laws is to be impious, and to subject a guilty man to public execration is to consign him to the anger of the Gods: sacer estod.20

But it is bad in that, being based on error and falsehood, it deceives men, makes them credulous and superstitious, and drowns the true cult of divinity in empty ceremonial. It is bad too when, becoming exclusive and tyrannical, it renders a people bloodthirsty and intolerant; in such a way that it exudes only murder and massacre, and believes it is carrying out a holy action by killing whomsoever does not accept its Gods. This places such a people in a natural state of war against all others, very harmful to its own security.

So there remains the Religion of man or Christianity, not that of today, but that of the Gospel, which is entirely different. Through this holy, sublime and genuine Religion men, as children of the same God, all recognize one another as brethren, and the society that unites them is not dissolved even at death.

But this Religion, having no particular relation with the body politic, allows to the laws only such force as they draw from themselves, without adding to them any other force; hence, one of the great bonds of particular societies remains ineffective. Even worse, far from attaching Citizens’ hearts to the State, it detaches them from it, as from all earthly things: I know of nothing more contrary to the social spirit.21

We are told that a people of true Christians would form the most perfect society imaginable. I see only one great difficulty in this supposition, which is that a society of true Christians would no longer be a society of men.

I even say that this supposed society, for all its perfection, would be neither the strongest nor the most durable. By dint of being perfect, it would lack cohesion; its destructive vice would lie in its very perfection.

Everyone would fulfil his duty. The people would submit to the laws, the rulers would be just and moderate, the magistrates would be honest and incorruptible, the soldiers would scorn death, there would be neither vanity nor luxury: all this is very fine, but let us look further.

Christianity is a wholly spiritual religion, concerned solely with Heavenly things: the Christian’s fatherland is not of this world. He does his duty, to be sure, but he does it with profound indifference as to the good or bad outcome of his efforts. Provided he has nothing with which to reproach himself, it matters little to him whether everything goes well or ill here below. If the State prospers, he scarcely dares to enjoy the public felicity, fearing to grow proud of his country’s glory; if the State declines, he blesses the hand of God that weighs heavily upon his people.

For society to be peaceful and harmony maintained, all Citizens without exception would have to be equally good Christians. But if a single ambitious man is unfortunately to be found there, a single hypocrite – a Catiline, for example, or a Cromwell – this man will very surely pay little heed to his pious compatriots. Christian charity does not easily allow anyone to think ill of his neighbours. Once he has found by some ruse the art of imposing himself upon them and seizing a portion of the public authority, behold a man set up in dignity: God wills that he be respected. Soon behold a power: God wills that he be obeyed. Does the man in whom that power is vested abuse it? He is the rod with which God punishes his children. You would scruple to drive out the usurper: it would be necessary to disturb the public peace, use violence, shed blood, all of which accords ill with Christian meekness. And after all, what does it matter if you are free or a serf in this vale of tears? The essential thing is to go to paradise, and resignation is simply one more means to that.

Does some foreign war break out? The Citizens march unconcernedly to battle, none of them thinks of fleeing. They do their duty, but without passion for victory; they know better how to die than how to win. Whether they are victors or vanquished, what matter? Does providence not know better than they what they need? Just imagine what advantage a proud, impetuous and impassioned enemy can draw from their stoicism! Pit against them those generous peoples who used to be consumed by ardent love for glory and the fatherland, imagine your Christian republic against Sparta or Rome; the pious Christians will be beaten, crushed, destroyed before having had time to gather their wits, or will owe their salvation only to the scorn that their enemy will conceive for them. The oath of Fabius’ soldiers22 was a fine one and to my liking: they did not swear to die or conquer; they swore to return victorious, and they kept their oath. Never would Christians have made its like; they would have thought they were tempting God.

But I err in speaking of a Christian Republic: each of these two words excludes the other. Christianity preaches only servitude and dependence. Its spirit is too favourable to tyranny for tyranny not always to benefit by it. True Christians are made to be slaves; they know this and are scarcely perturbed by it; this brief life has too low a price in their eyes.

Christian troops are excellent, we are told. I deny it. Let me be shown any such. As for me, I do not know of any Christian troops. People will cite the Crusades. Without disputing the valour of the Crusaders, I shall note that, far from being Christians, they were soldiers of the priest; they were Citizens of the Church: they were fighting for its Spiritual country, which it had made temporal, one knows not how. When all is said and done, this amounts to paganism. As the Gospel establishes no national Religion, a holy war is impossible among Christians.

Under pagan Emperors, Christian soldiers were brave; all Christian authors assert this, and I believe it. They were vying for honour against pagan Troops. As soon as the Emperors were Christians this rivalry ceased, and once the cross had driven out the eagle all Roman valour disappeared.

But leaving political considerations aside, let us return to right and determine its principles on this important point. The right that the social pact gives the Sovereign over its subjects, as I have said, does not go beyond the limits of public utility.* Hence, subjects must account to the Sovereign for their opinions only in as much as these opinions concern the community. Now, it does indeed concern the State that every Citizen should have a Religion that makes him love his duties; but the dogmas of this Religion are of interest to the State or to members only in as much as these dogmas have to do with morality and the duties which the person who professes them is bound to fulfil towards others. Everyone may in addition have such opinions as he pleases, without it being the Sovereign’s province to know them. For since no competency exists in the other world, whatever the fate of subjects may be in the life to come, that is not the Sovereign’s business, provided they are good citizens in this life.

So there is a purely civil profession of faith whose articles it is the Sovereign’s province to determine, not precisely like dogmas of Religion, but as feelings of sociability, without which it is impossible to be a good Citizen or a loyal subject.* Without being able to oblige anyone to believe them, the Sovereign can exile from the State anyone who does not believe them. It can exile him, not as impious, but as unsociable: as incapable of sincerely loving the laws and justice, or of sacrificing his life if need be to his duty. And if anyone, after having publicly recognized these same dogmas, conducts himself as though not believing them, may he be punished by death. He has committed the greatest of crimes, he has lied before the laws.23

The dogmas of the civil Religion24 must be simple, few in number, enunciated with precision and without explanations or commentaries. The existence of the powerful, intelligent, beneficent, prescient and provident Divinity; the life to come; the happiness of the just; the punishment of the wicked; the sanctity of the Social Contract and of the Laws: these are the positive dogmas. As for the negative dogmas, I restrict them to just one: viz. intolerance, which belongs to the cults we have excluded.

Those who distinguish civil intolerance and theological intolerance are mistaken, in my opinion. These two kinds of intolerance are inseparable. To live in peace with people you believe are damned is impossible; to love them would be to hate God, who punishes them. It is absolutely necessary to either bring them back to the fold or consign them to torment. Wherever theological intolerance is accepted, it is bound to have some civil effect;* and once it does, the Sovereign is no longer Sovereign, even in the temporal sphere. From then on Priests are the true masters; Kings are merely their officers.

Now that there is no longer, and can no longer be, an exclusive national Religion, we must tolerate all those which tolerate others, in so far as their dogmas have nothing contrary to the duties of the Citizen. But anyone who dares to say No salvation outside the Church must be driven from the State. Unless the State is the Church, and the Prince is the Pontiff. Such a dogma is good only in a Theocratic Government; in any other it is pernicious. The reason why Henri IV is said to have embraced the Roman Religion ought to cause any honest man to leave it, and especially any Prince who knows how to reason.

Chapter 9

Conclusion

Having set forth the true principles of political right and attempted to ground the State on this basis, what remains is to buttress it by its external relations, including the right of nations, commerce, the right of war and conquest, public right, leagues, negotiations, treaties, etc. But all this forms a new subject too vast for my short gaze, which I should always have fixed closer at hand.

End

Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

Prefatory Note

The chapter ‘Of the General Society of Mankind’, included in the draft version of the Social Contract but excised from the final text, is an important bridge between the published version and Rousseau’s earlier writings such as the Discourse on Inequality. It is also of great importance for understanding Rousseau’s conception of the relationship between political institutions and morality.

The chapter essentially consists of an engagement with an article which Denis Diderot had published on the topic of ‘Natural Right’ in 1755. Diderot’s article appeared in the same volume of the Encyclopédie as Rousseau’s entry on ‘Political Economy’. In that article, Diderot attempts to argue against a sceptic who sees what the demands of justice are but sees no reason to comply with them and prefers to take his chances in a world of mutual predation. Diderot argues that such a sceptic is unreasonable and fails a basic test of reciprocity. Diderot further argues for a thesis concerning the content of justice, which is determined by the general will of the human race as a whole. After canvassing the possibility of a kind of general assembly of the human race (and even of a broader circle of moral concern, including animals), Diderot suggests that we can locate the content in existing moral practice and institutions and by introspection: by each person looking into their heart and determining what it is reasonable for people to demand of one another. Rousseau’s somewhat incredulous response to Diderot emphasizes the importance of political institutions to the acquisition of moral sensibility. Diderot’s ‘violent interlocutor’, standing outside of such institutions, has no reason to recognize the claims of justice.

The present translation is based on the text contained in volume 3 of the Pléiade edition of Oeuvres Complètes produced under the direction of Bernard Gagnebin and Marcel Raymond in 1964. The paragraphs contained in square brackets are crossed-out in Rousseau’s original manuscript.

or
