A free people obeys, but it does not serve; there are leaders and not masters. It obeys the Laws, but obeys only the Laws; and it is through the strength of the Laws that it does not obey men. All the barriers to the power of Magistrates provided in Republics are established only to guarantee the sacred domain of the Laws against their violations. They are Ministers of the Laws, not their arbiters; they must maintain them, not infringe them. A People is free, whatever the form of its Government, when, in the one who governs it, it sees not the man but the organ of the Law. In a word, liberty always follows the fate of the Laws, it rules or perishes with them – I know nothing more certain.

You have good and wise Laws, whether in themselves or merely by virtue of the fact that they are Laws. Any condition imposed upon each by all can be burdensome to no one; and the worst of Laws is still preferable to the best master; for every master has preferences, and the Law never has such.

Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

CONSTITUTIONAL PROPOSAL FOR CORSICA

Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

Prefatory Note

The Corsican Republic, under the leadership of Pasquale Paoli, had proclaimed its independence from Genoa and sovereignty in 1755. Rousseau, an admirer of the new republic, had written:

There is still one country in Europe fit to be given laws: it is the Isle of Corsica. The valour and constancy with which that brave people has managed to recover and defend its liberty would deserve that some wise man should teach it to preserve that liberty. I have a feeling that one day that little island will astonish Europe. (Of the Social Contract, Book II, Chapter 10)

As a result of these words, a Corsican patriot and officer in the French army, Matthieu Buttafoco, wrote to ask him if he would be willing to draft a constitution for the republic. In his reply, on 22 September 1764, Rousseau declares himself daunted by the task given his lack of direct knowledge of the territory and the impossibility, in his state of health, of visiting the island in person. Buttafoco supplied Rousseau with further information, and the philosopher set to work in early 1765, producing the somewhat fragmentary text we have today. Had history turned out differently, Rousseau might have returned to the project, but the Genoese, perceiving correctly that they could not dislodge the republic, sold their interest to France, which invaded in 1768–9, ending the republic and forcing Paoli into exile. The main respect in which the island ended up astonishing Europe was not as a beacon of republican virtue, but rather by providing the world with the future French Emperor, Napoleon Bonaparte.

The text is an interesting example of Rousseau trying to apply the principles of the Social Contract to a real political subject. One noteworthy point is that Rousseau espouses a much more collectivist view of property in Corsica than he does elsewhere in his writings. The text was unpublished until an edition by G. Streickeisen-Moltou in 1861.

The present translation is based on the text contained in volume 3 of the Pléiade edition of Oeuvres Complètes produced under the direction of Bernard Gagnebin and Marcel Raymond in 1964.

Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

Constitutional Proposal for Corsica

Foreword

You ask for a Plan of Government fit for Corsica. It is asking more than you think. There are peoples who could not be well governed, however you might go about it, because among them the law has no purchase, and a government without laws cannot be a good government. The Corsican people, quite to the contrary, strikes me as most fortunately disposed by nature to receive a good administration. But this is not yet enough. All things have their abuses, often inevitable, and those of political institutions follow so hard upon their being established that it is hardly worth doing it only to see them degenerate so quickly.

People seek to guard against this inconvenience by mechanisms to maintain government in its primitive state. They bind it with a thousand chains, a thousand fetters, to keep it from declining; and they so burden it that, crushed by the weight of its irons, it remains inactive and immobile. If it does not slide towards its fall, neither does it advance towards its goal.

All this comes from the fact that they separate two inseparable things: viz. the body that governs and the body that is governed. As originally established these two bodies form but one; they separate only through abuse of that original establishment.

In such a case, wise men shape the government for the nation, ensuring appropriate relations. Yet there is something far better to do, which is to shape the nation for the government. In the former case, as the government declines while the nation remains the same, its appropriateness disappears. In the latter case, everything changes at the same pace; and the nation, forcibly dragging the government with it, maintains the government when it maintains itself, but causes its decline when it itself declines. They are appropriate to one another at all times.

The Corsican people is in the fortunate condition that makes good institutions possible: it can start off from the first point and take steps not to degenerate. Full of vigour and health, it can yield to a government that will keep it vigorous and healthy. However, the establishment of such a government is already bound to find obstacles. The Corsicans have not yet adopted the vices of other nations, but they have already adopted their prejudices. It is these prejudices that must be combated and destroyed in order to shape good institutions.

Proposal

The advantageous situation of the Island of Corsica and the happy nature of its inhabitants seem to offer them a reasonable hope of managing to become a prosperous people, and one day to make their appearance in Europe if, in the institutions they are contemplating, they turn their gaze in that direction. But the extreme exhaustion into which forty years of continuous warfare have cast them, the present poverty of their island, and the state of depopulation and devastation in which it finds itself, do not allow them at once to endow themselves with the costly administration that would be needed to civilize them for that purpose. Moreover, countless unconquerable obstacles would stand in the way of implementing such a plan. Genoa, still mistress of part of the coast and almost all the maritime strongholds, would repeatedly crush their infant navy, constantly exposed to the twofold danger of the Genoese and the Barbary pirates.1 They could rule the sea only with warships that would cost them ten times more than trade could bring them. Exposed on land and sea, forced to protect themselves on all sides, what would they become? They would be at everyone’s mercy, unable in their weakness to conclude any advantageous commercial treaty, and everyone would lay down the law to them. Amid so many risks, they would have only those profits that no one else would deign to make, and that would be reduced to nothing. And if, by some good fortune hard to comprehend, they overcame all these difficulties, their very prosperity, drawing upon them the eyes of their neighbours, would be a fresh danger to their ill-established liberty. A continual object of greed for the great powers and jealousy for the lesser, their island would be threatened at every moment by a fresh enslavement that it would no longer be able to escape.

To whatever end the Corsican nation may wish to civilize itself, the first thing it must do is to endow itself by its own endeavours with all the coherence it can achieve. Whosoever depends on others, and does not have his resources within himself, could never be free. Alliances, treaties, the pledged word of men – all this can bind the weak to the strong, but never binds the strong to the weak. So leave negotiations to the powers that be, and rely only on yourself. Noble Corsicans, who knows better than you all that men may draw from themselves? Without friends, without support, without money, without an army, enslaved to terrible masters, you alone have shaken off their yoke. You have seen the most formidable potentates of Europe band together turn by turn against you, swamping your island with foreign armies. You have overcome everything. Your constancy alone did what money could not have done: by seeking to preserve your wealth, you would have lost your liberty. Conclusions must not be drawn from other nations for your own. Maxims drawn from your own experience are the best according to which you could govern yourselves.

The important thing is not so much to become other than what you are, it is to know how to remain like that. The Corsicans have gained a lot since becoming free: they have combined prudence with courage, they have learned to obey their equals, they have acquired virtues and mores, and they had no laws. If they could remain thus by their own endeavour, I should see almost nothing to do. But when the danger that has united them recedes, the factions that it wards off will be reborn among them and, instead of combining their forces for the maintenance of their independence, they will use them against one another and have none left to defend themselves, if anyone comes again to attack them. So there you already have what needs to be prevented. The divisions among the Corsicans have from time immemorial been a device of their masters to render them weak and dependent; but this continually employed device has eventually produced an inclination, and has rendered them naturally restless, turbulent, hard to govern even by their own rulers. Good laws are needed, and a new constitution, in order to re-establish the concord for which tyranny has destroyed the very desire. Corsica, subjected to foreign masters whose hard yoke it has never borne patiently, was ever in turmoil. Its people must now make a new study, and must seek peace in liberty.

So these are the principles which in my view should serve as a basis for their legislation: to take advantage of their people and their country as far as possible; to cultivate and assemble their own forces, rely only upon these, and no more think about foreign powers than if none such existed.

Let us start off from this in order to establish the maxims of our foundation.

Since the island of Corsica cannot grow rich in money, it should strive to grow rich in men. The power that comes from population is more real than that which comes from finances, and produces its effect more surely. Use of manpower being impossible to hide, it always goes to its public destination. This is not the case with use of money, which flows and melts into private destinations. It is amassed for one purpose, it is dispensed for another. The people pays to be protected, but what it gives serves to oppress it. This means that a state rich in money is always weak, and that a state rich in men is always strong.

In order to multiply men, you must multiply their subsistence, hence agriculture. By this word I do not mean the art of paying attention to agriculture, establishing academies to talk about it, or making books to study it. I mean a constitution that will induce a people to spread across the whole surface of its territory, to settle there and cultivate it at every point, to love rural life and its related labours, to find in these the essentials and the charms of life so effectively that it will have not the slightest wish to abandon them.

The taste for agriculture is advantageous to population not merely in increasing men’s subsistence, but in endowing the body of the nation with a temperament and mores that cause men to be born in greater numbers. In all countries, dwellers on the land propagate more than city dwellers, whether thanks to the simplicity of rural life which forms better-constituted bodies, or thanks to the unflagging labour which prevents disorder and vice: for, all things being equal, the chastest women – those whose senses are less inflamed by recourse to pleasure – produce more children than others; and it is no less certain that men over-stimulated by debauchery, the inevitable effect of idleness, are less fit for reproduction than those whom a hardworking condition makes more temperate.

Peasants are far more attached to their soil than town-dwellers are to their cities. The equality and simplicity of rural life, for those who know no other, has a charm that gives them no wish to change it. Whence the contentment with his condition that makes man peaceable; whence the love of his fatherland that attaches him to its constitution.

Cultivation of the land forms patient, sturdy men such as are needed to become good soldiers. Those drawn from the towns are surly and soft, they cannot endure the fatigues of war, they melt away on the march, sicknesses consume them, they fight among themselves and flee before the enemy. Trained militia are the best and most reliable troops; the true education of the soldier is husbandry.

The only way to maintain a State in independence from others is agriculture. Should you have all the riches of the world, if you do not have the wherewithal to feed yourself you depend on others. Your neighbours can set whatever price they please on your money, because they can wait; but the bread we need has a price for us that permits no argument. In every kind of commerce, it is always the person in less haste who imposes his law on the other. I concede that in a system of finance you would have to operate according to other views; everything depends on the final target at which you are aiming. Commerce produces wealth, but agriculture ensures liberty.

You will say that it would be better to have both at once – but they are incompatible, as will be shown hereafter. In all countries, you will add, people cultivate the land. I agree. Just as in all countries there is commerce, everywhere people engage in a little business or a lot, but this does not mean that everywhere agriculture and commerce flourish. I am examining here not what takes place in the nature of things, but what results from the kind of government and general spirit of the nation.

Although the form of government that a people gives itself is more often the product of chance and luck than of any real choice, there are nevertheless qualities in the nature and soil of every country that provide it with a government more suitable than others, and each form of government has a particular strength that carries peoples towards one occupation or another.2

The form of government that we have to choose is on the one hand the least costly, because Corsica is poor, and on the other hand the most favourable for agriculture, because agriculture is for the moment the only occupation that can preserve for the Corsican people the independence it has won and give it the stability it needs.

The least costly administration is that which passes through the fewest degrees and requires the fewest different orders: such is generally the republican and in particular the democratic state.

The most favourable administration for agriculture is the one whose strength, not being concentrated at any point, does not involve an unequal distribution of the people but leaves the latter equally distributed across the territory: such is democracy.

In Switzerland you may see a very striking application of these principles. Switzerland is in general a poor and barren country. Its government is everywhere republican. But in cantons more fertile than the rest, like those of Berne, Soleure and Fribourg, the government is aristocratic. In the poorer ones, those where cultivation is more thankless and requires greater labour, the government is democratic. The State has only what is needed to subsist under the simplest administration. Under any other it would waste away and perish.

You will say that Corsica, more fertile and with a milder climate, can support a costlier government. That would be true at another time, but now, burdened by a lengthy enslavement and desolated by lengthy wars, the nation first and foremost needs to recover. Once it has put its fertile soil to good use, it will be able to think about becoming prosperous and endowing itself with a more splendid administration. The success of the original institution will subsequently make necessary its transformation. Cultivation of the fields cultivates the mind. Every cultivating people multiplies: it multiplies in proportion to the product of its land; and when this land is fecund, the people eventually multiplies so vigorously that the land can no longer provide for it; then it is forced to establish colonies, or to change its government.

When the country is saturated with inhabitants, it is no longer possible to employ the surplus in agriculture, and this surplus must be used for industry, for commerce, for the Arts, and this new system requires another administration. May the institutions that Corsica is going to create soon impose upon her the need to change in this way. But so long as she has no more men than she can feed, so long as an inch of fallow land remains on the island, she must stick to the rural system and change it only when the island is no longer sufficient for it.

The rural system, as I have said, prefers the democratic state. Thus the form we have to choose is given. It is true that in its application there are a few modifications to be made, because of the island’s size; for a purely democratic government suits a small Town rather than a nation. You could not assemble the whole people of a country like that of a city; and when the supreme authority is entrusted to deputies, the government changes and becomes aristocratic. What is suitable for Corsica is a mixed government, where the people assembles only through parties and where the depositaries of its power are often changed. This is what was seen very clearly by the author of the report drawn up at Vescovado in 1764,3 an excellent report that may be consulted with confidence on everything not explained in this one.

This well-established form will have two big advantages. Firstly, entrusting the administration only to a small number allows the choice of enlightened people. Secondly, ensuring that all members of the State contribute to the supreme authority places the whole people on a perfect level, thus allowing it to spread across the whole surface of the island and to populate it evenly everywhere. Herein lies the fundamental maxim of our institutions. Let us make them such that they will keep the population everywhere in equilibrium, and by this alone we shall have made them as perfect as they can be. If this maxim is good, our rules become clear and our work is simplified to an astonishing extent.

Part of this work is already done: we have fewer institutions than prejudices to destroy, it is less a matter of changing than of completing. The Genoese themselves prepared your institutions and, through a care worthy of Providence, thinking to reinforce tyranny they grounded liberty. They stripped you of almost all commerce, and indeed now is not the time to have any such. If commerce were open to the outside, it would have to be forbidden until your constitution had become well founded and until the interior provided you with all that you may derive from it. They obstructed the export of your staples. Your best interest is not that these should be exported, but that enough men should be born on the island to consume them.

The communes [pievi]4 and special jurisdictions the Genoese formed or preserved, in order to facilitate the collection of taxes and the execution of orders, are the only possible means to establish democracy in an entire people that cannot assemble all at once in a single place; these are also the only means to maintain the countryside independent of towns, which are more easily kept under the yoke. The Genoese also set about destroying the nobility, depriving it of its dignities and its titles, eliminating the great fiefs. It is lucky for you that they took upon themselves what was hateful in that enterprise, which you would perhaps not have undertaken had they not done so before you. Do not hesitate to complete their work: while believing that they were working for themselves, they were working for you. The aim alone is very different, since that of the Genoese concerned the thing itself, while yours concerns its effect. They sought only to debase the nobility; you are seeking to ennoble the nation.

This is a point upon which I see that the Corsicans do not yet have sound ideas. In all their supporting documents and in their Aix-la-Chapelle remonstrance, they complained about how Genoa had demeaned, or rather destroyed, their nobility.5 This was doubtless a grievance, but it was no misfortune; on the contrary, it was an advantage, without which it would be impossible for them to remain free.

To identify the dignity of a State with the titles of certain of its members is to take the shadow for the substance. When the Kingdom of Corsica belonged to Genoa, it could be useful to it to have marquesses, counts and titled nobles who might so to speak serve as mediators between the Corsican people and the Republic. But against whom might now be useful to the people such protectors, less fit to safeguard it from tyranny than themselves to usurp its place, protectors who would distress it with their vexations and their quarrels, until one of them, having subjugated the rest, made all his fellow citizens into his subjects?

Let us distinguish two kinds of nobility: the feudal nobility which belongs to monarchy, and the political nobility which belongs to aristocracy. The former has several orders or degrees, some with titles, some without, from great vassals to mere gentlemen. Its rights, though hereditary, are so to speak individual, particular, attached to every family, and so independent from one another that they are independent even from the constitution of the state and its sovereignty. The latter, on the other hand, united in a single, indivisible body all of whose rights belong to the body and not to its members, forms so essential a part of the body politic that it cannot survive without the latter nor the latter without it; and all the individuals who compose it, equal by birth in titles, privileges and authority, are merged beneath the common name of patricians.

It is clear from the titles borne by the ancient Corsican nobility, and from the fiefs that it owned, with rights coming close to actual sovereignty, that it belonged to the former category; and that it owed its origin either to Moorish or French conquerors, or to the princes in whom the Popes had vested the island of Corsica.6 Well, this kind of nobility can so little enter into a democratic or mixed republic that it cannot even enter into an aristocracy, since aristocracy allows only corporate rights and not individual rights. Democracy knows no other nobility after virtue than liberty, and aristocracy similarly knows no other nobility than authority. All that is alien to the constitution must be scrupulously banished from the body politic. Leave, therefore, to other states all those marquesses’ and counts’ titles that demean mere citizens. The fundamental law of your institutions must be equality. Everything must be related to that, even authority itself, which is established only to defend equality; everyone must be equal by right of birth. The State must grant distinctions only for merit, for virtues, for services rendered to the fatherland; and these distinctions must no more be hereditary than are the qualities upon which they are based. We shall soon see how different orders may be graduated for a people, without birth and nobility playing any part whatsoever.

All fiefs, homages, feudal rents and rights shall thus, if previously abolished, be so for ever; and the State shall redeem those that still survive, so that all seigneurial titles and rights shall remain extinguished and suppressed throughout the island.

In order that all parts of the State may so far as possible maintain the same level between one another that we are seeking to establish between individuals, the boundaries of districts, communes and jurisdictions shall be fixed in such a way as to diminish the extreme inequality discernible in them. The province of Bastia and Nebbio alone contains as many inhabitants as the seven provinces of Capocorso, Alleria, Porto Vecchio, Sartène, Vico, Salvi and Algagliola. That of Ajaccio contains more than its four neighbours. Without entirely removing the borders and disrupting the competencies, by a few slight changes these enormous disproportions can be moderated. For example, the abolition of fiefs makes it possible to form from those of Canari, Brando and Nonza a new jurisdiction, which, reinforced by the commune of Pietrabugno, will become almost equal to the jurisdiction of Capo Corso. The fief of Istria joined to the province of Sartène will still not make the latter equal to the province of Corte; and the province of Bastia and Nebbio, albeit diminished by a commune, can be divided along the line of the Guolo between two still very stable jurisdictions. This is simply an example to make myself understood; for I do not know the locality well enough to be able to determine anything.

By these slight changes the island of Corsica, which I am assuming to be wholly free,7 would find itself divided into twelve jurisdictions that would not be extremely disproportionate, above all once you had restricted the municipal rights of the towns as you should, so leaving them with less weight in their jurisdictions.

Towns are useful in a country insofar as commerce and the arts are cultivated in them, but they are harmful to the system we have adopted. Their inhabitants are farmers or idle. Well, farming is always carried out better by small-holders than by town dwellers, while it is from idleness that derive all the vices that have hitherto racked Corsica. The foolish pride of burghers merely demeans and discourages the husbandman. Given over to softness and to the passions it excites, they plunge into debauchery and sell themselves to satisfy it; interest makes them servile and laziness makes them restless, they are slaves or rebels, never free. This difference has made itself clearly felt during the present war, and since the nation broke its fetters. It is the vigour of your communes that made the revolution, it is their firmness that sustained it: this unbreakable courage that no reverse can shatter comes from them. The towns, peopled by mercenary men, sold their nation in order to keep for themselves a few little privileges that the Genoese skilfully knew how to point out to them; duly punished for their cowardice they remain nests of tyranny, while the Corsican people is already gloriously enjoying the liberty it has won at the price of its blood.

A farming people has no need at all to look covetously at life in towns, and enviously at the lot of the idlers who inhabit them; consequently, there is no need at all to encourage town-dwelling by advantages harmful to the general population and the nation’s liberty. A farmer must by birth be inferior to no man, must see above him only the laws and the magistrates, and must be able to become a magistrate himself if he is worthy of it on account of his knowledge and his probity. In a word, the towns and their inhabitants must no more than the fiefs and their owners retain any exclusive privilege; the whole island must enjoy the same rights, bear the same burdens, and become without distinction what in the country’s parlance is called terra di commune [communal land].8

Now if towns are harmful, capitals are still more so. A capital is an abyss wherein almost the entire nation is bound to lose its mores, its laws, its courage and its liberty. People imagine that large towns encourage agriculture because they consume a great quantity of its products, but they consume a still larger quantity of farmers, either because the latter are influenced by the wish to adopt a better occupation, or because of the natural deterioration of urban species, still recruited from the countryside. The surroundings of capitals have a semblance of life, but the further you move away the more everything is deserted. A plague is continuously exhaled from the capital, which undermines and eventually destroys the nation.

However, the government needs a centre, a meeting place and reference point for everything: it would be too great a disadvantage for the topmost administration to be obliged to move around. For the government to circulate from Province to Province, it would be necessary to divide the island into several little confederated States, each of which would hold the presidency in turn; but this system would complicate the functioning of the governmental machine, and its parts would be more disconnected. While the island is not large enough to make such a division necessary, it is too large to be able to do without a capital. But this capital must form the connection between all the jurisdictions without attracting their populations; everyone must communicate through it while everything remains in its place. In a word, the seat of the supreme Government must be less a capital than an administrative centre.

Necessity alone has directed the nation’s choice in this regard as reason itself would have done. The Genoese, remaining masters of the seaports, have left you only the town of Corte, no less fortunately situated for the Corsican administration than Bastia was for the Genoese administration. Corte, located in the middle of the island, has all the latter’s coastlines at almost equal distance. It is precisely between the two main parts9 di quà e di là dai monti [this side and beyond the mountains], within equal range of everywhere. It is far from the sea, which will safeguard its inhabitants’ mores, simplicity, probity and national character longer than if it was subject to the influx of foreigners. It is in the highest part of the island, in a very healthy atmosphere, but on not very fertile soil and almost at the source of the rivers, which makes access to crops more difficult, thus not allowing the town to grow too much. If only you add to all this the precaution of not making any of the great offices of State hereditary or even lifelong, it is to be presumed that public men, taking up only transitory residences there, will for long not give the town that fatal splendour which makes the lustre and the ruin of States.

Such are the first reflections suggested to me by a swift examination of the island’s situation. Before speaking now in greater detail about the Government, it is necessary to begin by seeing what it must do and upon what maxims it must conduct itself. This is what must finally determine its form, since every form of government has its spirit that is natural and appropriate for it, and from which it will never depart.

Until now we have so far as possible levelled the national territory; let us now attempt to trace upon it the plan of the edifice to be constructed. The first rule we have to follow is the national character. Every people has or should have a national character, and if it lacks one we should have to begin by giving it one. Islanders, being above all less mixed or intermingled with other peoples, usually have one that is more pronounced. Corsicans in particular have one that is very sensitive by nature; and if, disfigured by slavery and tyranny, it has become hard to recognize; on the other hand thanks to their isolated position it is also easy to restore and preserve.

The island of Corsica, Diodorus says,10 is mountainous, heavily wooded, and watered by big rivers. Its inhabitants live on milk, honey and meat, with which the land provides them in abundance. Among themselves, they observe rules of justice and humanity more scrupulously than other barbarians. The first person to find honey on the mountains and in the hollow of trees can be sure that no one will contest his claim to it. They are always certain to find their ewes, upon which each man puts his mark and which they then allow to graze in the fields without anyone to look after them: the same spirit of equity seems to govern them in all life’s encounters.

Great historians are able, in the simplest narratives and without any reasoning of their own, to make their readers aware of the reason behind every fact that they record.

When a country is not peopled by colonies, the primitive character of its inhabitants springs from the nature of the soil. A harsh terrain, irregular and hard to cultivate, must be more suitable for feeding animals than men: fields must be rarer there and pastures abundant. Whence the multiplication of livestock and the pastoral life. Individuals’ flocks roaming the mountains mingle and merge. Honey has no distinguishing mark beyond that of the original inhabitant; ownership can be neither established nor preserved except with public trust, and everybody must be honest otherwise nobody would have anything and the nation would perish.

Mountains, woods, streams, pastures. Might you not be reading a description of Switzerland? And indeed in former times the Swiss showed the same character that Diodorus ascribes to the Corsicans: equity, humanity, good faith. The sole difference was that, inhabiting a harsher climate, they were more hardworking. Buried in snow for six months, they were forced to make provision for the winter; they cultivated the rocks over which they were scattered with an exertion that made them sturdy; constant toil left them no time to know passions; communications were always arduous, and when snow and ice finally closed them each man in his hut was forced to suffice to himself and his family: whence a fortunate if crude industriousness, with every man practising all the necessary crafts at home – all were masons, carpenters, joiners, wheelwrights. The streams and torrents that separated them from one another provided everyone in return with the means to do without his neighbours; as saws, forges and mills multiplied, they learned to direct the watercourses as much to drive cogs as to increase irrigation. In this way, amid their cliffs and valleys, each man living on his own land managed to draw all that he needed from it; to find himself well off there and want nothing more than that. With interests and needs never crossing, and with no man dependent upon another, among them all there prevailed relations solely of kindliness and friendship. Amity and peace reigned effortlessly in their numerous families; they had almost nothing to discuss among themselves, other than marriages in which inclination alone was considered: marriages that ambition never arranged, and that interest or inequality never prevented. This people, poor but free from need, in the most perfect independence, thus multiplied in a unity that nothing could pervert. It had no virtues, since without vices to overcome doing good cost it nothing; and it was good and just without even knowing what justice or virtue were. The strength whereby this hardworking, independent life attached the Swiss to their fatherland produced two greater means of defending it, viz. commonality of resolution and courage in combat. When you consider the constant unity that reigned among men without masters, almost without laws, and how the Princes surrounding them strove to divide them by every political manoeuvre; when you see the unbreakable steadfastness, the constancy, the ferocity even that these terrible men displayed in combat, determined to die or to conquer, and having not the least notion of separating their lives from their liberty; you no longer have any difficulty in imagining the prodigies they have accomplished in defence of their country and their independence; you are no longer surprised to see the three greatest powers and the most warlike troops of Europe failing one after another in their attempts against this heroic nation,11 which its simplicity made as impervious to trickery as its courage made it to valour. There is the model, Corsicans, that you have to follow in order to return to your original condition.

But these rustic men, who at first knew only themselves, their mountains and their livestock, through defending themselves against other nations learned to know these. Their victories opened to them the frontiers of their neighbourhood, their reputation for bravery gave Princes the idea of employing them. Those Princes began to hire the troops whom they had been unable to defeat. Those noble men who had defended their liberty so well became oppressors of the liberty of others. People were astonished to see them bringing the same valour to the service of Princes that they had devoted to resisting them, the same loyalty that they had maintained to the fatherland; to see them selling for money the virtues that least have to be paid for and that money most rapidly corrupts. But in those early days they brought the same pride to the Princes’ service that they had devoted to resisting them; they saw themselves less as their satellites than as their defenders, and believed themselves to have sold them less their services than their protection.

Imperceptibly they sank to becoming merely mercenaries. Taste for money made them feel that they were poor; contempt for their condition imperceptibly destroyed the virtues that were its product; and Swiss soldiers could be hired for five pence as French could for four. Another more hidden cause corrupted that vigorous nation. Their isolated, simple life had made them independent as well as sturdy, each man knew no other master than himself, yet since all had the same interest and the same tastes they easily united to desire and to do the same things: for them, the uniformity of their lives was a substitute for law. But when association with other peoples had caused them to love what they should have feared and to admire what they should have despised, the ambition of their leaders caused them to alter their maxims; for those leaders felt that in order to dominate the people better they needed to give it more dependent tastes. Whence the introduction of commerce, industry and luxury, which, binding individuals to the public authority through their occupations and their needs, made them depend upon those who govern, far more than they had depended upon them in their original condition.

Poverty made itself felt in Switzerland only once money began to circulate there. Money introduced the same inequality into resources as into fortunes; it became a great means of acquisition removed from those who had nothing. Commercial and manufacturing establishments multiplied. Crafts took a multitude of hands away from agriculture. As men divided unequally, they multiplied, and they spread into the most favourably situated lands, where resources were still easier. Some deserted their fatherland, others became useless to it by consuming and producing nothing. The multitude of children became a burden. The country became noticeably less well peopled. As the towns became crowded, cultivation of the land grew more neglected and living needs grew more burdensome; foreign commodities thus became more necessary, placing the country in a greater dependency upon its neighbours. Idle lives introduced corruption and multiplied the pensioners of foreign powers. Love of the fatherland, extinguished in every heart, gave way to love of money alone. All those feelings that give motivation to the soul were stifled, so that neither firmness of conduct nor vigorous determination were any longer to be seen. Formerly a poor Switzerland laid down the law to France; now a rich Switzerland trembles when a French minister frowns.12

Here are some great lessons for the Corsican people. Let us see how it should apply them to itself. The Corsican people preserves a large number of its original virtues, which will greatly facilitate our constitution. It has also in servitude contracted many of the vices that it must remedy. Of these vices, some will disappear of their own accord along with the cause that engendered them; others need some cause to eradicate the passion that produces them.

In the former class, I place the indomitable and ferocious spirit that people ascribe to the Corsicans. People accuse them of being rebellious, but how do people know, since the Corsicans have never been governed justly? If they are constantly set in enmity against one another, people should foresee that this enmity might often turn against those who kindled it.

In the latter class, I place the propensity for robbery and murder that has made them hateful. The source of these two vices is idleness and impunity: this is clear as to the former, and easy to prove as to the latter, since the family hatreds and plans for vengeance that the Corsicans were forever engaged in satisfying spring from futile arguments, gain substance through gloomy meditation, and are implemented with ease thanks to the guarantee of impunity.

Who could fail to be horror-struck at a barbaric government which, when it saw those wretches cutting each other’s throats, spared no effort in spurring them on? Murder was not punished – nay, it was rewarded. The price of blood was among the revenues of the republic. The wretched Corsicans, in order to avoid total destruction, were obliged through a tribute to purchase the favour of being disarmed.13

The Genoese boast of having encouraged agriculture on the island, the Corsicans seem to agree. I would not agree likewise, since the poor success of agriculture proves that the Genoese adopted poor means. In this undertaking, the republic did not have the aim of multiplying the island’s inhabitants, since it so openly encouraged assassinations; nor that of helping them to live at ease, since it ruined them by its exactions; nor even that of facilitating the collection of land taxes [tailles],14 since it burdened the sale and transport of foodstuffs with duties and forbade their export. On the contrary, its aim was to make more onerous those same land taxes which it dared not increase; to keep the Corsicans for ever in servility, by so to speak binding them to their glebe, diverting them from commerce and crafts and all lucrative occupations, and preventing them from raising themselves, gaining an education or growing rich. Its aim was to have all foodstuffs at a very cheap price, through the monopolies of its officials. It took every measure to drain the island of money, in order to make money necessary there yet prevent it from returning there. The tyranny could not have used a more refined stratagem: by seeming to encourage agriculture it crushed the nation wholly; it sought to reduce it to a pack of base peasants living in the most deplorable misery.

What was the result? The Corsicans, disheartened, abandoned a toil that was enlivened by no hope. They preferred to do nothing than exhaust themselves for pure loss. A life of simple toil gave way to idleness, unemployment, all manner of vices. Robbery got them the money they needed to pay their land taxes, and that they could not derive from their crops: they left their fields in order to work on the highways.

May the Corsicans, brought back to a life of toil, lose the habit of wandering across the island as bandits! May their occupations, simple and equal, keep them concentrated in their families and leave them few interests to quarrel over among themselves! May their toil provide them easily with enough to survive on, they and their families! May those who have all things necessary for life not be also obliged to have cash money, whether to pay land taxes and other levies, or to provide for imagined needs and for a luxury which, without contributing to the well-being of the person who displays it, merely excites the envy and hatred of others!

You can easily see how the system to which we have given preference leads to these advantages, but this is not enough. It is a matter of persuading the people to adopt the practice of this system: of persuading the people to love the occupation that we wish to give it; to find its pleasures, its desires and its tastes in it; to derive the general happiness of its life from it; and to confine its ambitions and plans within it.

I see no prompter or more certain means of arriving at this than the two following: the first is so to speak to attach men to the land, by deriving their distinctions and their rights from it; the second is to reinforce this bond by that of the family, by making the latter necessary to the condition of fathers.

It has occurred to me that, in this view which bases the fundamental law upon distinctions drawn from the nature of things, you could divide the entire Corsican nation into three classes, the still personal inequality of which could be substituted satisfactorily for the inequality of race or domicile that results from the feudal municipal system we are abolishing.

The first class will be that of citizens.

The second that of patriots.

The third that of candidates.

The qualifications for being registered in each class, and the privileges enjoyed in it, will be made clear below.

This distinction by class must not be achieved by a census or headcount at the moment of the system’s inauguration, but determined subsequently of its own accord through the mere progress of time. The first act of the projected system should be a solemn oath sworn by all Corsicans aged twenty and over; and all those who swear this oath must be registered without distinction as citizens. It is quite right that all these brave men, who have delivered their nation at the cost of their blood, should enter into possession of all these advantages and be among the first to enjoy the liberty they have won.

But from the day that unity has been formed and the oath solemnly sworn, all those who though born on the island have not reached the right age will remain in the class of candidates, until under the following conditions they can rise to the other two classes.

Each candidate, married according to law, who has a holding of his own independently of his wife’s dowry, will be registered in the class of patriots.

Each patriot, married or widower, who has two living children, a residence of his own and a land-holding sufficient for his subsistence will be registered in the class of citizens.

This first step, sufficient to place the lands in credit, is not sufficient to place them under cultivation, unless the need for money, which has caused the island’s poverty under Genoese government, is removed. It must be established as a sure maxim that wherever money is a prime necessity, the nation becomes detached from agriculture, to plunge into more lucrative occupations. The condition of farm-worker is then either a target of commerce and a kind of manufacture for big farmers, or the last resort of destitution for the mass of peasants. Those who enrich themselves through commerce and industry, when they have earned enough, place their money in landed property, which others cultivate for them; the whole nation thus finds itself divided between wealthy idlers who own the land and wretched peasants who starve while cultivating it.

The more necessary money is to individuals, the more necessary it is to the government. Whence it follows that the more commerce flourishes, the higher taxes are. And in order to pay these taxes, in vain does the peasant cultivate his land if he does not sell the produce. It is fruitless for him to have wheat, wine and oil, he absolutely must have money; he must ferry his produce back and forth to the towns, make himself into a petty merchant, a petty seller, a petty rogue. His children, raised on selling, are lured away, attach themselves to the town, lose the taste for their condition and become sailors or soldiers rather than embrace their father’s estate. Soon the countryside is depopulated and the towns overflow with vagrants; little by little bread runs short, public destitution increases with the wealth of individuals, and both combine to introduce all the vices that eventually bring about a nation’s ruin.

I am so convinced that any commercial system is destructive of agriculture that I do not make an exception even for commerce in foodstuffs, which are the product of agriculture. For the latter to be able to survive in this system, it would have to be possible for the profit to be shared equally between the shopkeeper and the farmer. But that is just what is not possible, because the former’s trade being free and the latter’s coerced, the former will always lay down the law to the latter, a relationship devoid of balance that cannot create a stable and permanent state.

You must not imagine that, when the island has a great deal of money, it will thereby be richer. That is true vis-à-vis other peoples and in its external relations. But in itself a nation is neither richer nor poorer for having more or less money, or, which comes to the same thing, because the same amount of money circulates there with more or less activity. Not only is money a token; it is a relative token, that has no real effect other than through inequality of distribution. For supposing that each individual on the island of Corsica had just ten crowns, or that each individual had one hundred thousand crowns, the respective condition of all is absolutely the same in these two cases. Among themselves they are neither richer nor poorer, and the sole difference is that the latter supposition makes business more cumbersome. If Corsica needed foreigners, she would need money; but since she can be self-sufficient, she does not need any. And since money is useful only as a sign of inequality, the less that circulates on the island, the more real abundance will prevail there.

It must be seen whether what people do with money cannot be done without money; and, supposing that it can, the two methods must be compared in relation to our aim.

It is proved by the facts that the island of Corsica, even in its present state of neglect and exhaustion, suffices for its inhabitants’ subsistence, since during thirty-six years of war, when they handled arms more than the plough, not a single cargo of food or provisions of any kind for their use came in. It even has everything necessary, in addition to food, to place and keep them in a flourishing state, without borrowing anything from outside. It has wool for its fabrics, hemp and flax for ropes and linens, leather for shoes, timber for its navy, iron for its forges, copper for pans and coins. It has salt for its own use, and will have far more when it restores the Alleria saltpans, which the Genoese went to such trouble and expense to keep in a ruined state, yet which still produced salt in spite of them. Even if they wished to, the Corsicans could not trade outside by barter, unless they bought unnecessary things; so even in such a case they would not need money for trade, since it is the only commodity they would need to procure. Whence it follows that in these relations between nation and nation Corsica has no need of money.

Internally the island is quite large and cut up by mountains; its numerous, big rivers are scarcely navigable. Its parts do not communicate naturally with each other, but the difference in what they produce keeps them in mutual dependence, through the need they have for one another. The province of Cap Corse, which hardly produces anything but wine, has need of wheat and oil, with which Balagna provides it. Corte in the highlands likewise produces grain, but lacks everything else; Bonifacio below the peaks and at the other extremity of the island needs everything and provides nothing. Hence, the project of an equal population15 requires a circulation of staples, easy payment from one jurisdiction to another, and consequently internal trade.

But I have two comments here. Firstly, with the government’s help this trade can largely be accomplished by barter. Secondly, that with similar help and as a natural consequence of our institutions, this trade and this barter should diminish day by day and eventually be reduced to very little.

We know that in the exhaustion to which the Genoese have consigned Corsica, money, always flowing out and never flowing in, eventually became so rare that in certain of the island’s cantons cash was no longer known, and sales or purchases were made only by barter.

In their memoranda the Corsicans cited this fact among their grievances. They were right, since money was necessary to pay their land taxes; those poor people, who no longer had any, were dispossessed by warrant in their homes, saw themselves stripped of their most essential utensils, their furniture, their clothes and their rags, which had to be carried from place to place and whose sale did not fetch the tenth part of their worth, so that, for want of money, they would pay the tax ten times over.

But as in our system people will no longer be forced to pay the land tax in cash, lack of money, no longer being a sign of poverty, will not serve to increase it. Barter will be able to take place in kind and without intermediary values, and people will be able to live in plenty without ever handling a penny.

I see that under the Genoese administrations, which in innumerable ways forbade and obstructed trade in foodstuffs between one province and the next, the communes would establish warehouses for wheat, wine and oil, while awaiting a moment favourable and permitted for trade; and that these warehouses served the Genoese officials as a pretext for innumerable hateful monopolies. Not being new, the idea of these warehouses will thereby be all the easier to implement, and will provide the public and individuals with a convenient, simple means for barter, without risk of the disadvantages that used to make it burdensome for the people.

Even without having recourse to real warehouses or stores, a public double-entry register could be established in each parish, where individuals could record each year, on the one side, the kind and quantity of foodstuffs they have in excess, on the other those that they lack. By balancing and comparing these registers from province to province, it would be possible to regulate the price of staples and the amount of trade in such a way that each commune would see its surplus consumed and its necessities provided for, without there being either lack or excess in the quantity and almost as easily as if its harvest were tailored to its needs.

These operations can be effected with the greatest accuracy and without real money, either through barter or with the aid of a simple ideal currency that would serve as a term of comparison such as the pistoles in France,16 or else by taking as currency some real commodity that can be numbered, as the ox was among the Greeks or the ewe among the Romans, and that is fixed at its average value; for then an ox may be worth more or less than an ox and a ewe more or less than a ewe, a difference that makes the ideal currency preferable, because it is always exact, being taken only as an abstract number.

So long as you stick to this, trade will be kept in equilibrium; barter, being regulated solely in terms of the relative abundance or scarcity of staples and the greater or lesser ease of their transport, will always and everywhere remain in a balanced relationship; and all the island’s products, equally distributed, will of themselves adjust to the level of the population. I may add that the public administration will be able without disadvantage to preside over such trade and such barter, to keep them in balance, regulate their quantity and effect their distribution, because so long as that trade and that barter are effected in kind public officials will not be able to abuse them, or even have the temptation to do so; whereas the conversion of staples into money opens the door to every kind of extortion, every kind of monopoly, every kind of knavery habitual to people in power in such cases.

You must expect many obstacles at the beginning, but such obstacles are inevitable in any new order that is being initiated and that goes against an established usage. I may add that this system, once established, will become easier year by year, not simply through practice and experience, but through the successive diminution of trade that must necessarily result from it, until this is of itself reduced to the smallest possible quantity, which is the final aim you must set yourself.

Everyone must live and no one must grow rich. That is the fundamental principle of the nation’s prosperity, and the polity which I am proposing for its part moves towards this end as directly as possible.

Surplus foodstuffs, being neither an object of commerce nor converted into money, will be cultivated only in proportion to the need people have for necessities; and anyone who can at once procure the foodstuffs he lacks will be uninterested in having too much of them.

As soon as the products of the earth are no longer merchandise, their cultivation will gradually be adapted in each province, and even in each patrimony, to the general need of the province and to the individual need of the farmer. Everyone will strive to have all the things that are necessary to him in kind and through his own farming, rather than through barter, which will always be less reliable and less convenient however much it may be facilitated.

It is an incontestable advantage to give each soil what it is most fit to produce; by this arrangement you draw more from the land, and more easily, than by any other. But important as this consideration is, it is merely secondary. It is preferable for the land to produce a bit less and for the inhabitants to be better ordered. Among all these movements of trafficking and barter, it is impossible that destructive vices should not creep into a nation. The lack of certain advantages in the choice of soil can be compensated for by labour, and it is preferable to use fields badly than men. Besides, every farmer can and must make this choice on his lands, and every parish or community on its communal holdings, as is set out below.

You will fear, I can tell, that this economy may produce a contrary effect to that which I expect of it: that instead of stimulating agriculture, it may discourage it; that the farmers, having no sale for their foodstuffs, may neglect their labours; that they may limit themselves to subsistence, without seeking abundance; and that, content with harvesting what is absolutely necessary for themselves, they may for the rest let their land lie fallow. You will even seem confirmed by the experience of the Genoese administration, under which the ban on exporting foodstuffs outside the island had produced exactly that effect.

But it must be considered that under this administration, since money was of prime necessity, it formed the immediate object of labour; consequently all labour that could not produce any such was necessarily neglected; the farmer, overwhelmed by scorn, vexations and woes, viewed his condition as the direst misfortune and, seeing that he could not meet his needs thereby, would seek another or give way to discouragement, whereas under our system all views tend to make this condition happy in its mediocrity, respectable in its simplicity. Providing all the needs of life, all public taxes without selling and without trafficking, all means of consideration, it will not allow a better or nobler to be even imagined. Those who fill this condition, seeing no one above them, will glory in it; and making their way from it to the highest positions, they will fill it like the early Romans. Being unable to leave this condition, people will wish to distinguish themselves in it: to fill it better than others, achieve larger harvests, provide a stronger contingent to the State, merit the people’s votes in elections. Numerous well-fed and well-clad families will bring honour upon their heads; and since real plenty will be the sole object of luxury, everyone will wish to distinguish himself by that sort of luxury. So long as the human heart remains what it is, such institutions will not produce idleness.

What individual magistrates and family heads must do in each jurisdiction, in each commune, on each patrimony, in order not to need others, the general government of the island must do in order not to need the neighbouring peoples.

An accurate record of goods that have entered the island over a certain number of years will provide a sure and faithful list of those without which it cannot do; for the current situation there is not one where luxury and excess can exist. With careful observations both on what the island produces and on what it can produce, you will find that foreign necessities are reduced to very little; this is wholly confirmed by the facts, since in the years 1735 and ’36, when the island was blockaded by the Genoese navy and had no communication with the mainland, not only was nothing lacking there in terms of victuals, but no needs of any kind were unendurable. Those which were most keenly felt were war munitions, leather, cotton for wicks – and even this last was provided for by the pith of certain reeds.

From this small number of necessary imports, you must further cut out everything that the island does not provide now but can provide, if better cultivated and invigorated by industry. The more the idle arts, the arts of pleasure and softness, must be carefully eliminated, the more those that are useful for agriculture and advantageous to human life must be encouraged. We need neither sculptors nor goldsmiths, but we do need carpenters and blacksmiths; we need weavers, good workers in wool, and not embroiderers or drawers of gold thread.

You will begin by providing yourselves with the most essential raw materials, namely wood, iron, wool, leather, hemp and flax. The island used to abound in wood both for construction and for heating, but you should not rely on this abundance and leave the use and felling of forests merely to the discretion of their owners. As the island’s population grows and clearances increase, there will be rapid devastation of the woods that you will be able to repair only very slowly. Regarding this, precautionary lessons can be drawn from the country where I live. Switzerland was formerly covered by woods in such abundance that it was hampered by them. But the multiplication of pastures and the establishment of manufactures alike led to these being felled without restraint or method. Now those immense forests display only virtually bare rock. Luckily, warned by the example of France, the Swiss saw the danger and regulated matters so far as lay within their power. It remains to be seen whether their precautions are not too late; for if, despite these precautions, their woods dwindle daily, it is clear that they must eventually be destroyed.

Corsica, tackling things in better time, will not have the same danger to fear. You must establish rigorous control of the forests early on, and regulate their felling in such a way that reproduction matches consumption. You must not do as in France, where the Masters of Rivers and Forests,17 who have rights over the felling of trees, have an interest in destroying the lot: an aim that they pursue to the best of their ability. You must foresee the future well in advance. Although it is not at present the right time to establish a navy, the time will come when this will have to be done, and then you will be aware of the advantage of not having given up to foreign navies the fine forests that lie close to the sea. You must exploit or sell the old woods that are no longer profitable, but you must leave standing all those that are in their prime. There will be a use for them when the time comes.

People say that a copper mine has been found on the island, but iron mines are worth even more, and there certainly are some on the island. The situation of the mountains, the nature of the terrain, the thermal springs to be found in the province of Cap Corse and elsewhere – all this makes me think that many such mines will be found if you look carefully and use capable people for the search. On this assumption, you will not allow their exploitation indiscriminately, but will choose the most favourable sites, closest to woods and streams for the establishment of forges, and where you will be able to open up the easiest routes for transport.

You will pay the same attention to manufactures of every kind, each in its respective materials, in order to facilitate labour and distribution as much as possible. However, you will take care not to create these kinds of establishment in the most populous and most fertile parts of the island. On the contrary, all things being equal you will choose the most arid lands, ones that would remain deserted if they were not populated through industry. By doing this, you will have some additional problems in supplying them with what they need; but the advantages you will find thereby, and the disadvantages you will avoid, should easily outweigh any such consideration.

Firstly, we shall be following here our first great principle, which is not just to extend and multiply the population, but to equalize it as far as possible throughout the whole island. For if the barren places were not populated through industry, they would remain deserted and that would be so much the more lost for the potential advancement of the nation.

If you formed similar establishments in fertile places, the abundance of victuals and the profit of labour – necessarily greater in the arts than in agriculture – would, by diverting farmers or their families from rural concerns and gradually depopulating the countryside, oblige new settlers to be drawn in from far away in order to cultivate the latter. Hence, by overloading certain parts of the territory with inhabitants we should depopulate others, and by thus breaking the balance we should indirectly go against the spirit of our institutions.

The transport of staples, by making them more costly in the factories, will thereby diminish the profit of the workers; this will keep their condition closer to that of the farmer, thus better maintaining the balance between them. This balance, however, cannot be such that the advantage does not always lie with industry, either because the money that is in the state flows there in greater abundance, or through the chance means whereby power and inequality come into play, or thanks to the greater strength possessed by a number of men assembled, which the ambitious know how to harness to their own advantage. It is important, therefore, that this over-favoured part should remain dependent upon the rest of the nation for its subsistence; in case of internal divisions, it is in the nature of our institutions that it should be the farmer who lays down the law to the worker.

With precautions, you may safely encourage the establishment of useful arts on the island, and I doubt not but that these creations well run may be able to provide for all that is necessary, without needing to bring anything from outside, apart from a few trifles, for which you will allow a proportionate export, always carefully balanced by the administration.

I have so far shown how the Corsican people could subsist in ease and independence with very little trading; how the bulk of what little it will find necessary can easily be acquired by barter; and how it can reduce almost to nothing the need for imports from outside the island. You can see by this that, if the use of money and cash cannot be wholly abolished in the affairs of individuals, it can be reduced at least to so little that abuses are unlikely to arise from it; that no fortunes will be made by such means; and that if any could be made, they would become almost useless and give little advantage to their owners.

But how shall we govern the public finances? What revenues shall we assign to their administration? Shall we establish it as free, or how shall we regulate its upkeep? That is what we must now consider.

Financial systems are modern inventions. The word ‘finance’ was no more known to the ancients than were our land taxes or capitation.18 The word vectigal19 was understood differently, as will be made clear below. The sovereign instance would impose tribute on conquered or defeated peoples, never on its direct subjects especially in republics. Far from the people of Athens being burdened with taxes, the government used on the contrary to pay it. And Rome, to whom her wars must have been so costly, would often distribute wheat and even land to the people. The State nevertheless subsisted, maintained great armies on sea and land, carried out sizeable public works and incurred expenses at least as great as are made proportionately by modern States. How was this done?

Two epochs must be distinguished in States: their beginning and their growth. In the beginning of a State, it would have no other revenue than the public domain, and this domain would be considerable. Romulus formed it from a third of all estates. He allocated the second third for the upkeep of Priests and sacred things; the remaining part alone was shared among the citizens. It was little, but that little was freely held. Do you not think that the French husbandman would willingly be reduced to one-third of what he cultivates, on condition of having that third free from any land tax, quit-rent [cens] or tithe, and not paying any kind of duty?

Hence, the public revenue was not taken in money, but in foodstuffs and other produce. Expenditures were of the same kind as takings. Neither magistrates nor troops were paid, they were fed and provided with uniforms; and in times of pressing need, the extraordinary burdens on the people consisted of forced labour rather than money. Those splendid public works cost the State almost nothing; they were the work of those formidable legions, which toiled just as they fought, and which were made up not of riff-raff but of citizens.

When the Romans began to expand and became conquerors, they took the upkeep of their troops from the conquered peoples; when they paid them, their subjects were taxed, never the Romans. In times of pressing danger, the Senate raised a subscription, took out loans that it returned faithfully, and, during the whole course of the Republic, I do not know of the Roman people ever having paid a pecuniary tax, either by head or on its estates.

There is a fine model for you, O Corsicans! Do not be surprised at there being more virtue among the Romans than elsewhere: money was less necessary there. The State had small revenues and did great things. Its wealth was in the lives of its citizens. I might say that, thanks to the situation of Corsica and thanks to the form of her government, there will be none in the whole world less costly. For, being an island and a Republic, she will have no need of regular troops; and the leaders of the State, all reverting to equality, will not be able to draw anything from the common mass that will not very speedily return to it.

But this is not how I envisage the sinews of your public force. On the contrary, I wish a great deal to be spent on the State service. More precisely, I am arguing only about the choice of currency. I view finances as the fat of the body politic, which by congealing in certain muscular systems overloads the body with a useless corpulence and makes it heavy rather than strong. I wish to feed the State with a healthier diet, that will merge into its substance; that will change into muscle and fibre without clogging the vessels; that will give the limbs vigour rather than size; and that will strengthen the body without weighing it down.

Far from wishing the State to be poor, I should on the contrary wish it to have everything, and for each man to have a share of the common property only in proportion to his services. The acquisition of all the Egyptians’ goods to which Joseph persuaded the King would have been good, if he had not done too much or too little.20 But without going into such hypotheses, which distract me from my purpose, it is enough to elucidate my thought here: which is not to destroy individual property absolutely, because that is impossible, but to confine it within narrower limits; to give it a measure, a rule and a brake that may contain it, direct it, subjugate it, and keep it always subordinated to the public good. In a word, I wish the State’s property to be as large and strong, and that of citizens to be as little and weak, as possible. That is why I avoid putting it in things whose individual owner is too much the master, such as cash and money, which are easily hidden from public inspection.

The establishment of a public domain is, I admit, not as easy a thing to do today in Corsica, already shared out between her inhabitants, as it was in Rome at her birth, before her conquered territory as yet belonged to anyone. However, I know that there remains on the island a large quantity of excellent untilled land, of which it is very easy for the government to take advantage: either by alienating it for a certain number of years to those who will put it under cultivation; or by having it tilled through forced labour [corvées],21 organized in each community. One would need to have been on the ground, in order to judge how this land might be distributed, and what profit might be drawn from it. But I have no doubt but that, by means of a few exchanges and certain quite simple agreements, it would be possible in each jurisdiction and even each commune to procure communal funds, which may even increase before many years have gone by, thanks to the system about which we shall speak in relation to the law on inheritance.

Another still simpler means, which should provide a more definite, more certain and far more considerable income, is to follow an example that I have before my eyes in the Protestant cantons. During the Reformation in these cantons, they seized the ecclesiastical tithes; and these tithes, with which they maintained their clergy decently, formed the principal income of the State. I am not saying that the Corsicans should touch the revenues of the Church, God forbid! But I think that the people will not be very much put out if the State asks it for as much as is asked of it by the clergy, already adequately endowed with property in land. The basic funding for this tax will be established without trouble or impediment, and at almost no cost, since you need only double the ecclesiastical tithe and take half of it.

I draw a third kind of revenue, the most reliable and best, from men themselves, by using their labour, their arms and their hearts rather than their purses in the fatherland’s service, whether for its defence in the militia or for its comforts through forced labour on public works.

Let republicans not take fright at this term ‘forced labour’! I know that it is abominated in France, but is it in Switzerland? The roads there are built also by forced labour, and no one complains. The seeming convenience of payment can seduce only superficial minds; and it is a certain maxim that the fewer the intermediaries between the need and the service, the less burdensome the service should be.

Without daring to set out my thinking entirely, without here presenting forced labour and all private labour by citizens as an absolute good, I shall agree, if you will, that it would be better for it all to be done by payment if the means of payment did not introduce a host of unrestrained abuses and greater ills, more limitless than those which can result from constraint, especially when the person imposing the latter belongs to the same state as those upon whom it is imposed.

Moreover, in order that the contribution should be shared equally, it is right that a person who has no land, so cannot pay the tithe from its produce, should pay it with the labour of his arms; hence, forced labour should fall especially on the order of candidates. But citizens and patriots must lead them to labour and set them an example. Let all that is done for the public good always be honoured! Let the very magistrate, busy with other cares, show that these ones are not beneath him, like those Roman consuls who, to set an example to their troops, would be the first to turn their hands to camp labours!

As for fines and confiscations, which in republics constitute a fourth kind of revenue, I hope that thanks to these present institutions this may be reduced almost to nothing in our republic, so I take no account of it.

Since all these public revenues are in physical kind rather than in cash, they appear cumbersome to collect, to store and to use. And this is partly true, but what matters here is less the easiest administration than the healthiest; so it is preferable for it to be a little more cumbersome but engender less abuse. The best economic system for Corsica or for a republic is assuredly not the best for a monarchy or a great State. The one I am proposing would not succeed either in France or in England, and could not even be established there. But it has the greatest success in Switzerland, where it has been established for centuries and is the only system the country could have borne.

The revenues are farmed out in each jurisdiction; they are made in kind or in money as the taxpayer chooses; the payment of magistrates and officials is likewise effected for the most part in wheat, in wine, in fodder, in timber. In this way, tax collection is neither burdensome for the public nor onerous for individuals; but the disadvantage I see here is that there are men whose profession is to earn from the prince and to harass the subjects.

It is of extreme importance not to permit any financier by profession in the republic: less because of their dishonest profits than because of their principles and their example, which, spreading too rapidly throughout the nation, destroy all good sentiments through esteem for illicit plenty and its advantages; which heap scorn and opprobrium upon disinterestedness, simplicity, morals and all virtues.

Let us take care not to increase pecuniary wealth at the expense of moral wealth. It is the latter which truly places us in possession of men and all their power, whereas through the former we obtain only the semblance of their services, but cannot buy their will. It is preferable for the exchequer to be run by a family man and lose something than to be run by a usurer and take in more.

Let us, therefore, leave tax collection under state administration, even should it bring in far less. Let us even avoid making this administration into a profession, for that would have almost the same disadvantage as farming it out. What makes a financial system most pernicious is the role of financier. At all costs, there must be no publicans in the State.22 Instead of making collection by the state and public revenues into a lucrative profession, they should on the contrary be made into a test of the merit and integrity of young citizens. The tax administration must be, so to speak, the apprenticeship for public posts and the first step towards reaching magistracies.
