4.  pievi: A pieve (plural pievi) was originally a medieval ecclesiastical unit in Italy and in Corsica, roughly equivalent to a parish. Through Pisan administrative reforms in the eleventh century, the pievi of Corsica were established as the basic administrative units on the island, intermediate between communes and provinces. In Rousseau’s day, they were the principal administrative units, rendered here as ‘communes’. The boundaries of the sixtytwo pievi correspond exactly to those of today’s cantons.

5.  Aix-la-Chapelle remonstrance … their nobility: In 1748 the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle at the end of the War of Austrian Succession placed Corsica back under Genoese jurisdiction, despite remonstrations by Corsican patriots arguing that Genoese rule was intolerable to them, and complaining in particular because the Corsican nobility did not enjoy the same privileges as that of Genoa.

6.  the Popes had vested the island of Corsica: The Papacy played a major role in Corsica from the late eleventh century, and annexed the island to the Holy See in 1217, in an ultimately vain attempt to end the rival claims of Genoa and Pisa, cities which, later joined by Aragon, were to contend for mastery over it, and for Papal backing, for the next three centuries.

7.  wholly free: As opposed to the island’s actual condition of semifreedom, with its main ports still in Genoese hands.

8.  terra di commune: Communal land established in the early eleventh century, by a movement aimed at curbing feudal anarchy comparable to the Peace of God movement in Languedoc. In the course of the fourteenth century the entire north-east of the island (between Calvi, Bastia and Solenzara) was freed from feudal obligations; henceforth twelve autonomous communes, each with its own assembly headed by a Podestat, would band together as terra di commune, with the land either leased to individual peasants or left open for flocks. This effectively put an end to the wars between rival barons and petty lords in the north of the island, although the south remained wild.

9.  between the two main parts: Corsica is roughly divided by a mountain range running from south-east to north-west. The area closer to the Italian peninsula, comprising six provinces with forty-one pievi, is known as ‘di quà dai monti’ or ‘this side of the mountains’; the area facing across the Mediterranean to the Iberian peninsula, with three provinces containing twenty-one pievi, is known as ‘di là dai monti’ or ‘beyond the mountains’.

10.  Diodorus says: Diodorus of Sicily was a Greek historian writing in the first century BC, author of a monumental ‘Universal history from the origins of the world up to Caesar’, from which Rousseau takes this description.

11.  you are no longer surprised … against this heroic nation: The three attacks on Switzerland alluded to are presumably those of Austria in the fourteenth century, Burgundy in the fifteenth and the Holy Roman Empire under Maximilian I in the sixteenth.

12.  when a French minister frowns: The reference here is to the duc de Choiseul, principal minister of Louis XV, whom Rousseau blamed for intervening with the authorities of Berne and so causing his expulsion from Switzerland, as he recounts in Confessions, Book XII. He compares this with the time, prior to the Perpetual Peace signed with the Swiss in 1515 by François I, when France feared Swiss depredations.

13.  The wretched Corsicans … the favour of being disarmed: The Genoese raised considerable revenue in Corsica from the sale of permits to bear arms, and also from the sale of safe-conducts to persons guilty of murder. Confronted by an alarming rise in blood crimes, and by public indignation in Corsica, they eventually decided to forbid the bearing of arms. But in order to make up for the consequent loss of revenue, they imposed a new tax indiscriminately on the entire population. Not only did these measures do nothing to lessen the number of murders; they also proved so unpopular that they were a direct cause of the 1729 uprising.

14.  the collection of land taxes: The taille was a feudal direct tax on land; in France by the late fifteenth century it had become a purely royal prerogative, and it continued to be levied until the 1789 Revolution.

15.  the project of an equal population: Rousseau advances the idea that a territory should be evenly populated in Of the Social Contract, Book III, Chapter 13 above.

16.  the pistoles in France: The French name for the Spanish gold coin known in English as a ‘doubloon’, i.e. the double escudo. The louis d’or introduced by Louis XIII in 1640, upon which pre-revolutionary French coinage was based, was initially its equivalent.

17.  Masters of Rivers and Forests: The Grand maître des eaux et forêts was an important officer in feudal France, charged with protecting the royal domain especially in respect of hunting, fishing and wood-gathering rights. From the late sixteenth century on, the office was progressively subdivided, so that the maître des eaux et forêts became an essential official of local administration.

18.  capitation: Capitation or poll-tax was the main form of direct taxation in pre-revolutionary France, with amounts to be paid by head varying according to class.

19.   vectigal: Term used in ancient Rome for all the state’s revenues, but at the height of Roman power the bulk of these did indeed derive from external tribute.

20.  The acquisition … too much or too little: According to the Old Testament story (Genesis 47: 20–31), Joseph was sold by his brothers into slavery in Egypt, but rose to be the Pharaoh’s vizier after interpreting his dream. Following his advice, Egypt stored up goods during seven years of abundance in order to survive the seven years of famine that would follow. Towards the end of the seven lean years, however, even Egypt began to run short, so Joseph obliged its inhabitants – with exception made for the priestly caste – to sell all their property to the Pharaoh in return for seed, so that it became state property. Since they would henceforth be farming on state land, they would have to pay one-fifth of their produce to the Pharaoh.

21.  forced labour: The corvée is a form of unpaid labour imposed by force, as for instance in pre-revolutionary France.

22.  no publicans in the State: Publicans in the ancient world were public contractors, and notably – e.g. in Rome – tax collectors.

23.  Hôtel-Dieu in Paris … Lyons: Hôtel-Dieu, or ‘hostel of God’, was the old term for the principal hospital in French towns, that of Paris dating from 660 and that of Lyons from 1478.

24.  stealing from his creditors: The modern reader, accustomed to fiat currency, may find this passage puzzling since governments intent on fleecing their creditors now inflate away debt in a manner that reduces the value of the currency. However, in earlier times, such as Rousseau’s, currency purportedly derived its value fr0m its metallic content (often gold). Governments could therefore debase the coinage either by stamping a higher face value on coins of constant metallic content (the practice Rousseau refers to here) or by adulterating the metal or by clipping the coin

25.  Gazetteers: Journalists.

26.  the Catos: Members of a distinguished Plebeian family in ancient Rome, notably the statesmen Marcus Porcius Cato (234–149 BC) and his great-grandson Marcus Porcius Cato Uticensis (95–46 BC), both noted for their strict republican morality.

27.  Le prerogative che goderanno le sudette famiglie: The opening words of a quotation from Buttafoco’s report (see note 3 above), expressing support for an idea with which Rousseau strongly disagreed, namely that the privileges of the Corsican nobility should be restored.

CONSIDERATIONS ON THE GOVERNMENT OF POLAND

1.  Count Wielhorski’s description … government: The document Rousseau refers to has not been identified.

2.  end of the Social Contract: The reference is to the chapter on civil religion.

3.  there to take lessons in corruption: Rousseau had condemned the modern theatre for its corrupting effects on republican virtue in his Letter to d’Alembert.

4.  A proof of this … live in the memory: The Bar Confederation of 1768: an association of nobles determined to preserve Polish independence.

5.  black sauce: Spartan ‘black broth’ was a stew made from pork, salt, vinegar and blood; according to Plutarch the older inhabitants of Sparta were devoted to it, but it did not meet with favour elsewhere. The individual referred to is Brasidas.

6.  to be another Croesus: Croesus (596–c.547 BC) was king of Lydia in Asia Minor until his defeat by the Persians, proverbial for his wealth.

7.  what that much praised Tsar did: A reference to Tsar Peter I the Great, who obliged his court to adopt Western (especially French) apparel and customs.

8.  the Magnates: In reference to the Middle Ages, the term ‘magnate’ is widely used for major territorial landowners. Specifically in the Kingdom of Poland, and later in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, the magnates were a distinct social class of wealthy and influential nobility.

9.  duc d’Epernon … duc de Sully: Jean Louis de Nogaret, duc d’Epernon (1554–1642), was a Catholic nobleman who made a brilliant military career under Henri III; out of favour under Henri IV, he took part in various plots culminating in the latter’s assassination, after which he returned to public life and was involved in the persecution of Huguenots. Maximilien de Béthune, duc de Sully (1564–1640) was a prominent Huguenot nobleman, principal adviser to Henri IV from the latter’s accession in 1589 until his assassination in 1610, but obliged to withdraw from the court in 1611.

10.  ‘moot State’: By analogy with ‘moot courts’, ‘moot assemblies’, etc.

11.  three States combined in one: Greater Poland, Lesser Poland and Lithuania being three parts of the whole.

12.  the Dietines: The assemblies of each Palatinate.

13.  the legislator: Rousseau’s reference to the legislator here is confusing, and matters are not helped by the subsequent references in this chapter. He may be referring to the sovereign people who legislate rather than to a figure like the Legislator of Of the Social Contract, Book II, Chapter 7.

14.  the pacta conventa: Articles of agreement: a pledge made by each Polish king to uphold the constitution.

15.  in Of the Social Contract: See Of the Social Contract, Book III, Chapter 18.

16.  in his Polysynodie: See Of the Social Contract, Book IV, note 6, above.

17.  his authority: Again, this may not be a reference to a figure such as the Legislator of Of the Social Contract.

18.  liberum veto: A device that allowed any member of the assembly to bring a session to an end and nullify anything approved there by declaring ‘I do not allow’.

19.  where I advance it: Of the Social Contract, Book III, Chapters 12–13.

20.  The Legislator corporately: The reference to ‘the Legislator corporately’ strengthens the notion that this is a reference to the sovereign people, especially given the language so strongly reminiscent of the opening paragraph of Of the Social Contract, Book II, Chapter 3.

21.  the comitia: For the Roman comitia, see Of the Social Contract, Book IV, Chapter 4.

22.  Rugi: The Polish word rugi can be translated as ‘eviction’ or ‘exclusion’.

23.  Radom’s commissaries … the Tribunal: The dicastery of Radom was a kind of fiscal court scrutinizing accounts, made up of senators designated by the Diet and commissaries elected by the Dietines, abolished by the Diet in 1764 and replaced by a commission of the exchequer. The Tribunal was a supreme court of appeal held alternately at Piotrków and Lublin.

24.  Laudum: The confirmation sworn by officials in each Palatinate that a particular candidate had been duly elected.

25.  this Wilkes is a mere troublemaker: The reference is to John Wilkes (1725–97), the English radical journalist and politician, who in 1769 was elected to Parliament and disqualified three times, formally on the grounds that he had been an outlaw at the time of his election, but more substantially on the grounds of his unacceptability to King George III and the Court.

26.  Venice’s Golden Book: The Libro d’Oro or Golden Book was the formal register of nobles in the Republic of Venice.

27.  in every Grod: The Grod was the registry attached to every local administration.

28.  Now the law … balanced by their multiplicity: These remarks recall Rousseau’s discussion in Of the Social Contract, Book II, Chapter 3 of the difference between the general will and the will of all.

29.  the Palatines of Polock and Witebsk … the Starost of Samogitie: The Palatines of Polock and Witebsk, and the Starost (Elder) of Samogitie, whose status was equivalent to that of a Palatine, were appointed by the King and sat in the Senate; but their appointment went through a two-stage process of election by ‘popular’ assembly and then by the Dietine.

30.  I have discussed most carefully in the Social Contract: See Of the Social Contract, Book IV, Chapter 2.

31.  the Archbishop of Gniezno: The Roman Catholic Archbishop of Gniezno is traditionally Primate of the Polish Church.

32.  Denmark … England … Sweden: In 1770 the Danish royal doctor, Johann Friedrich Struensee (1737–72), who had become the Queen of Denmark’s lover, insinuated himself into a position of supreme power within the state, which he used to promote various Enlightenment reforms. He alienated both the nobility and the Danish people and was arrested and executed in 1772. Ironically, given the remarks here, Struensee was an admirer of Rousseau. In England, the radical John Wilkes (see note 25) was repeatedly disbarred and re-elected to Parliament in 1769. In Sweden, following half a century of parliamentary domination, King Gustav III (1746–92) came to the throne in 1771, and in 1772 led a coup d’état, with French support, that established him as an ‘enlightened despot’.

33.  the imperial capitulations: In 1519 the Imperial Diet and Grand Electors imposed ‘capitulations’ on the German Emperor in return for their recognition of the hereditary principle, and new guarantees were given in 1711 when Charles VI inherited the Habsburg domains and was elected Emperor.

34.  unanimity was required: See Rousseau’s assertion in Of the Social Contract, Book IV, Chapter 2 that the social pact is the only law which requires unanimity.

35.  the Pseudo-Diet of 1768: The last extraordinary Diet of Warsaw, convened under Russian pressure in October 1767, prorogued in March 1768, which listed a number of fundamental laws and constitutional provisions. Those referred to here were the first, that the republic of Poland was composed of three orders, the King, the Senate and the Equestrian Order; the fifth, that the election of kings must be unanimous and excluded heredity of the Crown; the ninth, confirming the indissoluble unity of the Crown and the Grand Duchy; and the eleventh, guaranteeing the equality and the prerogatives of the szlachta, body politic of the nation.

36.  men of the sword and men of the gown: In France, the noblesse d’épée referred to the traditional nobility rooted in medieval feudalism, while noblesse de robe – attained through the occupation of a range of public functions – was formalized in 1600; in European parlance it subsequently came to refer more generally to members of the legal professions and public servants.

37.  entails or Majorats: Majorat is the right of succession to property according to age (primogeniture). A majorat (fidéicommis) would be inherited by the eldest son, or if there was no son by the nearest male relative. The institution was designed to prevent the division of wealthy estates between many family members. In the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, majorat was known as ordynacja. Introduced in the late sixteenth century by King Stefan Batory, it assisted the creation of major magnate fortunes such as that of the Radziwills, and survived until the Communist period following the Second World War.

38.  the Bailiffs of the Canton of Berne: Berne was ruled by a Grand Council, whose members were known as Bailiffs (a term, widespread in Europe, that had lost its original meaning of royal steward and come merely to designate an important civic official). Rousseau’s earlier good opinion of the administration of Berne had given way to the harsh judgements expressed here, following his two expulsions from the canton.

39.  a people of Capuchins: Order of Friars Minor Capuchin, founded in 1520, originally as a reform movement within the Franciscans and aiming to return the latter to the poverty recommended by St Francis. Known for their austere way of life, often as hermits, they took their name from the cappuccio or hood that they wore.

40.  the infallible and natural effect: Rousseau sets out this criterion in Of the Social Contract, Book II, Chapter 9.

41.  Hôtel-Dieu: See Constitutional Proposal for Corsica, note 24, above.

42.  capitation: See Constitutional Proposal for Corsica, note 19, above.

43.  the Maréchal de Vauban and the abbé de Saint-Pierre: Sébastien Le Prestre, Marquis de Vauban (1633–1707), the great military theorist and engineer, also wrote widely on economic issues, including notably in his Projet d’une dixme royale (1707), which called for the imposition of a single 10 per cent tax on all agricultural output (payable in kind) and on income from trade and manufactures, with no exemptions. For Saint-Pierre, see Of the Social Contract, Prefatory Note, note 1, above.

44.  Antony and Crassus easily entered the territory of the Parthians: Marcus Licinius Crassus (115–53 BC) was a Roman politician and general, proverbially wealthy, and a member of the first Triumvirate (see Of the Social Contract, Book III, note 15, above). Given the governorship of Syria, he invaded the territory of the Parthian empire (in present-day Iran) in 53 BC, but was defeated and killed. Mark Antony (Marcus Antonius, 83–30 BC) was a Roman politician and general, a close supporter and ally of Julius Caesar, who following the latter’s assassination became a member of the second Triumvirate. He was involved in sporadic warfare against the Parthians between 41 and 33 BC, sometimes successfully, at other times leading to defeat on Parthian territory, notably in 37 BC.

45.  Themistocles: Themistocles (c.524–459 BC) was an Athenian politician and general, pre-eminent following the battle of Marathon and playing a vital role in the establishment of Athenian naval power and the defeat of the Persians at Salamis. He was widely viewed by later generations as the symbol of ancient Greek statesmanship.

46.  what I said in the Social Contract: See Of the Social Contract, Book II, Chapter 10.

47.  the Turkish war: The Russo–Turkish War of 1768–74 eventually turned into a decisive Russian victory, which brought southern Ukraine, northern Caucasus and the Crimea under Russian rule. In it Turkey was allied with the Polish Confederation of Bar, while Russia was allied with Great Britain.

48.  The Grand Turk: In eighteenth-century Europe, the Ottoman Sultan was commonly referred to as the Grand Turk, and his administration, headed by the Grand Vizier, as the Sublime Porte, or simply Porte, from the gate to the Divan at which the Vizier would receive diplomatic visitors.

49.  the King they sought to give you: Stanisław August Poniatowski (1732–98), a lover of Catherine the Great, was elected King of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1764, following a Russian-backed coup d’état. He supported Russian suppression of the Confederation of Bar in 1768–72, and was briefly taken prisoner by Confederate sympathizers in 1771. Although he did protest against the first partition of the Commonwealth in 1772, he was powerless to do anything about it. He remains a very controversial figure in Polish history.

Chronology

1707 Following acute conflict between the Genevan bourgeoisie and the ruling oligarchy, the leader of the democratic party, Pierre Fatio, is executed.

1712 Jean-Jacques Rousseau born on 28 June in Geneva; his mother Suzanne dies on 7 July.

1715 Death of Louis XIV of France.

1722 Rousseau’s father flees from Geneva. Rousseau is sent to live with the Lambercier family outside the city.

1724 Rousseau is apprenticed to an engraver in Geneva.

1728 Rousseau runs away and meets Mme de Warens at Annecy. She sends him to Turin, where he converts to Roman Catholicism.

1729 Rousseau returns to Annecy to live with Mme de Warens.

1738 Following further civil strife in Geneva, the Act of Mediation establishes a new constitution.

1740 Rousseau becomes a tutor to the de Mably family in Lyon. Frederick the Great comes to power in Prussia.

1742 Rousseau moves to Paris and unsuccessfully proposes a numerically based system of musical notation.

1743–4 Serves as secretary to the French Ambassador in Venice.

1744 Rousseau meets with Diderot and is inducted into French Enlightenment circles.

1745 He begins his lifelong relationship with Thérèse Levasseur.

1748 Montesquieu publishes The Spirit of Laws.

1749 On his way to visit the imprisoned Diderot, Rousseau experiences an epiphany on reading of an essay competition set by the Academy of Dijon.

1750 The Discourse on the Sciences and the Arts wins the prize from the Dijon Academy and Rousseau enjoys widespread fame.

1751 The first volume of the Encyclopédie, edited by Diderot and d’Alembert, appears.

1752 Rousseau’s opera Le Devin du Village enjoys success.

1754 Rousseau visits Geneva and reconverts to Protestantism in order to regain his citizenship.

1755 Rousseau publishes the Discourse on the Origin of Inequality and, as an entry in the Encyclopédie, the Discourse on Political Economy. The Lisbon earthquake. Pasquale Paoli proclaims Corsica a republic, independent of Genoa.

1756 Beginning of the Seven Years War.

1758 The Letter to d’Alembert on the Theatre signals Rousseau’s breach with the mainstream of the French Enlightenment.

1761 Publication of Julie, or the New Héloïse.

1762 Publication of the Social Contract and Emile. Condemnation in Paris and Geneva. Facing arrest, Rousseau flees to Môtiers in Switzerland. Catherine the Great comes to power in Russia.

1763 Rousseau renounces his Genevan citizenship. Treaty of Paris ends the Seven Years War.

1764 With Letters Written from the Mountains, Rousseau intervenes in the political debate in Geneva.

1766 At the invitation of David Hume, Rousseau travels to England, where he settles at Wootton in Staffordshire and begins work on the Confessions. Quarrels with Hume and becomes mentally unstable.

1767 Rousseau returns to France under an assumed name.

1768 Confederation of Bar forms to defend Polish independence against Russia.

1768-9 Genoa transfers its nominal sovereignty over Corsica to France. France invades Corsica and ends the Corsican Republic.

1770 Rousseau returns to Paris.

1772 First partition of Poland.

1776 Rousseau composes his final work, The Reveries of the Solitary Walker. American Declaration of Independence. Adam Smith publishes The Wealth of Nations.

1778 Rousseau dies on 2 July, aged sixty-six.

1789 Fall of the Bastille, the French Revolution begins.

1794 The French revolutionaries transfer Rousseau’s remains to the Panthéon in Paris.

1798 Geneva annexed by France.

1815 Geneva becomes a canton of Switzerland.

He just wanted a decent book to read ...

Not too much to ask, is it? It was in 1935 when Allen Lane, Managing Director of Bodley Head Publishers, stood on a platform at Exeter railway station looking for something good to read on his journey back to London. His choice was limited to popular magazines and poor-quality paperbacks – the same choice faced every day by the vast majority of readers, few of whom could afford hardbacks. Lane’s disappointment and subsequent anger at the range of books generally available led him to found a company – and change the world.

We believed in the existence in this country of a vast reading public for intelligent books at a low price, and staked everything on it’

Sir Allen Lane, 1902–1970, founder of Penguin Books

The quality paperback had arrived – and not just in bookshops. Lane was adamant that his Penguins should appear in chain stores and tobacconists, and should cost no more than a packet of cigarettes.

Reading habits (and cigarette prices) have changed since 1935, but Penguin still believes in publishing the best books for everybody to enjoy.We still believe that good design costs no more than bad design, and we still believe that quality books published passionately and responsibly make the world a better place.

So wherever you see the little bird – whether it’s on a piece of prize-winning literary fiction or a celebrity autobiography, political tour de force or historical masterpiece, a serial-killer thriller, reference book, world classic or a piece of pure escapism – you can bet that it represents the very best that the genre has to offer.

* ‘Scholarly studies on public law are often merely the story of ancient abuses, and people have been over-zealous when they have taken the trouble to pay them too much attention.’ Traité des intérêts de la Fr. avec ses voisins, par M. le Marquis d’Argenson (printed by Rey in Amsterdam). That is just what Grotius has done. [1782 edition]

* See a little treatise by Plutarch entitled: ‘Beasts are rational’ [Bruta animalia ratione uti].

* The Romans, who understood better and respected more the right of war than any other nation in the world, carried their scruples in this respect so far that a Citizen was not allowed to serve as a volunteer without having expressly engaged himself against the enemy, and against the particular enemy by name. When a Legion in which the young Cato was seeing his first service under Popilius was reorganized, Cato the Elder wrote to Popilius13 that if he wanted his son to continue to serve under him, he must make him swear a new military oath, because the former oath having been annulled he was no longer able to bear arms against the enemy. And that same Cato wrote to his son to take care not to present himself for combat if he had not sworn this new oath. I know that you could bring up against me the siege of Clusium and other specific events, but for my part I am citing laws and customs. The Romans are the people who least often infringed their laws, and they are the only people to have had such fine ones. [1782 edition]

* The true meaning of this word has been almost wholly erased in the modern world; most people today take a town for a City and a townsman for a Citizen. They are unaware that houses make a town but Citizens make a City. This same mistake once cost the Carthaginians dear. I have not read that the title Cives has ever been given to the subjects of any Prince, not even in olden times to the Macedonians, nor in our own day to the English, closer to liberty though they be than all the rest. The French alone adopt this title of Citizens quite casually, since as can be seen from their Dictionaries they have no real idea about it; otherwise by usurping it they would fall into the crime of Lèse-Majesté. Among them, this name expresses a quality, not a right. When Bodin thought to speak about our Citizens and Townsmen, he made a serious blunder in taking one for the other. M. d’Alembert did not fall into the same error, and in his article ‘Geneva’18 clearly distinguished the four orders of men (even five, counting mere foreigners) who exist in our town, and of whom two alone make up the Republic. No other French author, to my knowledge, has understood the true meaning of the word Citizen.

* Under bad governments this equality is only apparent and illusory; it serves only to maintain the poor man in his misery and the rich man in his usurpation. In fact, laws are always useful to those who own and harmful to those who have nothing. Whence it follows that the social state is advantageous to men only in so far as all have something and none has anything in excess.

Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

* For a will to be general, it is not always necessary that it be unanimous, but it is necessary that all votes be counted; any formal exclusion breaks its generality.

* ‘Every interest’, says M. d’A[rgenson], ‘has different principles. Agreement between two particular interests is formed through opposition to that of a third party.’ He might have added that agreement between all interests is formed through opposition to the interest of each. If there were no different interests, you would scarcely be aware of the common interest, which would never encounter any obstacle. Everything would proceed of its own accord, and politics would cease to be an art.

* ‘It is very true’, says Machiavelli, ‘that some divisions are harmful to the Republic, while some are beneficial: harmful are those associated with factions and followers; beneficial those maintained without factions or followers. The founder of a Republic being therefore unable to ensure that there are no enmities within it, he must at least ensure that there are no factions.’ History of Florence, L, 7. [Cited by Rousseau in Italian.]

* I beg of you, attentive readers, do not rush to charge me here with inconsistency. I have been unable to avoid it in my terms, given the poverty of the language. But wait.

Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

* By this word, I do not mean only an Aristocracy or a Democracy, but in general any government guided by the general will, which is the law. To be legitimate, the Government must not be confused with the Sovereign, but be its minister: then monarchy itself is a republic. This will be clarified in the following book.

* A people becomes famous only when its legislation begins to decline. We do not know for how many centuries before the rest of Greece ever took notice of the Spartans the institutions of Lycurgus ensured their well-being.

* Those who consider Calvin only as a theologian have poor knowledge of the scope of his genius. The drafting of our wise Edicts, in which he played a large part, does him as much honour as do his Institutes. Whatever revolution time may bring to our faith, the memory of that great man will never cease to be blessed in it, for as long as love of the fatherland and liberty have not been extinguished among us.

* ‘And in truth’, says Machiavelli, ‘there was never any ordainer of extraordinary laws in a people who did not have recourse to God, because otherwise they would not be accepted; for many good things are known to a prudent man that do not in themselves have manifest reasons such as to persuade others of them.’ Discourses on Titus Livius, L, I, c, XI.

* If two neighbouring peoples could not do without one another, it would be a very difficult situation for one and a very dangerous situation for the other. Every wise nation, in such a case, will strive with all haste to free the other from its dependence. The Republic of Tlaxcala, which formed an enclave within the Empire of Mexico, preferred to go without salt than to buy any from the Mexicans, or even to accept any from them as a gift. The wise Tlaxcalans saw the trap hidden beneath such generosity. They kept their liberty, and that little State surrounded by that great Empire was finally the instrument of the latter’s ruin.

* Do you wish then to give the State coherence? Bring the extreme degrees as close together as possible: do not tolerate either opulent persons or beggars. Those two conditions, naturally inseparable, are equally fatal to the common good. From one come the creators of tyranny, from the other come tyrants. It is always between them that public liberty is trafficked: one buys it, the other sells it.

† Some branches of external commerce, says the M[arquis] d’A[rgenson], scarcely provide anything other than false utility for a kingdom in general; they may enrich certain individuals, even certain towns, but the nation as a whole gains nothing from them, and the people is no better off.

Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

* Thus in Venice the College is called most serene Prince, even when the Doge is not present.1

* The Palatine of Poznan, father of the King of Poland, Duke of Lorraine.

† Clearly the word Optimists in the ancient world does not mean the best, but the most powerful.

* It is of great importance to regulate the form of elections of magistrates by laws. For if it is left to the will of the Prince, you cannot avoid falling into hereditary Aristocracy, as happened to the Republics of Venice and Berne. Thus the former has for long been a dissolved State, but the latter maintains itself through the extreme wisdom of its Senate; it is a very honourable and very dangerous exception.

* Machiavelli was an honest man and a good citizen. But, being attached to the house of Medici, he was forced under the oppression of his fatherland to disguise his love of liberty. The very choice of his execrable Hero shows clearly enough his secret intention; and the contrast between the maxims of his book on the Prince and those in his discourses on Titus Livius 10 and in his history of Florence shows that this profound political thinker has hitherto had only superficial or corrupt Readers. The Court of Rome severely proscribed his book, as I can well believe; for that court is what the book most clearly portrayed. [1782 edition]

* Tacitus, Histories, Book I.

† In The Statesman.

* This does not contradict what I said earlier in Book II, Chapter 9, on the disadvantages of large States. For there it was a matter of the Government’s authority over its members, while here it is a matter of its strength against its subjects. Its scattered members serve it as fulcra to act upon the people from afar, but it has no fulcrum to act directly upon those members themselves. Thus in one case the length of the lever makes for weakness, in the other for strength.

* We should follow the same principle in judging which centuries merit our preference in terms of the prosperity of mankind. We have admired too much those in which letters and arts have been seen to flourish, without grasping the secret aim of their cultivation, and without considering its fateful effect, idque apud imperitos humanitas vocabatur, cum pars servitutis esset [and the ignorant called it ‘human nature’, whereas it was part of slavery]. In the maxims of books, shall we never see the vulgar interest that makes their Authors speak? No, whatever they may say about it, when a country becomes depopulated in spite of its brilliance, it is not true that all is going well; and it is not enough for a poet to have an income of a hundred thousand livres for his century to be best of all. We should pay less regard to the apparent ease and tranquillity of rulers than to the well-being of whole nations, and above all of the most populous states. Hail may lay waste a few cantons, but it rarely brings a famine. Riots and civil wars greatly frighten rulers, but they do not cause the true misfortunes of peoples, which can even have some respite while argument rages over who will tyrannize them. It is their permanent state which gives birth to their real prosperity or their real calamities. It is when everything remains crushed beneath the yoke that everything declines, and that rulers, destroying them with ease, ubi solitudinem faciunt, pacem appellant [where they create solitude, call it peace]. When the bickerings of the Nobles were disrupting the kingdom of France, and the Coadjutor of Paris used to go to Parliament with a dagger in his pocket, that did not prevent the French people, happy and numerous, from living at their ease in respectability and liberty. In olden times Greece flourished amid the cruellest wars; blood flowed copiously, yet the whole land was filled with men. It seemed, Machiavelli says, that amid murders, banishments and civil wars our [Florentine] Republic grew all the more powerful; the virtue of its citizens, their morals and their independence had more effect in strengthening it than all its disputes had in weakening it. A little unrest gives vigour to the soul, and what makes the species truly prosper is not so much peace as liberty.15

* The slow formation and the progress of the Republic of Venice in its lagoons offers a notable example of this succession. And it is astonishing indeed that after more than twelve hundred years the Venetians seem still to be only at the second stage, which began at the Serrar del Consiglio in 1198. As for the old Doges who are brought up against them, whatever the Squitinio della libertà veneta may say about them, it is proven that they were not their Sovereigns at all. People will not fail to cite against me the Roman Republic, which they will claim followed a quite opposite progress, passing from monarchy to Aristocracy, and from Aristocracy to Democracy. I am very far from viewing things like this.

The first establishment of Romulus was a mixed Government, which quickly degenerated into Despotism. For specific reasons the State perished before its time, as a newborn child sometimes dies before having reached manhood. The expulsion of the Tarquins was the true epoch when the Republic was born. But it did not at first take a constant form, because by not abolishing the patriciate only half the work was done. For in this way the hereditary Aristocracy, which is the worst of legitimate administrations, remained in conflict with Democracy, so that the still uncertain and fluctuating form of Government was settled, as Machiavelli proved, only when the Tribunes were established; then alone was there a true Government and a true Democracy. In fact the people was then not merely Sovereign, but also magistrate and judge, the Senate was merely a subsidiary tribunal to moderate or concentrate the Government, and the Consuls themselves, albeit Patricians, albeit first Magistrates, albeit absolute Generals in war, in Rome were only the presidents of the people.

Thenceforth the Government too was seen to take its natural tendency and to incline strongly to Aristocracy. With the Patriciate being abolished almost of its own accord, Aristocracy was no longer in the body of Patricians as it is in Venice and Genoa, but in the body of the Senate made up of Patricians and Plebeians, even in the body of the Tribunes when these began to usurp an active power; for words do nothing to things, and when the people has rulers who govern for it, whatever name these rulers bear, it is always an Aristocracy. From the abuse of Aristocracy sprang the civil wars and the Triumvirate. Sulla, Julius Caesar, Augustus became in fact real Monarchs, and finally under the Despotism of Tiberius the State was dissolved. Roman history thus does not refute my principle, it confirms it.16

* Omnes enim et habentur et dicuntur Tyranni qui potestate utuntur perpetua, in ea Civitate qua libertate usa est [For all are both deemed and called Tyrants who use perpetual power, in that City which is used to liberty], Cornelius Nepos, Life of Miltiades. It is true that Aristotle in Nichomachean Ethics, Book VIII, chapter X, distinguishes the Tyrant from the King, in that the former governs for his own utility and the latter only for the utility of his subjects. But apart from the fact that all Greek authors generally took the word Tyrant in another sense, as appears above all from the Hieron of Xenophon, it would follow from Aristotle’s distinction that since the beginning of the world there would never have existed a single King.

* More or less in the sense given to this term in the Parliament of England. The similarity between these functions would have brought the Consuls and the Tribunes into conflict even if all jurisdiction had been suspended.

* To adopt in cold countries the luxury and softness of Orientals is to be willing to accept their chains, indeed to submit to these even more inevitably than they do.

* This is what I had proposed to do in the remainder of this work, when, in dealing with external relations, I came to confederations. This is a wholly new topic, and one whose principles remain to be established.

* Provided, of course, that he does not go away in order to evade his duty and excuse himself from serving his fatherland at the moment when it has need of him. Flight would then be criminal and punishable; that would no longer be withdrawal, but desertion.

Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

* This should always be understood in relation to a free State, for elsewhere family, goods, lack of refuge, necessity and violence may keep an inhabitant in the country unwillingly, and then his mere residence no longer presupposes his consent to the contract or to violation of the contract.

† In Genoa, the word Libertas may be read on the façade of prisons and the shackles of galley-slaves. This application of the motto is splendid and right. For it is only criminals of every condition who prevent the Citizen from being free. In a country where all such people were in the Galleys, you would enjoy the most perfect liberty.

* The name Rome, which is claimed to come from Romulus is Greek, and means strength. The name Numa is Greek too, and means Law. What is the likelihood that the two first Kings of that city should in advance have borne names so clearly related to what they did?

* Ramnenses.

† Tatienses.

‡ Luceres.

* I say on the Campus Martius, because it was there that the comitia assembled by centuries; in the two other forms the people would assemble at the forum or elsewhere, and then the Capite censi had as much influence and authority as the first Citizens.

* This century drawn thus by lot was called prae rogativa, because it was the first to be asked for its suffrage, and that is the source of the word prerogative.

* Custodes, Diribitores, Rogatores suffragiorum.

* This nomination would be made at night and in secret, as if they were ashamed to place a man above the laws.

* That is what he could not guarantee by proposing a Dictatorship, not daring to nominate himself and not being able to ensure that his colleague would nominate him.

* In this chapter I merely allude to what I dealt with at greater length in the Letter to M. d’Alembert.

† They were from another Island,16 which the delicacy of our language forbids me to name on this occasion. [1782 edition]

* Nonne ea quae possidet Chamos deus tuus tibi jure debentur? Such is the Vulgate text. Father Carrières has translated: Do you not believe in your right to possess what belongs to Chamos your God? I do not know the import of the Hebrew text, but I see that in the Vulgate Jephtha positively acknowledges the right of the God Chamos, and that the French Translator weakens this acknowledgement by an according to you that is not in the Latin.

† It is perfectly evident that the war of the Phocians known as the sacred war was not a war of religion at all. Its aim was to punish sacrilege, not to subdue unbelievers.

* It is noteworthy that it is not so much formal assemblies, like those of France, which bind the clergy into a body as it is the communion of Churches. Communion and excommunication are the social pact of the clergy, a pact by virtue of which it will always be the master of peoples and Kings. All priests who are in communion together are fellow citizens, even should they come from opposite ends of the earth. This invention is a masterpiece in politics. The pagan Priests had nothing like it; accordingly, they never formed a body of Clergy.

† See among other things, in a Letter from Grotius to his brother on 11 April 1643, what that learned man approves and what he condemns in the book De Cive. It is true that, being inclined to indulgence, he seems to forgive the author what is good for the sake of what is bad; but everyone is not so merciful.

* In the Republic, says M. d’A[rgenson], every man is perfectly free in what does not harm others. There is the invariable limit; it cannot be stated more accurately. I have been unable to deny myself the pleasure of sometimes quoting this manuscript, albeit unknown to the public, in order to pay honour to the memory of an illustrious and worthy man, who even in the Ministry had preserved the heart of a true citizen and upright, sound views on the government of his country.

* Caesar pleading for Catiline sought to establish the dogma of the soul’s immortality. Cato and Cicero, in order to refute it, did not amuse themselves by philosophizing. They contented themselves with showing that Caesar was speaking as a bad Citizen and advancing a doctrine harmful to the State. For that was what the Senate of Rome had to pass judgement on, not a question of theology.

* Marriage, for example, being a civil contract, has civil effects without which it is even impossible that society should survive. Let us then suppose that a Clergy manages to attribute to itself alone the right to approve this act; a right that it must necessarily usurp in every intolerant Religion. Is it not then clear that, in validating the authority of the Church in this respect, it will render vain that of the Prince, who will no longer have any more subjects than those whom the Clergy is willing to give him. Is it not clear that, by behaving prudently and standing firm, the Clergy – with the power to marry people or not depending on whether they do or do not have such and such a doctrine; depending on whether they accept or reject such and such a form; depending on whether they are more devout or less so – will alone dispose of the inheritances, offices and Citizens of the State itself, which would be unable to survive were it henceforth to be made up only of bastards? But, you may say, abuses will be appealed against, summonses will be issued, decrees made, temporal property seized. What a tragedy! The Clergy, provided it has I shall not say courage but common sense, will let this happen and continue as usual. It will calmly let abuse be appealed against, summonses be issued, decrees be passed, and seizures be made, and will end up as the master. It does not strike me as any great sacrifice to abandon a part when you are confident of capturing the whole.

Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

* Thus this analytical method offers reason only abysses and mysteries, where the wisest understands least. If you ask why manners become corrupted as minds become enlightened, being unable to find the cause they will have the audacity to deny the fact. If you ask why savages transported among us share neither our passions nor our pleasures, and are not concerned with all that we so ardently desire, they will never explain it, or will explain it only by my principles. They know only what they see, and have never seen nature. They very well know what a Burgher of London or Paris is, but they will never know what a man is.

Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

* Even that of God’s will, at least with respect to its application. For although it is clear that man ought to will whatever God wills, it is not clear that God wills some Government to be preferred to some other, nor that you should obey Jacques rather than Guillaume. Well, this is what the issue is.

* At the height of the initial hullabaloo caused by the proceedings of Paris and Geneva, the surprised Magistrate banned the two Books: but after his own examination this wise Magistrate simply changed his mind, above all with respect to Of the Social Contract.

* ‘In general’, says the author of the Letters [Written from the Country], ‘men are even more afraid of obeying than they are fond of commanding.’ Tacitus thought otherwise and knew the human heart. If the maxim were true, the Lackeys of the Great would be less insolent with Townsmen, and you would see fewer idlers lurking in the Courts of Princes. There are few men of sound enough heart to be able to love liberty. All wish to command; at that price, no one fears to obey. A petty upstart gives himself a hundred masters in order to acquire ten lackeys. You need only see the pride of the nobles in Monarchies; how vehemently they pronounce those words ‘service’ and ‘to serve’; how great and respectable they deem themselves when they can have the honour of saying ‘the King, my master’; how much they despise Republicans who are merely free, and who are certainly nobler than they.

Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

* In these estimates, you must have far more regard for persons than for isolated actions. True good is done with little show. It is through a uniform and sustained conduct, through private and domestic virtues, through all the duties of his estate well fulfilled, lastly through actions flowing from his character and his principles, that a man can deserve honours, rather than through a few great dramatic actions that already find their reward in public admiration. Philosophical ostentation is very fond of showy actions; but a person with five or six actions of this kind, very splendid, very clamorous, very much extolled, has no other aim than to falsify his account and to be all his life unjust and harsh with impunity. ‘Give us the small change for great actions.’ This saying by a woman is a very judicious saying.

Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

PENGUIN    CLASSICS

OF THE SOCIAL CONTRACT AND OTHER POLITICAL WRITINGS

JEAN-JACQUES ROUSSEAU was born in Geneva in 1712. Abandoned by his father at the age of ten, he tried his hand as an engraver’s apprentice before he left the city in 1728. From then on he was to wander Europe seeking an elusive happiness. At Turin he became a Catholic convert; and as a footman, seminarist, music teacher or tutor visited many parts of Switzerland and France. In 1732 he settled for eight years at Chambéry or at Les Charmettes, the country house of Madame de Warens, remembered by Rousseau as an idyllic place in the Confessions. In 1741 he set out for Paris, where he met Diderot, who commissioned him to write the musical articles for the Encyclopédie. In the meantime, he fathered five children by Thérèse Levasseur, a servant girl, and abandoned them to a foundling home. The 1750s witnessed a breach with Voltaire and Diderot and his writing struck a new note of defiant independence. In his Discourse on the Sciences and the Arts and the Discourse on the Origin of Inequality, he showed how the growth of civilization corrupted natural goodness and increased inequality between men. In 1758 he attacked his former friends, the Encyclopaedists, in the Letter to d’Alembert on Theatre, which pilloried cultured society. In 1757 he moved to Montmorency and these five years were the most fruitful of his life. His remarkable novel Julie, or the New Héloïse (1761) met with immediate and enormous success. In this and in Emile, which followed a year later, Rousseau invoked the inviolability of personal ideals against the power of the state and the pressures of society. The crowning achievement of his political philosophy was Of the Social Contract, published in 1762. That same year he wrote an attack on revealed religion, The Creed of a Savoyard Priest. He was driven from Switzerland and fled to England, where he only succeeded in making an enemy of Hume and returned to his continental peregrinations. In 1770 Rousseau completed his Confessions. His last years were spent largely in France, where he died in 1778.

CHRISTOPHER BERTRAM is Professor of Social and Political Philosophy at the University of Bristol. He is the author of Rousseau and The Social Contract (Routledge, 2004) and is a past president of the Rousseau Association. His main research interests are in social contract theory, in theories of justice and in public justification.

QUINTIN HOARE won his first translation prize (at school) for a rendering of Homer, and in 1968 produced one of the earliest versions of Walter Benjamin to appear in English. He has translated from Italian (Antonio Gramsci, Franco Moretti), French (Jean-Paul Sartre, Simone de Beauvoir, Paul Nizan, Germaine Tillion, Jacques Berque, Hélène Carrère d’Encausse), German (Hermann Grab, Richard Wagner, Siegfried Kracauer), Russian (Nikolai Chernyshevskii) and Bosnian (Mladen Vuksanović), winning the John Florio Prize in 1978/9, the Scott-Moncrieff Prize in 1984 and the Schlegel-Tieck Prize in 1989. He was general editor of the Pelican Marx Library, and since 1997 has been director of The Bosnian Institute. Married to the historian Branka Magaš, he has had a long association with the former Yugoslavia and its successor states.
