chapters.text:
Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

Introduction

Jean-Jacques Rousseau is one of the dominant intellectual figures of the modern era. According to the cover of a special edition of the French magazine Le Nouvel Observateur, he invented childhood, nature, equality, democracy and ‘the cult of the self’.1 Others have credited Rousseau as the great forerunner of Marx and Freud or as the theorist of participatory and deliberative democracy. Yet he has also been vilified as a charlatan, and accused of being the inspiration for the Great Terror of the French Revolution, for ‘totalitarian democracy’ and, thus, indirectly, for the evils of communism and fascism. Today, happily, we are to some extent free from the ideological blinkers of the Cold War and can assess Rousseau on his own merits rather than through the distorting lens of subsequent conflicts. And those merits are considerable. Rousseau was an unusual man with unusual gifts. Difficult to get along with, certainly mentally unbalanced, he was a Genevan outsider in the salons of Paris; a man who rejected religious orthodoxy, but could not bring himself to accept the scientism and scepticism of the Enlightenment; a late-developing autodidact, a dabbler in many fields and an expert in some; a lover of freedom but a pessimist about its realization, Rousseau was able to delineate many of the characteristic pathologies of modernity when the modern age was still being born.

Those who encounter Rousseau today are likely to get to know him through just one or two facets of his achievement. Students of philosophy or political science, for example, will probably read Of the Social Contract and, perhaps, the Discourse on the Origins of Inequality. But Rousseau contributed to a wide variety of fields. His Confessions, together with his other autobiographical writings such as the paranoid Dialogues and the elegiac Reveries of the Solitary Walker, support a claim that he invented autobiography in its modern sense. By giving an interior account of how Rousseau became himself, an account predicated on the notion that a person’s psyche could be shaped and fixed by small but traumatic incidents, Rousseau made possible modes of thinking about the self that later found literary expression in writers like Proust, scientific form in Freudian psychoanalysis, and are with us today in modern obsessions with therapies of the self. His writings on childcare and education, particularly Emile, have also been tributaries to that same stream. How can we bring up our children to lead happy and fulfilled lives in a world of conflict and competition? It is a question that millions of parents have asked themselves in the West over the past two centuries, but Rousseau was one of the first people to attempt an answer. By trying to think through the elementary forms of psychological development, and the meaning and character of the emotions, not only did Rousseau begin child psychology, but he also prepared a stream of philosophical exploration of related themes, with Hegel’s Phenomenology of Spirit being one prominent result. Rousseau was also a novelist, with his work Julie, or the New Héloïse being among the most popular creations of the eighteenth century, scandalizing and titillating both bourgeoisie and aristocracy but additionally providing a further vehicle for Rousseau’s wider psychological concerns.

If all that were not enough, we can mention his contribution to music, both as a composer and a theorist. Rousseau participated in one of the most significant ‘culture wars’ episodes of the past three centuries, the ‘Querelle des Bouffons’, in which he and his friends championed the aesthetic of Italian opera against the pomposity and bombast of its French counterpart. Yet despite condemning French as inherently unmusical, he composed an opera in the language, Le Devin du Village, which was the smash hit of 1752, earned him the offer of a pension for life from the King (Rousseau declined it) and stayed in the repertoire for a hundred years. As a music theorist and critic, Rousseau became one of the principal contributors to Diderot and d’Alembert’s Encyclopédie and wrote his own Dictionary of Music before, at the very end of his life, befriending and corresponding with the great reformer of opera Gluck. We can even add to this list of wider interests: Rousseau’s writings on botany, expressed in the form of a series of letters to an English noblewoman, were later transformed into a textbook used at the University of Cambridge.

The texts collected in this volume comprise some of Rousseau’s principal later writings in political philosophy and political science. However, they were composed against the background of a set of earlier studies, most notably the Discourse on the Sciences and Arts and the Discourse on the Origins of Inequality, which connect explicitly to the wider themes of Rousseau’s project. In those earlier studies, Rousseau had written about the fall of mankind and about the material and psychological causes of our modern unfreedom. In the Discourse on Inequality in particular, he paves the way for much later thinking about the development of the human species and about problems of cooperation and exploitation. From Marx to modern work in sociobiology and evolutionary psychology, we can discern the traces of Rousseau’s influence. Some of the details of Rousseau’s evolutionary story and its psychological dynamics are discussed below. Here, it is important to note its underlying motivation and the principle which unifies it. The idea that gives coherence to all this work is the one that finds expression right at the outset of the Social Contract. It is the idea that mankind is free by nature but is everywhere in chains: legal, material and psychological. Rousseau combines this idea with an attempt to think through how our freedom could be restored to us in some form. Rousseau’s opponents, from Voltaire to Nietzsche and beyond, have tried to pin on him the naive idea that the answer to mankind’s problems is a return to nature, to some pre-social Eden.2 Rousseau was indeed fascinated with nature and his appreciation of its beauty and grandeur helped to generate modern aesthetic sensibilities and finds expression in our contemporary concerns about our planet and the destruction of the environment. But Rousseau does not so much want to return to nature as to find a place for our nature in a world where it is both materially and psychologically impossible for us to recreate some lost paradise. At the beginning of Emile, he expresses this notion with the metaphor of a seedling that has taken root on a busy path. Left to nature alone, that seedling will quickly be trampled and die; to survive and flourish it needs protection and cultivation. In that work, the task is to form an individual who can grow to autonomous adulthood in a world of inequality and corruption. In Of the Social Contract, Rousseau is concerned with the possibility of a whole society combining the interdependence of modernity with the freedom and equality of individuals.

ROUSSEAU’S LIFE AND BACKGROUND

Jean-Jacques Rousseau was born in Geneva in 1712, the son of Isaac Rousseau, a watchmaker and a citizen of the independent city-state. Rousseau’s mother Suzanne died a few days after his birth, so he and his brother were brought up by their father. Jean-Jacques seems to have had a somewhat idiosyncratic education, involving much reading of the classics (especially Plutarch). Isaac appears to have been a fairly imprudent and impulsive individual, and, having managed to get himself into a dispute with a nobleman, was forced to flee Geneva when Jean-Jacques was ten years old. The boy was sent to live with a pastor’s family outside the city, an experience which is given a lively depiction in his Confessions. Later, Rousseau had to learn a trade and was apprenticed to an engraver, who, according to Rousseau’s later account, treated his charge with cruelty and violence. At the age of sixteen, having failed to get back inside the city gates before they were locked at curfew, the young apprentice decided not to return and face the beating he anticipated, but rather to seek a new life beyond Geneva.

The Geneva Rousseau abandoned was not the wealthy cosmopolitan city of today, but a republic founded on sectarian confessional principles by Jean Calvin himself in 1536. By the early eighteenth century, there was considerably more religious heterodoxy in Geneva than earlier, but it was still a Protestant fortress surrounded by hostile Catholic states, with a parallel system of religious law enforcement to punish moral deviation. In some formal sense, Geneva was democratic, in that its sovereign body was notionally the Grand Conseil, composed of all its citizens. But this apparently democratic constitution fell short of genuine popular sovereignty on two grounds. First, the hereditary citizens of the state had, by Rousseau’s time, become a minority of the population. Second, even those with political rights had very little effective power. In practice, control was in the hands of the interlocked group of a few families who controlled a much smaller body, the Petit Conseil. Much of Geneva’s recent political history had involved sharp and sometimes bloody contestation between those who sought to restore or establish citizen sovereignty and the small oligarchy who exercised power. Rousseau himself would become entangled in this controversy after the publication of the Social Contract in 1762, its banning by the Genevan authorities and subsequent protests by some of the Genevan bourgeoisie, a dispute that would lead to the composition of his Letters Written from the Mountains.

In 1728 the immediate alternative to Geneva appeared to Rousseau in the form of an attractive Catholic convert in Annecy, Françoise-Louise de Warens. Mme de Warens took the young Jean-Jacques under her protection before sending him to Turin for instruction in the Catholic faith. After converting and spending some time in service and starting to train for the priesthood, Rousseau then spent time as a travelling musician and music copyist before returning to the de Warens household near Chambéry in 1731. Rousseau remained there for most of the rest of the decade, becoming, for a while, de Warens’s lover. In 1740, whilst working as a tutor to the de Mably family in Lyon, Rousseau made his first contacts with leading figures of the Enlightenment such as Condillac and d’Alembert, before travelling to Paris in 1742 to present the Academy of Sciences with a novel numerical scheme for musical notation. This was not well received and Rousseau left Paris briefly to serve as secretary to the French ambassador in Venice, an episode which both made him familiar with a form of republican government other than Geneva’s and aroused a passion for Italian music. Returning to Paris in 1744, Rousseau befriended the philosopher Denis Diderot, and started to write on musical themes, with his contributions including articles for the Encyclopédie.3 The following year, he started a relationship with Thérèse Levasseur, a laundry-maid, with whom he had five children, all of whom were left at the foundling hospital shortly after birth, almost certainly to perish there.

Rousseau was now approaching middle age, with no substantial intellectual achievements to his name, a minor figure in the salons of fashionable Paris. Yet in 1749 Rousseau had an experience which, he claimed, transformed his life and outlook and certainly set him on a path to both fame and notoriety. Walking to the Château de Vincennes, where Diderot had been temporarily imprisoned for testing the limits of religious tolerance, Rousseau read in the Mercure de France newspaper of an essay competition set by the Academy of Dijon. The Academy invited submissions on the theme of whether the development of the arts and sciences had improved or corrupted public morals. Rousseau subsequently related that he had had some kind of epiphany on reading this question and had, in his dreamlike state, come to the realization that the human race is naturally good but is corrupted by society. He would often insist that it was this (somewhat elusive) thesis of natural goodness which gives unity to his works. He employed the idea to argue, in what was to become his Discourse on the Sciences and Arts, that the human race had indeed been morally corrupted by cultural and scientific ‘progress’. This both won Rousseau the prize and, perhaps more importantly, provoked a series of replies from figures including the exiled King of Poland. His future celebrity was assured.

After concentrating on musical issues for much of the early 1750s, Rousseau returned to social theory in a major way with the publication of his Discourse on the Origins of Inequality among Men in 1755. This work, conventionally known as the Second Discourse, was again written in response to a competition call by the Academy of Dijon. Rousseau did not win the prize a second time, but he did produce a much more mature work and it represents the first really systematic exposition of his ideas on human social evolution, moral psychology and philosophical anthropology. It also contains a long dedicatory essay full of praise for the city of Geneva, of which he had reclaimed his citizenship after formally reconverting to Calvinism in 1754. The political status of this dedication is a matter of controversy: is it sincere or is its praise for the idea of Geneva’s institutions an implicit critique of the working of its actual ones?

The Second Discourse marks a deepening of Rousseau’s intellectual and personal estrangement from the mainstream of the French Enlightenment, a process that would be completed in 1758 with the appearance of his Letter to d’Alembert on the Theatre, in which he opposed the Encyclopaedist’s proposal for the construction of a theatre in Geneva on the grounds that theatre is corrosive of the morals necessary for virtuous republican citizenship. This split with his erstwhile intellectual milieu began the most productive period of Rousseau’s life. Julie, or the New Héloïse appeared in 1761 and was an immediate literary sensation, followed in 1762 by both Emile and Of the Social Contract. Intellectual triumph was, however, accompanied by both personal and political catastrophe. Both of the latter two works contain passages of religious heterodoxy equally shocking to Parisian Catholics and Genevan Calvinists. As a consequence, Rousseau was obliged to flee, initially to Switzerland and then, in 1766, to England at the invitation of David Hume.

Rousseau’s stay in England has been the subject of much commentary. Rousseau developed paranoid fantasies about Hume, whom he erroneously believed to be implicated in a plot against him. It was certainly an unhappy time for the Genevan, though not unremittingly so. He spent much of it at Richard Davenport’s estate in Weaver Hills in Staffordshire, where he worked on the Confessions in a hermit’s grotto beside the house and botanized in the surrounding countryside. After fourteen months in Staffordshire, gripped by anxiety and paranoia, Rousseau fled again, to Lincolnshire and thence back to France, where he was still, technically, vulnerable to arrest.

Rousseau remained in France for the rest of his life, a somewhat isolated figure. Not that this period was without achievement: Rousseau completed some political works, notably his writings on Corsica and on Poland, but also made progress on his autobiographical writings. He completed the Confessions and the Dialogues, which – in a fit of derangement – he attempted to place on the altar at Notre Dame. His final and perhaps most beautiful work, the elegiac Reveries of the Solitary Walker, foretells his death and expresses his paranoid concern that his now all-pervasive enemies will attempt to publish forgeries in his name. Rousseau died in 1778 but his work grew in influence and, indeed, acquired cult status during the French Revolution. In 1794, the revolutionaries transferred his remains to the Panthéon.

MORAL PSYCHOLOGY AND HISTORY

One of the difficulties that any reader coming fresh to the text of the Social Contract or to some of the related writings is likely to have is that the argument there presupposes a wider one, which Rousseau only hints at. When he tells us, in the briefest possible terms, that mankind was born free but is still in chains, or that he assumes that men are forced to associate because they can no longer subsist from their individual forces alone, he is assuming, but not stating, an account of human psychology and history that he provides only in other places. The conjectural history that he gestures towards is sketched most fully in the Discourse on Inequality, though elements are also to be found in such places as the Essay on the Origin of Languages (unpublished in his lifetime). The moral psychology is given extensive treatment in both the Second Discourse and in Emile (especially in Book IV). In the first, draft, version of Of the Social Contract, known as the Geneva Manuscript, Rousseau makes more of an effort to provide this essential background, through a chapter which engages with an argument that Diderot had put in his article on ‘Natural Right’ for the Encyclopédie. That draft chapter, ‘On the General Society of the Human Race’, is translated as part of the present volume.

While the account Rousseau gives of his moral psychology varies somewhat from text to text in detail and in emphasis, the basic picture is reasonably clear. He posits two basic psychological propensities as innate: one is a disposition to care for one’s self; the other is an instinct to feel compassion (pitié) for another suffering person. The first of these, which Rousseau calls amour de soi, directs individuals to seek the nourishment and shelter necessary for survival and to flee from danger; the second moves a person to attend to another’s needs and to relieve their distress, provided that doing so is compatible with the reasonably safe pursuit of the first person’s basic interests. The original humans, he believes, were not naturally sociable creatures at all, but wandered alone through primeval forests, sometimes encountering one another to reproduce, but essentially pursuing their limited goals with the powers and capacities that they had as natural creatures. Crucially, for Rousseau, these powers were in balance with their needs so that they did not depend on the cooperation of others in order to provide for themselves.

A long period of development follows, during which human nature is gradually transformed. As human populations grow, encounters between individuals become more and more frequent, and elementary forms of cooperation in activities like hunting start to develop. Eventually, people start to live in small communities. At around this time an important change in human psychology occurs. Sex ceases to be a matter of what people get up to instinctually with members of the opposite sex whom they encounter at random in the forest, and starts to be a matter of people deliberately choosing their mates from an array of potentially suitable candidates. Crucially, they themselves also become objects of possible choice for others and become aware of themselves as such. In such an environment people start to see and imagine themselves as others see them, and to compare themselves with their possible sexual rivals. This new awareness brings with it the advent of jealousy and the crime of passion, as well as of pride in being attractive and of shame and self-loathing at not being desirable. Thus emerges a sense of self as a social being among others and having an existence for others.

Rousseau calls the new psychological drive that arises amour propre. Rousseau’s texts are not altogether consistent about whether this is a third psychological force alongside pitié and amour de soi or whether it is a transformation of amour de soi corresponding to the new socially aware state of the person. It does not matter much for our purposes here. What amour propre introduces is a disposition to care about one’s relative position, one’s ranking in a social group and the esteem in which one is held by others. Whereas the original amour de soi focused on whether certain absolute needs of the person had been achieved – am I warm, fed, rested, etc.? – amour propre always has this relative and comparative feature.

In the Discourse on Inequality, even a fairly attentive reader could be forgiven for taking the impression that Rousseau thinks of amour propre as something wholly destructive and negative. And indeed many readers of Rousseau have come away from his writings with this idea: that amour propre is something bad to be repressed. Yet his view is more complex than this would suggest. While Rousseau sees amour propre as being the source of much evil and unhappiness, he also believes that it generates a transformation in the human psyche that makes possible the development of morality, reason and justice. This is one reason why he thinks of the primitive societies in which amour propre first emerges as being the happiest era of human existence: in such societies, individuals have achieved a certain level of self-awareness and rationality such that they have overcome the purely instinctual stupidity of their wood-wandering ancestors, without yet suffering too much of the corrosive social pathologies that amour propre will generate among their descendants. Those social pathologies, Rousseau believes, pervade the modern world and are the primary source of social conflict and personal unhappiness.

In the Second Discourse, Rousseau imagines a dialectic developing, according to which human psychological and material needs constantly expand, making people increasingly dependent on one another yet also putting them mutually at odds. New technologies in metallurgy and agriculture increase the output of goods and the size and density of human populations, but they also require the cooperation of individuals in a division of labour. These technologies also explain the development of property, as people who have invested in agriculture seek to protect their crops by excluding others from what was once common to them all. As people require the help of others to get what they want, they also start to do what is necessary in order to secure that help. They flatter others and deceive them about their real beliefs and intentions, in order to get those others to behave as they wish. Looking at themselves as if through the eyes of others, they also start to change themselves in order to become desirable. Yet no one can find true satisfaction, since everybody knows that this misrepresentation is what people must do to secure their aims. As serial deceivers themselves they are all too bitterly aware that others are showing them the face that it is advantageous for them to see.

Increasingly complex and hierarchical societies are thus pervaded by insincerity and inauthenticity. Each person seeks the satisfaction of their amour propre, to know that they are loved, preferred or respected. But they also know that others have a self-serving motive to pretend to love and respect them. Bosses seek to exact respect from their subordinates and threaten dire consequences if it is not forthcoming, but they also know that their underlings – who may titter and gossip about them in private – say what they say because they must. Amour propre remains frustrated: it even becomes enraged as people react bitterly to perceived signs of disrespect and revenge themselves on those who treat them with contempt.

Much of this dismal picture is familiar from Thomas Hobbes’s state of nature in Leviathan (1651),4 a condition where people are driven to conflict not only by competition for scarce resources, but also out of desire to dominate others or outrage at being treated with less respect than they believe they deserve. Rousseau’s quarrel with Hobbes was that Hobbes believed that these sources of conflict were basic and original features of human nature, whereas Rousseau saw them as being the result of a long period of social development that had transformed human beings into creatures who could not live together in peace but equally could not live apart. Although the human race does not begin as a bunch of angry Hobbesians, that is pretty much where it ends up, and Rousseau concludes the Second Discourse with a collective escape from the state of nature into a political order.

The ‘social contract’ that Rousseau imagines at the end of that work consists of individuals making a choice to abjure conflict and to subject themselves to the rule of law. Property rights, hitherto uncertain, are to be respected and guaranteed by the state. Faced with a choice between this law-governed regime and continual insecurity and fear of violent death, even those who possess little or nothing agree to the new order. Rousseau thinks this is a mistake on their part, though an understandable one in the circumstances. For now the inequalities that have grown up in society receive official and collective sanction: the power of the rich over the poor is assured. People have gained security, but they have gained it at the price of being permanently dependent on their wealthy masters. But even those masters, who seem to have come out on top, have gained an unsatisfactory victory. For the social position of this elite depends on opinion and reputation, on a fragile, interlocking system of beliefs and expectations.

Rousseau is consistently pessimistic about our chances of extricating ourselves from this prison-house of mutual dependence and opinion. The drive to satisfy our amour propre in conditions of inequality and dependence draws us into a looking-glass world of inauthenticity, where we lose sight of the very selves we are trying to care for as we make ourselves into the persons that we hope and imagine others will value. Sometimes this pessimism drives him to despair (as at the outset of the Reveries of the Solitary Walker, where he contemplates withdrawal and isolation). But when Rousseau is non-despairing he proposes two solutions to this problem of social co-existence. The first, to be found in Emile, argues for the possibility of managing the development of the passions in such a way that amour propre does not take the corrosive form it has for most people, and of satisfying the individual’s craving for recognition and respect through a satisfactory and reciprocal love-relationship with a member of the opposite sex. The second, expressed in the political writings, including Of the Social Contract, involves securing for each individual the status of a free and equal citizen, subject to laws which he himself has chosen rather than living at the behest of some supposed superior.

THE POLITICAL PHILOSOPHY OF OF THE SOCIAL CONTRACT

Rousseau’s central aim in Of the Social Contract is to explain how the freedom of the individual can be reconciled with the authority of the state. Because of the process of social evolution sketched in other writings, but particularly in the Second Discourse, it is essential for human beings to associate together in order to fulfil their psychological and material needs. But this association carries with it the risk, indeed the probability, that our freedom will be extinguished and that we shall be subjected to the arbitrary will and opinions of others. Since, Rousseau believes, freedom is essential to our nature and is a condition of our having moral responsibility, it is vital to find a way of combining freedom and authority, but, at the same time, it is not at all clear how this can be done. States claim to act with authority: that their laws are commands that their subjects have an obligation to obey. How can a person be free and at the same time obliged to obey such instructions?

The General Will

The concept with which Rousseau carries out this attempted reconciliation is the general will. Rousseau argues that citizens who live in a state governed by the general will obey only themselves: freedom and obedience to law are thereby combined. Unfortunately, the concept of the general will as Rousseau deploys it is often unclear and ambiguous and he seems to operate with two contrasting and incompatible interpretations of it. This unclarity is the basis for many of the difficulties and subsequent controversies surrounding Rousseau’s ideas and their relationship to individual freedom and democracy. In one interpretation of the general will, it is simply what a people, voting as a body of sovereign legislators in their assembly, decides the law to be. The general will is thus the expression of popular sovereignty, of collective democratic choice. Yet at other times Rousseau seems committed to a different view according to which the general will corresponds to a fact of the matter concerning where the common interest lies, a fact of the matter that holds true quite independently of what the citizens actually believe or decide.5 This latter sense of the general will has featured prominently in attempts to suggest that Rousseau was in some sense responsible for later claims by dictatorial elites to speak in the name of the people; but Rousseau is consistently clear in the Social Contract that, though the people may make mistakes, they must legislate for themselves if the state is to be legitimate.

Although the two conceptions of the general will to be found in the Social Contract are in tension with one another, there are ways to reduce this tension. One possibility is to interpret Rousseau as thinking that there is a fact of the matter about where the common good lies and that, so long as the people legislate together under the right conditions, they can be more or less sure to decide on laws that align with and promote that common good. For Rousseau, it is crucial that the laws come from all citizens and apply to all citizens so that each person is simultaneously a maker of the law and subject to it. If this is so, he believes, voters will naturally be drawn to legislation that promotes their common interest at the same time as not being too demanding of them as individuals. For each person will be guided both by a sense that certain reciprocal restrictions on freedom are necessary for them to live together in a society and by a desire not to impose on themselves restrictions that go beyond what is necessary. This process of self-legislation has both a formal and a material aspect to it. One way of getting the citizens to go beyond a narrow selfish standpoint and to look on the law from a public and objective standpoint is built into the very notion of the law itself, since it applies indifferently to all citizens. So when a citizen wills that a proposition be incorporated into the law, he wills something that applies to himself as well as to everyone else. But Rousseau also sees that this objective aspect to the law is only actually even-handed in its effects on people where their material circumstances are roughly similar. As Anatole France is supposed to have remarked, the law forbids the rich and the poor alike from sleeping under bridges. A society that is already divided into extremes of wealth and poverty will not therefore be one in which the collective decisions of the citizenry reliably track the common good; indeed, there may not be much of common interest to track. Similarly, a society that is too large or diverse in morals and customs is likely to be one where the citizens have difficulty in discerning where the common good lies, if, indeed, there is a sufficient overlap in their interests.

Culture and the Legislator

To these formal and material factors, Rousseau sometimes adds a third, more subjective, one. Even citizens who are materially and culturally similar to one another and are choosing rules that apply to everyone will not reliably will the common good unless they have the right kind of psychology. The trick of looking upon oneself as a subject of the laws and thinking in terms of enlightened self-interest will not come naturally to a person who is excessively passionate, angry and has a short time horizon. Unfortunately, there is every danger that the individuals who initially form a society will lack the social perspective and public-spiritedness that are required of good citizens. These virtuous habits of mind in individuals come from long exposure to the laws and practices of a just society. Yet the initial founders of a society will have been pressed into their association under very different circumstances: almost certainly the quasi-Hobbesian nightmare depicted at the end of the Second Discourse, in which most people are aggressively concerned for their own relative status and seek to extract ‘respect’ from their peers. To survive together they need to be virtuous citizens who calmly discuss their common interests; in actuality they are jealous, resentful, proud, vain and quick to draw their swords.

Rousseau sees this problem and articulates a solution to it, but it is not one likely to convince his readers. Rousseau’s bridge between the violent anarchy of the pre-political stage and the stable consensus of the virtuous republic consists of a quasi-mythical individual: the legislator or lawgiver. The legislator is one of a group of similar characters in Rousseau’s writings whose task is to manipulate their subjects into a condition where they can take charge of their own lives (or, on a more sinister reading, acquire the illusion of being in charge of themselves). In Emile, the tutor has this role, leading his pupil through a series of stages until he is able to live as a free adult. In his novel Julie, the officially benign éminence grise is Wolmar, master of the Clarens estate. In all these cases, the same problems arise. If people are shaped by circumstances – as Rousseau makes clear he believes – and if the pre-political circumstances are intensely competitive and morally corrosive, then how does the legislator or the tutor acquire the skills and sensibility necessary for his job? Where could such a person come from? Rousseau has no satisfactory answer. The best that he can do is to point to a few historical examples of people who have inspired the laws of new societies: people like the Spartan Lycurgus and the Athenian Solon.6

Rousseau envisages the legislator as a kind of transitional fix. Good laws make for good citizens, but the first citizens are not yet virtuous enough or rational enough to will good laws on their own, nor are they yet in a condition to listen to rational arguments in favour of such laws. The legislator therefore has to use other methods to get them to vote the right way: he must ‘persuade without convincing’. He must employ non-rational means, including his own charismatic authority, to ensure that the citizens institute the laws that are in their long-term collective self-interest. Clearly this is unsatisfactory. If the laws are to be an expression of the citizens’ individual and collective freedom, a genuine reconciliation of freedom and authority, then the citizens ought to be choosing them with clear heads and undistorted vision. To read that they have to be inspired to support the laws by an implausible cult-leader figure leaves a sense that we are getting less than was originally advertised.

There are, however, things to be said in Rousseau’s defence. It may seem odd to claim Rousseau’s invocation of such an implausible figure as an instance of his ‘realism’, but, both in Of the Social Contract and in other places (particularly Considerations on the Government of Poland) Rousseau shows an openness to the idea that, if citizens are to live together in freedom and equality, we may need to foster among them feelings of patriotism and solidarity that have an emotive and not a rational basis. The lawgiver promotes such sentiments of identification not by argument but by practices such as children’s games and the use of music and dance. The creation of ‘we, the people’ cannot just be a matter of rational argument and cool calculation, but also depends on the immersion of the self in the collective.

Freedom

Rousseau’s claim that, in a state governed by the general will, freedom and authority are reconciled has encountered a great deal of scepticism over the years. But in order to evaluate it, we need a clear sense of what he means by freedom. It is no easy matter to work this out, especially since he fails to make explicit the most important understanding he has of the concept within the text of the Social Contract. When Rousseau introduces the task of the book, at I.6, he tells us that the new association will leave the citizens as free as they were before they entered it. However, this seems to be at best misleading, since he makes it clear that the sense in which the pre-political contractors were free (natural freedom) is quite different from any way in which the citizens of the new state are free. Indeed, that natural freedom, in which people’s capacity to act is limited only by their native abilities to get what they want, is permanently lost once they join together. What they get instead is civil freedom and the right to what they possess, a right specified and limited by the general will (I.8). Additionally, they get moral freedom, obedience to a law that they have prescribed to themselves. However, Rousseau frustratingly skates past the latter, telling us that it is not his subject.

The reader worried about the claim that authority and freedom have been reconciled is not going to be satisfied with the statement that the citizens have a new sort of freedom that is limited by the general will, because it is precisely the limitation of freedom by the general will that is likely to seem problematic to them. Similarly, the idea that citizens end up being morally free because they get to obey the laws that they have chosen for themselves invites the obvious objection that citizens who are out-voted in the assembly are subject to laws that other people have chosen. The sceptical reader is also unlikely to be persuaded that Rousseau has effected his reconciliation when he or she comes across the famous lines at I.7 where he tells us that the citizen constrained to obey the general will is thereby ‘forced to be free’.

That notorious passage, though, contains the crucial clue to Rousseau’s ideas, for there he says that submission to the general will frees individuals from personal dependence. The idea of freedom as a guarantee of non-subjection to the arbitrary will of another person is central to the classical republican tradition of which Rousseau is an inheritor. Rousseau does not make his allegiance to this idea explicit in Of the Social Contract’ but in other texts, most notably the eighth of the Letters Written from the Mountains, he is more forthcoming. There he tells us that liberty, ‘consists less in acting upon your wish than in not being subjected to the wish of others; it further consists in not subjecting the wish of others to our own’ (p. 185). Recall the final stages of the pre-political condition that Rousseau depicts in the Second Discourse. In that phase, individuals have become dependent on one another both materially and in terms of opinion. They can satisfy neither their physical needs nor their craving for respect and recognition without subjecting or enticing others to do their bidding. The rule of a law willed by all the citizenry and limiting their freedom only to the extent necessary for them to co-exist with others is Rousseau’s political alternative to this state of dependence, dominance and subjection. Individuals remain interdependent through the division of labour. That is unavoidable given the growth in their needs engendered in the process of historical development and technological change. But this interdependence is organized around fair terms of association that are the product of all the citizens choosing together in their assembly. Citizens are free because they are not at the beck and call of this or that rich or powerful person, but rather because they enjoy an equality of status7 and are subject only to constraints that they have chosen themselves.

What then of the other problem for Rousseau’s claim to have reconciled freedom and authority: that citizens who are in the minority cannot be said to be subject to a law that they have chosen for themselves? Rousseau would probably have conceded that if there are permanent majorities and minorities, rather than some people happening to be out-voted some of the time, then there is a real problem. But this is because a society with such entrenched factions cannot be said to have a genuinely general will at all. Part of his discussion in Book II of the Social Contract focuses on just this issue. Where the politics of a society is dominated by a faction – be it based on wealth, ethnicity or religion – then what happens is that the general will of that group, which is but a sectional interest of society as a whole, gets imposed as the choice of the entire people. In such a society there is no freedom, as some citizens are always subject to the alien choices of others. In the non-pathological case, where it is simply a matter of disagreement and the choices of others carry the day, Rousseau says something different. He tells us that the choice of the majority simply shows that the minority voter was wrong about where the general will lay, but, since that voter wants the general will, he is still subject to a law that he wills (IV.2). This will probably strike some readers as the worst kind of casuistry and evasion, but there are things that can be said in defence of the idea. The laws deal with the basic terms according to which citizens live together. We might think of legislation as involving two stages. In the first, since we want to live on fair terms with our neighbours, we are resolved on choosing from a range of possible conventions to solve practical problems. Shall we drive on the left or the right? Shall we strike a balance between individual freedom and social cohesion at this point or another? The legislative process then involves a choice from among these possibilities, where we are committed to the idea that some choice is better than none. The legislative process doesn’t just pick in an arbitrary way from among the possibilities, it also reflects the judgement of individuals about which option would be the best. Assuming a good level of competence among citizens, and assuming also that there is a fact of the matter about which option is best (or at least better than other options presented), there is good reason to believe that the assembly will converge on the optimal solution.

Government, Sovereign and Democracy

In the first two books of the Social Contract, Rousseau is principally concerned with the ideas of sovereignty, law and the general will. The sovereign people, in choosing the laws that define their terms of association, exercise their general will and govern themselves. Laws, however, by their very nature are general and abstract: they may specify that certain institutions are to exist, that if one thing occurs another thing should then happen, that all citizens have certain rights, and so on. The general form of the law is important for Rousseau because of its connection to the moral rectitude of the citizens. The law comes from all and applies to all, and each citizen, similarly situated to his fellows, is drawn to favour just principles which maximize freedom and guarantee equal status, because to do otherwise would be contrary to his own interest. However, the law neither interprets nor applies itself. To mention H. L. A. Hart’s famous example, the law may say that all vehicles are banned from the park, but it cannot specify in advance all the possible cases that might fall under its general principle.8 Particular cases need judgement: assuming that the law has been silent on the matter, someone needs to decide whether or not a child’s tricycle is a ‘vehicle’ for the purposes of the law. The law may specify that there should be a particular office or role in the state, perhaps with a title and remuneration; but, confined as it is to generalities, it cannot appoint a particular person to that role. And the law may give people title to their property, but it cannot decide particular property disputes, award compensation or punish thieves. For all these reasons (and many more besides) a society needs to apply general principles in particular cases. For Rousseau, this is the task of government or administration, a body that combines executive and judicial functions. The relationship between the government and the sovereign is both central to Rousseau’s political philosophy and the source of multiple difficulties in its interpretation.

Perhaps the first issue to be faced is that of who should fulfil this role of deciding in particular cases. Since people often come to Rousseau with an idea of him as some kind of participatory democrat, a view bolstered by some of his writings on sovereignty, they are perhaps naturally inclined to expect that he should be a democrat about government too, and it can come as a shock to discover that he is not. In fact, his thought is somewhat complex and nuanced, and sometimes his commitments look to be in tension with one another or even inconsistent. Rousseau rejects democracy as a form of government because he thinks it requires impossible levels of virtue in the citizenry. Legislating gives the individuals a more generalized and abstract perspective, seeing themselves as one among many; government, with its focus on the particular, has exactly opposite cognitive effects. Instead of thinking dispassionately about the rules and penalties that ought to apply to types of action, citizens, perhaps inflamed by the immediate facts, will be focused on how a particular decision applies to them. It is similar to the distinction between a sport where the players decide collectively on the rules but play subject to the authority of a referee and one where they referee each game as well. A consensus among footballers that players should not make dangerous challenges is easy to achieve; agreement among the players on the pitch that this challenge is dangerous is unlikely to be forthcoming. Referees will nearly always do a better job.

In Of the Social Contract Rousseau therefore favours government by a small group, an elective aristocracy. His account of the relationship between that group and the citizenry pulls in two directions. He spends much of Book III of the Social Contract discussing the threat that the magistrates pose to popular sovereignty. This threat arises from the nature of the problem they, and the wider society, face. In a small, equal and homogeneous society the laws will be few and simple, they will be widely understood and adhered to, and the conduct of citizens will be regulated as much by their shared sense of civic belonging as by any explicit regulations. In such a society, quite a large and loose collection of magistrates can share responsibility for the small amount of government that needs to be done. But as societies grow larger – Rousseau thought of population growth as the inevitable outcome of political success – and society becomes more diverse in its habits and ways of life, there may be more inequality, people know fewer and fewer of their fellow citizens and the polity becomes a distant abstraction. In larger and more anonymous societies, there will be more need for the magistrates to intervene, simply in order to remedy the fact that social order is no longer spontaneous. A large group of magistrates will be ineffective for this purpose because large committees are bad at deciding and acting. A small group takes charge of the machinery of the state, but also starts to think of itself as embodying the state. Eventually, thinks Rousseau, the magistrates will substitute their collective will for the general will of the citizenry, and inevitably the state will be brought to ruin.

Given that Rousseau sees this seizure of the proper rights of the sovereign by the magistrates as a mortal threat to the political order, it is surprising that he sometimes seems to favour the empowering of the magistrates at the expense of the citizens. In the Letters Written from the Mountains, for example, whilst deploring the long-term tendency of the government to undermine popular sovereignty, he stops short of permitting the citizens to have the positive rights to initiate new legislation. In Of the Social Contract he insists that no one can deprive citizens of the right to vote on legislation but nevertheless declares that ‘the Government always takes great care to confine to its own members [the right of voicing an opinion, proposing, dividing, and debating]’ (IV.1). Some critics have read these passages as expressing an elitist and undemocratic view and as sanctioning the domination of the supposedly sovereign people by the government. Others, however, read them as being in tension with the democratic spirit of the rest of the work and point out the somewhat ambiguous tone of the Social Contract passage, which is neither clearly normative nor descriptive.

The picture of the relationship between legislating people and government is also muddied by what he has to say about the idea of representation. Many modern readers of the Social Contract are almost instantly put off by his apparent rejection of representative government in III.15. However, he has often been misunderstood on just this point. Rousseau’s objection is to the representation of sovereignty. In Of the Social Contract, at least, he rejects the idea that the people, in deciding the laws that define their fundamental association, could hand over that task to representatives or deputies. If they were to do so, to hand over a general mandate to other people to decide such terms of association for them, they would be subject to laws that they had not themselves decided upon; they would, in his view, have enslaved themselves. But Rousseau’s conception of government, ideally run by an elective aristocracy, is very much a representative one. The distance between a Rousseauvian republic and a modern parliamentary democracy depends in part, then, on how we conceive of the divide between the laws and the decrees of the government. If, as often seems to be the case, the laws are very few in number and simple in nature (IV.1), then the legislative task of the people is really quite simple and requires little activity on their part: perhaps the occasional meeting to ratify some basic constitutional provision or other, whilst the elected government issues the day-to-day regulations. At other moments, though, Rousseau seems to have an altogether busier conception of citizenship (III.15), approximating the direct democracy of the ancient world. Even if we take the former view, however, it looks hard to reconcile universal participation in legislation with anything like the size of modern states.

Civil Religion

One of the oddities about reading Of the Social Contract more than two centuries after its composition is the profound disconnection between the way in which contemporary readers received the work and the manner in which it is often seen today. One section of the Social Contract that brings this out is the final proper chapter of the book, dealing with civil religion. At the time – and this was an important reason for its condemnation – the religiously orthodox objected to Rousseau’s Machiavelli-derived thought that true Christians make bad citizens and soldiers, that they would fight ineffectively for the republic because their loyalty is to an other-worldly power rather than to the state and the patrie. Today, it is the whiff of an official ideology that people find repellent, together with the suggestion that atheists have no place in the good society and that the death penalty might be appropriate for people who disbelievingly affirm their commitment to a supreme being but then conduct themselves as if they do not.

Rousseau’s own religious views were unorthodox, but this chapter is not where he affirms them. What it is about, rather, is toleration. The modern liberal political philosopher John Rawls has advanced the idea of an ‘overlapping consensus’ of what he calls ‘reasonable comprehensive doctrines’: the idea being that a liberal political order can be supported by people who converge on a set of basic principles and does not require more thoroughgoing agreement about philosophical and theological matters. Rousseau’s civil religion is, essentially, a similar idea. Though the exclusion of atheists is doubtless regrettable, Rousseau is promoting the idea that a stable and flourishing political society does not require religious uniformity and that Catholics, Protestants, Jews and others can co-exist and cooperate as citizens of equal standing. Their common affirmation of belief in the dogmas of civil religion helps to cement mutual trust among them; the limited nature of those dogmas that they can all assert from their separate doctrinal standpoints pushes sectarian disagreements out of the sphere of political power. Far from being evidence of an incipient totalitarianism on Rousseau’s part, this chapter, at least, reflects Rousseau’s concern to reconcile religious pluralism with the social unity necessary for any functioning political order.

BEYOND OF THE SOCIAL CONTRACT

The texts included in this volume provide evidence of another Rousseau besides the utopian dreamer of caricature. The now-reconstructed text of Principles of the Right of War shows us a savage and incisive critic of the received wisdoms of statists and international politicians everywhere. The state gets its supposed justification from the fact that it brings us peace and security, and its power and wealth call forth an array of philosophical and legal apologists for its actions, but in the international arena it turns out to be a formidable instrument of killing and oppression, often in the very name of high-sounding principles. It is hard to read Principles of the Right of War today without thinking both of the official rhetoric and legalese of interventions in Iraq, Afghanistan and elsewhere and the bloody reality of those conflicts. Rousseau’s text is a subversive reminder of the way in which we can use legal and moral reasoning as the self-deceiving cover for self-interest, hiding behind abstractions and concepts whilst the corpses pile higher.

The Letters Written from the Mountains, Constitutional Proposal for Corsica and Considerations on the Government of Poland show Rousseau’s connectedness to the real-world politics of his day and his willingness to revise and compromise his most abstract principles in the face of a concrete political problem. They also shed light back on Of the Social Contract, providing new materials on which to base our assessment of his political thought and perhaps rendering even more difficult any easy attempt to fit Rousseau into any simple ideological category. Partisans of a thoroughly democratic and participatory Rousseau will be given both encouragement and pause by the Letters Written from the Mountains. Rousseau’s incisive analysis of the ways in which governments work to steal sovereignty from the people is balanced by his refusal to give Geneva’s bourgeois faction everything they wanted in terms of the right to initiate legislation. And then there is the great lacuna of all his writings on Geneva, the refusal of the great advocate of the people’s sovereignty to speak about who gets included in ‘the people’: for Geneva’s citizenry were but a small fraction of the populace, many of whom included resident ‘foreigners’ of many generations’ standing, subject to the laws but with no part in the making of them.

The Constitutional Proposal for Corsica provides evidence of Rousseau’s economic egalitarianism, of his commitment to self-sufficiency and community, and of his view that independent self-government is incompatible with luxury. Modern readers are likely to see it either as a sign of the distance between Rousseau’s concerns and ours – of economic illiteracy and rejection of a global division of labour – or as the prescient image of some green future of zero-growth community. Considerations on the Government of Poland is valuable for two main reasons. First, it substantially complements the political sociology of the Social Contract, with its emphasis on mœurs, on culture and on nation-building, showing us that these are not minor concerns that we can separate out from Rousseau’s more formal treatments of will, law and legitimacy. Second, we see Rousseau taking a more permissive view of the representation of sovereignty than he had in Of the Social Contract. Poland was a large and diverse country, so he was open both to federalism and to the idea of people electing limited-term representatives subject to a system of public examination at the end of their service.

IMPACT AND INFLUENCE

Much of the twentieth century’s commentary on Rousseau, particularly from a liberal perspective, has sought to portray him as the source of totalitarianisms of various kinds, be they Jacobin, communist or fascist. There are various reasons behind thoughts of this kind, perhaps the most common ones being the claims of various self-proclaimed vanguards and elites from Robespierre to Lenin to incarnate the will of the people (or the proletariat) independently of the people’s actual choices; the somewhat sinister and non-rational aspects of Rousseau’s discussion of the legislator; worries about Rousseau’s conception of freedom (exacerbated by Isaiah Berlin’s famous distinction between positive and negative liberty);9 and Rousseau’s rejection of the idea that individuals have inalienable natural rights against the state.

So ingrained are some of these perceptions of Rousseau that they are likely to distort our view of him for some time to come. But all of them either are based on tendentious readings of what he has to say or turn out to be doctrines shared with thinkers whose liberal bona fides remain beyond question. The claim of vanguard elites to represent the general will, for example, may derive some support from Rousseau’s occasional remarks that there is a fact of the matter about the general will that holds even when the people prove incapable of perceiving it, but it founders on Rousseau’s repeated and consistent affirmation in Of the Social Contract that will, and especially the general will, cannot be represented: the people must speak for themselves. Rousseau’s rejection of the Lockean idea that people have natural rights against the state and its law and his assertion of the primacy of the general will over individuals may be positions that people can reasonably disagree upon, but it is essentially one shared by Kant in his affirmation that there are no conclusive rights to property in the state of nature and that the sovereign’s word is final in case of disputes about individual rights. Rousseau’s influence on Kant was profound and emerges in a number of places, including Kant’s formulations of the categorical imperative. But one way in which Rousseau’s political philosophy, as transmitted through Kant, is still with us is in the ideas of John Rawls and his liberal conception of a well-ordered society. Though Rawls does not share Rousseau’s ideal of an active, legislating citizenry, the idea of the general will is alive in the idea that principles of justice are those that would be chosen in circumstances of equality where citizens put aside their individual aims and try to adopt an impartial perspective.10

Some developments do, though, cast doubt on the continued relevance of Rousseau’s thinking. In Book I, Chapter 6 of the Social Contract, Rousseau argues for the necessity of quitting the state of nature at a certain point of human development, claiming that the human race would perish if it did not change its way of being. He suggests there is a fork between mutually destructive conflict among individuals inflamed by their amour propre and the creation of political and social institutions that reconcile freedom and authority. More than two centuries later, the interdependence that Rousseau worried about and which necessitated that association has become global, as have the environmental threats to the human race. The task of finding forms of association on a global scale that will defend and protect human beings at the same time as preserving their liberty is an altogether more daunting one.

NOTES

1.    ‘the cult of the self’: Le Nouvel Observateur, hors-série no. 7 (2010).

2.    to some pre-social Eden: The classic rebuttal is Arthur O. Lovejoy, ‘The Supposed Primitivism of Rousseau’s “Discourse on Inequality” ’, Modern Philology 21:2 (1923), pp. 165–86.

3.    for the Encyclopédie: Edited and directed by Denis Diderot (1713–84) and Jean le Rond d’Alembert (1717–83), the Encyclopédie was the major unifying intellectual project of the French Enlightenment, its first volume appearing in 1751.

4.    Leviathan: The influence of Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679) is pervasive throughout Rousseau’s political writings, though Rousseau often chooses to emphasize his disagreements with Hobbes.

5.    what the citizens actually believe or decide: The classic passage in which Rousseau discusses a possible divergence between the general will and what the people decide is Of the Social Contract II.3. His language there suggests a distinction between the sum of the selfish wills of individuals, ‘the will of all’, and the general will. However, readers should note that the phrase ‘the will of all’ does not consistently carry this connotation.

6.    The Spartan Lycurgus and the Athenian Solon: Lycurgus (800?–730? BC) was the legendary lawgiver of Sparta, supposedly inspired to give Spartan society its militarist and communalistic cast by the Oracle at Delphi. Solon (c.638–558 BC) was an Athenian statesman and lawgiver, often credited with laying the foundations of Athenian democracy.

7.    equality of status: Would this equality of status serve to satisfy the amour propre that has emerged in modern people? For a nuanced but sceptical view, see Frederick Neuhouser, Rousseau’s Theodicy of Self-Love (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2008), ch. 5.

8.    its general principle: See H. L. A. Hart, The Concept of Law (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1961), pp. 123–6.

9.    positive and negative liberty: See his ‘Two Concepts of Liberty’ in his Four Essays on Liberty (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1969).

10.  Though Rawls … an impartial perspective: See John Rawls, A Theory of Justice (Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1971).

Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

Further Reading

The standard French edition of Rousseau is currently the five-volume Oeuvres complètes, under the direction of Bernard Gagnebin and Marcel Raymond (Paris: Pléiade, 1959–95). It is likely to be superseded by a new Oeuvres complètes, published by Garnier under the direction of Jacques Berchtold, François Jacob and Yannick Séité, the first volumes of which will appear from 2011. Our understanding of some of the texts included in the Pléiade edition has been transformed by later scholarship, and this is particularly true of Rousseau’s writings on international affairs, for which Principes du droit de la guerre et Écrits sur la paix perpétuelle, edited by Bruno Bernardi and Gabriella Silvestrini (Paris: Vrin, 2008), should be consulted for now. The definitive edition of Rousseau’s correspondence is the Correspondance complète, ed. R. A. Leigh (Geneva and Oxford: Institut et Musée Voltaire and Voltaire Foundation, 1965–89).

The major biography of Rousseau in French is that by Jean Guéhenno, Jean-Jacques: histoire d’une conscience, 2 vols. (Paris: Gallimard, 1962). In English, the three-volume study by Maurice Cranston is comprehensive: Jean-Jacques: The Early Life and Work of Jean-Jacques Rousseau 1712–1754 (Harmondsworth: Penguin, 1983); The Noble Savage: Jean-Jacques Rousseau 1754–1762 (Harmondsworth: Penguin, 1991); and The Solitary Self: Jean-Jacques Rousseau in Exile and Adversity (Harmondsworth: Allen Lane, 1997). The single-volume study by Leo Damrosch, Jean-Jacques Rousseau: Restless Genius (New York: Houghton Mifflin, 2005), is highly readable and gives a compelling portrait of Rousseau the man. Readers interested in Rousseau’s life should, of course, consult his autobiographical works, starting with the Confessions. Christopher Kelly, Rousseau’s Exemplary Life: The ‘Confessions’ as Political Philosophy (New York: Cornell, 1987), provides a sensitive commentary and interpretation.

As a general introduction to Rousseau’s life, thought and themes, a good place to start is R. A. Wokler’s Rousseau (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1995). Wokler’s collected essays, to be published as Rousseau, the Age of Enlightenment and Their Legacies (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2012) will also be essential reading. Charles W. Hendel’s Jean-Jacques Rousseau: Moralist (New York: Bobbs-Merrill, 1934) is a comprehensive guide. The classic study in French is Jean Starobinski, Jean-Jacques Rousseau: la transparence et l’obstacle, 2nd edn (Paris: Gallimard, 1971), published in somewhat abbreviated form in English as Jean-Jacques Rousseau: Transparency and Obstruction (Chicago: Chicago University Press, 1988). A major impetus to new work on Rousseau in the anglophone world was provided by N. J. H. Dent, Rousseau: An Introduction to His Psychological, Social and Political Theory (Oxford: Blackwell, 1988), which revised the standard negative evaluation of amour propre. Dent’s subsequent Rousseau (London: Routledge, 2005) is also worthy of note and his A Rousseau Dictionary (Oxford: Blackwell, 1992) is a valuable resource. Dent’s contribution to our understanding of Rousseau’s moral psychology has been taken forward by Frederick Neuhouser in his Rousseau’s Theodicy of Self-Love (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2008). Alternatives to this approach are Jean Charvet, The Social Problem in Jean-Jacques Rousseau (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1974) and Marshall Berman, The Politics of Authenticity (New York: Atheneum, 1970). A comprehensive assessment of Rousseau as a philosopher is provided by Timothy O’Hagan, Rousseau (London: Routledge, 1999).

The classic work in English on Rousseau’s political writings is Roger D. Masters, The Political Philosophy of Rousseau (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1968). Other significant studies include Richard Fralin, Rousseau and Representation (New York: Columbia, 1978), which contains useful background to the later political writings and argues for Rousseau being a less democratic thinker than is commonly thought. James Miller, Rousseau: Dreamer of Democracy (New Haven: Yale, 1984) provides the opposite view. Helena Rosenblatt, Rousseau and Geneva (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1997) is a useful study of the specifically Genevan roots of Rousseau’s thinking. Joshua Cohen’s Rousseau: A Free Community of Equals (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2010) is a study of Rousseau by a leading analytical political philosopher. Zev Trachtenberg, Rousseau’s Political Theory of Culture (London: Routledge, 1993) is good on the interactions between institutions and psychology. Commentaries on Of the Social Contract include Christopher Bertram, Rousseau and The Social Contract (London: Routledge, 2004) and the somewhat Straussian view of Hilail Gildin, Rousseau’s Social Contract: The Design of the Argument (Chicago: Chicago University Press, 1973). Two important recent essays on the idea of the general will are Frederick Neuhouser, ‘Freedom, Dependence and the General Will’, Philosophical Review 102:3 (1993); and Gopal Sreenivasan, ‘What Is the General Will’, Philosophical Review 109:4 (2000). The question of Rousseau’s impact on the politics of the French Revolution is considered by James Swenson in his On Jean-Jacques Rousseau: Considered as One of the First Authors of the Revolution (Stanford: Stanford University Press, 2000).

Rousseau’s writings on international relations are the subject of Grace G. Roosevelt’s Reading Rousseau in the Nuclear Age (Philadelphia: Temple, 1990), and his views on war, together with his relations with Corsican and Polish republicanism, are ably covered in Karma Nabulsi’s Traditions of War (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1999).

Feminist writers from Mary Wollstonecraft in her A Vindication of the Rights of Women (1792) onwards have highlighted the contrast between the liberatory potential of Rousseau’s politics and the misogyny of some of his writings. Christopher Kelly and Eve Grace have edited a telling selection of Rousseau’s own writings on this subject, Rousseau on Women, Love and Family (Lebanon, N.H.: University Press of New England, 2009), and the subject is covered by works including Joel Schwartz, The Sexual Politics of Jean-Jacques Rousseau (Chicago: Chicago University Press, 1984); and Nicole Fermon, Domesticating Passions: Rousseau, Woman and Nation (Hanover, N.H.: University Press of New England, 1997).

OF THE SOCIAL CONTRACT

chapters.title: Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings
chapters.text:
Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

Prefatory Note

Rousseau’s fragment on political institutions is entitled Of the Social Contract or Principles of Political Right. Rousseau arrived at this title after a good deal of hesitation. In the manuscript of the draft version, now known as the Geneva Manuscript, Rousseau appears to have substituted Of Civil Society as his preferred choice before reverting to Of the Social Contract. That version also bears a different subtitle, ‘Essay on the Form of the Republic’, which replaces earlier choices including ‘Essay on the Constitution of the State’, ‘Essay on the Formation of the Body Politic’ and ‘Essay on the Formation of the State’. Maybe nothing much depends on these changes of mind, but they do underline the difficulty in classifying Rousseau’s text, which veers between political philosophy, constitutional law and political sociology.

Rousseau seems to have first had the idea to write a treatise on politics as early as 1743, when he was secretary to the French ambassador in Venice; at least, this is what he tells us in Book IX of the Confessions. The idea as originally conceived was broader in scope and, as is clear from the brief final chapter of the Social Contract, included plans to write on international relations and war. Some of that project may have survived in the form of the essay on Principles of the Right of War (included in this volume) and Rousseau’s commentaries on the Project for Perpetual Peace of the abbé de Saint-Pierre.1 The basic ideas for Of the Social Contract start to show in Rousseau’s work from about 1753: the dedication to Geneva of the Discourse on Inequality anticipates some of the ideas and Rousseau’s entry on ‘political economy’ for the Encyclopédie contains the key notion that a legitimate state should be governed according to the general will. Rousseau completed the final version in 1761 and it was finally published in April 1762 by Rousseau’s usual publisher, Marc-Michel Rey in Amsterdam.

The draft version of the Social Contract is reasonably close to the final text, the most important divergence being the inclusion of the chapter on the ‘General Society of Mankind’, which serves as an important bridge between the argument of the Social Contract and Rousseau’s earlier writings in moral psychology and philosophical anthropology such as the Discourse on Inequality. For this reason, we have included a translation of this ‘missing chapter’ in the present volume.

The present translation is based on the text contained in volume 3 of the Pléiade edition of Oeuvres Complètes produced under the direction of Bernard Gagnebin and Marcel Raymond in 1964. Gagnebin and Raymond followed the edition published by Marc-Michel Rey in Amsterdam in 1762. Pierre-Alexandre Du Peyrou, a friend and confidant of Rousseau, published an edition of his works in 1782 in Geneva. On a few occasions we have preferred the 1782 variant and have indicated this in the text.

chapters.title: Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings
chapters.text:
Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

Foreword

This little treatise is extracted from a more extensive work, undertaken years ago with no heed for my strength and long since abandoned. Of the various fragments that might be drawn from what was done, this is the most considerable and has seemed to me least unworthy of being presented to the public. The rest already exists no more.

chapters.title: Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings
chapters.text:
Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

BOOK I

I wish to explore whether in the civil order – taking men as they are1 and laws as they can be – there may be any legitimate and reliable rule of administration.2 In this study, I shall attempt always to ally what is permitted by right to what is prescribed by interest, so that justice and utility may not be divided.

I shall embark upon my theme without first proving the importance of my subject. People will ask if I am a prince or a legislator, to be writing about Politics. I reply that I am not, which is why I am writing about Politics. If I were a prince or legislator, I should not waste my time saying what ought to be done; I should do it, or I should hold my peace.

Since by birth I am a citizen of a free State and a member of its sovereign body, the right to vote on public affairs is enough to impose on me the duty to inform myself about these, however weak an influence upon them my voice may have. Fortunate indeed, whenever I reflect on Governments, always to find in my inquiries new reasons for loving that of my own country!

chapters.title: Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings
chapters.text:
Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

Chapter 1

Subject of This First Book

Man was born free, and everywhere he is in chains.3 A person deems himself the master of others, yet still remains more of a slave than they. How did this change come about? I do not know. What can make it legitimate? I think I can resolve that question.

If I were to consider force alone and the effect deriving from it, I should say: so long as a People is constrained to obey and obeys, it does well; as soon as it can cast off the yoke and casts it off, it does still better; for, in recovering its liberty by the same right whereby it was robbed of it, either it is entitled to seize back that liberty, or no one was entitled to remove it. But social order is a sacred right, serving as the basis for all others. Yet that right by no means comes from nature; hence, it is founded on conventions. The question is to know what those conventions are. Before tackling this, I must establish what I have just proposed.

Chapter 2

Of the First Societies

The oldest of all societies and the only natural one is that of the family. Yet children remain bound to their father only so long as they need him in order to survive. No sooner does this need cease than the natural bond is dissolved. The children released from the obedience they used to owe to their father, the father released from the care he used to owe to his children – all return alike to independence. If they do continue to remain united, this is no longer natural but voluntary, and the family itself is maintained only through convention.4

This common liberty is a consequence of man’s nature. His first law is to attend to his own survival; his first care is owed to himself and, once he reaches the age of reason, as sole judge of the means appropriate for survival he thereby becomes his own master.

So the family is, if you will, the first model for political societies; the ruler is the image of the father, the people is the image of the children, and all – having been born equal and free – alienate their liberty only where this is useful to them. The sole difference is that in the family a father’s love for his children repays him for the care he takes of them, while in the State the pleasure of commanding makes up for that love which the ruler does not have for his people.

Grotius5 denies that every human power is established in favour of those who are governed, citing the example of slavery. His preferred manner of reasoning is always to establish right by facts.*A more consistent method might be used, but not one more favourable to Tyrants.

Thus, according to Grotius, it is doubtful whether the human race belongs to a hundred men, or whether those hundred men belong to the human race; throughout his book he seems to lean towards the former opinion – which is also the view of Hobbes.6 So there we have the human race divided into herds of cattle, each with its ruler who tends it that he may devour it.

Just as a pastor’s nature is superior to that of his flock, the shepherds of men – who are their rulers – likewise are of a nature superior to that of their peoples. So reasoned the Emperor Caligula, by Philo’s account;7 fairly concluding from this analogy that kings were Gods, or that peoples were beasts.

Caligula’s reasoning is the same as that of Hobbes and Grotius. Before all of them Aristotle too had said that men are by no means naturally equal, but some are born for slavery and others for domination.

Aristotle was right, but he took the effect for the cause. Every man born in slavery is born for slavery, nothing is surer. Slaves lose all in their irons, even the desire to escape them; they love their servitude, just as Ulysses’ companions loved their brutish condition.*8 So if there are slaves by nature, it is because there have been slaves against nature. Force made the first slaves,9 their cowardice has perpetuated them.

I have said nothing about king Adam, nor about emperor Noah, father of three great Monarchs who divided the universe between them as had Saturn’s children,10 whom some people have thought to recognize in them. I hope that gratitude will be shown me for this moderation. For who knows whether I – descended directly from one of these Princes, and perhaps from the senior branch – might not, if titles were to be verified, find myself legitimate king of the human race? Be that as it may, it cannot be denied that Adam was Sovereign of the world like Robinson of his island, since he was its sole inhabitant; and what was convenient in that empire was that the monarch safe on his throne had nothing to fear from rebellions or wars or conspirators.

Chapter 3

Of the Right of the Strongest

The strongest is never strong enough to be forever master, if he does not transform his strength into right and obedience into duty. Whence the right of the strongest: a right in appearance meant ironically, and in reality established as a principle. But will this word ever be explained to us? Strength is a physical power; I cannot at all see what morality can result from its effects. Yielding to force is an act of necessity, not of will; at most it is an act of prudence. In what sense could this be a duty?

Let us assume this supposed right for a moment. I say its only result is an inexplicable muddle. For as soon as it is force that makes right, the effect changes with the cause; any force surmounting the first inherits its right.
