As soon as you can disobey with impunity, you can do so legitimately; and since the strongest is always right, all that matters is contriving to be strongest. But what right is it, that perishes when strength ceases? If you have to obey by force, you do not need to obey out of duty; and if you are no longer forced to obey, you are no longer obliged to do so. So it is clear that this word ‘right’ adds nothing to strength; it means nothing at all here.

Obey the powers that be. If that means: yield to force, the precept is good but superfluous: I respond that it will never be violated. Every power comes from God, I admit; but every ailment likewise comes from Him. Does that mean it is forbidden to call the doctor? Let a brigand surprise me in some corner of a wood: not merely must I perforce surrender my purse, but if I could hide it am I in all conscience obliged to hand it over, since the pistol he holds is after all also a power?

Let us agree then that strength does not make right, and that you are obliged to obey only legitimate powers. So my original question still recurs.

Chapter 4

Of Slavery

Since no man has a natural authority over his fellow, and since strength produces no right, conventions are left as the basis of every legitimate authority among men.

If an individual, Grotius says, can alienate his liberty and enslave himself to a master, why could not a whole people alienate its own and subject itself to a king? There are plenty of ambiguous words here requiring explanation, but let us confine ourselves to ‘alienate’. To alienate is to give or to sell. Now, a man who enslaves himself to another does not give himself, he sells himself, at the very least for his subsistence. But for what does a people sell itself? A king, far from providing his subjects with their subsistence, derives his own subsistence from them alone, and according to Rabelais a king does not live off a pittance. Do subjects then give their person on condition that their property too will be taken? I fail to see what they have left to preserve.

You will say that the despot guarantees civil peace to his subjects. Very well. But what do they gain thereby, if the wars into which his ambition draws them, his insatiable greed, and the humiliations of his rule inflict more desolation upon them than would their own disputes? What do they gain thereby, if that very peace is one of their miseries? One may live at peace even in a dungeon – is that enough to feel at ease there? The Greeks imprisoned in Cyclops’ cave11 lived there peacefully, awaiting their turn to be devoured.

To say that a man gives himself freely is to say something absurd and unthinkable. Such an action is illegitimate and null, if only because the person who performs it is not in his right mind. To say the same thing of an entire people is to assume a people of madmen: madness does not create right.

Even if each man could alienate himself, he cannot alienate his children. They are born men and free; their liberty belongs to them, they alone have the right to dispose of it. Before they have reached the age of reason, their father may in their name stipulate conditions to ensure their survival or their well-being; but not give them away irrevocably and without condition, for such a gift is contrary to the aims of nature and goes beyond the rights of fatherhood. Hence, for an arbitrary government to be legitimate, it would be necessary for the people in each generation to have the power to accept or reject it; but then that government would no longer be arbitrary.

To renounce your liberty is to renounce your character as a man – the rights and even the duties of humanity. There is no possible compensation for someone who renounces everything. Such a renunciation is incompatible with man’s nature. To strip his will of all liberty means to strip his actions of all morality. Stipulating on the one hand an absolute authority and on the other a boundless obedience is a vain and contradictory convention. For is it not obvious that you have no obligation to a person from whom you have the right to demand everything? And does not that circumstance – without equivalence, without exchange – of itself nullify the act? For what right could my slave have against me, since all that he has belongs to me; and since, his right being mine, this right of my own against myself has no meaning?

Grotius and others derive from war another source of the so-called right to enslavement. Since, according to them, the victor has the right to slay the vanquished, the latter may purchase his life in return for his liberty; an agreement all the more legitimate in that it benefits both parties.

But it is clear that this supposed right to slay the vanquished in no way results from the state of war. For the simple reason that men living in their primitive independence do not maintain sufficiently constant relations among themselves to constitute either a state of peace or a state of war; they are not natural enemies at all. It is the relationship between things not between men that constitutes war. And since the state of war cannot arise from mere personal relations, but only from property relations, a private war – or war between one man and another – cannot exist, either in the state of nature where there is no constant property, or in the social state where all is governed by laws.

Individual conflicts, encounters or duels are acts that do not constitute a state; and as for the private wars authorized by the legal code of King Louis IX of France and suspended by the Peace of God,12 they are abuses of feudal government, an absurd system if ever there was one, against the principles of natural law and every good polity.

Thus war is by no means a relationship between one man and another, but a relationship between one State and another, in which individuals are enemies only accidentally, not as men or even as citizens,* but as soldiers; not as members of the fatherland, but as its defenders. For any State may have only other States as enemies, not men, considering that no real relation may be fixed between things of differing nature.14

This principle even accords with the maxims established in every age and with the constant practice of all civilized peoples. Declarations of war are warnings less to powers than to their subjects. The foreigner – whether king, or individual, or people – who steals, kills or detains subjects without declaring war upon the prince is not an enemy, he is a brigand. Even in the thick of war, a just prince may indeed seize all that belongs to the public in an enemy country; but he respects the person and the goods of individuals, he respects rights upon which his own are based. Since the aim of war is destruction of the hostile State, you have the right to kill its defenders so long as they are bearing arms; but as soon as they lay them down and surrender, ceasing to be enemies or instruments of the enemy, they again become merely men and you no longer have any right over their lives. Sometimes you may kill the State without killing a single one of its members: well, war gives no right that is not necessary to its objective. These principles are not those of Grotius; they are not based on the authority of poets, but derive from the nature of things and are based on reason.

As for the right of conquest, it has no basis other than the law of the strongest. If war does not give the victor the right to massacre the peoples he has vanquished, this right that he does not have cannot be the basis for a right to enslave them. You have the right to kill an enemy only when you cannot make him a slave; thus the right to make him a slave does not come from the right to kill him. It is thus an unjust exchange to make him buy his life, upon which you have no right, at the price of his liberty. In establishing the right of life and death upon the right to enslave, and the right to enslave upon the right of life and death, is it not clear that you are falling into a vicious circle?

Even assuming this dreadful right to kill everyone, I say that a slave made in war – or a conquered people – has no obligation whatsoever towards his master, other than to obey him to the extent that he is forced to do so. By taking an equivalent to his life, the victor has by no means spared it: instead of killing him fruitlessly, he has killed him usefully. Hence, far from the victor having acquired any authority over him in addition to force, the state of war subsists between them as before, their very relationship is a consequence of it, and use of the right of war implies no peace treaty. They have made a convention, very well; but that convention, far from destroying the state of war, implies its continuation.

Thus, however you look at things, the right to enslave is non-existent, not just because it is illegitimate, but because it is absurd and means nothing. The words slavery and right are contradictory; they mutually exclude one another. Whether from a man to a man, or from a man to a people, this argument will always be equally preposterous: I make a convention with you entirely at your expense and entirely for my benefit, which I shall observe to whatever extent pleases me, and which you will observe to whatever extent pleases me.

Chapter 5

How It Is Always Necessary to Go Back to a Primary Pact

Even were I to accept all that I have hitherto rejected, the advocates of despotism would thereby be no further forward. There will always be a great difference between subduing a multitude and governing a society. In the fact that dispersed men may successively have been enslaved – in whatever numbers – to a single individual, I perceive only a master and slaves, and by no means a people and its ruler. It is an aggregation, if you will, but not an association; neither public good nor body politic is involved here. Had that man enslaved half the world, he is still just an individual; his interest, separated from that of other men, is still just a private interest. If this same man happens to perish, his empire after him is left dispersed and disconnected, just as an oak dissolves and falls in a heap of ashes once the fire has consumed it.

A people, Grotius says, can give itself to a king. According to Grotius, therefore, a people is a people before giving itself to a king. This very gift is a civil act, assuming some public deliberation. So before examining the act whereby a people elects a king, it would be useful to examine the act by virtue of which a people is a people. For since this latter act necessarily precedes the former, it is the true foundation of society.

If there were no prior convention, in fact, where would be the obligation for the minority – unless the election were unanimous – to submit to the choice of the majority? And whence do a hundred who wish for a master have the right to vote for ten who do not wish for one at all? The law of voting by plurality is itself established by convention, and assumes unanimity on at least one occasion.

Chapter 6

Of the Social Pact

I assume men arrived at the point where the obstacles impeding their preservation in a state of nature prevail, through their resistance, over the forces each individual can deploy to maintain himself in such a state. The primitive state can then no longer subsist, and mankind would perish if it did not change its way of being.15

Now, since men cannot engender new forces, but merely unite and direct those that exist, they no longer have any means of self-preservation other than to form by aggregation a sum of forces capable of overcoming the resistance, to bring these into play through a single motive force, and to make them act in concert.

This sum of forces can be born only from the cooperation of many: but since the strength and liberty of each man are the first instruments of his preservation, how shall he commit them without harming himself, without neglecting the care he owes to himself? In relation to my subject, this difficulty can be articulated in the following terms. How to find a form of association that will, with the whole common force,defend and protect the person and goods of each associate, and through which each individual, while uniting with all, will nevertheless obey himself alone and remain as free as before? Such is the fundamental problem to which the social contract gives the solution.

The clauses of this contract are so much determined by the nature of the act that the least modification would render them vain and ineffective; so that, although they have perhaps never been formally articulated, they are everywhere the same, everywhere tacitly accepted and recognized; until such time as the social pact has been violated, when each person is restored to his original rights and recovers his natural liberty, losing the liberty by compact for which he renounced the latter.

These clauses can all be reduced, of course, to one alone: namely, the total alienation of each associate with all his rights to the community as a whole. For initially, since each person surrenders himself entirely, the condition is equal for all; and since the condition is equal for all, no one has any interest in making it onerous for the rest.

Moreover, since the alienation is made without reservation, the union is as perfect as may be, and no associate has anything further to claim. For if individuals did retain some rights, there would be no common superior able to adjudicate between them and the public. Then everyone, being his own judge on certain matters, would soon claim to be his own judge on all. The state of nature would thus live on, and the association would necessarily become tyrannical or vain.

For since each person gives himself to all, he gives himself to no one. And since there is no associate over whom you do not acquire the same right that you grant him over yourself, you gain the equivalent of all that you lose, and more strength to preserve what you have.

So if you eliminate from the social pact what is not essential to it, you will find it is reduced to the following terms. Each of us places his person and all his power in common under the supreme direction of the general will; and as a body we receive each member as an indivisible part of the whole.

Instantly, in place of the particular person of each contracting party, this act of association produces a corporate and collective body16 composed of as many members as the assembly has votes: a body that receives from this very act its unity, its common self, its life and its will. This public person thus formed by the union of all the rest was formerly given the name of City,*17 and is now given the name of Republic or body politic; which is called a State by its members when it is passive, a Sovereign when it is active, a Power when comparing it with its likes. So far as the associates are concerned, they collectively take the name of people, and in particular are called Citizens as participants in the sovereign authority, and Subjects as subjugated to the laws of the State. But these terms are often confused and taken one for the other; it is enough to know how to distinguish them when they are used with full precision.

Chapter 7

Of the Sovereign

It is clear from this formula that the act of association involves a reciprocal engagement between private persons and the public. And that each individual, contracting so to speak with himself, finds himself engaged by a twofold relationship: namely, as a member of the Sovereign towards private persons, and as a member of the State towards the Sovereign. But you cannot here apply the maxim of civil right that no one is bound by engagements to himself; for there is a clear difference between incurring an obligation to yourself and incurring one to a whole of which you form part.

We must further note that public deliberation, which may involve all subjects in an obligation towards the Sovereign, thanks to the two different relations in terms of which each of them is viewed, cannot for the opposite reason involve the Sovereign in an obligation towards itself; and that it is thus against the nature of the body politic for the Sovereign to impose a law on itself that it could not infringe. Being unable to consider itself other than in terms of one single relation, it is thus in the same situation as a private person contracting with himself. From which it may be seen that there is not  and cannot be  any kind of fundamental law binding on the body of the people, not even the social contract. Which does not mean that this body cannot perfectly well engage itself to others in whatever does not infringe this contract; for in relation to foreigners it becomes a simple being, an individual.

But the body politic or Sovereign, drawing its being solely from the sanctity of the contract, can never incur an obligation  even towards another  for anything that infringes that primitive act, such as alienating some part of itself or submitting itself to another Sovereign. Violating the act whereby it exists would mean annihilating itself, and that which is nothing produces nothing.

As soon as the multitude is thus assembled into a body, you cannot harm one of its members without attacking the body; still less harm the body without the members feeling the effect. Thus duty and interest alike oblige the two contracting parties to help one another mutually, and the same men must seek to combine in this twofold relationship all the advantages flowing from it.

Now the Sovereign,19 being formed only by the individuals who make it up, neither has nor can have any interest contrary to theirs; hence, the Sovereign power has no need of a guarantor against its subjects, since it is impossible that the body should wish to harm all its members, and we shall see later that it cannot harm anyone individually. The Sovereign, merely by virtue of its existence, is always all that it must be.

But the same is not true for subjects against the Sovereign, to which despite the common interest nothing would guarantee their commitments, if it did not find means to ensure their loyalty.

Every individual may indeed as a man have a particular will contrary or dissimilar to the general will that he has as a Citizen. His particular interest can speak to him quite otherwise than the general will. His absolute and naturally independent existence can make him see what he owes to the common cause as a gratuitous contribution, the loss of which will be less harmful to others than payment of it is burdensome to himself. And viewing the corporate person which constitutes the State as a fictive being, since it is not a man, he would enjoy the rights of a citizen without wishing to fulfil the duties of a subject: an injustice that if it persisted would cause the ruin of the body politic.

Thus, in order that the social pact should not be a vain formula, it tacitly incorporates a commitment that alone can give force to the rest: namely, that whosoever refuses to obey the general will shall be constrained to do so by the entire body. This means nothing other than that he shall be forced to be free. For such is the condition that, by giving each Citizen to the Fatherland, guarantees him against all personal dependence:20 the condition that makes the artifice and play of the political machinery, and that alone gives legitimacy to civil engagements which without it would be absurd, tyrannical and subject to the most enormous abuses.

Chapter 8

Of the Civil State

This passage from the state of nature to the civil state produces a most remarkable change in man, by substituting justice for instinct in his behaviour and endowing his actions with the morality they previously lacked. Only then, when the voice of duty succeeds physical impulsion and law succeeds appetite, does man, who until now had thought only of himself, find himself forced to act according to other principles, and to consult his reason before heeding his inclinations. Although in this state he denies himself a number of advantages granted him by nature, he gains others so great in return  his faculties are exercised and developed, his ideas expanded, his feelings ennobled, his entire soul soars so high  that if the abuses of this new condition did not often degrade him below that from which he emerged,21 he ought continually to bless the happy moment that wrested him thence for ever, and out of a stupid, limited animal made an intelligent being and a man.

Let us reduce this whole balance to terms easily compared. What man loses through the social contract is his natural liberty, and a limitless right to all that tempts him and that he can reach. What he wins is civil liberty and ownership of all that he possesses. In order not to be mistaken about these compensations, a clear distinction must be made between natural liberty, which has no limits other than the powers of the individual, and civil liberty, which is limited by the general will; between possession, which is the result merely of force or the right of the first occupant, and property, which can be based only on a positive title.

Apart from the foregoing, to the gains of the civil state might be added moral liberty,22 which alone makes man truly master of himself; for the impulsion of mere appetite is slavery, while obedience to the law you have set yourself is liberty. But I have said too much already on this topic, and the philosophical meaning of the word ‘liberty’ is not my subject here.

Chapter 9

Of Real Estate

Each member of the community gives himself to it at the moment of its formation, just as he currently is: himself and all his powers, including the goods he possesses. It is not that by this act possession changes its nature in changing hands, and becomes property in the hands of the Sovereign. But since the powers of the City are incomparably greater than those of an individual, public possession in fact is also stronger and more irrevocable, without being more legitimate, at least for foreigners. For the State with respect to its members is master of all their goods through the social contract, which in the State serves as the basis for all rights; but with respect to other Powers it is master only through the right of the first occupant, which it derives from individuals.

The right of the first occupant, though more real than that of the strongest, becomes a true right only after establishment of the right of property. Every man naturally has a right to all that is necessary to him; but the positive act that makes him the owner of some good excludes him from all the rest. Once his share is allotted he must limit himself to that, and no longer has any right to common property. This is why the right of the first occupant, so weak in the state of nature, is respected by every civil man. What is respected in this right is less what belongs to another than what does not belong to you.

In general, in order to authorize the right of the first occupant over any piece of land, the following conditions are necessary. First, that this land not yet be occupied by anyone; secondly, that you occupy only so much of it as you need to subsist; in the third place, that you take possession of it not through some vain ceremony, but by labour and cultivation, the only sign of ownership that, in the absence of legal titles, should be respected by others.

For if you grant the right of first occupant to need and to labour, are you not extending that right as far as it will go? Is it possible to place no limits upon it? Will it be enough to set foot on a piece of common land, in order at once to claim you are master of it? Will it be enough to have the strength to keep other men out of it for a while, in order to deny them the right ever to return to it? How can a man or a people seize hold of an immense territory and deprive the entire human race of it, other than through a usurpation deserving of punishment, since it denies to all other men the residence and sustenance that nature gives them in common? When Nuñez Balboa on the coast took possession of the South Sea and all southern America in the name of the crown of Castile, was that enough to dispossess all its inhabitants and exclude from it all the Princes of the world?23 If such were the case, those ceremonies were multiplied to no purpose, and the Catholic King had only to take possession of the entire universe at a stroke from his study, subject to later subtracting from his empire what was already possessed by other Princes.

How the combined and contiguous lands of individuals become public territory is easily understood, and how the right of sovereignty, extending from the subjects to the land they occupy, becomes at once real and personal; which places the possessors in a greater dependence and makes their very forces into guarantees of their loyalty. An advantage that seems not to have been appreciated by the monarchs of old, who in calling themselves simply kings of the Persians, Scythians or Macedonians appeared to see themselves as rulers of men rather than masters of a country. Their counterparts today more astutely call themselves Kings of France, Spain, England, etc. By thus holding the land, they are quite sure of holding its inhabitants.

What is singular about this alienation is that the community, far from despoiling individuals of their goods when it accepts these, only ensures their legitimate possession of them, changing usurpation into a genuine right, use into ownership. Thus, with the possessors being considered as trustees of the public good, their rights respected by all members of the State and upheld with all the latters powers against foreigners, they have in a manner of speaking, through a transfer advantageous both to the public and still more to themselves, gained all that they have given. A paradox easily explained by the distinction between the rights the sovereign and the proprietor have to the same land, as we shall see later.

It may also happen that men begin to unite before they possess anything, and that later, seizing enough land for all of them, they use this in common or share it among themselves, either equally or according to proportions established by the Sovereign. In whatever way this acquisition is made, the right that each individual has over his own land is always subordinated to the right that the community has over all, without which there would be neither solidity in the social bond, nor real force in the exercise of Sovereignty.

I shall end this chapter and this book by a remark that should serve as the basis for the whole social system. It is that, rather than destroying natural equality, the fundamental pact on the contrary substitutes a corporate and legitimate equality for whatever physical inequality nature may have placed among men; and that, whereas they may be unequal in strength or intelligence, they all become equal through convention and by right.*

End of the First Book

chapters.title: Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings
chapters.text:
Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

BOOK II

Chapter 1

How Sovereignty Is Inalienable

The first and most important consequence of the principles established above is that only the general will can direct the forces of the State in keeping with the aim for which it was instituted, which is the common good. For if the conflict of particular interests made the establishment of societies necessary, it is the agreement of those same interests that made it possible. It is what those different interests have in common that forms the social bond, and if there were not some point at which all the interests agree, no society could exist. Now, it is solely on the basis of this common interest that society must be governed.

So I say that sovereignty, being merely the exercise of the general will, can never be alienated, and that the sovereign, which is merely a collective being, can be represented only by itself; power can indeed be transferred, but not will.

For if it is not impossible that an individual will may agree on some point with the general will, it is at least impossible that this agreement should be lasting and constant; for the individual will tends by its nature to partiality, the general will to equality. It is yet more impossible to have a guarantee of this agreement, even if it were still to exist, since it would be the result not of design but of chance. The Sovereign may well say: I currently will what such and such a man wills, or at least what he says that he wills. But it cannot say: what that man is going to will tomorrow, I shall still will. For it is absurd that will should shackle itself for the future; and it is inherent in no will to consent to anything opposed to the welfare of the being that does the willing. Hence, if the people promises simply to obey, by that act it dissolves itself and loses its quality as a people. As soon as there is a master there is no more Sovereign, and the body politic is destroyed forthwith.

This does not at all mean that the orders of rulers cannot be taken as general wills, so long as the Sovereign, being free to oppose them, does not do so. In such a case, the agreement of the people must be presumed from the universal silence. This will be explained at greater length.

Chapter 2

How Sovereignty Is Indivisible

For the same reason that sovereignty is inalienable, it is indivisible. For will is general,* or it is not; it is the will of the people as a body, or merely of one part. In the former case, this declared will is an act of sovereignty and constitutes law. In the latter, it is merely a particular will, or an act of magistracy; at most it is a decree.1

But our political thinkers, unable to divide sovereignty in its principle, divide it in its object. They divide it into force and will; legislative power and executive power; rights of taxation, justice and war; domestic administration and power over foreign affairs. Sometimes they mingle all these parts, and sometimes they separate them.2 They make the Sovereign into a fantastic being, composed of disparate pieces; it is as if they were putting a man together from various bodies, one of which had eyes, another arms, another feet, and nothing else. Mountebanks in Japan are said to dismember a child in full view of spectators, throw all its limbs one after another into the air, then bring the child down again alive and in one piece. Such, more or less, is the sleight-of-hand of our political thinkers: after dismembering the social body by a conjuring trick worthy of the fairground, they reassemble the pieces no one knows how.

This error comes from not having formulated precise notions of sovereign authority, and from having taken as parts of this authority what were mere emanations from it. Thus, for example, the act of declaring war and that of making peace have been seen as acts of sovereignty, which is not so. For each of these acts is no law, but only an application of the law, a particular act that decides the law in this case, as will be seen clearly once the idea attached to the word law has been fixed.

By scrutinizing the other divisions in the same way, you would find that whenever you believe you see sovereignty shared you are mistaken: the rights which you take to be parts of that sovereignty are all subordinated to it, and always presuppose supreme wills that these rights simply implement.

It would be hard to tell how much this lack of precision has obscured the conclusions of authors with respect to political right, when they have sought to adjudicate the respective rights of kings and peoples in keeping with the principles they had established. In chapters III and IV of the first book of Grotius,3 anyone can see how that learned man and his translator Barbeyrac become entangled, caught up in their sophisms, for fear of saying too much or too little, depending on their views, and offending the interests they had to reconcile. Grotius, having taken refuge in France and wishing to woo Louis XIII, to whom his book is dedicated, spares nothing to despoil peoples of all their rights and to cloak kings in these through every artifice. This would have been to the taste of Barbeyrac too, who dedicated his translation to George I, King of England; but unfortunately the expulsion of James II, which he calls an abdication, forced him to hold back, distort and prevaricate, in order to avoid making William into a usurper. If those two writers had adopted true principles, all difficulties would have been removed and they would always have been consistent; but they would sadly have told the truth and wooed only the people. Now, truth does not lead to fortune, and the people gives no embassies, chairs or pensions.

Chapter 3

Whether the General Will Can Err

From the foregoing it follows that the general will is always rightful and always tends to public utility. But it does not follow that the deliberations of the people always have the same rightness. You always will your own good, but you cannot always see it.4 The people is never corrupted, but it is often misled, and only then does it seem to will what is bad.

There is often a great deal of difference between the will of all and the general will: the latter takes account only of the common interest; the former takes account of private interest, and is only a sum of particular wills. But remove from these same wills the pluses and minuses that cancel each other out,* and what is left as the sum of differences is the general will.

If, when a properly informed people deliberates, Citizens held no communication with one another, the large number of small differences would always result in the general will and the deliberation would always be good. But when intrigues arise, and partial associations are formed at the expense of the greater one, the will of each of these associations becomes general in relation to its members and particular in relation to the State. You may then say that there are no longer as many voters as there are men, but only as many as there are associations. Differences become less numerous and give a less general result. Finally, when one of these associations is so large that it prevails over all the rest, you no longer have a sum of small differences as the result, but one single difference. Then there is no longer a general will, and the view that prevails is merely a particular view.

In order really to have the expression of the general will, it is thus important that there should be no partial society in the State, and that each Citizen should give only his own opinion.* Such were the unique and sublime institutions of the great Lycurgus. If there are partial societies, you must multiply their number and prevent inequality between them, as did Solon, Numa, and Servius.5 Such precautions alone are capable of ensuring that the general will is always enlightened, and the people never goes astray.6

Chapter 4

Of the Limits of Sovereign Power

If the State or the City is simply a corporate person [personne morale], whose life consists in the union of its members, and if the most important of its concerns is its own preservation, it must have a universal and coercive force to move and dispose each part in the manner most beneficial to the whole. Just as nature gives each man an absolute power over all his limbs, the social pact gives the body politic an absolute power over all its members; and it is this same power which, directed by the general will, bears, as I have said, the name of sovereignty.

But apart from the public person, we have to consider the private persons who make it up, and whose life and liberty are naturally independent of it. So it is a matter of clearly distinguishing between the respective rights of Citizens and the Sovereign,* and between the duties which the former have to fulfil as subjects and the natural right which they must enjoy as men.

We may agree that whatever of his power, his goods and his liberty each man alienates through the social pact is merely the part of it all whose use is important to the community; but it must also be agreed that the Sovereign alone can be the judge of this importance.

All the services a citizen may render to the State, he owes once the Sovereign demands them. But the Sovereign for its part cannot burden subjects with any fetter useless to the community. It cannot even will this, for under the law of reason nothing is done without cause, any more than under the law of nature.

The engagements that bind us to the social body are obligatory only because they are mutual, and their nature is such that by fulfilling them you cannot work for another without working also for yourself. Why is the general will always rightful, and why do all continuously wish for the happiness of each, unless it is because there is no one who does not appropriate that word each, and who does not think about himself in voting for all? This proves that equal rights, and the notion of justice they produce, derive from the preference that everyone accords to himself: hence, from the nature of man. And that the general will, to be truly general, must be so in its object as well as in its essence; that it must start off from all in order to apply to all; and that it loses its natural rightness when it tends towards some individual, determinate object. Because then, judging what is foreign to us, we have no true principle of equity to guide us.

For no sooner is it a matter of a particular fact or right, concerning a point that has not been settled by a general and previous convention, than the affair becomes contentious. It is an issue in which interested private individuals are one of the parties and the public is the other, but in which I can discern neither the law to be followed nor the judge who is to decide. It would be ridiculous to wish then to refer to an express decision of the general will, which can be only the conclusion of one of the parties, and which consequently for the other is only a foreign, particular will, inclined on this occasion to injustice and subject to error. Thus, just as a particular will cannot represent the general will, the general will in turn changes its nature if it has a particular object, and being general cannot pronounce either upon a man or upon a fact. When the people of Athens, for example, nominated or dismissed its rulers, granted honours to one and imposed penalties upon another, and by countless individual decrees exercised all acts of Government indiscriminately, then the people no longer had any general will properly speaking. It no longer acted as a Sovereign but as a magistrate. This will appear at variance with common views, but I must be allowed time to expose my own.

You must understand by all this that what generalizes will is less the number of votes than the common interest uniting them. For under these institutions everyone necessarily submits to the conditions he imposes on others. This admirable agreement between interest and justice gives common deliberations a character of equity, which can be seen to vanish in discussion of any particular affair, for lack of a common interest uniting and identifying the judge’s ruling with that of the party.

However we may trace our path back to the principle, we always reach the same conclusion: namely, that the social pact establishes such equality between citizens that they all engage themselves under the same conditions, and must all enjoy the same rights. Thus by the nature of the pact any act of sovereignty, that is to say any authentic act of general will, obliges or favours all Citizens equally, so that the Sovereign knows only the body of the nation and does not distinguish any one of those who make it up. So what really is an act of sovereignty? It is not a convention between a superior and an inferior, but a convention between the body and each of its members: a legitimate Convention, because it has as its basis the social contract; equitable, because it is common to all; useful, because it can have no object other than the general good; and solid, because it is guaranteed by public force and the supreme power. So long as subjects are subordinated only to such conventions, they obey no one, but only their own will; and to ask how far the respective rights of Sovereign and Citizens extend is to ask how far the latter can engage themselves to one another, each to all and all to each.

It is clear from this that the Sovereign power, absolute, sacred and inviolable though it be, does not and cannot exceed the limits of general conventions; and that every man may fully dispose of such of his goods and his liberty as these conventions have left him; so that the Sovereign is never entitled to burden one subject more than another, because with the affair then becoming particular its power is no longer competent.

Once these distinctions are conceded, it is so untrue that the social contract entails any real renunciation on the part of individuals that, as a result of that contract, their situation is found to be genuinely preferable to what it was previously. And, rather than an alienation, they have made only an advantageous exchange: of an uncertain and precarious way of being for a better and surer one; of natural independence for liberty; of the power to harm others for their own security; and of their force, which others might overwhelm, for a right that the social union renders invincible. The very life which they have devoted to the State is continuously protected by it; and when they expose that life in its defence, what are they then doing but giving back to the State what they have received from it? What are they doing that they did not do more frequently and at greater peril in the state of nature, when, engaging in inevitable conflicts, they would at the risk of their life defend what serves to preserve it? To be sure, everyone has to fight if need be for the fatherland, but then no one ever has to fight for himself. Do we not still gain, by risking for what ensures our security part of what we would have to risk for ourselves, were that security ever taken from us?

chapters.title: Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings
chapters.text:
Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

Chapter 5

Of the Right of Life and Death

Do you ask how individuals, having no right to dispose of their own life, can transmit to the Sovereign this very right that they do not have? The question seems hard to resolve only because it is badly put. Any man has the right to risk his own life in order to preserve it. Has it ever been claimed that someone who throws himself through a window in order to escape from a fire is guilty of suicide? Has such a crime ever been imputed even to someone who perishes in a storm of whose danger he was aware when embarking?

The social treaty has preservation of the contracting parties as its end. Who wills the end, wills also the means, and these means are inseparable from certain risks, even certain losses. Whosoever wishes to preserve his life at the expense of others must also give it for them when necessary. Now, the Citizen is no longer judge of the danger to which the law wishes him to expose himself. And when the Prince has told him: ‘It is expedient for the State that you should die,’ then he must die, since it is upon this condition alone that he has lived in safety hitherto, and since his life is no longer merely a bounty of nature but a conditional gift from the State.

The death penalty inflicted on criminals can be viewed more or less from the same viewpoint: it is in order not to fall victim to an assassin that you agree to die if you become one. In this treaty, far from disposing of your own life you think only of guaranteeing it; and it is not to be supposed that any of the contracting parties plans at the time to be hanged.

Moreover, any malefactor attacking society’s law becomes by his misdeeds a rebel and traitor to the fatherland; he ceases to be a member of it by violating its laws, he even makes war upon it. So preservation of the State is incompatible with his own, one of the two has to perish; and when the guilty man is put to death, it is less as a Citizen than as an enemy. The proceedings and judgement are the proof and declaration that he has broken the social treaty, and that consequently he is no longer a member of the State. Now, since he has acknowledged himself as such, at least by residence, he must be cut off from it either by exile as a violator of the pact, or by death as a public enemy. For such an enemy is not a corporate person, but a man, in which case the right of war allows the vanquished to be killed.

But you will say that the condemnation of a Criminal is a particular act. Granted; so this condemnation is not the province of the Sovereign, but a right that it may confer without being able to exercise it itself. All my ideas are consistent, but I cannot expound them all at once.

Besides, the frequency of executions is always a sign of weakness or indolence in the Government. There is no man so wicked that he cannot be made good for something. Even in order to set an example, you have the right to put to death only a person who cannot be kept without danger.

With respect to the right to pardon, or to exempt a guilty man from the penalty inflicted by the law and pronounced by the judge, this belongs only to the one who is above the judge and the law, in other words the Sovereign. Yet the latter’s right in this respect is not very clear, and the cases in which it may be used are very rare. In a well-governed State there are few punishments, not because many pardons are granted, but because there are few criminals. The large number of crimes ensures their impunity when the State is in decline. Under the Roman Republic, neither the Senate nor the Consuls ever attempted to grant pardons; the people itself did not do so, although it sometimes revoked its own decision. Frequent pardons proclaim that crimes will soon no longer need them, and anyone can see where that leads. But I feel my heart protest and check my pen; let us leave these questions to be discussed by the just man who has never sinned, and never himself been in need of pardon.

Chapter 6

Of the Law

Through the social pact we have given the body politic existence and life; it is now a matter of giving it movement and will through legislation. For the primitive act whereby this body forms and unites does not yet determine anything of what it must do to preserve itself.

What is good and favourable to order is such by the nature of things, and independently of human conventions. All justice comes from God, who alone is its source; but if we could receive it from so high up, we should need neither government nor laws. There is doubtless a justice emanating from reason alone,7 but for this justice to be accepted among us it must be reciprocal. Considering things in human terms, for want of natural sanction the laws of justice are vain among men; they merely benefit the wicked man and do harm to the just, if he observes them towards everyone while no one observes them towards him. So conventions and laws are needed in order to unite rights with duties and restore justice to its object. In the state of nature, where everything is common, I owe nothing to those to whom I have promised nothing, I recognize as another’s only what is of no use to myself. It is otherwise in the civil state, where all rights are fixed by law.

But what is a law after all? So long as you are content with attaching only metaphysical ideas to this word, you will continue to reason without reaching agreement; and even when you have stated what a law of nature is, you will have no better notion of a law of the State.

I have already said that there is no general will concerning a particular object. For this particular object is either within the State or outside the State. If it is outside the State, a will that is foreign to it cannot be general with respect to it. And if this object is within the State, it is part of it. Then a relation is formed between the whole and its part which makes them into two separate beings, one of which is the part, the other the whole minus that same part. But the whole minus a part is not the whole; and so long as this relation persists there is no more whole, but two unequal parts. Whence it follows that the will of one part is never general either with respect to the other part.

But when the entire people rules over the entire people, it is considering itself alone; and if a relation is then formed, it is one between the whole object from one viewpoint and the whole object from another viewpoint, without any division at all. Then the matter ruled upon is general, as is the will that rules. It is this act that I call a law.

When I say that the object of laws is always general, I mean that the law considers subjects in a body and actions as abstract, never a man as an individual or a particular action. Thus the law may well rule that there will be privileges, but it cannot grant these to anyone by name. The law can make several Classes of Citizen, even assign the qualities that will grant entry to these classes, but it cannot name such and such persons to be admitted to them. It can establish a royal Government and a hereditary succession, but it cannot elect a king or name a royal family. In a word, any function relating to an individual object is not the province of the legislative power.

On this view, you can see at once that you no longer need to ask whose task it is to make laws, since they are acts of the general will; nor if the Prince is above these laws, since it is a member of the State; nor if the law can be unjust, since no one is unjust to himself; nor how we can be both free and subject to laws, since these register only what we will.

It is also clear that since the law combines the universality of the will with that of its object, what any man, no matter who, orders on his own authority is no law. What even the Sovereign orders with respect to a particular object is not a law either, but a decree; not an act of sovereignty, but one of magistracy.

So I call Republic any State ruled by laws, under any form of administration whatsoever: for only then does the public interest govern, and is the res publica a reality. All legitimate Government is republican.* I shall explain later what Government is.

Laws properly speaking are only the conditions of civil association. The People subjected to laws must be their author. It is the province only of those who associate in a society to regulate its conditions, but how will they do so? Will it be by common agreement, by sudden inspiration? Does the body politic have some organ to express its will? Who will give it the foresight necessary to formulate its acts and declare them in advance, or how will it proclaim them in time of need? How should a blind multitude, which often does not know what it wants, because it rarely knows what is good for it, by itself implement so great and difficult an undertaking as a system of legislation? The people of itself always wants what is good, but it does not of itself always see it. The general will is always rightful, but the judgement guiding it is not always enlightened. It must be brought to see objects such as they are, and sometimes such as they should appear; it must be shown the true path that it seeks; it must be safeguarded from the seduction of particular wills; places and times must be brought closer to its gaze; the charm of present, perceptible advantages must be weighed against the danger of distant, hidden ills. Individuals see the good they reject; the public wills the good that it does not see. All are equally in need of guides. The former must be obliged to adapt their wills to their reason; the latter must be taught to know that which it wills. Public enlightenment then results in the union of understanding and will in the social body, leading to exact cooperation of the parts and ultimately the greatest strength of the whole. Thence arises the need for a Legislator.

Chapter 7

Of the Legislator

In order to discover the best social rules appropriate for Nations, a superior intelligence would be necessary, which would live all the passions of men but experience none of them; which would have no part of our nature, but would know it through and through; whose happiness would be independent of us, yet which would be willing to concern itself with us; which finally, storing up a distant glory for itself over the course of time, would be able to work in one century and find enjoyment in another.* Gods would be necessary in order to give men laws.

What Caligula argued on the basis of reality, Plato argued on the basis of right when in his book on ruling he sought to define the civil or kingly man.8 But if it be true that a great Prince is a rare man, what will be the case for a great Legislator? The former has only to follow the model that the latter has to propose. The latter is the engineer who invents the machine, the former is only the workman who installs and operates it. At the birth of societies, Montesquieu says, it is the rulers of republics who make the institutions, and thereafter it is the institutions that mould the rulers of republics.

Anyone who dares undertake to give a people institutions must feel capable of so to speak changing human nature; of transforming every individual, who in himself is a perfect and solitary whole, into part of a greater whole from which this individual in a sense receives his life and his being; of substituting a partial and corporate existence for the physical and independent existence that we have all received from nature. In a word, he must strip man of his own forces in order to give him others that are alien to him, and of which he cannot make use without another’s help. The more those natural forces are dead and destroyed, the more those gained are great and lasting, and the more too are the institutions solid and perfect. So that if every Citizen is nothing and can do nothing other than through all his fellows; and if the force acquired by the whole is equal or superior to the sum of natural forces of all the individuals; then legislation may be said to be at the highest point of perfection it could attain.

The Legislator is in all respects an extraordinary man in the State. If he must be so by virtue of his intelligence, he is just as much so by virtue of his function. This is not magistracy, nor is it sovereignty. This function, which constitutes the republic, forms no part of its constitution. It is a particular and superior function that has nothing in common with human power. For if he who commands men must not command the laws, neither must he who commands the laws command men. Otherwise those laws, catering to his passions, would often only perpetuate his injustices; and he could never guard against particular views impairing the sanctity of his work.

When Lycurgus gave laws to his fatherland, he began by surrendering his Royal status. It was the custom in most of the Greek cities to entrust the establishment of their laws to foreigners. The modern Republics of Italy often imitated this practice; that of Geneva did the same and prospered by doing so.* Rome in her finest age saw all the crimes of Tyranny reborn in her bosom, and saw herself on the verge of perishing, because she had united legislative authority and sovereign power on the same brows.

Yet the Decemvirs9 themselves never claimed the right to pass any law by their authority alone. Nothing of what we propose to you, they would say to the people, can pass into law without your consent. Romans, be yourselves the authors of the laws that are to ensure your happiness.

The man who draws up the laws thus has, or should have, no legislative right; and the very people, even should it wish to, cannot strip itself of that incommunicable right. Because, according to the fundamental pact, it is the general will alone that puts individuals under an obligation; and because you can never ensure that an individual will is in conformity with the general will, unless you have first submitted it to the free votes of the people. I have already stated this, but it is worth repeating.

So in the work of lawgiving you can find at one and the same time two things that seem incompatible: an undertaking that is beyond human powers, and for its execution an authority that is nothing.

There is another difficulty that deserves attention. Wise men intent on speaking their own language to the common man instead of his could not be understood by him. But there are innumerable kinds of idea that cannot be translated into the language of the people. Views too general and objects too remote are equally beyond its range. It is hard for any individual, appreciating no other plan of government than that relating to his particular interest, to discern the advantages he is to draw from the constant privations that good laws impose. For a nascent people to be able to appreciate healthy maxims of political thought and follow the fundamental rules of raison d’État, effect would have to succeed in becoming cause; the social spirit that must be the work of institutions would have to preside over the institutions themselves; and prior to laws men would have to be what they must become through them. Hence, since the Legislator is thus unable to use either force or reason, it is a necessity for him to have recourse to an authority of a different order, which may compel without violence and persuade without convincing.10

This is what, throughout time, forced the fathers of nations to have recourse to the intervention of heaven and ascribe their own wisdom to the Gods, so that peoples – subjected to the laws of the State as to those of nature, and acknowledging the same power in man’s formation and that of the city – might obey in liberty, and bear the yoke of public happiness with docility.

This sublime reasoning, which soars above the reach of common men, is that whereby the Legislator puts decisions in the mouth of the immortals, in order through divine authority to compel those whom human prudence could not shake.* But it is not the province of all men to make the Gods speak, nor to be believed when they announce themselves as their interpreters. The Legislator’s great soul is the true miracle that should prove his mission. Any man can engrave tablets of stone, or buy an oracle, or feign secret traffic with some divinity, or train a bird to whisper in his ear, or find other crude means with which to impose upon the people. The man who knows this alone may even by chance manage to assemble a flock of crazy people; but he will never found an empire, and his outlandish construction will soon perish with him. Empty illusions create an ephemeral bond, it is wisdom alone that can make it lasting. The Judaic law which still lives on, and that of Ishmael’s child which for ten centuries has ruled half the world, proclaim to this day the great men who dictated them. And whereas proud philosophy or blind partisanship see in them only lucky imposters, the true political thinker admires in their institutions the great and powerful genius that presides over enduring creations.

From all this it would be wrong to conclude with Warburton11 that among us political thought and religion have a common object, but rather that in the origin of nations the latter serves as an instrument of the former.

Chapter 8

Of the People

Just as the architect, before erecting a great building, observes and plumbs the ground to see if it can bear the weight, so the wise founder of institutions does not begin by drafting laws good in themselves, but first examines whether the people for which he intends them is capable of supporting them. This is why Plato refused to give laws to the Arcadians and Cyrenians, knowing that those two peoples were rich and could not tolerate equality. This is why in Crete you saw good laws and wicked men, because Minos had imposed discipline only upon a people weighed down by vice.12

Countless nations have glittered upon this earth which could never have tolerated good laws; and even those which could have done so had throughout their span only a very short time for it. Most peoples like most men are docile only in their youth, becoming incorrigible as they grow older. Once customs are established and prejudices take root, it is a dangerous and vain undertaking to seek to reform them. The people cannot even endure its ills being touched in order to destroy them, like those stupid and cowardly patients who shudder at the sight of the doctor.

It is not that, just as some illnesses throw men’s minds into turmoil and strip them of all memory of the past, there are not sometimes violent epochs in the life of States wherein revolutions have the same effect on peoples as certain crises have upon individuals; in which horror of the past takes the place of forgetting; and in which the State, set aflame by civil wars, is so to speak reborn from its ashes and recovers the vigour of youth as it emerges from the arms of death. Such was Sparta in the time of Lycurgus, such was Rome after the Tarquins, and such among us have been Holland and Switzerland after the expulsion of their Tyrants.13

But these events are rare; they are exceptions, the reason for which is always to be found in the particular constitution of the exceptional State. They could not even take place twice for the same people; for it can free itself so long as it is merely barbarous, but can do so no longer once the civil order is eroded. Then troubles can destroy it without revolutions being able to re-establish it; and as soon as its fetters are broken, it falls in fragments and no longer exists. Henceforth it needs a master, not a liberator. Free peoples, remember this maxim: ‘you can win liberty, but you can never regain it’!

Youth is not childhood. For Nations, as for men, there is a time of youth or if you will of maturity, that must be awaited before subjecting them to laws; but the maturity of a people is not always easy to know, and if you anticipate it the undertaking is a failure. One people is susceptible to discipline at its birth, another is not after ten centuries. The Russians will never truly be civilized, because they were civilized too soon. Peter had a genius for imitation;14 he did not have true genius, that which creates and makes everything out of nothing. Some of the things he did were good; most were inappropriate. He saw that his people was barbarous, he failed to see that it was not ripe for civilization; he wished to civilize it when what was needed was merely to harden it. He wished first to make Germans or Englishmen, when it was necessary to begin by making Russians; he prevented his subjects from ever becoming what they might have become, by persuading them that they were what they are not. That is how a Tutor in France trains his pupil to shine for a moment in childhood, and thereafter never to be anything. The Empire of Russia will seek to subjugate Europe, and will itself be subjugated. The Tartars – its subjects or its neighbours – will become its masters and ours. This revolution seems to me inevitable. All the Kings of Europe are working in concert to hasten its coming.

Chapter 9

Of the People – continued

Just as nature has set limits to the stature of a well-formed man, beyond which she makes only Giants or Dwarfs, similarly with respect to the best constitution of a State there are limits to the extent it may have, so that it is neither too large to be well governed nor too small to maintain itself independently. In every body politic there is thus a maximum of strength that it would be unable to surpass, and from which it often moves away by dint of growing larger. The further the social bond stretches, the looser it grows; and in general a small State is proportionately stronger than a large one.

Countless reasons confirm this maxim. First, administration grows more irksome over large distances, just as a weight grows heavier at the end of a large lever. It also grows more onerous as its levels multiply. For at first every town has its administration, paid for by the people; every district has its own, again paid for by the people; then every province, then such major levels of government as Satrapies or Viceroyalties, which have to be paid for more dearly as you rise higher, and always at the expense of the unhappy people; finally comes the supreme administration, which crushes all. The subjects are constantly exhausted by so many additional burdens. Far from being governed better by these various orders, they are less well governed than if they had but a single one over them. Meanwhile there are barely any resources left for emergencies; and when it has to resort to them, the State is always on the brink of ruin.

That is not all. Not only does the Government have less vigour and promptness in ensuring observance of the laws, correcting abuses, or forestalling seditious undertakings that may occur in far-off places; but the people has less affection for its rulers, whom it never sees, for the fatherland, which seems to it like the world, and for its fellow citizens, most of whom are strangers to it. The same laws cannot be appropriate for so many diverse provinces, which have different mores, live under contrasting climates, and cannot tolerate the same form of government. Different laws engender only turmoil and confusion among peoples which, living under the same rulers and in constant communication, intermingle or intermarry and, being then subjected to other customs, never know if their patrimony is truly their own. Talents are buried, virtues ignored and vices unpunished in this multitude of men, unknown to one another, assembled in one place by the seat of the supreme administration. The Rulers, overwhelmed by the weight of business, see nothing for themselves; functionaries govern the State. In short, the measures that have to be taken to maintain the general authority, which so many distant Officials wish to evade or to exploit, absorb all the public concern. Nothing is left for the well-being of the people, hardly anything for its defence in case of need, which is why a body too large for its own constitution grows weak and perishes crushed beneath its own weight.

On the other hand, the State must give itself a certain base in order to have solidity; in order to bear up under the shocks it will not fail to experience and the efforts it will be obliged to make to maintain itself. For all peoples have a kind of centrifugal force, whereby they continuously act against each other and tend to expand at the expense of their neighbours, like Descartes’ vortices.15 So the weak risk being soon engulfed, and scarcely can any people preserve itself except by setting itself in a kind of equilibrium with all that will render the pressure more or less equal everywhere.

From this it may be seen that there are reasons to expand and reasons to contract; and that it is not the least talent of a political thinker to find, between the former and the latter, the proportion most advantageous for preservation of the State. You may say in general that the former reasons, being only external and relative, should be subordinated to the latter, which are internal and absolute. A healthy, strong constitution is the first thing to be sought; and you must rely more on the vigour born of a good government than on the resources provided by a large territory.

Moreover, we have seen States so constituted that the need for conquests formed part of their very constitution, and in order to maintain themselves they were forced constantly to expand. Perhaps they used to congratulate themselves greatly on this happy necessity; yet it showed them, along with the limit on their size, the inevitable moment of their downfall.

Chapter 10

Of the People – continued

A body politic may be measured in two ways: namely, by the extent of its territory and by the number of its people; and between these two measurements there is an appropriate ratio for giving the State its true greatness. It is men who make the State, and its territory that feeds the men. The appropriate ratio is thus that the land should be sufficient for the upkeep of its inhabitants, and that there should be as many inhabitants as the land can feed. It is in this proportion that the maximum force of a people of given number lies. For if there is an excess of territory, guarding it is burdensome, it is insufficiently cultivated, and its product is superfluous; this is the proximate cause of defensive wars. If there is not enough territory, the State finds itself looking to its neighbours to supplement it; this is the proximate cause of offensive wars. Any people that through its position has only the alternatives of trade and war is weak in itself. It depends on its neighbours, it depends on events, it never has anything other than an uncertain, brief existence. Either it subjugates and changes its situation, or it is subjugated and is nothing. It can keep itself free only by being small or large.

No fixed ratio can be worked out between the extent of land and the number of men that suffice for one another: as much because of the differences that occur in the quality of the land, its degree of fertility, the nature of its production, and the influence of its climate as because of the differences to be noted in the temperament of the men living on it, some of whom consume little in fertile country while others consume much on unrewarding soil. Account must also be taken of the greater or lesser fecundity of the women, of what is more or less favourable to population in the country, of the amount the legislator can hope to contribute through his institutions. So that he must not base his judgement on what he sees, but on what he foresees; nor dwell so much upon the present state of the population as upon the state it should naturally reach. After all, there are countless occasions when the particular incidentals of the place require or permit more territory to be incorporated than seems necessary. Thus you will expand a great deal in a land of mountains, where natural production in the shape of forests and pastures requires less labour, where experience teaches that women are more fecund than on the plains, and where extensive sloping terrain provides little flat land, that alone may be relied upon for vegetation. On the sea coast, by contrast, even among almost barren rocks and sands you may contract, because fishing can largely make up for terrestrial production, because men have to cluster more closely to repel pirates, and because too, by means of colonies, you will find it easier to deliver the country from the inhabitants with which it is overburdened.

To these conditions for giving a people institutions must be added one that cannot replace any other, but without which they are all useless: this is that you should enjoy abundance and peace. For the time when a State is in order, like the time when a battalion is formed, is the instant when the body is least capable of resistance and easiest to destroy. One would resist better in absolute disorder than in a moment of ferment, when everyone is concerned about his rank and not about danger. If war, famine or sedition occurs in this time of crisis, the State is infallibly overthrown.

Not that many governments have not been established during such storms; but then it is these governments themselves that destroy the State. Usurpers always bring on, or choose, such times of upheaval in order to put through, under cover of the public panic, destructive laws that the people would never adopt in cold blood. Choice of the right moment to form institutions is one of the surest features by which you may distinguish the work of the Legislator from that of the Tyrant.

So which people is fit to be given laws? A people that, finding itself already bound by some link of origin, interest or convention, has not yet borne the real yoke of laws; one that has no well-rooted customs or superstitions; one that does not fear being overwhelmed by a sudden invasion, and that, without entering its neighbours’ disputes, can on its own resist any one of them, or use the help of one to repel another; one each of whose members can be known by all, and in which you are not forced to load a man with a burden greater than a man can carry; one that can do without other peoples, and that any other people can do without;* one that is neither rich nor poor, and can be sufficient unto itself; finally one that combines the resistance of an ancient people with the docility of a new people. What makes the work of legislation irksome is less what must be established than what must be destroyed; and what makes success so rare is the impossibility of finding the simplicity of nature combined with the needs of society. All these conditions, to be sure, are hard to find together. So few well-constituted States are seen.

There is still one country in Europe fit to be given laws: it is the Isle of Corsica.16 The valour and constancy with which that brave people has managed to recover and defend its liberty would merit that some wise man should teach it to preserve that liberty. I have a feeling that one day that little island will astonish Europe.

Chapter 11

Of the Various Systems of Legislation

If you look for precisely what constitutes the greatest good for all, which must be the aim of every system of legislation, you will find that it is reduced to these two main objects: liberty and equality. Liberty, because every particular dependence is so much strength removed from the body of the State; equality, because liberty cannot exist without it.

I have already stated what civil liberty is. As for equality, this word must not be taken to mean that degrees of power and wealth should be absolutely identical, but that in the case of power it should stop short of all violence, and never be exerted other than in keeping with rank and the laws; and in the case of wealth no citizen should be so opulent as to be able to buy another, and none so poor as to be forced to sell himself. This implies moderation in goods and influence on the part of the great, moderation in avarice and covetousness on the part of the humble.*

This equality, people say, is a speculative fantasy that cannot exist in practice. But if abuse is inevitable, does it follow that it should not at least be regulated? It is precisely because the force of things always tends to destroy equality that the force of legislation must always tend to maintain it.

But these general aims of all good institutions must be modified in each country by the relations engendered alike by the local situation and the character of the inhabitants; and it is on the basis of these relations that each people must be assigned a particular system of institutions, which is perhaps best not in itself but for the State for which it is destined. For instance, is the soil unrewarding and barren, or the land too restricted for the inhabitants? Turn then towards industry and crafts, the products of which you will exchange for the commodities you lack. On the other hand, do you occupy rich plains and fertile slopes? On good land, do you lack inhabitants? Give all your concern then to agriculture, which multiplies men; and drive out crafts, which would only complete the depopulation of the land, by herding the few inhabitants there are onto certain parts of the territory.† Do you occupy an extensive, open coast? Cover the sea with ships, foster trade and navigation; you will have a brief and glorious existence. Does the sea on your shores wash only against almost inaccessible rocks? Remain ichthyophagous barbarians; you will live more tranquilly for that, perhaps better, and certainly more happily. In a word, apart from the maxims common to all, every People contains within itself some cause that orders these in a particular way and makes its legislation suitable for it alone. Thus formerly the Hebrews and recently the Arabs had Religion as their main aim, the Athenians letters, Carthage and Tyre commerce, Rhodes seafaring, Sparta war and Rome virtue. The author of The Spirit of Laws17 showed in a host of examples the skill with which the legislator directs institutions towards each of his aims.

What makes the constitution of a State truly solid and lasting is when conventions are observed in such a way that natural relations and laws always coincide on the same points, so that the latter in a manner of speaking only ensure, accompany and rectify the former. But if the Legislator, erring in his aim, takes a different principle from that which springs from the nature of things – if one principle tends towards servitude, the other towards liberty; one towards riches, the other towards population; one towards peace, the other towards conquest – then you will see laws imperceptibly weaken, the constitution deteriorate, and the State will not cease to be in turmoil until it is destroyed or changed, and until invincible nature has reasserted its sway.

Chapter 12

Division of Laws

For the whole to be set in order, or the best possible form given to the res publica, various relationships must be considered. First, the action of the whole body acting upon itself: in other words, the relation of the whole to the whole, or of the Sovereign to the State. And this relationship is made up of relations between intermediate terms,18 as we shall see below.

The laws regulating this relationship bear the name of political laws, and are also called fundamental laws, not without some reason if these laws are wise. For if in each State there is only one good way to set it in order, the people which has found this must hold fast to it. But if the established order is bad, why should you take laws to be fundamental that prevent it from being good? Whatever happens, moreover, a people is always in a position to change its laws, even the best; for if it is pleased to harm itself, who has the right to prevent it from doing so?

The second relationship is that of members with one another or with the whole body; and this relationship must in the former case be as little as possible, in the latter as great as possible. So that each Citizen should be perfectly independent of all the others, and excessively dependent upon the City; which is always achieved by the same means, since it is only the force of the State that can make its members free. It is from this second relationship that civil laws spring.

A third kind of relationship between man and the law may be considered: namely, that between disobedience and punishment; and this gives rise to the establishment of criminal laws, which are basically not so much laws of a particular kind as the sanction of all the others.

To these three kinds of law a fourth may be added, the most important of all, which is engraved neither on marble nor on brass, but in the hearts of citizens; which makes the true constitution of the State; which gains new strength every day; which, when other laws grow old or fade away, rekindles or replaces them, preserves a people in the spirit of its institutions, and imperceptibly substitutes the force of habit for that of authority.
