Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

BOOK I

Chapter 2

Of the General Society of Mankind

Let us begin by inquiring whence the necessity for political institutions arises.

Man’s strength is so proportionate to his natural needs and to his primitive state that no sooner does this state change and his needs increase than the assistance of his fellows becomes necessary to him; and when his desires finally embrace the whole of nature, the help of all mankind is scarcely enough to assuage them. Thus it is that the same causes which make us wicked make us also slaves, enslaving us by depraving us. The sense of our weakness comes less from our nature than from our cupidity: our needs draw us closer even as our passions divide us, and the more we become enemies to our fellows the less we can do without them. Such are the first bonds of the general society; such are the foundations of that universal goodwill whose acknowledged necessity seems to stifle feeling, whose fruits each man would like to pluck without being obliged to cultivate them. For, so far as natural identity goes, its effect is null in this respect, since for men it is as much a source of conflict as of unity, and as often sets rivalry and jealousy among them as good intelligence and agreement.

From this new order of things arise a host of relations, without measure or rule or consistency, which men continually alter and change, a hundred working to destroy them for each one who works to fix them. And since the relative existence of a man in the state of nature depends upon countless other relations that are in continual flux, he can never be certain of being the same through two moments of his life. Peace and happiness are for him but a lightning flash; nothing is permanent except the wretchedness that results from all these vicissitudes. Even might his feelings and his ideas attain the love of order and the sublime notions of virtue, it would be impossible for him ever to make a certain application of his principles in a state of affairs that would not let him discern either good or evil, either the honest man or the wicked.

The general society such as our mutual needs may engender thus offers no effective assistance to man become wretched; or at least gives new strength only to the man who already has it in excess, while the weak man, lost, stifled, crushed in the multitude, finds no shelter in which to take refuge, no crutch for his weakness, and finally dies a victim to that deceptive unity from which he expected his happiness.

[If you are once convinced that among the motives leading men to unite among themselves by voluntary ties there is nothing relating to the point where they come together; and that, far from proposing a goal of common felicity whence each may derive his own, one man’s happiness makes his fellow’s misfortune; and finally if you consider that, instead of all tending towards the general good, men draw closer to one another only because all are moving away from it; then you must also feel that, even if such a state could exist, it would be merely a source of crime and wretchedness for men, each of whom would see only his own interest, follow only his own inclinations and listen only to his own passions.]

Hence, the sweet voice of nature is no longer an infallible guide for us, nor is the independence we have received from nature a desirable state. Peace and innocence eluded us for ever before we had tasted their delights. Inaccessible to the brutish men of the earliest days, eluding the enlightened men of later days, the happy life of the golden age was always a state alien to the human race, either because humans were unaware of it when they might have enjoyed it or because they lost it when they might have known it.

There is yet more. Even had that perfect independence and that unregulated liberty remained united with the ancient innocence, they would always have had an essential defect, harmful to the progress of our most excellent faculties: namely, the lack of that bond between the parts which constitutes the whole. The earth would be covered with men among whom there would be almost no communication; we would touch one another at certain points, without being joined at any of them; each person would remain isolated among the rest, each would think only of himself; our understanding would be unable to develop; we should live without feeling anything, we should die without having lived; all our happiness would consist in not knowing our wretchedness; there would be neither kindness in our hearts nor morality in our actions, and we should never have tasted the most delightful feeling of the soul, which is the love of virtue.

[Assuredly the word mankind offers the mind merely a collective idea supposing no real unity among the individuals who constitute it. Let us add, if you will, this Supposition: let us conceive mankind as a corporate person possessing, along with a feeling of common existence that gives it individuality and constitutes it as one, a universal motivation that makes each part act for a general end relating to the whole. Let us conceive that this common feeling is that of humanity, and that natural law is the active principle of the entire machinery. Let us then observe what results from man’s constitution in his relations with his fellows; and, quite otherwise from what we imagined, we shall find that the progress of society stifles humanity in people’s hearts, by awakening private interest; and that the notions of natural Law, which should rather be called the law of reason, begin to develop only when the earlier development of the passions renders all its precepts powerless. Thus it is seen that this supposed social treaty dictated by nature is a veritable pipe-dream; for its conditions are always unknown or impracticable, and must necessarily be ignored or infringed.

If the general society existed anywhere other than in the systems of Philosophers, it would, as I have said, be a corporate [moral] Being that would have qualities of its own distinct from those of the particular Beings constituting it, rather as chemical compounds have properties that they do not derive from any of the elements that make them up. There would be a universal language that nature would teach all men, and that would be the first instrument of their mutual communication. There would be a kind of common sensorium enabling all the parts to correspond. The public good or ill would not be merely the sum of individual goods or ills as in a simple aggregation, but would reside in the bond uniting them and be greater than that sum. And far from public felicity being established upon the happiness of individuals, it would be the source of the latter.]

It is false that, in the state of independence, reason leads us to contribute to the common good from a perception of our own interest. Far from individual interest allying itself to the general good, they exclude one another in the natural order of things, and social laws are a yoke that everyone wishes to impose upon others, but not to be burdened with himself. ‘I am aware that I bring terror and distress to mankind,’ says the independent man whom the wise man stifles;1 ‘but I must either be wretched or make others wretched, and no one is dearer to me than myself.’ ‘In vain,’ he might add, ‘would I seek to reconcile my interest with that of others; all that you tell me about the advantages of the social law might well be right, if while observing it scrupulously towards others I was sure that all would observe it towards me. But what assurance of that can you give me? And can my situation be any worse than to see myself exposed to all the injuries that stronger men may wish to do me, without daring to recompense myself at the expense of the weaker? Either give me guarantees against every unjust action or do not hope that I in turn shall abstain from such. It is fruitless for you to tell me that, by renouncing the duties imposed upon me by natural law, I at the same time deprive myself of its rights, and that my acts of violence will authorize all those that people may wish to use against me. I grant it all the more readily since I do not at all see how my moderation could guarantee me against them. Furthermore, it will be my concern to win the strong to my interests by sharing with them the spoils from the weak. This will be worth more than justice for my advantage and my security.’ The proof that this is how the enlightened and independent man would have reasoned is that this is how every sovereign society reasons, accounting for its conduct only to itself.

What solid reply can be given to such arguments, if you do not wish to bring Religion to the aid of ethics, and have the will of God intervening directly to unite the society of men? But the sublime notions of the God of the wise, the sweet laws of brotherhood imposed by him, the social virtues of pure souls that are the true worship he wishes from us, will always elude the multitude. Foolish Gods will always be made for the latter in its own image, to whom it will sacrifice minor comforts only to yield to a thousand horrible and destructive passions in their honour. The whole earth would overflow with blood and mankind would soon perish if Philosophy and the laws did not hold back the furies of fanaticism, and if the voice of men were not stronger than that of the Gods.

In fact, if the notions of the great Being and natural law were innate in every heart, it was a quite superfluous concern to teach both of these expressly. That was teaching us what we already knew, and the way people set about it would have been far more apt to make us forget it. If these notions were not innate, then all men to whom God has not given them would be excused from knowing them. Once you needed specific forms of education for this, every People has its own – proved to it to be the only good ones – whence Carnage and murder more often derive than concord and peace.

So let us leave aside the sacred precepts of the various Religions, abuse of which causes as many crimes as use of them can spare, and let us yield to the Philosopher the examination of a question that the Theologian has only ever treated to mankind’s detriment.

But the former will send me back to face mankind itself, which alone has the right to decide, because the greatest good of all is the sole passion it has. It is to the general will that the individual must address himself, the Philosopher will tell me, in order to know how far he must be man, Citizen, Subject, Father, child, and when he should live and die. ‘I certainly see there, I confess, the rule that I can consult,’ our independent man will say; ‘but I do not yet see the reason that should subject me to that rule. It is not a matter of teaching me what justice is; it is a matter of showing me what interest I have in being just.’ For no one will deny that the general will is in each individual a pure act of comprehension, reasoning in the silence of passions upon what man may demand of his fellow and upon what his fellow has the right to demand of him. But where is the man who can thus separate himself from himself? And if concern for his own preservation is the first precept of nature, can you force him thus to view the species in general, in order to impose upon himself duties whose connection with his individual constitution he can by no means perceive? Do not the foregoing objections still subsist, and does it not still remain to be seen how his private interest requires him to submit to the general will?

There is more. Since the art of thus generalizing your ideas is one of the hardest and most belated exercises of human comprehension, will the average man ever be capable of drawing the rules of his behaviour from this manner of reasoning? And if it were necessary to consult the general will about a particular act, how often would it not befall a well-intentioned man to be mistaken about the rule or about its application, and to follow only his own inclination while thinking to obey the law? What shall he then do to guard himself against error? Shall he listen to his inner voice? But this voice, people say, is formed only by the habit of judging and feeling within society and according to its laws, so it cannot serve to establish these; moreover, it would be necessary for his heart not to have harboured any of those passions that speak more loudly than conscience, drown its timid voice, and cause philosophers to maintain that this voice does not exist. Shall he consult the principles of written law, the social actions of all peoples, the tacit conventions of the very enemies of mankind? The former difficulty always recurs, and it is only from the social order established among us that we draw our ideas about the one we imagine. We conceive the general society according to our particular societies, the institutions of small Republics make us think about the great Republic, and we begin truly to become men only after having been Citizens, whereby we can see what is to be thought of those supposed Cosmopolitans who, justifying their love for the fatherland by their love for mankind, boast of loving everyone in order to have the right to love no one.

What reasoning shows us in this respect is entirely confirmed by the facts, and we need only go back to high antiquity in order to see easily that the sound ideas of natural law and common brotherhood of all men spread quite belatedly, making such slow progress in the world that it was Christianity alone which generalized them sufficiently. Indeed even in the Institutes of Justinian2 we find the ancient forms of violence authorized in many respects, not merely against declared enemies, but against all that was not subject to the Empire; so that the humanity of the Romans extended no further than their dominion.

Indeed, as Grotius observes, it was long believed permissible to rob, pillage and mistreat foreigners, especially barbarians, and even reduce them to slavery. From this it comes that people would ask strangers, without shocking them, if they were Brigands or Pirates; for the craft, far from being disgraceful, was then considered honourable. The first Heroes like Hercules and Theseus who waged war against Brigands did not refrain from practising brigandage themselves; and the Greeks often called peace treaties those made between peoples who were not at war at all. The words stranger and enemy were for long synonyms among several ancient peoples, even among the Latins: Hostis enim, says Cicero, apud majores nostros [is] dicebatur, quem nunc peregrinum dicimus.3 Thus Hobbes’s error is not to have established the state of war among men once independent and grown sociable, but to have supposed that state natural to the species, and to have made it the cause of those vices of which it is the effect.4

But although there is no natural and general society among men; although they become wretched and wicked as they become sociable; although the laws of justice and equality mean nothing to those who live at once in the liberty of the state of nature and subjugated to the needs of the social state; far from thinking that there is neither virtue nor happiness for us and that heaven has abandoned us irrevocably to the depravity of our species, let us strive to draw from the malady itself the remedy that should cure it. Let us if possible correct through new associations the lack of the general association. Let our violent interlocutor himself be the judge of our success. Let us in perfected art show him redress for the ills that incipient art caused to nature. Let us show him all the wretchedness of the state he thought solid. Let him see in a better constitution of things the reward of good deeds, the punishment of evil ones, and the sweet harmony of justice and happiness. Let us enlighten his reason with new knowledge, let us warm his heart with new feelings, and may he learn to expand his being and his felicity by sharing them with his fellows. If my zeal does not blind me in this undertaking, let us not doubt that with a strong soul and a right direction this enemy of mankind will finally abjure his hatred along with his errors; that the reason which led him astray will bring him back to humanity; that to his apparent interest he will learn to prefer his interest rightly understood; that he will become good, virtuous, sensitive and finally, in sum, rather than the fierce Brigand he sought to be, the firmest bulwark of a well-ordered society.

PRINCIPLES OF THE RIGHT OF WAR

chapters.title: Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings
chapters.text:
Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

Prefatory Note

Rousseau tells us at the very beginning of the Social Contract that it is but a small piece of a much larger project which he has come to realize is beyond his powers. We know from the Confessions that this project would have been a more thoroughgoing account of political institutions. The final one-paragraph chapter of the Social Contract also tells us that the account he gives there needs to be supplemented by a theory of the external relations of states, including such questions as the right of war. To this evidence we can add a letter from Rousseau to his publisher, Marc-Michel Rey, of 9 March 1758. Rousseau informs Rey that he envisages the publication of a section of that work, under the title Principles of the Right of War, as a free-standing work. The text we now have is, very probably, most of a developed working draft of this.

The text presented here of the Principles of the Right of War is, in effect, the translation of a previously unpublished text by Rousseau. Fragments of this text have been available in earlier editions, but what we present here is a more continuous and coherent piece of writing than existed before, the version contained in the Gagnebin and Raymond Oeuvres Complètes being based on C. E. Vaughan’s attempt in 1914 to make something of a few pages published by Dreyfus Brissac in 1896 (pages that Rousseau had included with papers given to Pierre-Alexandre du Peyrou). Subsequently, further textual materials were discovered and published by Bernard Gagnebin. An important breakthrough was made in Rousseau scholarship when Grace G. Roosevelt argued that the various pieces of this text had probably been assembled in the wrong order by previous editors and proposed a reconstruction. Now Bruno Bernardi and Gabriella Silvestrini, working anew with the various manuscript materials, have put forward what looks like a comprehensive and rational version of Rousseau’s intended piece, which now fills an important lacuna in his available writings. Bernardi and Silvestrini have also done important work on the dating of the text, which they believe to have been composed in 1755–6. This dating means that Rousseau’s thinking in the piece pre-dates his engagement with the work of the abbé de Saint-Pierre.

The text presented here is based on the translation and arrangement presented by Bruno Bernardi and Gabriella Silvestrini in their edition of Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Principes du droit de la guerre, Écrits sur la paix perpetuelle (Paris: Vrin – Librairie Philosophique, 2008), under the direction of Blaise Bachofen and Céline Spector. The content of this prefatory note draws on the ‘Présentation de l’édition’ by Bernardi and Silvestrini in that volume, which readers wanting a more comprehensive account of the textual reconstruction should consult.

chapters.title: Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings
chapters.text:
Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

Principles of the Right of War

I open books on right and on ethics; I listen to scholars and jurisconsults and, convinced by their ingratiating arguments, I deplore the miseries of nature; I admire the peace and justice established by the civil order; I bless the wisdom of public institutions, and console myself for being a man by seeing myself as a citizen. Well instructed upon my duties and my good fortune, I close the book, leave the classroom, and look around me. I see wretched peoples groaning beneath an iron yoke, the human race crushed by a handful of oppressors, a host overwhelmed by misery and starved for bread whose blood and tears the rich man quaffs in peace, and everywhere the strong armed against the weak with the formidable power of the laws. All this takes place peacefully and without resistance: it is the calm of Ulysses’ companions imprisoned in the cavern of the Cyclops, waiting to be devoured. They must languish in silence. Let us draw an eternal veil over these objects of horror. I raise my eyes to gaze afar. I see fire and flame, deserted fields, towns being pillaged. Cruel men, whither are you dragging those wretches! I hear a frightful din, such commotion and such screams, I approach and perceive a scene of murder, ten thousand men butchered, the dead stacked in heaps, the dying trampled underfoot by horses, bearing the image of death and its last agony. So that is the fruit of those pacific institutions. Pity and indignation well up in the depths of my heart. O barbarous Philosopher! come read us your book on a battlefield.

What human bowels would not be stirred by those sad sights; but it is no longer permitted to be a man and plead the cause of humanity. Justice and truth must be bent to the interest of the most powerful, that is the rule. The People bestows no pension, no post, no chair, no place in the academy; for what reason should it be protected? Princes, magnanimous beings from whom we expect all, I speak in the name of the world of letters. Oppress the people with a clear conscience; it is from you alone that we expect all, the people will never be of any use to us.

How could so frail a voice make itself heard through so much venal clamour? Alas, I must hold my tongue; but might my heart’s voice not pierce so dismal a silence? No, without entering into odious details which would be taken as satirical for the very reason that they would be true, I shall limit myself as I have always done to examining human institutions by way of their principles; to correcting if possible the false ideas about them that partisan authors give us; and to ensuring at least that injustice and violence do not brazenly parade as right and equity.

The first thing I note when considering the position of the human species is a manifest contradiction in its constitution, rendering it forever unstable. From one man to the next, we live in a civil state and subject to laws. From one people to the next, each enjoys natural liberty. But this basically makes our situation worse than if these distinctions were unknown. For, living at once in social order and a state of nature, we are subjected to the disadvantages of both without finding safety in either. The perfection of social order consists, to be sure, in the collaboration of force and law; but for this it is necessary that law should direct force. Whereas in princes’ ideas about absolute independence force alone, addressing Citizens in the name of law and foreigners in the name of raison d’état, renders the latter unable and the former unwilling to resist, so that the vain name of justice serves everywhere only as a shield for violence. As for what is commonly called the right of nations,1 it is certain that for want of sanction its laws are merely chimaeras, weaker even than the law of nature. The latter at least speaks in individual hearts, whereas, since the law of nations has no guarantee apart from its usefulness to the person who submits to it, its decisions are respected only insofar as interest confirms them. In the mixed condition wherein we find ourselves, and whichever of the two systems we may favour, by doing either too much or too little we have done nothing, and placed ourselves in the worst state in which we could possibly be. This strikes me as the true origin of our public calamities.

Let us for a moment contrast these ideas with the horrible system of Hobbes, and we shall find, running quite counter to his absurd doctrine, that far from the state of war being natural to man, war was born from peace, or at least from the precautions men took to ensure a lasting peace. But before entering into this discussion, let us attempt to settle how we should conceive of the state of war.

What the State of War Is

Although these two words war and peace appear to correlate exactly, the latter contains a far broader meaning, given that you may interrupt or disturb peace in a number of ways without going so far as war. Repose, unity, concord, all the ideas of benevolence and mutual affection seem contained in this sweet word peace. It brings a plenitude of feeling to the soul, causing us to love at once our own existence and that of others; it represents the bond between beings that unites them in the universal system; it attains its full extent only in the spirit of God, who can be harmed by nothing that exists and who seeks the preservation of all the beings he has created.

The constitution of this universe does not allow all the sentient beings which compose it to share simultaneously in mutual happiness; but since the well-being of one is another’s harm, in keeping with the law of nature each gives preference to himself; and when he works for his own advantage against the interest of another, peace is instantly disturbed in regard to the one who suffers. Not only is it thus natural to repel the harm that pursues us, but when an intelligent being sees that this harm comes to him by the ill will of another, he is angered and seeks to turn it back against its author. Thence are born discord and disputes, sometimes conflicts, but not yet war.

At last, when things have reached the point where a being endowed with reason is convinced that concern for his own preservation is incompatible not just with the well-being but with the very existence of another, then he arms himself against the latter’s life and seeks to destroy him with the same passion with which he seeks to preserve himself and for the same reason. The one under attack, feeling that the security of his existence is incompatible with the existence of the aggressor, in turn with all his strength attacks the life of the one who threatens his own. This demonstrated will to mutual destruction, and all the acts that flow from it, produce a relationship between the two enemies that we call war.

It follows from this that war by no means consists in one or several unpremeditated conflicts, nor yet in homicide and murder committed in some fit of anger, but in the steady, well-considered and manifest will to destroy our enemy. For to judge that the existence of this enemy is incompatible with our well-being demands a cool head and reason, producing a durable resolve; and for the relationship to be mutual, the enemy in turn, knowing that his life is under threat, must be intent on defending it at the expense of our own. All these ideas are contained in this word war.

The public effects of this ill will reduced to action are called hostilities; but whether there are hostilities or not, the relation of war, once established, can cease only through a formal peace. Otherwise each of the two enemies, having no proof that the other has ceased to threaten his life, could not or should not cease to defend it at the expense of the other’s.

These differences give rise to certain distinctions in terminology. When parties keep one another in mutual tension by constant hostilities, that is what is properly known as waging war. On the other hand, when two declared enemies remain calm and carry out no offensive action against one another, their relationship is not thereby changed, but so long as it has no current effect it is called merely a state of war. Long wars of which parties grow weary but which they cannot bring to a halt commonly produce this state. Sometimes their animosity, far from subsiding through inaction, is merely awaiting a favourable moment to surprise the enemy; and often the state of war that relaxation produces is more dangerous than war itself.

There has been argument as to whether truces, cease-fires, the Peace of God,2 are a state of war or of peace. As the foregoing notions make clear, all these are just a modified state of war, in which the two enemies tie their hands without losing or disguising the will to harm one another. Preparations are made, arms and siege materials are amassed, all military operations other than ones specified continue. This shows clearly enough that the intentions remain unchanged. The same is true again when two Enemies meet on neutral ground without attacking one another.

Who can have imagined without shuddering the senseless system of a natural war of all against all? What a strange animal it must be that would believe its well-being depended on the destruction of its entire species. And how is it conceivable that this species, so monstrous and so detestable, could last even two generations? Yet that is how far one of the finest geniuses ever to have lived was led by his desire, or rather his passion, to establish despotism and passive obedience. So savage a principle was worthy of its purpose.

The social state, which constrains all our natural inclinations, is nevertheless incapable of annihilating them; despite our prejudices and despite ourselves they still speak in our innermost hearts, often bringing us back to the true which we abandon for pipe-dreams. If that mutual and destructive enmity was part of our constitution, then it would still make itself felt, and would thrust us back despite ourselves through every social chain. The dreadful hatred of humanity would gnaw at man’s heart. He would be anguished by the birth of his own children, would rejoice at the death of his brethren – and when he found one of them asleep, his first impulse would be to kill him.

The benevolence that causes us to participate in the happiness of our fellows, the compassion that identifies us with the person who suffers and that distresses us at his grief, would be unknown sentiments directly contrary to nature. A feeling, merciful man would be a monster, and we should be naturally what we find it so hard to become amidst the depravity that dogs us.

In vain would the sophist say that this mutual enmity is not innate and immediate, but based on the inevitable competition engendered by every individual’s right to all things; for the sentiment of this supposed right is no more natural to man than the war that the sophist derives from it. I have already said and cannot repeat too often: the mistake of Hobbes and other philosophers is to confuse natural man with the men they see before them, and to transport into one system a being who can survive only in another. Man wishes for his well-being and all that can contribute to it; that is undeniable. But in nature man’s well-being is limited to what is physically necessary. For when he has a healthy soul and his body does not ail him, what does he lack to be happy in keeping with his constitution? He who has nothing desires little; he who commands no one has little ambition. But superfluity arouses greed: the more you get, the more you desire. He who has much wants to have everything, and the lunacy of universal monarchy has never tormented the heart of any but a great king. Such is the course of nature; such is the development of the passions. A superficial philosopher observes souls kneaded and fermented countless times in the leaven of society and believes that he has observed man. But in order to know him well, you must know how to disentangle the natural gradation of his sentiments; and it is by no means among those who live in great cities that you should seek nature’s first feature imprinted on the human heart.*

But even were it true that this boundless and unconquerable greed had developed in all men to the extent that our sophist assumes, it would still not produce that state of universal war of each against all, the odious image of which Hobbes dares to outline. That unbridled desire to appropriate everything is incompatible with the desire to destroy all one’s fellows; and the victor who, having killed everyone, had the misfortune to remain alone in the world would enjoy nothing there, just because he would have everything. What good are even riches, if not to be handed on? What use would it be to him to own the entire universe, if he were its only inhabitant? What? Will his stomach devour all the fruits of the earth? Who will collect the products of all climates for him? Who will bear witness to his empire in the vast wastes that he will not inhabit? What will he do with his treasures, who will consume his foodstuffs, to what eyes will he display his power? I see. Instead of massacring everyone, he will clap everyone in irons in order at least to have Slaves. That at once changes the whole question. Since it is no longer a matter of destroying them, the state of war is abolished. Let the reader suspend his judgement here. I shall not forget to deal with this point.

Man is naturally peaceable and timorous. At the least sign of danger, his first impulse is to flee. He becomes warlike only by dint of habit and experience. Honour, interest, prejudice, vengeance, all the passions that can lead him to brave dangers and death are far from him in the state of nature. It is only after having kept company with some man that he takes the decision to attack another; and he becomes a soldier only after having been a citizen. You do not see any great propensity here to wage war on all his fellows. But I am devoting too much time to a system as revolting as it is absurd, and that has already been refuted countless times.

So there is no general war of man against man, and the human species has not been created solely in order to destroy one another. What remains to be considered is the accidental and particular war that may arise between two or more individuals.

If the law of nature were written only in human reason, it would hardly be capable of directing most of our actions. But it is engraved too in the heart of man in indelible characters, where it speaks to him more loudly than all the precepts of the Philosophers; where it cries out to him that only to preserve his own life is he allowed to sacrifice that of his fellow, and fills him with horror at spilling human blood other than in anger, even when he finds himself obliged to do so.

I suppose that in such unregulated disputes as may arise in the state of nature an angry man may sometimes kill another, either in open combat or by surprise. But when a genuine war is involved, just imagine what a strange position this same man must be in if he can preserve his life only at the expense of another’s and, by virtue of a relation established between them, one has to die for the other to live. War is a permanent state presupposing constant relations, and such relations very rarely obtain between one man and another, where among individuals everything is in a continual flux which ceaselessly changes relations and interests. So that a subject of dispute arises and ceases almost instantaneously, a quarrel begins and ends in a day, and there may be fights and murders but never or very rarely protracted enmities and wars.

In the civil state, where the life of all citizens is in the sovereign’s power and no one has the right to dispose of his own life or anyone else’s, the state of war can likewise not exist between individuals; and as for Duels, challenges, cartels, invitations to single combat, apart from the fact that these involved an illegitimate and barbarous abuse of a wholly military constitution, the result was not a genuine state of war but an individual affair that would be settled within a limited time and space, so that for a second fight a new challenge was necessary. Exception must be made for the private wars that were suspended by daily truces called ‘the Peace of God’, and that received sanction from the legal code of Saint Louis.3 But this example is unique in history.

It may further be asked if Kings, who are de facto independent of human power, might engage in personal, individual wars between themselves, independent of those of the State. This is surely a pointless question, since Princes are notoriously not in the habit of sparing others in order to expose themselves personally. Moreover, this question depends upon another, which is not up to me to decide: namely, whether or not the Prince is himself subject to the laws of the State. For if he is subject to them, his person is bound to the State and his life like that of the least Citizen belongs to it. But if the Prince is above the laws, he lives in the pure state of nature and owes no account for any of his actions either to his subjects or to Anybody.

Of the Social State

We now enter a new order of things. We are going to see men united by an artificial concord assemble to cut each other’s throats, and all the horrors of war arise from the efforts they had made to avert it. But it is important first to form more precise notions about the essence of the body politic than we have done so far. Let the reader merely reflect that it is a question here not so much of history and facts as of right and justice, and that I mean to examine things in terms of their nature rather than our prejudices.

The first society formed necessarily leads to formation of all the rest. People have to belong to it, or unite to resist it. People have to imitate it, or let themselves be swallowed up by it.

Thus the entire face of the earth is changed; everywhere nature has disappeared; everywhere human contrivance [art] has taken its place; natural independence and liberty have given way to laws and to slavery, there no longer exists any free Being; the philosopher seeks a man and no longer finds one. But it is futile to think of abolishing nature; it is reborn and reveals itself where it was least expected. The independence wrested from men takes refuge in societies; and these great bodies, given over to their own impulses, produce shocks more terrible in proportion as their mass exceeds that of individuals.

But, you will say, since each of these bodies has so solid a footing, how can they possibly ever clash with one another? Should their own constitution not keep them in everlasting mutual peace? Must they, like men, look outside for the wherewithal to meet their needs? Have they not within themselves all that is necessary for their preservation? Are competition and exchange a source of inevitable discord? But in all the countries of the world did the inhabitants not exist before commerce? Irrefutable proof that they could subsist without it.

I could content myself with replying to this with facts, without needing to fear any rejoinder. But I have not forgotten that I am reasoning here about the nature of things, and not about events that can have a thousand particular causes independent of the common principle. But let us consider attentively the constitution of political bodies. Although in the last resort each suffices for its own preservation, we shall find that their mutual relations do not fail to be far more intimate than those of individuals. For man basically has no necessary relationship with his fellows; he can survive without their help in all possible vigour. He needs not so much the care of men as the fruits of the earth; and the earth produces more than is needed to feed all its inhabitants. Add that man has a measure of strength and size fixed by nature, beyond which he cannot go. However he may view himself, he finds all his faculties limited. His life is short, his years are numbered. His stomach does not grow larger with his wealth. However much his passions increase, his joys have their measure. His heart has bounds like all the rest. His capacity for enjoyment is always the same. However high he raises himself in thought, he still remains small.

The State, by contrast, being an artificial body, has no determinate measure. The size pertaining to it is undefined; it can always increase this. It feels weak so long as any are stronger than it. Its security and self-preservation require it to make itself more powerful than all its neighbours; it can increase, sustain and exert its forces only at their expense. And if it does not need to seek its subsistence outside itself, it constantly seeks new members there who may give it a more unshakeable stability. For inequality between men has limits set by the hands of nature, but inequality between societies can grow constantly until one absorbs all the rest.

Hence, since the size of the body politic is purely relative, it is forever obliged to compare itself in order to know itself. Depending upon all that surrounds it, it must take an interest in all that occurs there. For, however much it may wish to remain within itself without gain or loss, it becomes small or large, weak or strong, according to whether its neighbour expands or contracts and grows stronger or weaker. Lastly, its very solidity, by rendering its relations more constant, gives all its actions a surer outcome and makes all its quarrels more dangerous.

People seem to have undertaken to overturn all true ideas about things. Everything inclines natural man to repose; eating and sleeping are the only needs he knows; and hunger alone drags him from idleness. People have made him out to be a madman, always ready to torment his fellows through passions of which he is wholly unaware; meanwhile such passions, heightened in society by all that can inflame them, are held not to exist there. Countless writers have dared to declare that the body politic is passionless, and that no raison d’état exists other than reason itself, as if it were not evident, on the contrary, that the essence of society consists in the activity of its members, and that a State without movement would be merely a dead body, as if all the histories of the world did not show us that the best-constituted societies are also the most active. Both within and without, the continual action and reaction of all their members testifies to the vigour of the whole body.

The difference between human contrivance and the works of nature makes itself felt in its effects. However much citizens may call themselves members of the State, they cannot become joined to it as real members are joined to the body. It is impossible to prevent each of them from having a separate, individual existence, through which he alone can provide for his own survival. The nerves are less sensitive, the muscles have less vigour, all the bonds are looser, the least mishap can dismember everything.

If you consider how inferior the public force is in the aggregate of the body politic to the sum of individual forces, and how much friction there is so to speak in the working of the whole mechanism, then you will find that the feeblest man has more strength for his self-preservation, all other things being equal, than the sturdiest State has for its own.

Hence, for this State to survive, the intensity of its passions must replace that of its movements, and its will must quicken even as its power grows slack. This is the law of conservation that nature itself establishes between species, and that maintains them all despite their inequality. It is also the reason incidentally why small States have proportionately more vigour than large ones. For public sensitivity does not increase with territory: the more this expands, the more the will cools, the more the movements weaken, and that great body overburdened by its own weight collapses, languishes and withers away.

Having seen the earth covered with new States, having discovered among them a general relationship tending towards their mutual destruction, it remains for us to see in what precisely their existence, their well-being and their life consist, in order then to find by what manner of hostilities they may attack and harm one another.

It is from the social pact that the body politic receives its unity and common self. Its government and laws make its constitution more or less sturdy. Its life is in the hearts of its citizens; their courage and their morals make it more or less durable. The only actions that it performs freely, and that may be imputed to it, are dictated by the general will; and it is by the nature of these actions that you may judge if the being which produces them is well or badly constituted.

Hence, so long as there exists a common will to observe the social pact and the laws, this pact still survives; and so long as this will manifests itself through external acts, the State is not abolished. But without ceasing to exist, it may find itself in a condition of vigour or decline, strong or weak, healthy or sick, and tending to self-destruction or self-assertion. Its well-being may increase or diminish in an infinity of ways, almost all of which depend upon it. These myriad cases are outside my scope, but here is a summary of those that do relate to it.

General Idea of War between State and State

The life principle of the body politic and so to speak the heart of the State is the social pact: once wounded there, it instantly dies, falls and is dissolved. But this pact is no charter in parchment, needing only to be torn up in order to be destroyed; it is written in the general will, where revoking it is not so easy.

Hence, being unable at first to divide the whole, they attack it in its parts. If the body is invulnerable, they wound the limbs in order to weaken it. If they cannot rob it of its existence, at least they affect its well-being. If they cannot reach the seat of life, they destroy what maintains it: they attack its government, laws, mores, goods, possessions, men. The State must surely perish, when all that preserves it is annihilated.

All these means are employed, or can be, in war between one power and another; and they are frequently also the conditions imposed by a victor in order to continue harming the vanquished once disarmed.

For the purpose of all the harm you do to your enemy through war is to force him to suffer you to do still more of the same through peace. There are no hostilities of this kind of which history does not furnish us with examples. I need not speak about pecuniary contributions, in merchandise or in foodstuffs; nor about territory stolen and inhabitants transplanted. Annual tribute in men is not even something rare. Without going back to Minos and the Athenians, we know that the emperors of Mexico attacked their neighbours only in order to have captives to sacrifice; and in our day the mutual wars of the kings of Guinea,4 and their treaties with the peoples of Europe, had no other object than tribute and trade in slaves. Neither is it hard to justify the fact that the aim and effect of war is sometimes only to change the constitution of the enemy State. The Republics of Greece used to attack each other less in order to deprive each other of liberty than to change their form of government; and they would change the government of the defeated only the better to keep them under their sway. The Macedonians and all conquerors of Sparta always made a great point of abolishing the laws of Lycurgus there, and the Romans believed that they could give no greater mark of clemency to a subjugated people than to let it keep its own laws. We also know that it was a maxim of their policy to foment among their enemies and ward off from themselves the effeminate, sedentary arts that enervate and soften men. Let us leave to the Tarentines their angry Gods, Fabius used to say, when urged to bring to Rome some of the statues and pictures with which Tarentum was adorned; and the initial decadence of Roman mores was rightly imputed to Marcellus, because he did not follow the same policy at Syracuse.5 For it is true that a skilful conqueror sometimes harms the vanquished more by what he leaves them than by what he takes from them; and that on the other hand a greedy usurper often damages himself more than his enemy by the unrestrained harm he does to him. This influence of morals has always been viewed as very important by truly enlightened princes. The only hardship that Cyrus imposed on the rebellious Lydians was a soft, effeminate life; and the way the tyrant Aristodemos went about keeping the inhabitants of Cumae beneath his sway is too curious not to be related.6

These examples suffice to give an idea of the various means whereby you may weaken a State, and those whose use is seemingly authorized by war in order to harm your enemy. With respect to the treaties for which some of these means are conditions, what at bottom are such forms of peace other than a continuation of war, with all the more cruelty in that the vanquished enemy no longer has the right to defend himself? I shall speak about this elsewhere.

Add to all this such tangible manifestations of ill will, proclaiming the intention of doing harm, as denying some power the titles due to it; failing to acknowledge its rights; rejecting its claims; depriving its subjects of commercial liberty; stirring up enemies against it; in short, infringing the right of nations in its regard upon any pretext whatsoever.

These various ways of injuring a body politic are not all equally practicable or equally useful for the one who employs them; those which redound to both our own advantage and the enemy’s detriment are naturally preferred. Land, money, men – all the spoils you can appropriate – thus become the principal objects of mutual hostilities; and since such base greed insensibly changes the ideas of things, war finally degenerates into brigandage, while little by little enemies and warriors turn into Tyrants and thieves.

Lest we unwittingly adopt these changed ideas, let us first fix our own with a definition, and try to make this so simple as to be impossible to misuse.

I call war between one power and another, therefore, the effect of a constant, demonstrated, mutual disposition to destroy the enemy State, or at least to weaken it, by all possible means. This disposition reduced to actions is war properly speaking; so long as it remains without effect it is merely the state of war.

I foresee an objection. Since according to me the state of war is natural among powers, why does the disposition from which it results need to be demonstrated? My answer is that I spoke earlier about the natural state; that I am speaking here about the legitimate state; and that I shall show later how, in order to make the latter legitimate, war needs to be declared.

Fundamental Distinctions

I beg readers not to forget that I am seeking not what makes war advantageous to the one who wages it, but what makes it legitimate. There is almost always a cost to being just. Are you then exempted from being so?

If there never was, nor could be, a genuine war between individuals, who then are those between whom it takes place, and who may really call themselves enemies? I answer that they are public persons. And what is a public person? I answer that it is the corporate being called sovereign, which the social pact has endowed with existence and all of whose wills bear the name of laws. Let us here apply the foregoing distinctions: regarding the effects of war, it is the sovereign that may be said to do harm and the State to suffer it.

If war takes place only between corporate beings, there is no hostility towards men, and it can be waged without taking anyone’s life. But this needs to be explained.

Viewing things only in strict terms of the social pact, land, money, men and all that is included within the confines of the State belongs to it unreservedly. But since the rights of society, being based on those of nature, cannot abrogate these, all such objects must be considered in a twofold light: to whit, the land as both public territory and the patrimony of individuals; goods as belonging in one sense to the sovereign and in another to the owners; inhabitants as citizens and as men. Since the body politic is basically only a corporate person, it is only a fictive being. Take away public convention, this being is instantly destroyed without the least change for the worse in whatever makes it up; and never could all the conventions of men change anything in the physical nature of things. What then does it mean to wage war on a sovereign? It means to attack public convention and all that flows from it; for the essence of the State consists in that alone. If the social pact could be severed with a single blow, there would instantly be no more war; and by that one blow the State would be killed, without a single man dying. Aristotle says that, in order to authorize the cruel treatment meted out to the Helots in Sparta, the Ephors on taking office would solemnly declare war upon them.7 This declaration was as superfluous as it was barbaric. A state of war necessarily existed between them, for no other reason than that they were respectively the masters and the slaves. Since the Lacedaemonians used to kill Helots, the Helots undoubtedly had every right to kill Lacedaemonians.
