In their memoranda the Corsicans cited this fact among their grievances. They were right, since money was necessary to pay their land taxes; those poor people, who no longer had any, were dispossessed by warrant in their homes, saw themselves stripped of their most essential utensils, their furniture, their clothes and their rags, which had to be carried from place to place and whose sale did not fetch the tenth part of their worth, so that, for want of money, they would pay the tax ten times over.

But as in our system people will no longer be forced to pay the land tax in cash, lack of money, no longer being a sign of poverty, will not serve to increase it. Barter will be able to take place in kind and without intermediary values, and people will be able to live in plenty without ever handling a penny.

I see that under the Genoese administrations, which in innumerable ways forbade and obstructed trade in foodstuffs between one province and the next, the communes would establish warehouses for wheat, wine and oil, while awaiting a moment favourable and permitted for trade; and that these warehouses served the Genoese officials as a pretext for innumerable hateful monopolies. Not being new, the idea of these warehouses will thereby be all the easier to implement, and will provide the public and individuals with a convenient, simple means for barter, without risk of the disadvantages that used to make it burdensome for the people.

Even without having recourse to real warehouses or stores, a public double-entry register could be established in each parish, where individuals could record each year, on the one side, the kind and quantity of foodstuffs they have in excess, on the other those that they lack. By balancing and comparing these registers from province to province, it would be possible to regulate the price of staples and the amount of trade in such a way that each commune would see its surplus consumed and its necessities provided for, without there being either lack or excess in the quantity and almost as easily as if its harvest were tailored to its needs.

These operations can be effected with the greatest accuracy and without real money, either through barter or with the aid of a simple ideal currency that would serve as a term of comparison such as the pistoles in France,16 or else by taking as currency some real commodity that can be numbered, as the ox was among the Greeks or the ewe among the Romans, and that is fixed at its average value; for then an ox may be worth more or less than an ox and a ewe more or less than a ewe, a difference that makes the ideal currency preferable, because it is always exact, being taken only as an abstract number.

So long as you stick to this, trade will be kept in equilibrium; barter, being regulated solely in terms of the relative abundance or scarcity of staples and the greater or lesser ease of their transport, will always and everywhere remain in a balanced relationship; and all the island’s products, equally distributed, will of themselves adjust to the level of the population. I may add that the public administration will be able without disadvantage to preside over such trade and such barter, to keep them in balance, regulate their quantity and effect their distribution, because so long as that trade and that barter are effected in kind public officials will not be able to abuse them, or even have the temptation to do so; whereas the conversion of staples into money opens the door to every kind of extortion, every kind of monopoly, every kind of knavery habitual to people in power in such cases.

You must expect many obstacles at the beginning, but such obstacles are inevitable in any new order that is being initiated and that goes against an established usage. I may add that this system, once established, will become easier year by year, not simply through practice and experience, but through the successive diminution of trade that must necessarily result from it, until this is of itself reduced to the smallest possible quantity, which is the final aim you must set yourself.

Everyone must live and no one must grow rich. That is the fundamental principle of the nation’s prosperity, and the polity which I am proposing for its part moves towards this end as directly as possible.

Surplus foodstuffs, being neither an object of commerce nor converted into money, will be cultivated only in proportion to the need people have for necessities; and anyone who can at once procure the foodstuffs he lacks will be uninterested in having too much of them.

As soon as the products of the earth are no longer merchandise, their cultivation will gradually be adapted in each province, and even in each patrimony, to the general need of the province and to the individual need of the farmer. Everyone will strive to have all the things that are necessary to him in kind and through his own farming, rather than through barter, which will always be less reliable and less convenient however much it may be facilitated.

It is an incontestable advantage to give each soil what it is most fit to produce; by this arrangement you draw more from the land, and more easily, than by any other. But important as this consideration is, it is merely secondary. It is preferable for the land to produce a bit less and for the inhabitants to be better ordered. Among all these movements of trafficking and barter, it is impossible that destructive vices should not creep into a nation. The lack of certain advantages in the choice of soil can be compensated for by labour, and it is preferable to use fields badly than men. Besides, every farmer can and must make this choice on his lands, and every parish or community on its communal holdings, as is set out below.

You will fear, I can tell, that this economy may produce a contrary effect to that which I expect of it: that instead of stimulating agriculture, it may discourage it; that the farmers, having no sale for their foodstuffs, may neglect their labours; that they may limit themselves to subsistence, without seeking abundance; and that, content with harvesting what is absolutely necessary for themselves, they may for the rest let their land lie fallow. You will even seem confirmed by the experience of the Genoese administration, under which the ban on exporting foodstuffs outside the island had produced exactly that effect.

But it must be considered that under this administration, since money was of prime necessity, it formed the immediate object of labour; consequently all labour that could not produce any such was necessarily neglected; the farmer, overwhelmed by scorn, vexations and woes, viewed his condition as the direst misfortune and, seeing that he could not meet his needs thereby, would seek another or give way to discouragement, whereas under our system all views tend to make this condition happy in its mediocrity, respectable in its simplicity. Providing all the needs of life, all public taxes without selling and without trafficking, all means of consideration, it will not allow a better or nobler to be even imagined. Those who fill this condition, seeing no one above them, will glory in it; and making their way from it to the highest positions, they will fill it like the early Romans. Being unable to leave this condition, people will wish to distinguish themselves in it: to fill it better than others, achieve larger harvests, provide a stronger contingent to the State, merit the people’s votes in elections. Numerous well-fed and well-clad families will bring honour upon their heads; and since real plenty will be the sole object of luxury, everyone will wish to distinguish himself by that sort of luxury. So long as the human heart remains what it is, such institutions will not produce idleness.

What individual magistrates and family heads must do in each jurisdiction, in each commune, on each patrimony, in order not to need others, the general government of the island must do in order not to need the neighbouring peoples.

An accurate record of goods that have entered the island over a certain number of years will provide a sure and faithful list of those without which it cannot do; for the current situation there is not one where luxury and excess can exist. With careful observations both on what the island produces and on what it can produce, you will find that foreign necessities are reduced to very little; this is wholly confirmed by the facts, since in the years 1735 and ’36, when the island was blockaded by the Genoese navy and had no communication with the mainland, not only was nothing lacking there in terms of victuals, but no needs of any kind were unendurable. Those which were most keenly felt were war munitions, leather, cotton for wicks – and even this last was provided for by the pith of certain reeds.

From this small number of necessary imports, you must further cut out everything that the island does not provide now but can provide, if better cultivated and invigorated by industry. The more the idle arts, the arts of pleasure and softness, must be carefully eliminated, the more those that are useful for agriculture and advantageous to human life must be encouraged. We need neither sculptors nor goldsmiths, but we do need carpenters and blacksmiths; we need weavers, good workers in wool, and not embroiderers or drawers of gold thread.

You will begin by providing yourselves with the most essential raw materials, namely wood, iron, wool, leather, hemp and flax. The island used to abound in wood both for construction and for heating, but you should not rely on this abundance and leave the use and felling of forests merely to the discretion of their owners. As the island’s population grows and clearances increase, there will be rapid devastation of the woods that you will be able to repair only very slowly. Regarding this, precautionary lessons can be drawn from the country where I live. Switzerland was formerly covered by woods in such abundance that it was hampered by them. But the multiplication of pastures and the establishment of manufactures alike led to these being felled without restraint or method. Now those immense forests display only virtually bare rock. Luckily, warned by the example of France, the Swiss saw the danger and regulated matters so far as lay within their power. It remains to be seen whether their precautions are not too late; for if, despite these precautions, their woods dwindle daily, it is clear that they must eventually be destroyed.

Corsica, tackling things in better time, will not have the same danger to fear. You must establish rigorous control of the forests early on, and regulate their felling in such a way that reproduction matches consumption. You must not do as in France, where the Masters of Rivers and Forests,17 who have rights over the felling of trees, have an interest in destroying the lot: an aim that they pursue to the best of their ability. You must foresee the future well in advance. Although it is not at present the right time to establish a navy, the time will come when this will have to be done, and then you will be aware of the advantage of not having given up to foreign navies the fine forests that lie close to the sea. You must exploit or sell the old woods that are no longer profitable, but you must leave standing all those that are in their prime. There will be a use for them when the time comes.

People say that a copper mine has been found on the island, but iron mines are worth even more, and there certainly are some on the island. The situation of the mountains, the nature of the terrain, the thermal springs to be found in the province of Cap Corse and elsewhere – all this makes me think that many such mines will be found if you look carefully and use capable people for the search. On this assumption, you will not allow their exploitation indiscriminately, but will choose the most favourable sites, closest to woods and streams for the establishment of forges, and where you will be able to open up the easiest routes for transport.

You will pay the same attention to manufactures of every kind, each in its respective materials, in order to facilitate labour and distribution as much as possible. However, you will take care not to create these kinds of establishment in the most populous and most fertile parts of the island. On the contrary, all things being equal you will choose the most arid lands, ones that would remain deserted if they were not populated through industry. By doing this, you will have some additional problems in supplying them with what they need; but the advantages you will find thereby, and the disadvantages you will avoid, should easily outweigh any such consideration.

Firstly, we shall be following here our first great principle, which is not just to extend and multiply the population, but to equalize it as far as possible throughout the whole island. For if the barren places were not populated through industry, they would remain deserted and that would be so much the more lost for the potential advancement of the nation.

If you formed similar establishments in fertile places, the abundance of victuals and the profit of labour – necessarily greater in the arts than in agriculture – would, by diverting farmers or their families from rural concerns and gradually depopulating the countryside, oblige new settlers to be drawn in from far away in order to cultivate the latter. Hence, by overloading certain parts of the territory with inhabitants we should depopulate others, and by thus breaking the balance we should indirectly go against the spirit of our institutions.

The transport of staples, by making them more costly in the factories, will thereby diminish the profit of the workers; this will keep their condition closer to that of the farmer, thus better maintaining the balance between them. This balance, however, cannot be such that the advantage does not always lie with industry, either because the money that is in the state flows there in greater abundance, or through the chance means whereby power and inequality come into play, or thanks to the greater strength possessed by a number of men assembled, which the ambitious know how to harness to their own advantage. It is important, therefore, that this over-favoured part should remain dependent upon the rest of the nation for its subsistence; in case of internal divisions, it is in the nature of our institutions that it should be the farmer who lays down the law to the worker.

With precautions, you may safely encourage the establishment of useful arts on the island, and I doubt not but that these creations well run may be able to provide for all that is necessary, without needing to bring anything from outside, apart from a few trifles, for which you will allow a proportionate export, always carefully balanced by the administration.

I have so far shown how the Corsican people could subsist in ease and independence with very little trading; how the bulk of what little it will find necessary can easily be acquired by barter; and how it can reduce almost to nothing the need for imports from outside the island. You can see by this that, if the use of money and cash cannot be wholly abolished in the affairs of individuals, it can be reduced at least to so little that abuses are unlikely to arise from it; that no fortunes will be made by such means; and that if any could be made, they would become almost useless and give little advantage to their owners.

But how shall we govern the public finances? What revenues shall we assign to their administration? Shall we establish it as free, or how shall we regulate its upkeep? That is what we must now consider.

Financial systems are modern inventions. The word ‘finance’ was no more known to the ancients than were our land taxes or capitation.18 The word vectigal19 was understood differently, as will be made clear below. The sovereign instance would impose tribute on conquered or defeated peoples, never on its direct subjects especially in republics. Far from the people of Athens being burdened with taxes, the government used on the contrary to pay it. And Rome, to whom her wars must have been so costly, would often distribute wheat and even land to the people. The State nevertheless subsisted, maintained great armies on sea and land, carried out sizeable public works and incurred expenses at least as great as are made proportionately by modern States. How was this done?

Two epochs must be distinguished in States: their beginning and their growth. In the beginning of a State, it would have no other revenue than the public domain, and this domain would be considerable. Romulus formed it from a third of all estates. He allocated the second third for the upkeep of Priests and sacred things; the remaining part alone was shared among the citizens. It was little, but that little was freely held. Do you not think that the French husbandman would willingly be reduced to one-third of what he cultivates, on condition of having that third free from any land tax, quit-rent [cens] or tithe, and not paying any kind of duty?

Hence, the public revenue was not taken in money, but in foodstuffs and other produce. Expenditures were of the same kind as takings. Neither magistrates nor troops were paid, they were fed and provided with uniforms; and in times of pressing need, the extraordinary burdens on the people consisted of forced labour rather than money. Those splendid public works cost the State almost nothing; they were the work of those formidable legions, which toiled just as they fought, and which were made up not of riff-raff but of citizens.

When the Romans began to expand and became conquerors, they took the upkeep of their troops from the conquered peoples; when they paid them, their subjects were taxed, never the Romans. In times of pressing danger, the Senate raised a subscription, took out loans that it returned faithfully, and, during the whole course of the Republic, I do not know of the Roman people ever having paid a pecuniary tax, either by head or on its estates.

There is a fine model for you, O Corsicans! Do not be surprised at there being more virtue among the Romans than elsewhere: money was less necessary there. The State had small revenues and did great things. Its wealth was in the lives of its citizens. I might say that, thanks to the situation of Corsica and thanks to the form of her government, there will be none in the whole world less costly. For, being an island and a Republic, she will have no need of regular troops; and the leaders of the State, all reverting to equality, will not be able to draw anything from the common mass that will not very speedily return to it.

But this is not how I envisage the sinews of your public force. On the contrary, I wish a great deal to be spent on the State service. More precisely, I am arguing only about the choice of currency. I view finances as the fat of the body politic, which by congealing in certain muscular systems overloads the body with a useless corpulence and makes it heavy rather than strong. I wish to feed the State with a healthier diet, that will merge into its substance; that will change into muscle and fibre without clogging the vessels; that will give the limbs vigour rather than size; and that will strengthen the body without weighing it down.

Far from wishing the State to be poor, I should on the contrary wish it to have everything, and for each man to have a share of the common property only in proportion to his services. The acquisition of all the Egyptians’ goods to which Joseph persuaded the King would have been good, if he had not done too much or too little.20 But without going into such hypotheses, which distract me from my purpose, it is enough to elucidate my thought here: which is not to destroy individual property absolutely, because that is impossible, but to confine it within narrower limits; to give it a measure, a rule and a brake that may contain it, direct it, subjugate it, and keep it always subordinated to the public good. In a word, I wish the State’s property to be as large and strong, and that of citizens to be as little and weak, as possible. That is why I avoid putting it in things whose individual owner is too much the master, such as cash and money, which are easily hidden from public inspection.

The establishment of a public domain is, I admit, not as easy a thing to do today in Corsica, already shared out between her inhabitants, as it was in Rome at her birth, before her conquered territory as yet belonged to anyone. However, I know that there remains on the island a large quantity of excellent untilled land, of which it is very easy for the government to take advantage: either by alienating it for a certain number of years to those who will put it under cultivation; or by having it tilled through forced labour [corvées],21 organized in each community. One would need to have been on the ground, in order to judge how this land might be distributed, and what profit might be drawn from it. But I have no doubt but that, by means of a few exchanges and certain quite simple agreements, it would be possible in each jurisdiction and even each commune to procure communal funds, which may even increase before many years have gone by, thanks to the system about which we shall speak in relation to the law on inheritance.

Another still simpler means, which should provide a more definite, more certain and far more considerable income, is to follow an example that I have before my eyes in the Protestant cantons. During the Reformation in these cantons, they seized the ecclesiastical tithes; and these tithes, with which they maintained their clergy decently, formed the principal income of the State. I am not saying that the Corsicans should touch the revenues of the Church, God forbid! But I think that the people will not be very much put out if the State asks it for as much as is asked of it by the clergy, already adequately endowed with property in land. The basic funding for this tax will be established without trouble or impediment, and at almost no cost, since you need only double the ecclesiastical tithe and take half of it.

I draw a third kind of revenue, the most reliable and best, from men themselves, by using their labour, their arms and their hearts rather than their purses in the fatherland’s service, whether for its defence in the militia or for its comforts through forced labour on public works.

Let republicans not take fright at this term ‘forced labour’! I know that it is abominated in France, but is it in Switzerland? The roads there are built also by forced labour, and no one complains. The seeming convenience of payment can seduce only superficial minds; and it is a certain maxim that the fewer the intermediaries between the need and the service, the less burdensome the service should be.

Without daring to set out my thinking entirely, without here presenting forced labour and all private labour by citizens as an absolute good, I shall agree, if you will, that it would be better for it all to be done by payment if the means of payment did not introduce a host of unrestrained abuses and greater ills, more limitless than those which can result from constraint, especially when the person imposing the latter belongs to the same state as those upon whom it is imposed.

Moreover, in order that the contribution should be shared equally, it is right that a person who has no land, so cannot pay the tithe from its produce, should pay it with the labour of his arms; hence, forced labour should fall especially on the order of candidates. But citizens and patriots must lead them to labour and set them an example. Let all that is done for the public good always be honoured! Let the very magistrate, busy with other cares, show that these ones are not beneath him, like those Roman consuls who, to set an example to their troops, would be the first to turn their hands to camp labours!

As for fines and confiscations, which in republics constitute a fourth kind of revenue, I hope that thanks to these present institutions this may be reduced almost to nothing in our republic, so I take no account of it.

Since all these public revenues are in physical kind rather than in cash, they appear cumbersome to collect, to store and to use. And this is partly true, but what matters here is less the easiest administration than the healthiest; so it is preferable for it to be a little more cumbersome but engender less abuse. The best economic system for Corsica or for a republic is assuredly not the best for a monarchy or a great State. The one I am proposing would not succeed either in France or in England, and could not even be established there. But it has the greatest success in Switzerland, where it has been established for centuries and is the only system the country could have borne.

The revenues are farmed out in each jurisdiction; they are made in kind or in money as the taxpayer chooses; the payment of magistrates and officials is likewise effected for the most part in wheat, in wine, in fodder, in timber. In this way, tax collection is neither burdensome for the public nor onerous for individuals; but the disadvantage I see here is that there are men whose profession is to earn from the prince and to harass the subjects.

It is of extreme importance not to permit any financier by profession in the republic: less because of their dishonest profits than because of their principles and their example, which, spreading too rapidly throughout the nation, destroy all good sentiments through esteem for illicit plenty and its advantages; which heap scorn and opprobrium upon disinterestedness, simplicity, morals and all virtues.

Let us take care not to increase pecuniary wealth at the expense of moral wealth. It is the latter which truly places us in possession of men and all their power, whereas through the former we obtain only the semblance of their services, but cannot buy their will. It is preferable for the exchequer to be run by a family man and lose something than to be run by a usurer and take in more.

Let us, therefore, leave tax collection under state administration, even should it bring in far less. Let us even avoid making this administration into a profession, for that would have almost the same disadvantage as farming it out. What makes a financial system most pernicious is the role of financier. At all costs, there must be no publicans in the State.22 Instead of making collection by the state and public revenues into a lucrative profession, they should on the contrary be made into a test of the merit and integrity of young citizens. The tax administration must be, so to speak, the apprenticeship for public posts and the first step towards reaching magistracies. What suggested this idea to me is the comparison between the administration of the Hôtel-Dieu in Paris, whose depredations and brigandry are known to one and all, and that of the Hôtel-Dieu in Lyons,23 which offers an example of order and disinterestedness that has perhaps no equal on earth. Whence does this difference come? Are the Lyonnais in themselves worth more than the Parisians? No. But in Lyons that administrative office is a state of passage. You must begin by filling it well in order to become a town councillor [échevin] or municipal leader [prévôt des marchands], whereas in Paris administrators are such by profession for life. They arrange to derive the greatest possible advantage from a post that is no kind of test for them, but a profession, a recompense, a calling so to speak attached to other callings. There are certain positions whose income, it is understood, will be augmented by the right to rob the poor.

And you should not think that this work requires more experience and learning than young people can have; it requires merely an activity for which they are particularly suited. And since they are normally less greedy, less harsh in exaction than older people – on the one hand, sensitive to the poor man’s miseries; on the other, keenly interested in filling well a post that serves them as a test – they conduct themselves in it exactly as the matter requires.

Each parish’s tax collector will present his accounts to his commune, each commune’s to his jurisdiction, and each jurisdiction’s to the auditing chamber, which will be made up of a certain number of State councillors and presided over by the Doge. The public exchequer will in this way consist for the most part of foodstuffs and other produce, scattered among small warehouses throughout the realm; and it will consist partly of money, which will be lodged in the general coffers, after the disbursement of minor expenses to be made on the spot.

As individuals will always be free to pay their quota in money or in staples, at a rate that will be fixed annually in each jurisdiction, once the government has calculated the best ratio that should obtain between these two types of contribution, as soon as this ratio alters it will be able forthwith to register the alteration, seek its cause and remedy it.

Here is the key to our political government, the only part that requires skill, calculation and mediation. This is why the auditing chamber, which everywhere else is merely a very junior court, will here be at the centre of affairs, give impetus to the entire administration and be composed of the State’s foremost brains.

When the collection of foodstuffs exceeds its target and that of money fails to attain it, that will be a sign that all is well with agriculture and the population, but that useful industry is being neglected and will have to be revived somewhat, for fear that individuals may also grow too isolated, independent and wild, hence may no longer sufficiently value the government.

But this lack of proportion, an infallible sign of prosperity, will always hold few fears and be easy to remedy. The same will not be the case with the opposite lack, which as soon as it makes itself felt is already of the greatest consequence and cannot be too soon corrected. For when the taxpayers provide more money than food, that will be a sure sign that there is too much exporting abroad; that commerce is becoming too weak; that profit-making skills are spreading on the island at the expense of agriculture; hence, that simplicity and all its attendant virtues are starting to decline. The abuses that produce this deterioration indicate the remedies that should be applied; but these remedies require great wisdom in the manner of administering them, for here it is far easier to prevent the malady than to destroy it.

If you merely put duties on luxury items, close your ports to foreign commerce, suppress manufactures, and halt the circulation of specie, you will only cast the people into idleness, misery and discouragement. You will cause money to disappear without increasing foodstuffs. You will remove the resource of wealth without re-establishing that of labour. Interfering with the price of currencies is still a bad course of action in a republic. Firstly, because it is then the public which steals from itself, which means nothing at all. Secondly, because between the quantity of tokens and the quantity of things there is a proportion that always likewise regulates their respective values; and because, when the Prince wishes to change the tokens, he changes only the names, since then the value of things necessarily changes in the same proportion. With kings things are different, and when the Prince raises the face value of the coinage he derives the real advantage of stealing from his creditors.24 But once this operation is repeated, the advantage is offset and erased by the loss of public trust.

Establish sumptuary laws, then, but always make them harsher for the foremost in the State, relax them for the lower orders. Ensure that there is pride in being simple, and that a rich man will be unable to derive honour from his money. These are by no means impracticable fantasies. For it is thus that the Venetians grant only to their nobles the right to wear their coarse, ugly black Padua cloth, so that the best citizens will consider it an honour to have the same permission.

When there is simplicity in mores, agrarian laws are necessary; for then the rich man, being unable to place his wealth in anything else, accumulates his estates. But neither agrarian laws nor any other laws can ever have retroactive effect; and no lands legitimately acquired can be confiscated, whatever their quantity may be, on the basis of a later law forbidding ownership of so much.

No law can strip any individual of any portion of his property. The law can merely prevent him from acquiring more of it. Then, if he infringes the law, he deserves punishment and the unlawfully acquired surplus can and should be confiscated. The Romans saw the necessity of agrarian laws when it was too late to establish them; and, for lack of the distinction I have just made, they finally destroyed the Republic by a means that should have preserved it: the Gracchi wished to strip the patricians of their lands, whereas they should have been prevented from acquiring them. It is quite true that subsequently those same patricians acquired more lands in spite of the law; but the fact was that the evil was deeply rooted when the law was introduced, and it was too late to remedy it.

Fear and hope are the two instruments with which to govern men. But instead of employing both indiscriminately, they must be used according to their nature. Fear does not stimulate, it restrains; and its use in penal laws is not to induce to act well but to prevent from doing wrong. We do not even see fear of destitution make idlers hardworking. Hence, to stimulate among men a genuine emulation in work, it should be presented to them not as a means of avoiding hunger, but as a means of advancing to prosperity. Let us, therefore, posit this general rule: that no one should be punished for having abstained, but for having done.

Thus to awaken a nation’s activity you must present it with great desires, great hopes, great positive motives for acting. The great motivations that make men act are reduced, when examined carefully, to two: sensual delight [volupté] and vanity. Moreover, if you remove from the former all that belongs to the latter, you will find in the last analysis that everything is reduced almost solely to vanity. It is easy to see that all those who find delight in display are merely vain. Their supposed delight is mere ostentation: it consists more in being shown or described than in being savoured. True pleasure is simple and peaceful, it loves silence and contemplation; the one who savours it is wholly absorbed therein and does not spend his time saying: ‘I feel pleasure!’ Well, vanity is the fruit of opinion, born from it and fed by it. With the consequence that the arbiters of a people’s opinion are arbiters of its actions too. The people seeks things in proportion to the price it puts on them; showing it what it should esteem is telling it what it should do.

This term ‘vanity’ is not well chosen, because it is merely one of the two branches of amour propre. I must explain. The opinion that puts a high price on frivolous objects produces vanity; but that which falls upon objects that are great and fine in themselves produces pride. You can thus make a people proud or vain depending on the choice of objects towards which you direct its judgements.

Pride is more natural than vanity, since it consists in esteeming yourself for truly estimable qualities; whereas vanity, putting value on what has no value, is the work of prejudices slow to arise. You need time to fascinate the eyes of a nation. As there is nothing more truly fine than independence and power, every people that is formed is at first proud. But never was a new people vain, since vanity by its nature is individual; it cannot be the instrument of so great a thing as forming a national body.

Two opposite states cast men into the torpor of idleness. One is that peace of mind which ensures that you are satisfied with what you possess; the other is an insatiable covetousness which proclaims the impossibility of satisfying it. The man who lives without desires and the man who knows he cannot obtain what he desires alike remain inactive. In order to act, you must both aspire to something and have some hope of attaining it. Any government wishing to stimulate activity in the people must take care to place within the latter’s reach objects capable of tempting it. Ensure that work offers citizens great advantages, not merely in your own estimation, but in theirs; you will infallibly make them hardworking. Among these advantages, not only are riches not always the most attractive, but they can be less so than any other, as long as they do not serve as a means to attain those by which one is tempted.

The most general and most reliable way you can have to satisfy your desires, whatever these may be, is power. Thus to whatever passions a man or a people may be inclined, if such passions be vigorous he will have a vigorous aspiration to power, either as an end if he is proud or vain, or as a means if he is vengeful or a sensualist.

Hence, it is in the well-arranged economy of civil power that the great art of government consists, not merely in order to maintain itself, but in order to extend activity and life throughout the State; in order to make the people active and hardworking.

Civil power is exercised in two ways: one legitimate, through authority; the other abusive, through wealth. Wherever wealth dominates, power and authority are usually separated, because the means of acquiring wealth and the means of attaining authority, not being the same, are rarely employed by the same people. Hence, apparent power is in the hands of magistrates and real power is in the hands of the wealthy. Under such a government, everything proceeds at the whim of men’s passions, nothing tends towards the institutional ends.

It then happens that the object of desire divides: some aspire to authority in order to sell its use to the wealthy and by this means enrich themselves; others, more numerous, aim directly at wealth, with which they are sure one day to have power, by buying either authority or those who are its depositaries.

Suppose that in a State thus constituted, on the one hand honours and authority are hereditary, and on the other hand the means of acquiring wealth are within reach of only a small number, and depend upon credit, favour, friends. It is then impossible that, while a few adventurers proceed to fortune and thereby gradually to employment, the bulk of the nation should not be overwhelmed by universal discouragement and cast into listlessness.

[Disconnected fragments]

Hence, in every rich nation the government is generally weak, and I term as such alike the government that acts only with weakness and, which comes to the same thing, that which needs violent means to maintain itself.

I can clarify my thought no better than by the example of Carthage and Rome. The former would massacre and crucify her generals, her magistrates and her members, and was merely a weak government forever frightened and shaken by everything. The latter would take no one’s life, nor even seize his goods; the accused criminal could depart in peace and the trial end there. The vigour of that admirable government had no need for cruelty. The greatest of misfortunes was to be excluded from its membership.

Peoples will be industrious when work is honoured, and it is always up to the government to make it so. If esteem and authority are within the Citizens’ reach, they will strive to attain them; but if they see them as too far away, they will not take a step. What casts them into despond is not the scale of the work but its futility.

I shall be asked if it is by tilling your field that you acquire the necessary talents to govern. I shall answer yes, in a simple and upright government like our own. Great talents are a substitute for patriotic ardour; they are necessary to guide a people that does not love its country and does not honour its leaders. But make the people feel affection for the res publica, seek virtues, and leave your great talents be they would do more harm than good. A government’s best motivation is love of the fatherland, and this love is cultivated along with the land. Common sense is enough to guide a well-constituted State, and common sense is developed as much in the heart as in the head; men not blinded by their passions always act well.

Men are naturally lazy, but enthusiasm for work is the first fruit of a well-regulated society; and when a people relapses into idleness and discouragement, it is always thanks to the abuse of that same society, which no longer accords work the price it has a right to expect.

Wherever money rules, that which the people gives to maintain its liberty is always the instrument of its enslavement, and what it pays voluntarily today is used to force it to pay tomorrow.

Every child born in the Island shall be a citizen and member of the Republic when he comes of age while following the statutes, and no one shall be able to become such other than in that way.

Hence, it will not be possible to grant civil rights to any foreigner – except once in fifty years, to just one, if he should present himself and be judged worthy, or the most worthy of those presenting themselves; his reception will be a general festival throughout the Island.

Every Corsican who on completing forty years is not married and never has been shall be excluded from Civil rights for his entire life.

Every individual who in changing domicile moves from one commune to another shall lose his Civil rights for three years, and at the end of this time shall be registered in the new commune by paying a due, without which he shall continue to be excluded from Civil rights until he has paid.

All those who perform some public office shall be exempted from the foregoing provision; they must be admitted to all Civil rights in whichever commune they may find themselves in, so long as they are on duty.

The Corsicans were subjected to the Genoese. It is well known what kind of treatment obliged them to revolt, almost forty years ago. Since that time they have maintained themselves in independence. Yet the Gazetteers25 still call them rebels, and who knows for how many centuries they will continue to call them thus. The present generation has not seen servitude: it is hard to conceive how a man born free, and who keeps himself such, is a rebel, while a fortunate usurper after two or three years is a consecrated monarch, a legitimate King. Thus the amnesty takes place only in favour of Tyranny, it is never admitted in favour of liberty. This attitude is as rational in itself as it is honourable for its supporters. Fortunately words are not things. Redeemed at the cost of their blood, the Corsicans, rebels or no, are free and worthy of being so despite the Genoese and the Gazetteers.

In each commune a register shall be kept of all the lands that each individual holds.

No one shall be able to own lands outside his commune.

No one shall be able to own more than … plots of land. Anyone having this quantity shall be able, through exchanges, to acquire similar quantities but no larger, even of less good land. And all gifts or bequests that may be made to him in land shall be null.

Because for three years you have governed a free people justly, it entrusts the same administration to you for a further three years.

No man under age shall be able to make a will, but all his property shall pass to the community.

Corsicans, be silent, I am going to speak in the name of everyone. Let those who do not agree depart, and let those who do agree raise their hands.

This act will have to be preceded by a general proclamation, enjoining upon everyone to repair to the place of his domicile within a time that will be prescribed, on pain of losing his born and natural rights.

I. The whole Corsican nation shall through a solemn oath come together in a single body politic, of which both the bodies that must form the nation and individuals will henceforth be members.

II. This act of union shall be celebrated on the same day throughout the island, and all Corsicans shall attend so far as possible, each in his town, village or parish, as he is more specifically instructed.

III. Formula for the oath, pronounced in the open air with hand on Bible:

In the name of all-powerful God and on the holy Gospels, by a sacred and irrevocable oath I unite my body, my goods, my will and all my power with the Corsican nation, to belong to it in full ownership, myself and all that depends upon me. I swear to live and die for it, to observe all its laws and obey its legitimate leaders and magistrates, in everything that conforms with the laws. So may God succour me in this life and have mercy on my soul. May liberty, justice and the Republic of the Corsicans live for ever. Amen.

All shall raise their right hands and reply: Amen.

Each parish shall keep an accurate register all those who have attended this solemn celebration. Their name, their father’s name, their age and their domicile shall be noted down in it.

As for those who are unable, because of valid impediments, to attend this solemn celebration, they shall be allocated other days to take the same oath and have themselves registered, within a period of three months at the latest after the solemn oath: after this period, all those who have neglected to fulfil this duty shall be debarred from their right, and shall remain in the Class of foreigners or candidates to be discussed below.

A country enjoys its greatest independent strength when the land in it produces as much as possible, in other words when the land has as many farmers as it requires.

For each child he has above the number of five, he shall be allocated a patrimony by the commune.

Fathers who have absent children shall be able to register them only after their return, and those remaining outside the Island for a whole year shall no longer be able to be registered, even after their return.

They will be diverted from superstition by keeping them very busy with their duties as citizens; by investing national festivals with pomp; by greatly reducing the time accorded to ecclesiastical ceremonies, in order to give it to civil ceremonies; and with a little adroitness this can be done without angering the Clergy, by ensuring that it always does play some part, but that this part is small enough for public attention not to remain fixed upon it.

Of all ways of living, that which most binds men to their country is rural life.

The Guardians of the Laws shall be able to convoke the states general as often as they please and, from the day of convocation until the morrow of the assembly, the authority of the grand Podestat and the council of State shall be suspended.

The person of the guardians of the laws shall be sacred and inviolable, and there shall be no one in the island having the power to arrest them.

Each commune shall have the right to recall its people and replace them with others, as often as it pleases; but unless they have been expressly recalled, they shall be for life.

Once the states general have been convoked extraordinarily by the Senate, they shall not be able to be dissolved unless the Senate or the grand Podestat have been overturned.

The Laws regarding estates must always tend to bring things back to equality, so that each man may have something and no one have too much.

Every Corsican who leaves his commune to go and reside in another shall lose his civil rights for three years. At the end of this time, upon his request and a proclamation, if nothing comes up against him he shall be inscribed in the registers of the new commune, and into the same order in which he was inscribed in the other: citizen if he was a citizen, patriot if he was a patriot, and candidate if he was only a candidate.

And the Corsicans had to pay tribute in order to win the favour of being disarmed.

There shall be no carriage in the Island: Ecclesiastics and women will be able to use two-wheeled chaises. But lay people of any rank whatsoever shall be able to travel only on foot or horseback, unless they are crippled or seriously ill.

No one shall be admitted to the oath in matters concerning his own interests. But the oath …

No one shall be able to be imprisoned for debt, and even in such seizures as may be made in the house of a debtor he shall be left, apart from the clothes to cover himself, with his plough, his oxen, his bed, and his most indispensable items of furniture.

Every boy who marries before the age of a full twenty years, or only after the age of a full thirty years, or who weds a girl having less than a full fifteen years, or a person – girl or widow – whose age differs from his own by more than twenty years, shall remain excluded from the order of citizens, unless he attains it as a public reward for services rendered to the State.

In view of the unequal distribution of the island’s produce, communications must not be closed; in some things regard must be shown for the prejudices and short-sightedness of the people. Seeing that it was not allowed to go about the neighbourhood to seek from among its compatriots the foodstuffs that it lacked, the people would accuse our laws of caprice and harshness; it would mutiny against them, or hate them in secret.

If we were able to do without money and have all the advantages that money gives, we should enjoy those advantages far better than with riches, since we should have them separated from the vices that poison them, and that money brings with it.

No one should be a magistrate by station or a soldier by station. Everyone should be ready to fulfil indiscriminately those functions that the fatherland imposes upon them. There should be no other permanent station in the Island than that of citizen, and that station alone should embrace all others.

So long as money is useful to the Corsicans, they will love it; and so long as they love it, the Republic will foster agents and traitors who will influence its deliberations and, so to speak, keep the State on the purse-strings of its former masters.

You must not rely upon a lively but always short-lived enthusiasm in the wake of your recovered liberty. Popular heroism is a moment of passion followed by languor and slackness. The liberty of a people must be based on its way of being, and not on its passions. For passions are transitory and change their object; but the effect of a good constitution lasts as long as it does; and no people would be able to remain free for longer than it was satisfied with liberty.

Let them remember well that privileges of every kind are advantageous to the individuals who obtain them, and burdensome to the nation that grants them.

This is the ridiculous contradiction into which all violent governments fall: seeking to keep peoples in a state of weakness, they nevertheless through them seek to place themselves in a state of strength.

The nation will not be illustrious, but it will be happy. It will not be talked about; it will not be held in high esteem abroad, but it will have plenty, peace and liberty at home.

Any advocate who has rejected the arbitration of the elders, or who after accepting it refuses to rely upon their judgement, if he loses his case in ordinary justice will be noted down and unable for five years to exercise any public function.

Any citizen’s daughter who marries a Corsican, of whatever class he may be, will receive a dowry from the husband’s commune; this dowry will always be a plot of land, and will be enough if he is a candidate to raise him to the class of patriots.

Of all governments, the Democratic is always the least costly, because public luxury consists only in abundance of men; and where the people is master, its power has no need of any spectacular sign.

For if two or several States are subjected to the same prince, that has nothing contrary to law or reason. But if a State is subjected to another State, that seems incompatible with the nature of the body politic.

Although I know that the Corsican nature has prejudices very opposed to my principles, my intention is not to employ the art of persuasion to make them adopt the latter. On the contrary, I seek to tell them my opinion and my reasons with such simplicity that there is nothing that might seduce them, because it is very possible that I am mistaken, and because I should be very vexed were they to adopt my view to their own disadvantage.

What caused the conflicts, quarrels and civil wars that racked Corsica for so many years, forcing her eventually to have recourse to the Pisans, and then the Genoese? Was all that not the work of her nobility? Was it not the latter that reduced the people to despair, forcing it to choose a tranquil enslavement over the ills it used to suffer under so many Tyrants? Now that the yoke has been cast off, does the people wish to return to the condition that obliged it to accept that yoke?

I shall not preach morality to them, I shall not order them to have virtues, but I shall place them in such a position that they will have virtues without knowing the word; such that they will be good and just without knowing much about what justice and goodness are.

I do not know how it comes about, but I do know that those operations for which the largest number of records and account-books are kept are precisely those in which there is most theft.

Such were those young Romans who would begin by being quaestors or treasurers of armies before commanding them. Such financiers would not be base men; it would never so much as enter their heads that it was possible to make a profit from the public purse; and the military coffers could without risk be entrusted to the Catos.26

Instead of [suppressing] luxury by sumptuary laws, it is better to prevent it by an administration that makes it impossible.

I am convinced that if you search thoroughly you will find iron mines on the Island; it would be better to find iron mines there than gold mines.

And even when in doubt, it is better to begin by the state that leads naturally to the other, and from which you may always pass on to the latter if you hope to be happier there, rather than by the state from which you can no longer return to the former, and which has nothing ahead of it except destruction and ruin.

Le prerogative che goderanno le sudette famiglie …27 [The prerogatives that the families mentioned below will enjoy …].

This provision is destructive of the spirit of the republic, which requires the soldier to be thoroughly subordinated to the magistrate and to see himself merely as the minister of the ministers of the law. It is extremely important that the soldier should not in himself be an estate, but an accidental form of the estate of citizen. If the nobility had prerogatives and Army distinctions, military Officers would soon believe themselves above civil officials; the leaders of the Republic would be seen merely as Lawyers, and the State under military government would very rapidly succumb to despotism.

An excellent means of learning to relate everything to the law is to see the man who has been so much respected while in office return to private life; and for him himself it is a great lesson to uphold the rights of individuals to be assured that one day he will find himself among their number.

For example, the province of Cap Corse being unable to produce anything other than wine, you must prevent so much being cultivated in all the rest of the Island that this part is no longer able to sell its own.

For individual property being so weak and so dependent, the Government needs but little strength and guides peoples, so to speak, by moving a finger.

Where are the Princes who think of assembling Theologians to consult about whether what they wish to undertake is legitimate?

Pre[face]

I have a deep respect for the Republic of Genoa. I respect every sovereign in particular, although I sometimes tell them all rather harsh truths. And may it please heaven, for their own advantage, that people should dare tell them such more often, and that they should sometimes deign to hear them.

Note well, I beg you, that I do not present corvées or any kind of forced labour here as an absolute good; it would be better for all that to be done freely and for payment, if the means to pay did not introduce a measureless infinity of abuses and greater and more limitless ills than those that can result from this constraint, above all when those who impose it are of the same estate as those subject to the imposition.

For when there will be only one kind of revenue, viz. the fruits of the earth, there will be only one kind of goods too, namely the land itself.

For the true spirit of public ownership is that individual ownership should be very strong in the direct line, and very weak or null in the collaterals.

And raise rates in order to place commodities in credit and depreciate cash money.

The Corsicans are almost still in the natural and healthy state, but great skill is needed to keep them there, because their prejudices take them away from it. They have precisely what is suitable for them, but they wish for what is not good for them. Their feelings are sincere, it is their false knowledge that deceives them. They see the false brilliance of neighbouring nations and yearn to be like them, because they are not aware of their misery and do not see that they themselves are infinitely better.

Preventing the export of commodities means cutting off large holdings at the root.

Noble people, I do not wish to give you artificial, systematic laws invented by men, but bring you back beneath the sole laws of nature and order, which rule hearts and do not tyrannize wills.

Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

CONSIDERATIONS ON THE GOVERNMENT OF POLAND

chapters.title: Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings
chapters.text:
Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

Prefatory Note

Rousseau’s Considerations on the Government of Poland is his final political work. Just as his text on Corsica was provoked by a request by a Corsican patriot, Buttafoco, this long discussion of Polish history, politics and institutions came about because Rousseau was approached by a Polish patriot, Count Wielhorski, acting on behalf of the Confederation of Bar, an association of wealthy noblemen and landowners who had risen up in 1768 to resist Russian domination and the proposed reforms of Poland’s pro-Russian king, Poniatowski. Rousseau was not alone in being courted in this way: another republican thinker, Gabriel Bonnot de Mably, was also approached and produced a text.

It is far from clear that Rousseau knew much about Poland before he embarked on the project, and the fact that this group of Polish nobles would seek him out and that he would write for them looks surprising given their political character. Poland had been in decline for several centuries and was dominated by a caste of wealthy landowners, the Magnates, who resisted political change. Change was, in any case, extraordinarily difficult within the system they defended, because of the institution of the liberum veto according to which any session of the Sejm, the legislative assembly, could be abandoned and its decisions nullified by the declaration of a single member. This requirement of unanimity placed the political order at the mercy of anyone who stood to lose by change, or, for that matter, anyone bribable by foreign powers or outside interests.

Among the matters that animated the Confederation’s resistance was pressure to accord greater religious toleration to non-Catholics. Since religious toleration was a key principle for Rousseau in the Social Contract, it is hard to imagine that he would have sympathized with the nobles on that matter.

Rousseau worked on the project, drawing on materials supplied by Wielhorski, from 1770 to 1771, but the work was not published in his lifetime. One of the principal reasons for this is that any such plans had become moot because of the so-called First Partition of Poland in 1772 which divided Poland between Prussia, Russia and Austria. A version finally appeared in 1782.

Students of Rousseau have several reasons to take an interest in this text, which, like Corsica, constitutes an attempt by him to apply his ideas to a concrete political subject. At the end of the second book of the Social Contract, Rousseau had stressed that the most important part of the legislator’s work consists not in the elaboration of particular institutions but rather in changing the mores and sensibilities of a people. Along with education, games and patriotic festivals are an important part of this nation-building project and this theme, already present in the Letter to d’Alembert on the Theatre, features prominently in Poland. Rousseau feared, with good reason, that the Poles would be unable to preserve their political independence. He nevertheless advised them that, by focusing on national culture and the preservation of a distinct Polish character, they would be able to resist being digested by these stronger powers.

Poland also show us a pragmatic side to Rousseau’s thinking about politics. Whereas he had been, in the Social Contract (Book III, Chapter 15), an emphatic opponent of the representation of the sovereign people by deputies sitting in an assembly, the size of the Polish nation compelled him to revise this opposition.

The present translation is based on the text contained in volume 3 of the Pléiade edition of Oeuvres Complètes produced under the direction of Bernard Gagnebin and Marcel Raymond in 1964.

chapters.title: Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings
chapters.text:
Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

Considerations on the Government of Poland

AND ON ITS PROPOSED REFORMATION

[I] State of the Question

Count Wielhorski’s description of the government of Poland, and his accompanying reflections, are instructive documents for anyone wishing to form a regular plan for the recasting of this government.1 I know no one more capable of outlining such a plan than he himself, since to the general knowledge required by this task he adds every kind of knowledge concerning the place, and concerning the particular details impossible to convey in writing yet necessary to be known in order to make any institutions suited to the people for which they are destined. If you do not know thoroughly the Nation for which you are working, the work you will make for it, however excellent it may be in itself, will always go astray in its application; and far more so when a nation already fully constituted is involved, whose tastes, manners, prejudices and vices are too deep-rooted to be able easily to be smothered by new sowings. Good institutions for Poland can be the work only of the Poles, or of someone who has studied carefully on the spot the Polish nation and its neighbours. A foreigner can scarcely give other than general views, to enlighten rather than to guide the lawmaker. Even when my wits were in full vigour, I should not have been able to grasp the ensemble of those large relationships. Today, when I barely retain the ability to connect ideas, in order to obey Count Wielhorski and display my ardour for his fatherland I must limit myself to giving him an account of the impressions made upon me by reading his work, and the reflections it has suggested to me.

Reading the history of Poland’s government, you can hardly comprehend how a State so bizarrely constituted has been able to survive for so long. A large corpus formed out of a large number of dead members and a small number of disunited members; all of whose movements – almost independent from one another – far from having a common aim, destroy each other; which is forever busy but does nothing; which can offer no resistance to whoever seeks to do it harm; which falls into dissolution five or six times in every century; which falls into paralysis whenever it seeks to make any effort, or provide for any need; and which, in spite of all this, is alive and retains its vigour: this seems to me one of the most remarkable spectacles to be encountered by a thinking being. I see all the States of Europe rushing to their ruin. Monarchies, Republics, all those nations with such magnificent institutions, all those fine governments so sensibly balanced, have fallen into decay and look destined for an imminent death. While Poland, this depopulated, devastated, oppressed region, open to its aggressors, in the midst of its misfortunes and its anarchy, still shows all the fire of youth. She dares to demand a government and laws, as if she has only just been born. She is in fetters, and discusses the means to keep herself free; she senses within herself the strength which that of tyranny cannot subjugate. I picture Rome under siege calmly governing the lands upon which her enemy has just established his camp. Brave Poles, take care; take care that you do not make your situation worse by seeking to better yourselves too much. In thinking about what you wish to gain, do not forget what you may lose. Correct, if possible, the abuses of your constitution; but do not scorn the one that has made you what you are.

You love liberty, you are worthy of it, you have defended it against a powerful and wily aggressor who, feigning to offer you bonds of friendship, weighed you down with fetters of servitude. Now, weary of your fatherland’s troubles, you yearn for tranquillity. I think this may very easily be obtained; but preserving it in liberty, that is what I consider difficult. It is in the midst of that anarchy which is hateful to you that were formed those patriotic souls which safeguarded you from the yoke. They were slumbering in a lethargic repose; the storm awakened them. Having broken the fetters planned for them, they now feel the weight of fatigue. They would like to combine the peace of despotism with the sweets of liberty. I am afraid they may be wishing for contradictory things. Repose and liberty seem to me incompatible: a choice must be made.

I am not saying that things must be left in the state in which they are; but I do say that tampering with this requires extreme circumspection. At this moment you are more struck by the abuses than by the advantages. The time will come, I fear, when you will better feel those advantages, and unfortunately that will be when you have lost them.

Though it is easy, if you will, to make better laws, it is impossible to make ones that men’s passions do not abuse, as they abused the former laws. Foreseeing and weighing all these future abuses is perhaps an impossible task for the most consummate man of State. Placing law above man is a problem in politics that I compare to that of squaring the circle in geometry. Solve this problem well, and the government based on that solution will be good and free from abuse. But until then be assured that where you think to make laws hold sway, it will be men who hold sway.

There will never be any good and solid constitution other than one in which the law holds sway over the hearts of citizens. So long as the force of legislation does not reach that point, laws will always be eluded. But how to reach hearts? This is something that our lawmakers, who always see only force and punishment, never think about; and it is something that material rewards would perhaps have no greater success in achieving. Even the most righteous justice does not achieve it, because justice like health is a good that you enjoy without being aware of it, which inspires no enthusiasm, and whose price you become aware of only after losing it.

So how to move hearts, and inspire love for the fatherland and its laws? Shall I dare to say it? Through children’s games, through institutions pointless to the eyes of superficial men, but which form cherished habits and invincible attachments. If I am raving here, I am at least doing so utterly, for I confess that I see my madness wearing the features of reason.

[II] Spirit of the Institutions of Antiquity

When you read ancient history, you think yourself transported into another universe and among other beings. What do the French, the English, the Russians have in common with the Romans and the Greeks? Almost nothing but the face. The strong souls of the latter appear exaggerations of history to the others. How would those who feel so small imagine that there have been such great men? Yet they did exist, and they were men like us. What prevents us from being men like them? Our prejudices, our mean philosophy, and the passions of low interest, concentrated with egoism in all hearts by inept institutions that genius never dictated.

I look at the modern nations. I see many makers of laws and not one legislator. Among the ancients, I see three of them who deserve particular attention: Moses, Lycurgus and Numa. All three devoted their main attention to objects that would seem risible to our doctors. All three had successes that would be judged impossible if they were less well attested.

The first shaped and carried out the astonishing enterprise of constituting into a national body a swarm of wretched fugitives, without arts, without weapons, without talents, without virtues, without courage, and who, not having a single inch of land of their own, formed an alien troop on the face of the earth. Moses dared to make this wandering, slavish troop into a body politic, a free people, and while it was wandering in the deserts without having a stone on which to rest its head, he gave it those lasting institutions, tested by time, fortune and conquerors, which five thousand years have not been able to destroy or even alter, and which still survive today at full strength, even when the national body no longer survives.

In order to prevent his people from melting away among alien peoples, he gave it manners and customs impossible to blend with those of other nations; he burdened it with rites and particular ceremonies; he troubled it in a thousand ways to keep it constantly in suspense and render it always alien among other men; and all the bonds of brotherhood that he placed between the members of his republic were so many barriers that kept his people separate from its neighbours and prevented it from mingling with them. This is how that singular nation, so often subjugated, so often dispersed and apparently destroyed but always idolizing his rules, nevertheless preserved itself until our day, scattered among others without merging into them; and how its manners, its laws, its rites, survive and will last as long as the world, despite the hatred and persecution of the rest of mankind.

Lycurgus undertook to give institutions to a people already degraded by servitude and the vices that result from it. He imposed on it an iron yoke, the like of which no other people ever bore; but he attached the people to it, as it were identifying the people with the yoke by keeping it ever present. He constantly showed the fatherland to the people in its laws, in its games, in its homes, in its loves, in its feasts; he did not leave it a moment of relaxation to be on its own, and that continual constraint, ennobled by its object, engendered in it that ardent love of the fatherland which was always the strongest or rather sole passion of the Spartans, and which made them beings above humanity. Sparta was just a city, it is true; but by the sole strength of its institutions that city gave laws to all Greece, became its capital, and made the Persian Empire tremble. Sparta was the source from which his legislation spread its effects all around her.

Those who have seen Numa merely as an institutor of rites and religious ceremonies have judged that great man very ill. Numa was the true founder of Rome. If Romulus had merely assembled brigands whom one reverse could scatter, his imperfect work would not have been able to resist time. It was Numa who made it solid and durable, by uniting those brigands into an indissoluble body; by transforming them into Citizens, less through laws, of which their rural poverty hardly as yet had need, than through gentle institutions which attached them to one another and all to their soil; lastly by rendering their city holy through his apparently frivolous and superstitious rites, of whose strength and effect so few people are aware, yet whose first foundations had been laid by Romulus, the fierce Romulus himself.

The same spirit guided all the ancient Legislators in their institutions. All sought bonds that would attach Citizens to the fatherland and to one another; and they found them in particular customs, in religious ceremonies that by their nature were always exclusive and national (see the end of the Social Contract);2 in games that kept citizens frequently gathered together; in exercises that along with their vigour and strength used to increase their pride and self-esteem; in spectacles which, reminding them of the history of their ancestors – their misfortunes, their virtues and their victories – would engage their hearts, inflame them with lively emulation, and attach them strongly to the fatherland that was constantly kept present to them. It is Homer’s poems, recited to the Greeks in solemn assembly, not in stalls or on benches paying cash, but in the open air and as a national body; it is the tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, often played out before them; it is the prizes with which, to the acclamation of all Greece, the victors in their games would be crowned – it is these which, continually setting them ablaze with emulation and glory, raised their courage and their virtues to a degree of energy that has no comparison today, and that is even inconceivable to modern men. If the latter have laws, it is solely in order to teach them to obey their masters well, not to pick pockets, and to give a lot of money to public rogues. If they have manners, it is only to tickle the idleness of easy women and display their own with grace. If they assemble, it is in Temples for a cult that has nothing to do with the nation, does nothing to remind them of the fatherland and is almost an object of derision; or it is in tightly closed halls and by paying money, to see ham actors declaim and prostitutes simper on effeminate, dissolute stages where love is the only subject, and there to take lessons in corruption,3 which alone bring benefit of all those claimed to be on offer there; or it is in festivals where the people is always despised and always without influence, where public blame and approbation produce nothing; or it is in licentious throngs, to form secret liaisons, to seek the pleasures that separate and isolate most men, and that most loosen hearts. Are these stimulants for patriotism? Should we be surprised that such dissimilar ways of living should produce such different effects, and that the moderns no longer find in themselves any of that vigour of soul that everything inspired in the ancients? Forgive these digressions due to a remnant of warmth you have rekindled. I return with pleasure to the one among all peoples today that separates me least from those of which I have just been speaking.

[III] Application

Poland is a large State surrounded by still more considerable States, which by virtue of their despotism and their military discipline have great offensive strength. Rendered weak, however, by her anarchy, despite Polish valour she is exposed to all their insults. She has no strongholds to halt their incursions. Her depopulation renders her almost absolutely incapable of defence. No economic order; few or no troops; no military discipline, order or subordination; always divided within, always threatened without, by herself she has no stability and depends upon the whim of her neighbours. In the present state of things, I see but one means to give her the stability that she lacks. This is, as it were, to instil in the whole nation the soul of the confederates. It is to so establish the Republic in the heart of the Poles that it survives there despite all the efforts of its oppressors, since that seems to me to be the sole refuge where strength can neither reach nor destroy it. A proof of this has just been seen that will always live in the memory.4 Poland was in Russia’s fetters, but the Poles remained free: a great example that shows you how you can brave the power and ambition of your neighbours. If you cannot prevent them from swallowing you up, at least ensure that they cannot digest you. However you may go about it, before you have given Poland all that she lacks in order to be capable of resisting her enemies, she will be overwhelmed a hundred times. The virtue of her citizens, their patriotic ardour, the particular form that national institutions can give to their souls – there is the sole rampart always ready to defend her, and that no army could breach. If you make sure that a Pole can never become a Russian, I answer for it that Russia will not subjugate Poland.

It is national institutions which form the genius, the character, the tastes and the manners of a people, causing it to be itself and no other; which instil in it the ardent love of the fatherland that is based on customs impossible to eradicate: customs that cause it to die of boredom among other peoples amid delights of which it is deprived in its own country. Remember the Spartan, sated with delicacies at the great King’s Court, who was reproached because he pined for black sauce.5 ‘Oh well,’ he told the satrap with a sigh, ‘I know your pleasures, but you don’t know ours.’

Today there are no longer Frenchmen, Germans, Spaniards, even Englishmen, whatever may be said about it. There are only Europeans. All have the same tastes, the same passions, the same manners, because none has received a national form through particular institutions. All, in the same circumstances, will do the same things. All will say they are disinterested but be rogues; all will talk of the public good while thinking only of themselves; all will praise mediocrity while wishing to be another Croesus.6 They have ambition only for luxury, they have no passion but for gold: sure of having with the latter all that tempts them, all will sell themselves to the first man willing to pay them. What does it matter to them which master they obey, the laws of which State they follow? Provided they find money to steal and women to corrupt, they are in their own country everywhere.

Give another inclination to the passions of the Poles, you will give their souls a national physiognomy that will distinguish them from other peoples, and prevent them from merging, feeling at ease, or intermarrying with the latter; a vigour that will replace the excessive use of vain precepts, and make the Poles do out of preference and passion what is never done enough when it is done only out of duty or interest. Such are the souls over which a well-adapted legislation will take hold. They will obey the laws and not elude them, because those laws will suit them and have the internal assent of their will. Loving the fatherland, they will serve it zealously and with all their heart. With this feeling alone, even bad legislation would make good Citizens; and it is good Citizens alone who make the strength and prosperity of the State.
