I shall explain later the administrative regime that, almost without affecting the basis of your laws, strikes me as capable of carrying patriotism and the virtues inseparable from it to the highest possible degree of intensity. But whether you adopt this regime or not, still begin by giving the Poles a high opinion of themselves and their fatherland: after the way in which they have just displayed themselves, this opinion will not be false. The circumstance of the present event must be grasped to raise souls to the pitch of those of the ancients. It is certain that the Confederation of Bar saved the expiring fatherland. That great epoch must be carved in sacred letters in all Polish hearts. I should like a monument to be raised in its memory; I should like the names of all the Confederates to be placed on it, even those who subsequently may have betrayed the common cause, since so great an action should erase a whole life’s faults; I should like a periodic ceremony to be instituted in order to celebrate it every ten years, with a pomp that is simple, proud and republican rather than showy and frivolous; I should like those virtuous citizens who had the honour to suffer for the fatherland in the enemy’s fetters to be praised in a dignified manner, but without bombast; I should like their families to be granted even some honorific privilege that would always recall this noble memory to the public gaze. I should not, however, like any invective against the Russians to be permitted on these solemn occasions, nor for them even to be spoken of: that would do them too great honour. This silence, the memory of their barbarity, and the praise for those who resisted them will say all that needs to be said about them: you should despise them too much to hate them.

I should like all the patriotic virtues to be blazoned by honours and by public rewards; should like Citizens constantly to be busied with the fatherland, for it to be made their principal concern and kept ceaselessly before their eyes. In this way, I admit, they would have fewer means and less time to enrich themselves, but they would also have less desire or need to do so; their hearts would learn to know another happiness than that of fortune; and there you have the art of ennobling souls and making them into an instrument more powerful than gold.

The succinct account of the manners of the Poles with which M. de Wielhorski has been good enough to supply me is not enough for me to be informed about their civil and domestic customs. But a large nation that has never mingled too much with its neighbours must have many such that are specific to it, and that are perhaps degenerating daily thanks to the general tendency in Europe to adopt the tastes and manners of the French. The old customs must be maintained and re-established, and suitable ones introduced that are specific to the Poles. These customs, should they be indifferent, should they even be bad in certain respects, provided they are not essentially bad, will always have the advantage of inspiring the Poles with affection for their country, and giving them a natural repugnance for mingling with the foreigner. I regard it as fortunate that they have a particular style of clothing. Preserve this advantage carefully: do exactly the opposite of what that much praised Tsar did.7 Let neither the King, nor the Senators, nor any public man ever wear any other apparel than that of the nation, and let no Pole dare to appear at Court dressed in the French style.

A great many public games, at which the good mother country may delight to see her children at play. May she be often concerned with them, so that they are always concerned with her. Even at Court, in order to set an example, you must abolish the usual court amusements – gaming, theatres, comedy, opera, all that makes men effeminate, all that distracts them, isolates them, makes them forget their fatherland and their duty, all that makes them feel content everywhere provided they are amused; you must devise games, festivals, ceremonies that are so specific to this particular Court that they are to be found in no other. People must amuse themselves more in Poland than in other countries, but not in the same way. In a word, you must reverse an execrable proverb and cause every Pole to say in his innermost heart: Ubi patria ibi bene [where the fatherland is, there am I well off].

If possible, nothing exclusively for the Great and the rich. Many spectacles in the open air, where ranks are distinguished with care, but where the whole people takes part equally, as among the ancients, and where on certain occasions young nobles may test their strength and skill. Bull fights have contributed no little to maintaining a certain vigour in the Spanish nation. Those circuses in which the youth formerly used to exercise in Poland should be carefully re-established; they should be made for her into theatres of honour and emulation. Nothing would be easier than to replace the old contests with less cruel exercises, in which strength and skill would nevertheless play a part and in which the victors would similarly receive honours and rewards. Horse-riding, for example, is a very fitting exercise for the Poles, and very well able to provide a brilliant spectacle.

Homer’s Heroes would all distinguish themselves by their strength and their skill, and thereby in the people’s eyes would show that they were made to command it. Knightly tournaments would form men who were not merely valiant and courageous, but thirsty for honour and glory and apt for all virtues. The use of firearms, by making those bodily faculties less useful for glory, has caused them to fall into discredit. The result is that – aside from mental qualities, which are often ambiguous, inappropriate, about which there are countless ways to be mistaken and on which the people is a poor judge – a man with the advantage of birth has nothing in him that distinguishes him from another, justifies fortune or shows in his person a natural right to superiority. And the more those external signs are ignored, the more those who govern us grow effeminate and corrupt with impunity. Yet it does matter, and more than is thought, that those who must one day command others should from their youth show themselves superior to them in every way, or at least strive to do so. It is good, moreover, that the people should often be present at agreeable occasions with its leaders; that it should know them, grow used to seeing them and share its pleasures with them. Provided that subordination is always maintained and that it never merges with them, this is the way for it to develop an affection for them and combine attachment to them with respect. Lastly, a taste for bodily exercises distracts from a dangerous idleness, from effeminate pleasures and spiritual luxury. It is above all for the soul’s sake that the body must be exercised, which is what our petty wiseacres are far from seeing.

By no means neglect a certain public display; let it be noble and imposing, and may the magnificence characterize men rather than things. You would not credit to what extent the people’s heart follows its eyes, and how much it is influenced by ceremonial. This gives authority an air of order and regularity, which will inspire confidence and dispel the image of whim and fantasy associated with that of arbitrary power. It is necessary only to avoid, in the trappings of the ceremonies, the gleam, glitter and luxury adornments that are customary in courts. The festivals of a free people must always be redolent of decency and seriousness, and only objects worthy of its esteem should be presented there for its admiration. The Romans, in their triumphs, displayed immense luxury, but it was the luxury of the conquered; the more it shone, the less seductive it was; its very sheen was a great lesson for the Romans. Captive Kings were chained with chains of gold and precious stones. That was luxury, to be sure. You may often reach the same goal by two opposite routes. The two bales of wool placed by the chancellor’s seat in England’s House of Lords form in my view a touching and sublime ornament. Two sheaves of wheat similarly placed in Poland’s Senate would to my mind have just as fine an effect there.

The vast disparity in fortunes separating the Magnates8 from the minor nobility is a big obstacle to the reforms necessary to make love of the fatherland the dominant passion. So long as luxury rules among the Magnates, cupidity will rule over all hearts. The object of public admiration will always be the object of individual wishes; and if it is necessary to be rich in order to shine, the dominant passion will always be to be rich, a great means of corruption that must be weakened as much as possible. If other attractive objects, if marks of rank distinguished highly placed men, those who were merely rich would be deprived of them; secret wishes would naturally direct themselves towards these honourable distinctions, in other words those of merit and virtue, if such were the only way to succeed. The Consuls of Rome were often very poor, but they had lictors, the trappings of those lictors were envied by the people, and plebeians rose to the Consulate.

Where inequality rules, I must confess that removing luxury entirely strikes me as a very difficult undertaking. But would there not be some way of changing the objects of that luxury and making its example less pernicious? For example, in former times impoverished noblemen in Poland would attach themselves to the Magnates, who would give them education and subsistence in their retinues. That was a truly great and noble luxury; I am perfectly sensible of its disadvantage, but at least far from degrading souls it elevates them, giving them feelings and motivation, and it was free from abuse among the Romans for as long as the Republic lasted. I have read that the duc d’Epernon, on meeting one day the duc de Sully,9 wanted to provoke him to a fight; but, having only six hundred gentlemen in his retinue, he did not dare attack Sully, who had eight hundred. I doubt that luxury of this kind leaves much room for a luxury of trinkets; and the example of it will at least not seduce the poor. Convince the Magnates in Poland to have only this kind; it will perhaps lead to divisions, parties and quarrels, but it will not corrupt the nation. After that, let us tolerate military luxury, that of weapons and horses; but let all effeminate finery be held in scorn, and if it is impossible to get women to renounce it, let them at least be taught to reprove and disdain it in men.

Besides, it is not by sumptuary laws that you will succeed in extirpating luxury. It is from people’s innermost hearts that it must be torn, while implanting there healthier and nobler tastes. Forbidding things that you should not do is an inept, futile expedient, if you do not begin by causing them to be hated and despised; and the disapproval of the law is effective only when it comes to support that of judgement. Whoever ventures to devise institutions for a people must be able to dominate opinions and govern men’s passions through them. This is true above all in the object of which I am speaking. Sumptuary laws provoke desire by constraint rather than extinguish it by punishment. Simplicity in manners and dress is less the fruit of law than that of education.

[IV] Education

This is the important point. It is education that must give souls national strength, and so direct their opinions and their tastes that they may be patriots by inclination, passion and necessity. A child opening its eyes must see the fatherland and until death must see no more than that. Every true republican sucked with his mother’s milk the love of his fatherland, in other words the love of laws and liberty. This love makes his whole existence; he sees only the fatherland, he lives for it alone; once he is alone, he is nothing; once he no longer has a fatherland, he is no more; and if he is not dead, he is worse.

National education belongs only to free men; it is they alone who have a common existence, and who are truly bound by the Law. A Frenchman, an Englishman, a Spaniard, an Italian, a Russian are all more or less the same man. He leaves school already fully moulded for a degree: in other words, for servitude. At twenty a Pole must not be another man, he must be a Pole. I want him, when learning to read, to read about his country’s affairs; to know at ten all its products, at twelve all its provinces, roads and towns, at fifteen to know the whole of its history and at sixteen all its laws. I want there not to have been in all Poland a fine action or an illustrious man of which his memory and his heart are not full, and of which he cannot instantly give an account. You may judge by this that it is no ordinary studies, directed by foreigners and priests, that I should like to have children pursue. The law must regulate the content, order and form of their studies. As teachers they must have only Poles, all married if possible, all distinguished by their morals, their probity, their good sense and their knowledge, and all destined, when after a certain number of years they have fulfilled this job well, not for more important or more honourable posts, since that is not possible, but for ones that are less arduous and more brilliant. Beware above all of making the condition of pedagogue into a profession. Every public man in Poland must have no other permanent state than that of Citizen. All the posts he fills, and above all those that are important to him, must like this one be considered only as testing grounds, and as rungs for rising higher once he has deserved it. I exhort the Poles to pay attention to this maxim, which I shall often stress. I consider it the key to one of the State’s great resources. We shall see below how in my view it can be made applicable without exception.

I do not at all like those distinctions between schools and academies which ensure that the rich nobility and the poor nobility are raised differently and separately. All, being equal by virtue of the State’s constitution, should be raised together and in the same way; and if a wholly free public education cannot be established, it must at least be set at a price that the poor can pay. Would it not be possible in each school to set up a certain number of purely free places, viz. at the State’s expense, and which in France are called bourses [scholarships]? These places, given to the children of impoverished gentlemen who had deserved well of the fatherland, not as an act of charity but as a reward for the fathers’ good services, would on this account become honourable, and could produce a twofold advantage that would not be negligible. For that it would be necessary for nomination for them not to be arbitrary, but to be made by a kind of judgement that I shall speak of later. Those who would fill these places would be called children of the State, and distinguished by some honourable mark that would give them precedence over other children of their age, not excepting those of the Magnates.

In all Schools a gymnasium or place for bodily exercises must be established for the children. This badly neglected point is in my view the most important part of education, not just in order to form robust, healthy temperaments, but still more for its moral purpose, which is either neglected or fulfilled only by a mass of futile, pedantic precepts that are so many wasted words. I shall never repeat enough that good education must be negative. Prevent vices from arising, and you will have done enough for virtue. The means to do so is extremely easy in good public education. It is always to keep children expectant, not through boring studies where they understand nothing, and which they come to hate simply because they are forced to remain in their place; but through exercises that please them, satisfying the need to move about that their body has as it grows, and whose appeal for them will not be limited to this.

You must not allow them to play separately at their whim, but all together and in public, so that there is always a common aim to which all aspire and which stimulates competition and emulation. Parents who prefer home education, and who raise their children under their own eyes, must still send them to these exercises. Their instruction can be domestic and individual, but their games must always be public and common to all. For it is a matter here not simply of keeping them busy, giving them a robust constitution, or making them agile and sturdy, but of accustoming them early on to rules, equality, fraternity and competitions; to live beneath the gaze of their fellow citizens and desire public approbation. For that, it is necessary that the prizes and rewards of the victors should not be distributed arbitrarily by games masters or by school heads, but by acclamation and according to the judgement of the spectators. And you may rely on these judgements always being just, above all if you take care to make these games attractive to the public, by arranging them with a little pomp and in such a way as to make a spectacle of them. It can then be assumed that all decent people and all good patriots will find it a duty and a pleasure to attend them.

In Berne, there is a very singular exercise for young Patricians leaving school. It is what is called the ‘moot State’ [Etat extérieur].10 It is a miniature copy of everything that makes up the government of the Republic: a Senate, Avoyers, Officers, Ushers, Orators, trials, verdicts, ceremonies. The moot State even has a small government and a few revenues; and this institution, authorized and protected by the sovereign, is the nursery for the Statesmen who will one day direct public affairs in the same functions that they first perform only in play.

Whatever form is given to public education, into the details of which I shall not enter here, a College of Magistrates of the first rank should be established to have supreme authority over it, and to appoint, dismiss and change at their discretion not merely the school Principals and heads, who will themselves as I have said be candidates for the top magistracies, but also the games masters, whose zeal and vigilance will be carefully stimulated by the higher posts that will be open or closed to them according to the manner in which they have filled their present ones. Since it is upon these establishments that the hope of the Republic and the glory and fate of the nation depend, I confess I find them to have an importance I am very surprised people have nowhere thought to accord them. I am distressed for humanity that so many ideas that seem to me good and useful should always, though quite practicable, be so far removed from whatever is done.

Besides, I am here merely giving an indication; but it is enough for those whom I am addressing. These badly developed ideas show from afar the paths unknown to the moderns by which the ancients used to lead men to that vigour of soul, to that patriotic zeal, to that esteem for truly personal qualities, ignoring what is merely alien to man, of which there are no examples among us, but the yeasts of which are waiting to ferment in all men’s hearts once they have been activated by suitable institutions. By directing the education, the habits, the customs and the manners of the Poles in this spirit, you will develop in them that yeast which has not yet been rendered stale by corrupt maxims, by outworn institutions, by a selfish philosophy which preaches what kills. The nation will date her second birth from the terrible crisis from which she is emerging and, seeing what her as yet undisciplined members have done, she will expect much and obtain more from well-balanced institutions. She will cherish and respect laws that flatter her noble pride, that render and keep her happy and free. Plucking from her bosom those passions that lead to evasion of the laws, she will nourish there those which cause them to be loved. In short, by as it were herself accomplishing her renewal, she will in this new age recover all the vigour of a nation newly born. But without these precautions, expect nothing from your laws. However wise, however far-sighted they may be, they will be evaded and futile, and you will have corrected a few abuses that bother you only to introduce others that you will not have foreseen. So much for some preliminaries I thought indispensable. Let us now cast our eyes upon the constitution.

[V] Radical Defect

Let us, if possible, avoid rushing with our very first steps into chimaerical projects. What undertaking, Gentlemen, concerns you for the moment? That of reforming the Government of Poland: in other words, endowing the constitution of a large kingdom with the same stability and vigour as that of a small republic. Before working to implement this project, it should first be seen if success in it is possible. The size of nations! – the extent of States! – first and principal source of the misfortunes of mankind, and above all of the innumerable calamities that undermine and destroy well-ordered peoples. Almost all small States, whether republics or monarchies, prosper for the sole reason that they are small; because all citizens know one another and look at one another; because the leaders can themselves see the evil that is done and the good they have to do; and because their orders are carried out before their eyes. All large peoples crushed by their own masses either groan like you in anarchy or groan beneath the subaltern oppressors whom their Kings are forced to impose on them in a necessary gradation. It is God alone who can govern the world, and merely human faculties would not be enough to govern large nations. It is astonishing, it is miraculous that the vast extent of Poland has not a hundred times already caused the government to be converted into despotism, caused the souls of the Poles to degenerate, and corrupted the mass of the nation. It is a unique example in history that after centuries such a State should have come merely to anarchy. The slowness of its progress is due to advantages inseparable from the handicaps from which you wish to deliver yourselves. Oh, I could not repeat it too often: think well before tinkering with your laws, above all those which made you what you are. The first reform you would need is that of your extent. Your vast provinces will never allow the strict administration of small Republics. Begin by contracting your frontiers, if you wish to reform your government. Perhaps your neighbours are thinking about rendering you that service. That would doubtless be a great evil for the dismembered parts; but it would be a great benefit for the body of the Nation.

But if these reductions do not take place, I see only one means perhaps to substitute for them, and fortunately that means is already in the spirit of your institutions. Let the separation of the two Polands be as distinct as Lithuania’s from them: have three States combined in one.11 If possible, I should like you to have as many as you have Palatinates. Form as many particular administrations in each. Perfect the form of the Dietines,12 extend their authority in their respective Palatinates. But mark their boundaries carefully, and ensure that nothing can break the bond between them of common legislation and subordination to the body of the Republic. In short, apply yourselves to extending and perfecting the system of federative Governments, the only one that could suit you. If you ignore this advice, I doubt whether your work could ever be successful.

[VI] Question of the Three Orders

I hardly ever hear people speak of government without finding an appeal to principles that strike me as false or ambiguous. The Republic of Poland, it has often been said and repeated, is made up of three orders: the equestrian Order, the Senate, and the King. I should prefer to say that the Polish nation is made up of three orders: the nobles, who are everything; the burghers, who are nothing; and the peasants, who are less than nothing. If you count the Senate as an order in the State, why not also count as such the chamber of Deputies, which is no less distinct and has no less authority? Furthermore, in the very sense in which it is put forward this division is obviously incomplete; for you would have to add the Ministers, who are neither Kings, nor Senators, nor Deputies, and who in all independence are invested nonetheless with full executive power. How shall I ever be brought to understand how a part existing only through the whole nevertheless forms, in relation to that whole, an order independent of it? The Peerage in England, given that it is hereditary, does, I admit, form an order existing by itself. But in Poland, if you remove the equestrian Order there is no longer a Senate, since no one may be a Senator if he is not first a Polish noble. Similarly, there is no longer a King, since it is the equestrian order that appoints him and the king can do nothing without it. But if you remove Senate and King, the equestrian order, and thereby the State and the sovereign, remain in their entirety; and tomorrow already, if it so please the latter, there will be a Senate and a King as before.

But because it is not an order in the State, that does not mean the Senate counts for nothing there. Even were it not the corporate depositary of the laws, its members, independently of that corporate authority, would still be the depositaries of legislative power. To prevent them from voting in the full Diet whenever it is a matter of making or repealing laws would be to strip them of a right they hold by birth; but then it is no longer as Senators that they are voting, but merely as Citizens. As soon as the legislative power speaks, everyone reverts to equality; every other authority falls silent before it; its voice is the voice of God on earth. The King himself, presiding over the Diet, does not then have the right, I maintain, to vote in it unless he is a Polish nobleman.

You will doubtless tell me here that I am proving too much, and that if Senators as such do not have votes in the Diet, no more should they have votes as Citizens, since members of the equestrian order do not vote there individually, but only through their representatives, among whom the Senators are not included. And why should they vote as individuals in the Diet, since no other nobleman, unless he is a deputy, can vote there? This objection strikes me as valid in the present state of affairs, but when the planned changes have been made, it will no longer be valid; because the Senators will then themselves be permanent representatives of the nation, albeit ones who will be able to act in the legislative domain only in concert with their colleagues.

Hence, let it not be said that the concert of King, Senate and equestrian order is necessary to create a law. That right belongs to the equestrian order alone, of which the Senators are members like the deputies, but with which the Senate has nothing to do corporately. Such is, or should be, the law of the State in Poland. But the law of nature, that sacred, imprescriptible law that speaks to man’s heart and to his reason, does not allow legislative authority to be thus restricted, nor laws to bind anyone who has not voted on them personally, as the deputies have done, or at least through their representatives, as the nobles have done corporately. That sacred law is not violated with impunity; and the state of weakness to which so great a nation sees itself reduced is the work of that feudal barbarism which causes the body of the State to be shorn of its most numerous and sometimes healthiest part.

God forbid that I should think it necessary here to prove what a little good sense and compassion suffice to make everyone feel! And whence does Poland claim to draw the power and the forces that she so wantonly stifles within her bosom? Noble Poles, be more, be men. Only then will you be happy and free; but do not ever pride yourselves on being that, so long as you keep your brothers in irons.

I am aware that the plan of emancipating your peoples is difficult. What I fear is not merely the ill-conceived interest, the amour propre and the prejudices of the masters. That obstacle once overcome, I should fear the vices and the cowardice of the serfs. Liberty is succulent fare, but hard to digest; it takes a very strong stomach to tolerate it. I laugh at those debased peoples who, letting themselves be stirred up by plotters, dare to speak of liberty without having the least idea of it; and who, their hearts filled with all the vices of slaves, imagine that in order to be free it is enough to be mutineers. Proud and sacred liberty! If those poor wretches could be acquainted with you, if they knew at what cost you are won and kept, if they were aware of how much more severe your laws are than the tyrant’s yoke is harsh; their weak souls, slave to passions that ought to be stifled, would fear you a hundred times more than servitude; they would flee you in terror like a burden about to crush them.

To emancipate the peoples of Poland is a great and fine undertaking, but risky and perilous, one that must not be attempted thoughtlessly. Among the precautions to be taken, one is indispensable and takes time. This is, before anything else, rendering the serfs you are seeking to emancipate worthy of liberty and able to endure it. I shall explain below one of the means that may be employed for this. It would be rash of me to guarantee its success, although I have no doubt of it. If there is any better means, let it be adopted. But whatever it may be, think that your serfs are men like you; that they have the stuff within them to become all that you are. Work first at releasing this, and free their bodies only after having freed their souls. Without this preliminary, be assured that your undertaking will turn out badly.

[VII] Means of Maintaining the Constitution

Poland’s legislation has been made successively and piecemeal, like all those in Europe. As people would see an abuse, they would make a law to remedy it. From this law other abuses would arise, which had again to be corrected. This way of operating has no end, and leads to the most terrible of all abuses, which is to enfeeble all laws by dint of multiplying them.

The weakening of legislation has taken place in Poland in a quite particular and perhaps unique way. Namely, it has lost its strength without having been subjugated by the executive power. For the time being, the legislative power still preserves all its authority; it is inactive, but without seeing anything above it. The Diet is as sovereign as it was upon its establishment. However, it is devoid of strength; nothing dominates it, but nothing obeys it. This state is remarkable and merits reflection.

What has hitherto preserved legislative authority? It is the continuous presence of the legislator.13 It is the frequency of Diets and the frequent renewal of Deputies that have maintained the Republic. England, which enjoys the former of these advantages, lost its liberty through having neglected the latter. The same Parliament lasts so long that the Court, which would ruin itself in buying it every year, is quite happy to buy it for seven and does not fail to do so. First lesson for you.

A second means whereby the legislative power has been preserved in Poland is, firstly, the division of the executive power, which has prevented those invested with the latter from acting in concert to oppress the former; and, secondly, the frequent passage of that same executive power through different hands, which has prevented any consistent system of usurpation. Every King would in the course of his reign take a few steps towards arbitrary power. But the election of his successor would force the latter to retreat rather than press on; and at the beginning of every reign Kings would be obliged by the pacta conventa14 all to start off from the same point, so that, despite the habitual inclination, there was no real progress towards despotism.

It was the same for the Ministers and high Officials. Independent both from the Senate and from each other, all had an unbounded authority in their respective departments. But apart from the fact that these offices balanced each other out mutually, by not being perpetuated within the same families they carried no absolute strength, and all the power, even usurped, would always return to its source. It would not have been the same if all the executive power had been either in a single Body like the Senate, or in one family through the heredity of the crown. This family or this body would probably sooner or later have oppressed the legislative power, and thereby placed the Poles beneath the yoke that all nations bear, and from which they alone are still exempt; for I already no longer count Sweden. Second lesson.

There you have the advantage; it is doubtless large, but here is the drawback, which is scarcely any smaller. The executive power shared among several individuals lacks harmony between its parts, and causes a continuous conflict incompatible with good order. All those invested with part of that power place themselves, by virtue of that part, in every respect above the magistrates and the laws. They do, to be sure, acknowledge the authority of the Diet; but acknowledging only this, when the Diet is dissolved they acknowledge none at all: they despise the courts and flout their rulings. They are so many little Despots, who, without precisely usurping the sovereign authority, do not fail to oppress Citizens singly; they set a disastrous and too persistent example of violating the rights and the liberty of individuals without scruple and without fear.

I think that this is the first and principal cause of the anarchy that holds sway in the State. In order to remove this cause, I see only one means. It is not to arm the individual tribunals of the public force against these little tyrants: for that force, at times badly administered and at times overcome by a superior force, might provoke disturbances and disorders capable of turning by degrees into civil wars. But it is to arm with the full executive force a respectable and permanent body, such as the Senate, able by virtue of its stability and its authority to hold to their duty the Magnates tempted to depart from it. This means strikes me as effective, and would certainly be so; but the danger in it would be terrible and very difficult to avoid. For as can be seen in the Social Contract,15 every body invested with the executive power aims strongly and continuously to subjugate the legislative power, and sooner or later succeeds in doing so.

In order to guard against this drawback, you are urged to divide the Senate into a number of councils or departments, each presided over by the Minister responsible for that department; this Minister, like the members of each Council, would change at the end of a fixed term and rotate with those of the other departments. This idea may be good; it was that of the abbé de Saint-Pierre, and he developed it well in his Polysynodie.16 The executive power thus divided and transitory will be more subordinate to the legislative, and the various parts of the administration will be more thorough and better dealt with separately. However, do not rely too much on this means. If the parts are always separated, they will lack coordination and soon, blocking each other mutually, they will use up almost all their strength against one another, until one of them has won ascendancy and dominates them all; or else, if they do achieve agreement and coordination, they will really constitute but a single body and have but a single mind, like the chambers of a Parliament. And in any case I consider it impossible for independence and equilibrium to be so well maintained between them that they do not always produce a centre or focus of administration, where all the individual forces will always come together to oppress the sovereign. In almost all our republics, the Councils are distributed thus among departments that in their origin were independent from one another, but that soon ceased to be so.

The invention of this division into chambers or departments is modern. The ancients, who knew better than we do how liberty is maintained, had no knowledge of this expedient. The Senate of Rome governed half the known world, and never dreamed of such a division. Yet that Senate never managed to oppress the legislative power, though the Senators were for life. But the laws had Censors, the People had Tribunes, and the Senate did not elect the Consuls.

For the administration to be strong and good, and serve its purpose well, all the executive power must be in the same hands. But it is not enough for these hands to change; they must if possible act only in sight of the Legislator, who must be the one to guide them. That is the true secret, if they are not to usurp his authority.17

So long as Estates meet and Deputies change frequently, it will be difficult for the Senate or the King to oppress or usurp the legislative authority. It is noteworthy that the Kings have hitherto not sought to make Diets rarer, even though they were not forced like their English counterparts to call them frequently on pain of being left without money. Either things must always have been in a state of crisis that rendered the royal authority insufficient to achieve it, or the Kings must have been persuaded by their intrigues in the Dietines that they still had the majority of Deputies at their disposal, or thanks to the liberum veto18 they must have been confident of always halting any deliberations that displeased them and dissolving Diets at will. When all these reasons no longer obtain, it must be expected that the King, or the Senate, or both together, will make great efforts to get rid of Diets and make them as rare as possible. That is what you must above all anticipate and forestall. The means I have proposed is the only one; it is simple and cannot fail to be effective. It is quite remarkable that before the Social Contract, where I advance it,19 no one should have been aware of it.

One of the greatest drawbacks of large States, and precisely that which makes liberty most difficult to preserve, is the fact that the legislative power cannot show itself directly, but can act only by delegation. That has its bad and its good side, but the bad prevails. The Legislator corporately20 is impossible to corrupt, but easy to deceive. His representatives are hard to deceive, but easily corrupted, and it rarely happens that they are not. You have before your eyes the example of the Parliament of England, and thanks to the liberum veto that of your own nation. Now an assembly that is mistaken cannot be enlightened, but how may one that sells itself be restrained? Without being informed about the affairs of Poland, I should wager everything on earth that there is more knowledge in the Diet and more virtue in the Dietines.

I see two means of averting this terrible evil of corruption, which turns the organ of liberty into the instrument of servitude.

The first, as I have already said, is the frequency of Diets, which by often changing the representatives makes their seduction more costly and more difficult. On this point your constitution is preferable to that of Great Britain, and once you have removed or modified the liberum veto I see no other change to be made to it, unless it be to add a few obstacles to sending the same deputies to two consecutive Diets, and to prevent their being elected a great many times. I shall return to this point later on.

The second means is compelling representatives to follow their instructions precisely, and to provide their constituents with a strict account of their conduct in the Diet. On this head, I can only marvel at the negligence, the carelessness and, dare I say, the stupidity of the English Nation, which, having armed its deputies with supreme power, adds no brake to control the use they may make of it over the seven whole years that their mandate lasts.

I see that the Poles are insufficiently aware of the importance of their Dietines, or of all that they owe them, or of all that they can obtain from them by extending their authority and giving them a more regular form. For my part, I am convinced that, if the Confederations saved the fatherland, it is the Dietines which have preserved it, and that is where the true Palladium of liberty is to be found.

The Deputies’ instructions must be drawn up with great care, both on matters announced in the royal summons and on other current needs of the State or Province. This must be done by a commission presided over, if you will, by the Marshal of the Dietine, but for the rest made up of members chosen by a majority of votes; and the nobility must not disperse before these instructions have been read, discussed and agreed in plenary assembly. In addition to the original of these instructions, delivered to the Deputies with their credentials, a copy signed by them must remain in the archives of the Dietine. Upon their return, they must account for their conduct at reporting Dietines, which must absolutely be re-established, in the light of these instructions; and it is on the basis of this account that they must either be excluded from any other subsequent mandate as deputy, or once again be declared admissible if they have followed their instructions to the satisfaction of their constituents. This scrutiny is of the utmost importance. It would be impossible for too much attention to be devoted to it, or its effect recorded too meticulously. Whenever the Deputy utters a single word in the Diet, whenever he takes an initiative there, he must see himself in advance beneath the gaze of his constituents and be aware of the influence their judgement will have, upon both his plans for advancement and the esteem of his compatriots, indispensable for realization of those plans. For, after all, it is not so that Deputies may voice their individual sentiments there, but so that they may express the wishes of the Nation, that she sends them to the Diet. This restraint is absolutely necessary in order to bind them to their duty and forestall all corruption, from any source whatsoever. Whatever people may say about it, I see no disadvantage to this hindrance, since the chamber of Deputies has or ought to have no part in the details of administration, hence can never have to deal with any unforeseen matter. Besides, provided that a deputy does nothing contrary to the express will of his constituents, they would not blame him for having offered an opinion, as a good Citizen, on a matter they had not foreseen and regarding which they had not decided anything. Lastly I must add that, even if there really were some drawback to thus keeping Deputies bound to their instructions, there would be none capable of outweighing the immense advantage that the law would never be anything but the real expression of the nation’s wishes.

But also, if these precautions are taken, there should never be a conflict of jurisdiction between the Diet and the Dietines; and once a law has been enacted by the full Diet, I do not even grant the Dietines any right of protest. Let them punish their deputies. If need be, let them even have those deputies’ heads cut off if they have been corrupt. But let the Dietines obey fully, always, without exception, without protest; let them as is proper pay the penalty for their bad choice; at the next Diet, however, if they think it relevant, let them make representations as vigorous as they please.

Being frequent, Diets have less need to be long; and a duration of six weeks strikes me as quite sufficient for the ordinary needs of the State. But it is contradictory that the sovereign authority should impose fetters on itself, above all when it is directly in the hands of the nation. Let this duration of ordinary Diets continue to be fixed at six weeks, very well. But it will always be open to the assembly to prolong this term by an express decision when affairs so require. For after all, if the Diet, which by its nature is above the law, says: ‘I wish to remain,’ who will say to it: ‘I do not wish you to remain’? There is just the one case when a Diet might wish to last for more than two years, but would not be able to do so: its powers would then come to an end and those of another Diet would begin with the third year. The Diet, which can do everything, can unquestionably prescribe a longer interval between Diets: but this new law could apply only to subsequent Diets, and the one enacting it cannot profit by it. The principles from which these rules may be deduced are established in the Social Contract.

With respect to extraordinary Diets, good order in fact requires that they be rare, and convoked only for urgent necessities. When the King judges them to be such, I admit that he should be believed. But such necessities might exist without his acknowledging it. Should the Senate then be the judge? In a free State, all that can attack liberty must be foreseen. If the Confederations remain, they can in certain cases replace extraordinary Diets; but if you abolish the Confederations, rules for such Diets become a necessity.

It strikes me as impossible for the law to be able to fix the duration of extraordinary Diets rationally, since this depends absolutely upon the nature of the affairs causing it to be convoked. Speed is usually necessary; but since this speed is relative to the matters to be dealt with, which do not come under the heading of current affairs, nothing can be ruled on this in advance; and you might find yourselves in such a state that it would be important for the Diet to remain assembled, until either that state is changed or the time for an ordinary Diet terminates the powers of the present one.

In order to conserve the precious time of the Diets, you should endeavour to rid these assemblies of futile discussions that serve only to waste it. You do, of course, need not just rules and order in them, but ceremonial and majesty too. I should even wish you to pay particular attention to this point and, for example, feel the barbarism and horrible impropriety of seeing the panoply of arms profane the sanctuary of law. Poles, are you more warlike than the Romans were? Yet never in the most troubled times of their Republic did the sight of a blade defile the comitia21 or the Senate. But I should also like you to concentrate on important and necessary things, while avoiding anything that can be done equally well elsewhere. The Rugi,22 for instance, when the Deputies’ legitimacy is scrutinized, is a waste of time in the Diet. Not that this scrutiny is not an important thing in itself, but because it can be done as well or better in the same place where they were elected, where they are best known and where all their rivals are. It is in their Palatinate itself, in the Dietine that mandates them, that the validity of their election may best be confirmed and in less time, as is the practice with Radom’s commissaries and with deputies to the Tribunal.23 That done, the Diet should admit them without any discussion on the Laudum24 they present, in order to prevent not merely obstacles that may delay election of the Marshal, but especially those intrigues whereby the Senate or the King may interfere with elections and quibble over subjects who are not to their liking. What has just taken place in London is a lesson to the Poles. I am well aware that this Wilkes is a mere troublemaker.25 But the example of his exclusion has set a precedent, and henceforth only subjects acceptable to the Court will be admitted to the House of Commons.

You should begin by paying more attention to the selection of members with a vote in the Dietines. In this way it would be easier to identify those who are eligible to serve as deputies. Venice’s Golden Book26 is one model to follow, because it is so simple. It would be convenient and very easy to keep a precise register in every Grod27 of all nobles with a right, under the conditions specified, to appear and vote in the Dietines. You would enter them in the register of their district as soon as they reached the age specified by the laws, and you would erase those to be excluded as soon as they come into that category, noting down the reason for their exclusion. By means of these registers, to which a very authentic form should be given, you would easily distinguish both legitimate members of the Dietines and subjects eligible to serve as deputies, and the length of discussions in this regard would be greatly shortened.

Better discipline in the Diets and Dietines would assuredly be a very useful thing; but I shall never repeat too often that you must not seek two contradictory things at the same time. Discipline is all very well, but freedom is worth more; and the more you trammel liberty with formalities, the more these formalities will provide means for usurpation. All those that you may use to prevent licence in the legislative order, however good in themselves, will sooner or later be used to oppress it. Lengthy, futile orations that waste such precious time are a great evil; but it is a far greater one when a good Citizen does not dare to speak when he has useful things to say. As soon as there are only certain mouths that open in the Diets, and these are forbidden to speak freely, they will no longer say anything except what may please the powerful.

After the indispensable changes in appointments to functions and the distribution of favours, there will probably be fewer futile orations and less toadying addressed to the King in this form. However, in order to prune somewhat the circumlocution and bombast, you might oblige each orator to enunciate at the start of his speech the proposal he is seeking to make, and after inferring his reasons to give his summary conclusions, as the King’s officials do in the courts. If this did not shorten the speeches, it would at least restrain those who wish to speak without having anything to say or to waste time doing nothing.

I am not sure what the form established in the Diets for ratifying laws is, but I do know that, for reasons explained earlier, this form ought not to be the same as in the Parliament of Great Britain; that Poland’s Senate ought to have administrative rather than legislative authority; that on any legislative matter the Senators ought to vote solely as members of the Diet, not as members of the Senate; and that the votes ought to be counted by head equally in both chambers. Perhaps the custom of liberum veto has prevented this distinction being made, but it will be very necessary when the liberum veto is removed, all the more because this will be of immense benefit at least in the chamber of Deputies, for I do not imagine that the Senators, still less the Ministers, have ever shared in this right. The veto of the Polish Deputies represents that of the people’s Tribunes in Rome. Now, the latter did not exercise this right as Citizens, but as Representatives of the Roman People. Loss of the liberum veto thus affects only the chamber of Deputies, and the Senate, corporately losing nothing, consequently gains by it.

Having established this, I see a defect to be corrected in the Diet. This is the fact that, since the number of Senators is almost equal to that of Deputies, the Senate has too large an influence in deliberations, and can easily, through its standing in the equestrian order, win the small number of votes it needs to be always preponderant.

I say that it is a defect; because the Senate, being a particular body in the State, necessarily has corporate interests different from those of the nation, and which can even in certain respects be contrary to the latter. Now the law, which is merely the expression of the general will, is indeed the result of all the particular interests combined and balanced by their multiplicity.28 But corporate interests, constituting too considerable a weight, would break the equilibrium and should not enter it collectively. Every individual must have his vote, but no body whatsoever should have one. Now, if the Senate had too much weight in the Diet, it would not only introduce its own interest, but render this preponderant.

A natural remedy for this defect presents itself directly; this is to increase the number of Deputies; but my fear would be that this might agitate the State too much and bring it too close to the Democratic tumult. If it were absolutely necessary to change the proportion, rather than increase the number of Deputies, I should prefer to decrease the number of Senators. And I do not really see why, already having a Palatine there at the head of each province, Grand Castellans are also needed. But let us never lose sight of the important maxim of changing nothing, either to subtract or to add, unless necessary.

It is preferable in my view to have a less numerous Council and leave more liberty to those who make it up, rather than to increase its number and hamper the liberty of its deliberations, as one is always forced to do when this number becomes too large. To which I should add, if it is permitted to anticipate good as well as ill, that you must avoid making the Diet as numerous as possible, in order not to deprive yourselves of the means one day to admit new Deputies without any fuss, if you ever come to ennoble the Towns and emancipate the serfs, as is desirable for the strength and happiness of the nation.

Let us then seek a means to remedy this defect in another way, and with the least change possible.

All Senators are appointed by the King, and are consequently his creatures. Moreover, they are for life, and by virtue of this form a body independent both of the King and of the equestrian order, which as I have said has its own separate interest and must aim at usurpation. And you must not accuse me here of contradiction, because I admit the Senate as a distinct body in the Republic, although I do not admit it as a constituent order of the Republic, since that is very different.

First of all, you must remove the King’s right to appoint the Senate, not so much because of the power he thereby retains over Senators, which may not be very great, as because of that which he has over all those who aspire to being Senators, and through them over the entire body of the Nation. In addition to the effect of this change to the constitution, it will have the inestimable advantage of quelling the spirit of sycophancy among the nobles, and replacing it by the spirit of patriotism. I see no disadvantage in Senators being appointed by the Diet, and I see great benefits in it, too obvious for me to need to detail them. This appointment can take place straight away in the Diet, or initially in the Dietines with a number of subjects being presented for each vacant seat in their respective Palatinates. Among those elected the Diet would make its choice; or else it would elect a lesser number of them, from among whom the king could still be left the right to choose. But to proceed straight away to the simplest, why should each Palatine not be elected definitively in the Dietine of his province? What disadvantage has been seen to arise from such elections for the Palatines of Polock or of Witebsk, and for the Starost of Samogitie;29 and what would be wrong with the privilege of these three provinces becoming a common right for all? Let us not lose sight of how important it is for Poland to turn her constitution towards the federative form, in order as far as possible to avoid the ills attached to the size, or rather extent, of the State.

In the second place, if you arrange that Senators should no longer be for life, you will considerably weaken the corporate interest aiming at usurpation. But this operation has its difficulties: firstly, because it is hard for men accustomed to handling public affairs to see themselves suddenly reduced to the private state without having incurred any blame; secondly, because Senatorial seats are joined with the titles of Palatine and Castellan, and with the local authority that is attached to these; unrest and grievances would thus flow from any permanent transfer of these titles and this authority from one individual to another. Moreover, this removability cannot be extended to Bishops, and perhaps ought not to be extended to Ministers, whose posts require particular talents and are not always easy to fill adequately. If Bishops alone were for life, the authority of the clergy, already too great, would increase considerably; and it is important that this authority should be balanced by Senators who, like the bishops, are for life and have no greater fear than they do of being demoted.

Here is what I should devise in order to remedy these various disadvantages. I should wish Senatorial seats of the first rank to continue to be for life. That would make, counting in addition to Bishops and Palatines all Castellans of the first rank, eighty-nine immovable Senators.

As for Castellans of the second rank, I should like them all to have a fixed mandate, either for two years allowing for a fresh election in every Diet, or for longer if this is judged appropriate; but always leaving the seat when each mandate is over, subject to electing anew those whom the Diet would like to retain, which I should permit a certain number of times only, in keeping with the plan to be found below.

The obstacle of the titles would be a minor one, since as these titles grant almost no function apart from sitting in the Senate, they could be suppressed without any disadvantage; and instead of the title of bench Castellans, they could simply bear that of deputy Senators. Thanks to the reform the Senate, invested with executive power, would be in permanent session with a certain number of its members; so a proportionate number of deputy Senators would similarly be obliged to attend, again by turns. But this is not the place for such details.

Through this scarcely perceptible change, those Castellans or deputy Senators would become so many real representatives of the Diet, providing a counterweight to the body of the Senate and strengthening the equestrian order in the Nation’s assemblies. In this way the Senators for life, albeit grown more powerful thanks to abolition of the veto and the diminution of royal and Ministerial power, now partly absorbed by themselves as a body, would nevertheless be unable to make the spirit of this body dominant there. And the Senate, now divided between temporary members and life members, would be as well constituted as possible in order to make an intermediary power between the chamber of Deputies and the King, having at once enough stability to run the administration and enough dependency to be subject to the laws. This arrangement seems good to me, because it is simple and yet very effective.

In order to moderate the abuses of the veto, it is proposed no longer to count the Deputies’ votes by head, but to count them by Palatinates. As much reflection as possible must be given to this change before adopting it, even though it has its advantages and is favourable to the federative form. Votes taken en masse and collectively always serve the common interest less directly than those taken individually and separately. It will very often happen that among the Deputies of a Palatinate one of them, in their particular deliberations, will gain ascendancy over the rest and sway the majority to his view, which he would not achieve if each vote remained independent. Hence, corrupters will have less to do and better know whom to approach. Moreover, it is preferable that each Deputy should have to answer for himself to his Dietine, so that none may pass blame to the rest, the innocent and the guilty may not be confused, and distributive justice may be better observed. Many reasons can be adduced against a form that would greatly loosen the common bond and at every Diet might expose the State to division. By making the Deputies more dependent on their instructions and their constituents, you gain more or less the same advantage without any drawback. This supposes, to be sure, that suffrages are not cast by ballot, but by show of hands, so that the conduct and the opinion of each Deputy at the Diet should be known, and that he should answer for them in his own, personal name. But as this matter of suffrages is one of those that I have discussed most carefully in the Social Contract,30 it is superfluous to repeat myself here.

As for the elections, you will perhaps at first find some awkwardness in appointing so many deputy Senators at the same time in every Diet, and generally in electing a large number out of a larger number as will sometimes recur in the plan I have to propose. But by resorting to a ballot in this case, you would easily remove this awkwardness, by means of printed, numbered cards that you would distribute to the electors on the eve of the election, and that would contain the names of all the candidates among whom a choice must be made in this election. The next day the electors would queue up to return all their cards into a basket, after each had marked on his own card those whom he selects or those whom he rejects, depending on the decision noted at the top of his card. The tallying of these same cards would be carried out at once in the presence of the assembly by the Diet secretary, assisted by two other secretaries ad actum appointed on the spot by the Marshal from among the deputies present. By this method the operation would become so short and simple that the whole Senate would easily be filled without conflict or fuss in one sitting. It is true that a rule would still be needed to determine the list of candidates; but this point will have its place and will not be forgotten.

It remains to talk about the King, who presides over the Diet, and who must by his position be the supreme administrator of the Laws.

[VIII] Of the King

It is a great evil that the Head of a nation should be the born enemy of the liberty of which he ought to be the defender. This evil, in my opinion, is not so inherent in that position that it cannot be detached from it, or at least considerably lessened. There is no temptation without hope. Make usurpation impossible for your Kings, you will rid them of that fantasy; and all the efforts that they now put into enslaving you they will put into your good governance and your defence. Poland’s lawmakers, as Count Wielhorski has noted, did indeed give thought to depriving her Kings of the means to do harm, but not of the means to corrupt, and the favours they distribute give them this means in abundance. The difficulty is that, by taking away their ability to distribute favours, you appear to deprive them of everything. But this is what should not be done; for you might just as well not have a King at all, and I consider it impossible for a State as large as Poland to do without one, in other words without a supreme head who is for life. Now unless the head of a nation is entirely null, and consequently useless, he must be able to do something, and however little he does it must necessarily be good or bad.

At the moment the whole Senate is appointed by the King: it is too much. If he plays no part in its appointment, that is not enough. Although the Peerage in England is also appointed by the King, it is far less dependent, because this Peerage once given is hereditary, whereas the Bishoprics, Palatinates and Castellanies, being only for life, revert to the King’s appointment upon the death of every title-holder.

I have said how it seems to me that such appointment should take place, namely the Palatines and Grand Castellans for life by their respective Dietines, the second-ranking Castellans for a term and by the Diet. With respect to the Bishops, it strikes me as difficult, unless you have them elected by their chapters, to remove their appointment from the King, so I think you may leave this to him; always excepting that of the Archbishop of Gniezno,31 which naturally belongs to the Diet, unless you separate from it the Primacy, which must be in the gift of the Diet alone. As for Ministers, especially senior Generals and Grand Treasurers, although their power which counterbalances that of the King must be diminished in proportion to his, it does not strike me as prudent to leave to the King the right to fill these posts with his creatures; and I should like him at least only to have a choice from among a small number of subjects presented by the Diet. I agree that, no longer being able to take those posts away having once given them, he can no longer rely absolutely on those who fill them; but they give him enough power over candidates, if not to enable him to change the face of the government, at least to leave him with the hope of doing so, and it is this hope above all that must at all costs be taken away from him.

As for the Grand Chancellor, he should in my view be a royal appointment. Kings are born judges of their peoples; it is for this function, even though they have all abandoned it, that they were established. It cannot be taken away from them; and if they are not willing to exercise it themselves, the appointment of proxies for this function is their right, because it is always they who must answer for judgements delivered in their name. The nation can give them assessors, to be sure, and must do so when Kings do not act as judges themselves. Hence, the Crown court, where the Grand Chancellor, not the King, presides, is under the nation’s supervision; and it is right that the Dietines should appoint the other members. If the King dispensed justice in person, I consider that he would have the right to do so alone. In any case, it would always be in his interest to be just, and iniquitous judgements were never a good path to usurpation.

Regarding other dignities, be they Crown or Palatine, which are merely honorific titles and bring more glitter than credit, you can do no better than to leave them entirely at the King’s disposal: let him be able to honour merit and flatter vanity, but let him not be able to confer power.

The majesty of the throne should be maintained with splendour, but it is important that you leave the King to make as little as possible of all the expenditure necessary for this purpose. It would be desirable for the wages of all the King’s officials to be paid by the Republic rather than by him; and for all the royal revenues to be reduced in proportion, in order to lessen the King’s handling of money as far as possible.

It has been proposed to make the Crown hereditary. Be assured that the moment such a law is passed Poland can bid farewell to her liberty for ever. People think this can be sufficiently provided for by limiting the royal power. They do not see that such limits imposed by the laws will in the course of time be breached by gradual usurpations, and that a system adopted and uninterruptedly followed by a royal family must eventually prevail over a legislation that by its nature constantly tends to slacken. If the King cannot corrupt the Magnates with favours, he can always corrupt them with promises guaranteed by his successors; and since the plans formed by the royal family are perpetuated with it, people will have far more confidence in its commitments and rely far more on their being fulfilled than when an elective crown makes clear that the monarch’s projects end with his life’s end. Poland is free because each reign is preceded by an interval during which the nation, having regained all its rights and rediscovered a fresh vigour, halts the progress of abuses and usurpations, and during which legislation is restored and recovers its original impetus. What will become of the pacta conventa, Poland’s aegis, when a family established in perpetuity on the throne occupies it without any such interval, between the father’s death and the son’s coronation, leaving the nation only an empty shadow of ineffectual liberty, soon to be erased by the pretence of an oath taken by all Kings at their consecration, and by all forgotten forever an instant later? You have seen Denmark, you see England, and you will soon see Sweden.32 Profit by these examples to learn once and for all that, however many precautions you may amass, heredity in the throne and liberty in the nation will forever be incompatible things.

The Poles have always had a propensity for transmitting the Crown from Father to son, or to the next in succession, though always by right of election. This inclination, if they continue to follow it, will sooner or later lead them to the tragedy of making the crown hereditary. And they should not hope to struggle for as long in this way against the royal power as the members of the German Empire struggled against that of the Emperor. For Poland does not have within herself any sufficient counterweight to keep a hereditary King in legal subordination. Despite the power of several members of the Empire, without the accidental election of Charles VII the imperial capitulations33 would already be no more than an empty formula, as they were at the beginning of this century. And the Pacta Conventa will become far hollower still, once the royal family has had time to consolidate itself and subordinate all the rest. To sum up my sentiments on this point, I think that an elective Crown with the most absolute power would still suit Poland better than a hereditary Crown almost devoid of power.

In place of that fatal law which would make the Crown hereditary, I should propose a quite contrary one, which if it were accepted would maintain Poland’s liberty. This would be to ordain through a fundamental law that the Crown would never pass from father to son, and that every son of a King of Poland would be forever excluded from the throne. I say that I should propose this law if it were necessary; but, as I have in mind a plan that would achieve the same effect without it, I shall defer the explanation of this plan to its proper place. And assuming that it will result in sons being excluded from their father’s throne, at least immediately, it seems to me that a secure liberty will not be the sole advantage to flow from that exclusion. Another very considerable one will be engendered by it: namely, by taking away from Kings all hope of usurping and transmitting to their children an arbitrary power, to direct all their activity towards the glory and prosperity of the State, the only prospect that remains open to their ambition. It is thus that the Head of the Nation, ceasing to be its born enemy, will become its first Citizen. It is thus that he will make it his prime concern to illustrate his reign by useful works that will render him dear to his people and worthy of respect from his neighbours, who will ensure that after him his memory is blessed. And it is thus that, aside from means of harming and seducing, which must never be left to him, it will be advisable to increase his power in all that can contribute to the public weal. He will have little immediate, direct force to act by himself, but he will have a great deal of authority, with powers of supervision and inspection in order to hold everyone to their duty and direct the Government to its true purpose. Presiding over the Diet, the Senate and all bodies; strict scrutiny of the conduct of all office holders; a great concern to maintain justice and integrity in all the courts, to preserve order and tranquillity within the State and give it a good standing without; command of the armies in wartime, useful works in peacetime – these are duties that belong particularly to his office as king, and that will occupy him enough if he wishes to perform them by himself. For since the details of administration are entrusted to Ministers created for this, it should be a crime for a King of Poland to entrust any part of his own to favourites. Let him do his job in person, or let him give it up, an important point regarding which the nation should never grow lax.

It is on similar principles that you should establish the balance and weighting of the powers that make up the legislation and the administration. These powers, as equitably distributed as possible among those invested with them, should be directly proportionate to their number and inversely proportionate to the time they remain in place. The constituent parts of the Diet will follow this equitable distribution quite closely. The chamber of Deputies, the most numerous, will also be the most powerful, but all its members will change frequently. The Senate, less numerous, will play a lesser part in legislation, but a greater part in the executive power; and its members, taking part in the constitution from both extremes, will in part be for a fixed term and in part for life, as befits an intermediary body. The King, presiding over the whole, will continue to be for life; and his power, still very great with respect to inspection, will be limited by the chamber of deputies with respect to legislation and by the Senate with respect to administration. But in order to maintain the constitution’s principle of equality, nothing in it must be hereditary apart from the nobility. If the Crown were hereditary, to preserve a balance the Peerage or Senatorial order would have to be hereditary likewise, as in England. Then the humbled equestrian order would lose its power, since the chamber of Deputies does not like the House of Commons have the power to open and close the public treasury annually, and the Polish constitution would be overturned from top to bottom.

[IX] Particular Causes of Anarchy

The Diet, thus well proportioned and well balanced in all its parts, will be the source of a good legislation and a good government. But for this its orders must be respected and followed. The contempt for the laws and the anarchy in which Poland has lived hitherto have clearly visible causes. I have already noted the main one above, and indicated the remedy. The other contributory causes are: 1. the liberum veto; 2. the confederations; 3. abuse by individuals of the right left to them to have men at arms in their service.

This last abuse is such that, if you do not begin by removing it, all other reforms are useless. So long as individuals have the power to resist the executive power, they will believe that they have the right; and so long as they have little wars between them, how do you think the State could be at peace? I concede that strongholds need guards; but why should you need any such that are strong only against Citizens and weak against the enemy? I fear that this reform may encounter difficulties. However, I do not think it impossible to overcome these, and if only a powerful Citizen be reasonable, he will easily agree to no longer having his own men at arms when no one else has them.

I plan to speak subsequently about military institutions; so I shall defer until then what I might have said about them here.

The liberum veto is not in itself a pernicious right, but as soon as it goes beyond its limit it becomes the most dangerous of abuses: it was the guarantor of public liberty; it is now merely the instrument of oppression. In order to eliminate this fatal abuse, the only way left is to destroy the cause of it entirely. But man’s heart leads him to be more attached to individual privileges than to greater and more general advantages. It is only a patriotism enlightened by experience that can teach him to sacrifice for greater benefits a glorious right grown pernicious through abuse, and from which such abuse is henceforth inseparable. All Poles must feel keenly the ills that this wretched right has made them suffer. If they love order and peace, they have no means to establish among them either of these, so long as they allow this right to survive, a right that is good when the body politic is being formed or is fully perfect, but that is absurd and disastrous so long as changes remain to be made. And it is impossible that changes should not always remain to be made, above all in a large State surrounded by powerful and ambitious neighbours.

The liberum veto would be less irrational if it affected only fundamental points of the constitution; but what is utterly unacceptable is its general use in all deliberations in the Diets. It is a defect of the Polish constitution that legislation and administration are not distinguished sufficiently, and that the Diet, while exercising legislative power, also performs administrative functions; that it performs acts of sovereignty and government indiscriminately, and often even mixed acts in which its members are all at once magistrates and legislators.

The proposed changes aim to distinguish these two powers more clearly, thus marking more clearly the limits of the liberum veto. For I do not think it ever occurred to anyone to extend it to matters of pure administration, which would be to nullify civil authority and government as a whole.

By the natural right of societies, unanimity was required34 for the formation of the body politic and for the fundamental laws pertaining to its existence: for example, the first as amended, the fifth, the ninth and the eleventh, all recorded in the Pseudo-Diet of 1768.35 Now, the unanimity required for the enactment of these laws must be required equally for their abrogation. So there you have some subjects on which the liberum veto can continue to exist. And since there is no question of abolishing it totally, Poles who without much grumbling saw this right restricted by the illegal Diet of 1768 ought easily to see it reduced and limited in a freer and more legitimate Diet.

You must weigh and consider carefully those capital points which you will establish as fundamental laws, and bring to bear on these points alone the force of the liberum veto. In this way you will render the constitution solid and the laws so far as possible irrevocable. For it is against the nature of the body politic to impose laws upon itself that it cannot revoke; but it is neither against nature nor against reason that it should be able to revoke those laws only with the same formality that it adopted to enact them. There you have the only chain with which it can bind its future. This will suffice both to reinforce the Constitution and to satisfy the Poles’ love of the liberum veto, without exposing itself thereafter to the abuses the veto has engendered.

As for that plethora of items that have ridiculously been added to the number of fundamental laws, and that constitute merely the body of legislation, as with all those that are classified under the heading of State matters, by the changing nature of things they are subject to inevitable variations which do not allow unanimity to be required on them. It is still absurd that, in any case whatsoever, a member of the Diet should be able to halt its activity, and that the withdrawal or the protest of a Deputy or of several should be able to dissolve the assembly and thus nullify the sovereign authority. This barbarous right must be abolished, and capital punishment be imposed upon anyone who might be tempted to avail himself of it.
