If there were cases of protest against the Diet, which cannot happen so long as it is free and complete, it would be Palatinates and Dietines which could be granted this right, but never Deputies, who as members of the Diet must not have any degree of authority over it or challenge its decisions.

Between the veto, which is the greatest individual power that members of the sovereign can have and which must be applied only for genuinely fundamental laws, and majority, which is the least and which relates to matters of mere administration, there are various proposals regarding which the preponderance of views can be determined in proportion to the importance of the topic. For example, when it is a matter of legislation, at least three-quarters of the suffrages can be required, two-thirds on matters of State, a simple majority for elections and other current, ephemeral business. This is simply an example to explain my idea, and not a proportion that I have fixed on.

In a State such as Poland where souls still have great energy, perhaps this fine right of liberum veto might have been preserved in its entirety without much risk, and perhaps even with advantage, provided that the right had been made dangerous to exercise, and serious consequences had been attached to it for anyone availing himself of it. For it is extravagant, I venture to say, that he who interrupts the activity of the Diet and leaves the State without recourse should go off home to enjoy, tranquil and unpunished, the public desolation he has caused.

So if, in an almost unanimous resolution, a single opponent retained the right to nullify it, I should like him to answer with his head for his opposition, not merely to his constituents in the post-assembly Dietine, but then to the whole nation he has injured. I should like it to be decreed by law that six months after his opposition he would be ceremoniously judged by an extraordinary court established for that sole purpose, made up of all the nation’s wisest, most illustrious and most respected men, and which could not simply acquit him, but would be obliged to condemn him to death without hope of pardon, or else to grant him a reward and public honours for his whole life, without ever being able to take any middle course between these two alternatives.

Institutions of this kind, so favourable to vigorous courage and the love of liberty, are too far removed from the modern spirit for it to be hoped they might be adopted or appreciated; but they were not unknown to the ancients, and were the means whereby their lawmakers were able in the hour of need to uplift souls and fire them to a truly heroic ardour. In Republics where still harsher laws prevailed, generous Citizens were known to risk death when the fatherland was in peril, in order to advance an opinion that might save it. A veto followed by the same danger may save the State on occasion, and will never be a cause for great alarm.

Should I venture here to speak about the confederations and not share the view of scholars? They see only the evil that these do; the evil that they prevent ought also to be seen. Indubitably confederation is a violent state in the Republic; but there are extreme evils which make extreme remedies necessary, and which you must seek to cure at all costs. Confederation in Poland is what Dictatorship was among the Romans: both cause the laws to fall silent in time of pressing danger, but with this great difference: that Dictatorship, directly contrary to Rome’s Legislation and the spirit of its government, finished by destroying the latter; while Confederation, on the contrary, being merely a means of reinforcing and restoring the constitution shaken by great efforts, can aim to strengthen the loosened mainspring of the State without ever being able to break it. This federative form, which in its origin perhaps had a fortuitous cause, strikes me as a masterpiece of politics. Wherever liberty reigns, it is ceaselessly attacked and very often in peril. Every free State in which great crises have not been foreseen is in danger of perishing from every storm. It is the Poles alone who have been capable of drawing from these very crises a new means of upholding the Constitution. Without the Confederations, the Republic of Poland would long ago have ceased to exist, and I fear she will not last long after them, if the decision is taken to abolish them. Cast your eyes upon what has just taken place. Without the Confederations, the State was subjugated; liberty was annihilated for ever. Do you wish to take away from the Republic the resource that has just saved it?

And let it not be thought that when the liberum veto is abolished and majority re-established, the confederations will become useless, as if their entire advantage consisted in that majority. It is not the same thing. The executive power attached to the confederations will always give them at moments of dire need a vigour, an activity, a speed that the Diet cannot have, forced as it is to advance at a slower pace, with more formalities, and unable to make a single irregular move without overturning the constitution.

No, the Confederations are the buckler, the refuge, the sanctuary of that constitution. So long as they survive, it seems impossible to me that it should destroy itself. They must be left, but they must be regulated. If all abuses were taken away, the confederations would become almost useless. The reform of your Government must bring about this effect. Violent undertakings alone will necessitate having recourse to them, but such undertakings are in the nature of things to be foreseen. So instead of abolishing the confederations, decide on the cases in which they may legitimately take place, and then carefully regulate their form and effect, in order to give them so far as possible a legal sanction, without hampering their formation or their activity. Situations may even arise when for that very reason all Poland should be instantly confederated. When, for example, upon any pretext whatsoever and outside a situation of open warfare, foreign troops set foot in the State. For after all, whatever the motive for such entry and even had the government itself agreed to it, confederation at home is not hostility to others. When, for whatever reason it may be, the Diet is prevented from assembling at the time prescribed by the law; when, at the instigation of whosoever it may be, men at arms appear at the time and place of its assembly; or when its form is altered; or when its activity is suspended; or when its liberty is trammelled in any way whatsoever: in all these cases, general Confederation ought for that very reason to exist. Private assemblies and signatures are merely its offshoots, and all its Marshals should be subordinated to whichever has been appointed first.

[X] Administration

Without going into administrative details about which I lack knowledge and opinions alike, I shall venture only, upon the two subjects of finance and war, a few ideas that I must express because I think them good, though I am almost sure they will not be appreciated. But first of all I shall make a comment on the administration of justice which is a little less far removed from the spirit of the Government of Poland.

The two estates of men of the sword and men of the gown36 were unknown to the ancients. Citizens were not soldiers or judges or priests by profession: they were everything by duty. There you have the true secret of ensuring that everyone moves towards the common goal; of preventing the spirit of estate from taking root in bodies at the expense of patriotism, and the hydra of dissension from devouring a nation. The function of judge, as much in the highest tribunals as in the land courts, should be a temporary and trial estate, on the basis of which the nation can assess the merit and probity of a Citizen, in order subsequently to raise him to the most eminent positions of which he is found to be capable. This way of viewing themselves cannot fail to make judges very careful in shielding themselves from all reproach, and to endow them generally with all the care and all the integrity that their position demands. It is in this way that in the golden days of Rome you would pass by way of the Praetorship to reach the Consulate. There you have the means whereby justice may be well administered, even with few clear and simple laws and even with few judges, by leaving judges the power to interpret the laws, and if need be supplement them with the natural wisdom of righteousness and good sense. Nothing is more puerile than the precautions taken in this respect by the English. In order to eliminate arbitrary judgements, they have submitted to a thousand iniquitous and even eccentric judgements: swarms of legal men devour them, unending trials consume them, and with the mad idea of wishing to anticipate everything they have made their laws into an immense maze, where memory and reason alike get lost.

It is necessary to make three codes. One political, another civil, and another criminal. All three as clear, brief and precise as possible. These codes will be taught not only in the universities, but in all schools, and no other body of law is needed. All the rules of natural law are better inscribed in men’s hearts than in all Justinian’s jumble. Simply make them honest and virtuous and I promise you they will know enough law. But all Citizens and especially public men must be instructed in the positive laws of their country and the particular rules according to which they are governed. They will find them in those codes, which they must study. And all nobles, before being registered in the golden book that will give them entry to a Dietine, must undergo an examination on these codes, especially the first, that is no mere formality, and on the basis of which, if they are not sufficiently instructed, they will be rejected until such time as they are more so. With respect to Roman and customary law, all that, if it exists, must be removed from the schools and courts. No authority must be recognized in them except for the Laws of the State; these must be uniform in all provinces, in order to dry up a source of trials; and questions not decided in them must be decided by the good sense and integrity of the judges. Be assured that when the magistracy for those who exercise it is only a trial estate in order to rise higher, this authority will not be as much abused by them as might be feared; or, if such abuse does occur, it will still be less than that of those proliferating and often contradictory laws, the number of which makes trials unending and the conflict between which makes judgements just as arbitrary.

What I say here about judges must be understood as applying a fortiori to Lawyers. This estate, so respectable in itself, is degraded and abased as soon as it becomes a profession. The lawyer should be the first and harshest judge of his client. His job should be, as it was in Rome and as it still is in Geneva, the first step to reaching the magistracies; and lawyers are indeed highly regarded in Geneva, and deserve to be. They are candidates for the Council, very careful to do nothing that might expose them to public disapprobation. I should like all public functions thus to lead from one to another, so that no one by arranging to remain in his own could make it into a lucrative profession and place himself above the judgement of men. This arrangement would perfectly fulfil the aim of making the children of rich citizens pass through the lawyer’s estate, in this way rendered honourable and temporary. I shall develop this idea more clearly in a moment.

I must say here in passing, since it comes into my mind, that it is against the system of equality in the equestrian order to establish entails or Majorats.37 Legislation must always aim at diminishing the great inequality of fortune and power that puts too much distance between the Magnates and the mere nobles, and that a natural progression always tends to increase. With respect to the Census through which the quantity of land is fixed which a noble must own to be admitted to the Dietines, seeing good and bad in this and not knowing the country well enough to compare the effects, I absolutely do not dare to decide on this question. It would indubitably be desirable that a Citizen with the right to vote in a Palatinate should own some lands there; but I should not much like the quantity of these to be fixed: in counting possessions for a great deal, should men then count for nothing at all? What, then! Because a Gentleman has little or no land, does he thereby cease to be free and noble, and is his poverty alone a crime serious enough to make him lose his right as a Citizen?

Besides, no law must ever be allowed to fall into disuse. Even if it is indifferent or bad, it must be formally abrogated or kept in force. This maxim, which is fundamental, will make it necessary to pass under review all ancient laws, to abrogate many of them, and to endow any you wish to keep with the severest sanction. It is seen as a State maxim in France to close your eyes to many things, which is what despotism always imposes; but in a free Government it is the means to enfeeble legislation and undermine the constitution. Few laws, but well digested and above all well observed. All abuses that are not forbidden are still without consequence. But whoever pronounces a law in a free State pronounces something at which every Citizen trembles, and the King first of all. In a word, allow everything rather than waste the resource of the laws; for once this resource is wasted, the State is ruined without recourse.

[XI] Economic System

Choice of the economic system Poland should adopt depends upon the objective she sets herself in correcting her constitution. If you wish only to become noisy, glittering, formidable and have an effect on the other peoples of Europe, you have their example, apply yourself to imitating it. Cultivate the sciences, the arts, commerce, industry, have regular troops, strongholds, Academies, above all a good system of finances which makes money circulate well, which thereby multiplies it, and which procures you a great deal of it. Work at making it very necessary, in order to keep the people highly dependent, and to that end foment both material luxury and luxury of the spirit, which is inseparable from it. In this way you will form a scheming, hot-blooded, greedy, ambitious, servile and rascally people like the rest, always with no middle term between the two extremes of destitution and opulence, licence or enslavement. But you will be counted among the great powers of Europe, you will enter all political systems, in all negotiations your alliance will be sought, you will be bound by treaties. There will be no war in Europe in which you do not have the honour of being mixed up. If fortune has it in for you, you will manage to regain your old possessions, perhaps conquer new ones, and then say like Pyrrhus or like the Russians, in other words like children: ‘When the whole world is mine, I shall eat a lot of sugar.’

But if by chance you would prefer to form a free, peaceful and wise nation that neither fears nor needs anyone, that suffices for itself and is happy, then you must adopt a quite different method: retain or re-establish among yourselves simple manners, healthy tastes and a martial spirit without ambition; form courageous and disinterested souls; apply your peoples to agriculture and to the arts necessary to life; make money contemptible and if possible useless, seeking and finding more powerful and reliable resources in order to achieve great things. I concede that by following this path you will not fill the gazettes with the noise of your festivities, your negotiations or your exploits; that philosophers will not shower praise upon you; that poets will not hymn you; that you will be little spoken of in Europe. Perhaps people will even affect to disdain you. But you will live in genuine abundance, in justice and in liberty. No one will seek to provoke you, people will fear you without seeming to, and I promise you neither the Russians nor anyone else will any longer come to lord it over you, or if they do have the misfortune to come they will be in a far greater hurry to leave. Above all, do not try to ally these two plans. They are too contradictory, and seeking to advance on both in a combined march would mean failing in both. So choose, and if you prefer the former path, stop reading me here. For of all that remains for me to propose, there is nothing relative to anything but the latter.

There are indubitably excellent economic opinions in the papers that have been communicated to me. The fault I perceive in them is that of being more favourable to wealth than to prosperity. With respect to new institutions, you must not be satisfied with seeing their immediate effect; it is necessary to see clearly their remote but inevitable consequences also. For example, the plan for the sale of elderships (starostwa) and for the way of using the proceeds strikes me as well conceived and easy to implement in the system established throughout Europe of doing everything with money. But is this system good in itself and does it achieve its aim? Is it certain that money is the sinew of war? Rich peoples have always been beaten and conquered by poor peoples. Is it certain that money is the mainspring of a good government? Financial systems are modern. I see nothing good or great proceeding from them. Ancient Governments did not even know that word ‘finance’, and what they did with men is prodigious. Money is at most men’s supplement, and the supplement will never equal the thing itself. Poles, leave all that money to others, or content yourselves with what they will have to give you, since they have more need of your wheat than you do of their gold. It is preferable, believe me, to live in abundance than in opulence; be better than moneyed, be rich. Cultivate your fields well, without caring for the rest, soon you will be harvesting gold, and more than you need to procure the oil and wine you lack, since apart from these Poland abounds or can abound in everything. To keep yourselves happy and free, it is heads, hearts and arms that you need: that is what makes the strength of a State and the prosperity of a people. Financial systems make venal souls, and as soon as you seek only to earn, you always earn more by being a rogue than an honest man. The use of money goes astray and becomes hidden; it is destined for one thing and used for another. Those who handle it soon learn to divert it, and what are all the overseers you may give them but other rogues whom you send to share with them. If there were only public, evident wealth; if the progress of gold left a visible mark and could not be hidden; there would be no more convenient expedient for buying services, courage, fidelity, virtues. But in view of its secret circulation, it is even more convenient for making plunderers and traitors, and for putting liberty and the public weal up for auction. In short, money is at once the weakest and most futile mainspring I know for making the political machine advance to its goal, the strongest and most reliable for diverting it from that goal.

You can make men act only through their interest, I know. But pecuniary interest is the worst of all, the basest, the most apt for corruption, and even, I repeat with confidence and shall always maintain, the least and weakest in the eyes of anyone who knows well the human heart. In all hearts, there are naturally great passions in reserve; when the passion for money alone still remains there, it is because all others that needed to be aroused and developed have been enfeebled and stifled. The miser has no real passion dominating him: he craves money only out of forethought, to satisfy those passions that may come to him. Know how to foment and satisfy them directly, without that resource: it will soon lose all its value.

Public expenditures are inevitable, I again concede. Make them with anything else but money. You still see to this day in Switzerland officials, magistrates and other public stipendiaries being paid in kind. They have tithes, wine, wood, rights both useful and honorific. All public service is done through obligatory duties [corvées], the State pays almost nothing in money. Money is needed, you will say, for paying the troops. This point will be attended to in a moment. This manner of payment is not without its disadvantages: there is loss and wastage; the administration of these kinds of goods is more cumbersome, and is especially unappealing to those charged with it since they find less profit there. All this is true. But how small the evil is, in comparison with the host of evils that it saves! Should a man seek to embezzle, he would not be able, at least without being seen to do so. You will counter me with the Bailiffs of the Canton of Berne;38 but whence do their outrages spring? From the pecuniary fines they impose. These arbitrary fines are already a great evil in themselves. However, if they could demand them only in kind, it would be almost nothing. The money they extort is easily hidden, storehouses could not be hidden in like fashion. Ten times more money is handled in the Canton of Berne alone than in all the rest of Switzerland; so its administration is iniquitous in proportion. Seek in every country, in every government and throughout the world. You will not find a single great evil in either morals or politics that does not involve money.

You will tell me that the equality of fortunes prevailing in Switzerland makes parsimony in the administration easy; whereas all those powerful houses and great Lords that exist in Poland require great expenditures for their upkeep and finances to provide for these. Not at all. Those great Lords are rich by virtue of their inherited wealth, and their expenditures will be less when luxury ceases to be honoured in the State, without thereby distinguishing them any the less from inferior fortunes, which will follow the same proportion. Pay their services with authority, with honours, with high positions. Inequality of rank is compensated in Poland by the advantage of nobility, which makes those who fill the various ranks more jealous of honours than of profit. In graduating and distributing these purely honorific rewards as appropriate, the Republic is storing up a treasure that will not ruin it and that will give it heroes as Citizens. This treasury of honours is an inexhaustible resource for a people that has honour. If Poland could only hope to exhaust that resource. Oh, happy the nation that will no longer find within it possible distinctions for virtue!

To the defect of not being worthy of virtue, pecuniary rewards add that of not being sufficiently public, of not forever speaking to eyes and hearts, of vanishing as soon as they are granted, and of leaving no visible trace that may fire emulation by perpetuating the honour that should accompany them. I should wish that all grades, all functions and all honorific rewards be marked by external signs; that a man in high office never be allowed to walk incognito; that the marks of his rank or his dignity follow him everywhere, so that the people would always respect him and he would always respect himself; that he be able in this way always to dominate opulence. I should wish that a rich man who is merely rich, and constantly overshadowed by poor Citizens with titles, find neither consideration nor esteem in his fatherland; that he be forced to serve it in order to shine in it, forced to be honest by ambition, and forced to aspire despite his wealth to ranks accessible only through public approval, and from which blame can always exclude. That is how to weaken the power of wealth, and make men who are not for sale. I insist a great deal on this point, quite convinced that your neighbours, and especially the Russians, will spare no effort to corrupt your high officials, and that your Government’s main task is to work at making these incorruptible.

If I am told that I am seeking to make Poland a people of Capuchins,39 I answer first that this is merely a French style of argument, and joking is not reasoning. I answer further that my maxims must not be exaggerated beyond what I intend and beyond reason; that my plan is not to suppress the circulation of currency, but merely to slow it and, above all, prove how important it is that a good economic system should not be a system of finance and money. Lycurgus, in order to uproot cupidity in Sparta, did not abolish coinage, but he made one out of iron. For my part, I intend to proscribe neither money nor gold, but to make them less necessary and ensure that whosoever has none, though poor, should not be a beggar. Basically, money is not wealth, but merely its sign; it is not the sign that should be multiplied, but the thing represented. In spite of travellers’ tales, I have seen that the English amid all their gold are individually no less needy than other peoples. And what does it matter to me, after all, to have a hundred guineas instead of ten, if those hundred guineas do not bring me an easier subsistence? Pecuniary wealth is merely relative, and, depending on ratios that can change for a thousand reasons, you can find yourself successively rich and poor with the same sum. But not with goods in kind; for, as directly useful to man, they always have their absolute value that does not depend on any commercial operation. I shall grant that the English people is richer than the rest, but it does not follow that a London burgher lives more comfortably than a Paris burgher. As between peoples, the one that has more money has some advantage; but this has nothing to do with the fate of individuals, nor is it wherein the prosperity of a nation resides.

Encourage agriculture and the useful arts, not by enriching farmers, which would merely incite them to quit their estate, but by making the latter honourable and agreeable for them. Establish manufactures that are a prime necessity; constantly multiply your hamlets and your men, without concerning yourself with the rest. The surplus product from your lands, which thanks to the multiplication of monopolies the rest of Europe will lack, will necessarily bring you more money than you have need of. Beyond this necessary and reliable product, you will be poor so long as you want to have; as soon as you know how to do without, you will be rich. That is the spirit I should like to have prevail in your economic system. Think little about abroad, worry little about commerce; but at home multiply both staples and consumers as much as possible. The infallible and natural effect40 of a free and just Government is population. So the more you perfect your Government, the more you will multiply your people without even giving it a thought. You will thus have neither beggars nor millionaires. Luxury and indigence will imperceptibly disappear together, and the Citizens, cured of the frivolous tastes that opulence gives and the vices attendant upon destitution, will devote their efforts and their glory to serving the fatherland well and will find their happiness in their duties.

I should like you always to tax men’s arms more than their purse; to provide for roads, Bridges and public buildings, or service to Prince and State, through corvées rather than money payments. This kind of tax is basically the least onerous, and above all is least open to abuse. For money vanishes as it leaves the hands that pay it; but everyone sees what men work at, so they cannot be overburdened to no purpose. I know this method is impracticable where luxury, commerce and the arts hold sway: but nothing is as easy among a simple people with virtuous manners, and nothing is more useful for keeping their manners virtuous. That is one more reason to prefer it.

So I return to the elderships, and I concede from the outset that the plan of selling them with a view to using the proceeds for the benefit of the public exchequer is good and well conceived with regard to its economic aim. But as for the political and moral aim, this plan is so little to my taste that, if the elderships were sold, I should like them to be bought back and made into a fund for the salaries and rewards of those who serve the fatherland or deserve well of her. In short, if possible I should like there to be no public exchequer, and the treasury to be unacquainted with money payments. I am aware that such a thing strictly speaking is impossible; but the spirit of government must always aim to make it possible, and nothing is more contrary to that spirit than the sale in question. The Republic would be richer, it is true; but the government’s vigour would thereby be proportionately weaker.

I admit that the management of public property would become more difficult, and above all less agreeable for the managers, if all such property were in kind rather than in money. But this management and its supervision must then be made into so many tests of good sense, vigilance and above all integrity, for attaining more exalted posts. In this respect, you will simply imitate the municipal administration established at Lyons, where it is necessary to begin by being Administrator of the Hôtel-Dieu41 before other positions in the city can be attained; and it is on the basis of how you acquit yourself in that position that people judge whether you are worthy of the others. The integrity of the Quaestors of Roman armies was unsurpassed, since the Quaestorship was the first step to reaching curule positions. In posts that may invite cupidity, it must be ensured that this is restrained by ambition. The greatest benefit flowing from this is not elimination of swindles; it is paying honour to disinterestedness, and making poverty respectable when it is the fruit of integrity.

The Republic’s revenues do not meet its expenditures. I can well believe it: its Citizens want to pay nothing at all. But men who wish to be free should not be slaves to their purses, and where is the State in which liberty is not paid for, often very dearly? You will bring up Switzerland; but, as I have already said, in Switzerland Citizens themselves perform the functions that everywhere else they prefer paying to have others perform for them. They are soldiers, officials, magistrates, labourers; they are everything for the State’s service and, always ready to pay with their person, they have no need to pay also with their purse. When the Poles wish to do the same, they will have no more need of money than the Swiss; but if so large a State refuses to behave in accordance with the maxims of small Republics, it must not expect the advantages of the latter, or seek the effect while rejecting the means to obtain it. If Poland, as I should wish, were a confederation of thirty-three small States, it would combine the strength of large Monarchies with the liberty of small Republics; but for that it would have to renounce ostentation, and I fear this would be the most difficult thing.

Of all the ways to establish a tax, the most convenient and least costly is unquestionably capitation.42 But it is also the most forcible and most arbitrary. That is doubtless why Montesquieu relates it to slavery, although it was the only one practised by the Romans and still exists in the present day in several Republics; under other names, to be sure, as in Geneva, where it is called ‘paying the Guards’, and where the tax is paid by Citizens and Burghers alone, whereas residents and natives pay others. This is the exact opposite of Montesquieu’s idea.

But as it is unjust and senseless to tax people who have nothing, levies on property are always preferable to those on the person. However, those that are difficult and costly to collect must be avoided, and especially those that are eluded by contraband, which devalues assets, fills the State with smugglers and brigands, and corrupts Citizens’ loyalty. Taxation must be so well balanced that the bother of fraud outweighs its benefits. So never any tax upon what can easily be hidden, like lace or jewels; it is better to forbid the wearing of these than their import. In France the temptation of contraband is stimulated without restraint, and that makes me think that the Tax administration benefits from the existence of smugglers. This system is abominable and contrary to all good sense. Experience teaches that tax stamps are singularly burdensome for the poor, and frustrating for commerce; they generate endless quibbles and cause the people to complain wherever they are established. I should not advise you to consider them. A duty on livestock strikes me as far better, provided you avoid fraud, since any possible fraud is always a source of ills. But it can be a burden on the taxpayers, in that it has to be paid in money; and the proceeds from this kind of duty are too subject to being diverted from their destination.

The best tax, in my view, the most natural, and one that is not subject to fraud at all, is a proportional tax on estates, and on all estates without exception, as the Maréchal de Vauban and the abbé de Saint-Pierre43 have proposed. For, after all, it is that which produces that should pay. All properties – of King, nobility, Church and commoner – should pay equally: in other words, proportionately to their extent and their yield, whoever their proprietor may be. This levy would seem to require a preliminary operation that is long and costly, namely a general land registry. But this expense may very easily be avoided, and even with advantage, by basing the duty not directly upon the land, but upon its yield, which would be still fairer. In other words by establishing, in whatever proportion may be deemed appropriate, a tithe to be levied in kind on the harvest, like the church tithe; and in order to avoid the trouble of their retail and storage, these Tithes could be farmed out to the highest bidder, as parish priests do. In that way individuals would be obliged to pay the Tithe only on their harvest, paying it out of their purses only if they preferred to do so, at a tariff set by the government. The pooled Tithes could be used as an object of commerce, since the foodstuffs they produce could be sold off abroad via Danzig or Riga. In this way you would also avoid all collection and management costs, all those swarms of agents and clerks so odious to the people, so inconvenient for the public; and, most important point of all, the republic would have money without citizens being obliged to give any. For I shall never repeat enough that what makes the land tax [taille] and all duties burdensome to the farmer is the fact that they are pecuniary, and that before he can pay he is first obliged to sell.

[XII] Military System

Of all the Republic’s expenditures, the upkeep of the army of the Crown is the most considerable; and the services that this army renders are certainly not commensurate with what it costs. However, you will say at once, troops are needed to protect the State. I should agree if those troops did indeed protect it; but I cannot see that this army has ever safeguarded the State from any invasion, and I greatly fear it will not safeguard it any more in future.

Poland is surrounded by warlike powers, which constantly maintain at the ready large numbers of highly disciplined troops, whom, try as she may, she will never be able to match like for like, without exhausting herself in a very short space of time, especially in the deplorable state in which she will be left by the brigands ravaging her. Besides, she would not be allowed to do it; and if, with the resources of the most vigorous administration, she sought to place her army on a respectable footing, her neighbours, intent on preventing her, would very swiftly crush her before she could implement her plan. No, if she wishes merely to imitate them, she will never stand up to them.

The Polish nation is different by temperament, government, manners and language not merely from its neighbours but from all the rest of Europe. I should wish her to be different also by military constitution, tactics and discipline; always to be herself and no other. It is only then that she will be all that she can be, and that she will draw from her bosom all the resources that she is capable of having. The most inviolable law of nature is the law of the strongest. There is no legislation, no constitution, that can exempt you from that law. To pursue the means to safeguard yourself from the invasions of a neighbour stronger than you is to pursue a pipe-dream. It would be a still greater one to seek to make conquests and endow yourself with an offensive strength: that is incompatible with your form of government. Whosoever seeks to be free must not seek to be a conqueror. The Romans were conquerors out of necessity and, in a manner of speaking, despite themselves. War was a necessary remedy for the defect of their constitution. Always attacked and always victorious, they were the only disciplined people amid those barbarians, and became masters of the world while still defending themselves. Your position is so different that you would not even know how to defend yourselves against anyone who attacked you. You will never have offensive strength; you will not have defensive strength for a long while; but you will soon have, or rather you already have, the preservative strength that will safeguard you from destruction even if you are subjugated, and that will preserve your government and your liberty in its sole true sanctuary, which is the hearts of Poles.

Regular troops, the plague and depopulators of Europe, are good for two ends alone: either for attacking and conquering neighbours or for chaining and enslaving Citizens. These two ends are equally alien to you; so renounce the means whereby they are arrived at. The State must not be left without defenders, I know; but its true defenders are its members. Every citizen must be a soldier out of duty, none must be a soldier by profession. Such was the military system of the Romans; such today is that of the Swiss; such must be that of every free State, and especially of Poland. In no position to pay for a sufficient army to defend herself, she must when needed find that army among her inhabitants. A good militia, a proper and well-trained militia, is alone capable of fulfilling this aim. This militia will cost the Republic little, will always be ready to serve her, and will serve her well, because after all you always defend your own property better than you do another’s.

Count Wielhorski proposes to levy one Regiment per Palatinate, and to keep it always at the ready. This assumes that the army of the Crown, or at least the infantry, would be discharged. For I think that the upkeep of these thirty-three Regiments would overburden the republic too much if she had the crown’s army to pay in addition. This change would have its utility and appears easy to effect; but it may still become burdensome, and preventing abuses will be difficult. I would not counsel scattering the soldiers to keep order in towns and villages; that would be bad for their discipline. Soldiers, especially professional ones, ought never to be left to their own devices, still less charged with any control over citizens. They should always march and be quartered as a body: always subordinated and overseen, they should be simply blind instruments in the hands of their officers. Should they be entrusted with the least degree of control, it would lead to violence, harassment and countless abuses; soldiers and inhabitants would become enemies to one another. This is an evil attendant upon regular troops everywhere; those permanently standing regiments would adopt their spirit, and this spirit is never favourable to liberty. The Roman republic was destroyed by its legions when the remoteness of its conquests forced it to keep them always standing. Once again, the Poles should not cast their gaze about them in order to imitate what is done there, even excellently. This excellence in relation to quite different constitutions would be an evil in their own. They should follow only what is appropriate for them and not what others do. Why, then, instead of regular troops a hundred times more burdensome than useful to any people that does not have the spirit of conquest, should you not establish a real militia in Poland, exactly like that established in Switzerland, where every inhabitant is a soldier, but only when he needs to be? The serfdom established in Poland does not, I admit, allow you to arm the peasants so soon: arms in servile hands will always be more dangerous than useful to the State. But while waiting for the happy moment of their enfranchisement to arrive, Poland abounds with towns, the inhabitants of which once enrolled could in time of need furnish numerous troops, whose upkeep outside of that time of need would cost the State nothing. Most of these inhabitants, having no lands, would thus pay their quota in service, and this service could easily be distributed in such a way as not to be burdensome to them, yet they would be properly drilled.

In Switzerland every individual who marries is obliged to be equipped with a uniform that becomes his holiday wear, a rifle of military calibre, and a foot-soldier’s full equipment; and he is enrolled in his local company. During the summer, these militias are drilled on Sundays and holidays in the order of their enrolment, first in small squads, then in companies, then in regiments; until, when their turn comes, they assemble in the field and form a succession of small encampments, in which they are drilled in all manoeuvres appropriate for infantry. So long as they do not leave their place of residence, not being distracted much or at all from their labours, they receive no pay; but as soon as they march out into the field, they have army rations and are in the State’s employ. And no one is allowed to send another in his place, so that each may himself be drilled and all do service. In a State such as Poland, you can draw from its vast provinces the wherewithal easily to replace the army of the Crown by a sufficient number of militias always at the ready, but which, changing at least every year and taken in small detachments from all units, would not be very burdensome to individuals, whose turn would come barely once every twelve or fifteen years. In this way, the whole nation would be drilled, you would have a fine and numerous army always ready when needed, and which would cost much less, especially in peacetime, than the army of the Crown costs today.

But in order to carry out this operation successfully, you would have to begin by changing public opinion in this respect concerning an estate that will indeed be wholly changed; and ensure that in Poland a soldier is no longer seen as a bandit who to live sells himself for five sous a day, but as a Citizen who serves the fatherland and is on duty. That estate must be restored to the same honour in which it was formerly held, and still is in Switzerland and at Geneva, where the finest Burghers are as proud in their corps and under arms as in the town hall and in the Sovereign Council. For this, it is important that in the choice of officers you should pay no regard to rank, reputation or fortune, but solely to experience and talent. Nothing is easier than to make skill at handling arms a point of honour, so that everyone trains zealously to serve the fatherland in sight of his family and his intimates; a zeal that cannot be aroused in the same way among riff-raff enrolled at random, who feel only the hardship of training. At Geneva, I saw the time when Burghers would manoeuvre far better than regular troops; but the Magistrates, finding that this provoked a military spirit among the Burghers that did not accord with their views, took pains to stifle such emulation, and succeeded only too well.

In the implementation of this plan, you could without risk yield to the King the military authority naturally attached to his position; for it is not fitting that the Nation should be used to oppress itself, at least when all those comprising it will share in its liberty. Only with regular and permanently standing troops can the executive power ever enslave the State. The great Roman armies were free of abuses so long as they changed with every Consul, and until Marius it never so much as occurred to any Consul that he might use them as a means to enslave the Republic. It was only when the great remoteness of their conquests forced the Romans to keep the same armies standing for a long while, to recruit them from vagabonds, and to perpetuate command of them in the hands of Proconsuls, that the latter began to sense their independence and seek to use it to establish their own power. The armies of Sulla, Pompey and Caesar became proper regular troops, who substituted the spirit of military government for that of republican government; so much so that Caesar’s soldiers felt greatly offended when, at a moment of mutual dissatisfaction, he addressed them as Citizens, Quirites. In the plan that I imagine, and that I shall soon finish outlining, all Poland will become warlike, as much in defence of her liberty against the schemes of the Prince as against those of her neighbours; and I shall venture to say that, once this plan has been well implemented, you might suppress the post of Grand General and reattach it to the Crown without the least danger for liberty resulting, unless the Nation were to let itself be seduced by plans for conquest, in which case I should no longer answer for anything.

Why would the equestrian order, true home of the republic, not itself follow a plan similar to that which I propose for the infantry? Establish cavalry corps in all Palatinates in which the whole nobility would be enrolled, and which would have its officers, its General staff, its standards, its designated quarters in case of alarms, its appointed times to assemble every year: let that fine nobility be trained to form squadrons, to make all manner of moves and turns, to invest its manoeuvres with order and precision, to learn military subordination. I should not wish it to imitate slavishly the tactics of other nations. I should wish it to create its own specific tactics, which would develop and perfect its natural and national temperament; wish it to train above all for speed and lightness, for breaking, scattering and reforming without trouble or confusion. I should wish it to train for what is called small warfare, in all manoeuvres suitable for light troops: the art of flooding an area like a torrent; attacking everywhere without ever being attacked; always acting in concert though separate; severing communications; intercepting convoys; charging rearguards; cutting off vanguards; surprising detachments; harassing large units marching and camping in a body. I should wish it to adopt the way of the ancient Parthians, as it has the same valour, and learn like them to defeat and destroy the best-disciplined armies without ever giving battle and without allowing them a breathing space. In short, have infantry since you must, but rely only upon your cavalry, and omit nothing to devise a system that will put the whole outcome of the war in its hands.

It is not advisable for a free people to have strongholds. These do not suit the Polish genius, and everywhere they sooner or later become nests of tyrants. Those strongholds that you think you are fortifying against the Russians you will infallibly be fortifying for them; and for you they will become fetters from which you will never release yourselves. Ignore the advantages even of bases, and do not ruin yourselves on artillery; all that is not what you need. A sudden invasion is no doubt a great misfortune, but permanent chains are a far greater one. You will never succeed in making it hard for your neighbours to enter your territory; but you can succeed in making it hard for them to leave with impunity, and you should put all your efforts into that. Antony and Crassus easily entered the territory of the Parthians,44 but to their own misfortune. A country as vast as yours always provides its inhabitants with places of refuge and great possibilities for eluding its attackers. The sum of human skill would not be able to prevent the sudden action of the strong against the weak, but it can preserve energies for a reaction; and once experience has taught that leaving your territory is so hard, people will be in less of a hurry to enter it. So leave your country entirely open, like Sparta, but like her build strong citadels in Citizens’ hearts; and as Themistocles45 used to take Athens with him onto his fleet, if necessary take your towns with you onto your horses. The spirit of imitation produces few good things, and never produces anything great. Each country has advantages that are specific to it, and that its institutions must extend and encourage. Preserve and cultivate those of Poland, and she will have few other nations to envy.

One thing alone suffices to make her impossible to subjugate: love of fatherland and liberty, prompted by the virtues inseparable from it. You have just given a forever memorable example of it. So long as this love burns in your hearts, though it may not safeguard you from an ephemeral yoke, sooner or later it will explode, shake off the yoke and make you free. So labour unremittingly, ceaselessly, to raise patriotism to the highest degree in all Polish hearts. I indicated earlier some of the means suitable to that end: all that remains for me to do here is to expand on that which I think strongest, most powerful, even infallibly bound to succeed, if it is well implemented. This is to ensure that all Citizens feel themselves constantly in the public’s gaze; that no one may advance or succeed other than through public favour; that no position or function be filled other than by the nation’s wish; and that lastly, from the humblest nobleman or even the humblest villein up to the King, all should if possible be so dependent upon public esteem that without it they may do nothing, acquire nothing, attain nothing. The effervescence this common emulation stimulates will give rise to that patriotic intoxication which alone is capable of raising men above themselves, and without which liberty is merely an empty word and legislation a pipe-dream.

In the equestrian order, this system is easy to establish, if you take care everywhere to follow a gradual advancement, and admit no one to State honours and dignities without his first having passed through the inferior grades, which will serve as an entry and trial before he can reach a higher station. Since equality among the nobility is a fundamental law of Poland, the career of public affairs must always begin there by junior functions, in the spirit of the constitution. These must be open to any Citizen induced by his zeal to put himself forward, and who feels himself capable of filling them successfully. But they must be the first indispensable step for whosoever, great or small, seeks to advance in this career. Each is free not to put himself forward for it; but as soon as anyone does enter it, unless he withdraws voluntarily he must advance, or be rejected with disapprobation. In all his conduct, seen and judged by his fellow citizens, he must know that his every step is followed, that his every action is weighed, and that a faithful account is kept of the good and the bad, an account whose influence will extend over all the rest of his life.

[XIII] Plan for Subjecting All Members of the Government to a Gradual Advancement

In order to graduate this advancement, here is a plan that I have tried to adapt as well as possible to the form of the established government, reformed only with respect to the appointment of Senators, in the manner and for the reasons set out earlier.

All active members of the Republic, I mean those who will take part in its administration, shall be divided into three classes identified by as many distinct signs which those comprising these classes shall carry on their persons. The orders of chivalry that were formerly proofs of virtue are now merely signs of the favour of Kings. The ribbons and jewels denoting them have the look of trinkets or feminine adornments, a look that must be avoided in our system. I should like the badges of the three orders that I propose to be medals made from various metals, whose material price would be in inverse proportion to the grade of those wearing them.

The first step in public affairs will be preceded by a trial period for the young, in posts as Lawyers, Assessors, even judges in lower courts, managers of some portion of the public funds, and generally in all junior posts which give those filling them an opportunity to display their merit, their capability, their accuracy, and above all their integrity. This trial status should last at least three years, at the end of which, armed with certificates from their superiors and with the testimony of public opinion, they shall present themselves to the Dietine of their province; there, after a strict scrutiny of their conduct, those who are judged worthy will be honoured by a gold medal bearing their name, that of their province, the date of their acceptance, and this inscription underneath in larger letters: Spes Patriae [hope of the fatherland]. Those who have received this medal shall always wear it attached to the right arm or over the heart; they will take the title of ‘State Servants’, and in the equestrian order it will only ever be State Servants who may be elected Deputies to the Diet, Tribunal Deputies, or Commissaries in the chamber of accounts, or entrusted with any public function belonging to sovereignty.

In order to reach the second grade, it will be necessary to have thrice been a Deputy to the Diet, and each time to have obtained the approval of one’s constituents at the reporting Dietines; and no one will be able to be appointed as a Deputy for a second or third time if he is not armed with this document for his previous mandate. Service in the Tribunal, or as a commissary or Deputy in Radom, will be the equivalent of a deputy’s mandate, and it will be enough to have sat thrice in any one of these assemblies, but always with approval, in order to reach the second grade by right. So that on the basis of the three certificates presented to the Diet, the State Servant who has obtained them shall be honoured with the second medal and the title of which it is the badge.

This medal will be of silver and have the same shape and size as the previous one; it will bear the same inscriptions, except that instead of the two words Spes Patriae, the two following will be engraved on it: Civis electus. Those wearing these medals will be called ‘Citizens-Elect’, or simply ‘Elect’, and will no longer be able to be mere Deputies, Tribunal Deputies, or Commissaries in the Chamber: they will be so many candidates for Senatorial seats. No one shall be able to enter the Senate unless he has passed through this second grade and worn its badge, and all Deputy Senators who in accordance with the plan will immediately be drawn from this grade will continue to wear its badge until they reach the third grade.

It is from among those who have reached the second grade that I should wish to choose the school Principals and inspectors of children’s education. They might be obliged to fill such posts for a certain time before being admitted to the Senate, and would be expected to present the Diet with their approval by the College of educational administrators; without forgetting that such approval like all the rest should always be confirmed by public opinion, which there are a thousand ways of consulting.

The appointment of Deputy Senators will take place in the chamber of Deputies on the occasion of each ordinary Diet, so that they will remain in place for only two years. But it will be possible to reappoint them or appoint them anew twice more, provided that each time upon leaving their seat they have first obtained from the same chamber a document of approval similar to that which must be obtained from the Dietines in order to be elected deputy for a second or third time. For without such a document obtained in each session no further appointment will be possible; and in order to avoid exclusion from government, the sole recourse will be to start again through the lower grades. This must be permitted, in order not to deprive a zealous citizen, whatever fault he may have committed, of all hope of expunging it and achieving office. Furthermore, no individual committee should ever be given the task of forwarding or rejecting these certificates of approval; such judgements must always be handed down by the whole chamber. This will be done without trouble or loss of time, if the same method of Cards is followed for judging Deputy Senators when they leave their seats that I proposed for appointing them.

You will perhaps say here that all these certificates of approval given first by individual bodies, then by the Dietines, and lastly by the Diet, will be less in tune with merit, justice and truth than extorted by intrigue and credit. To that I have but one thing to say in reply. My belief has been that I was addressing a people which, without being exempt from vice, still had energy and virtues; and on that assumption, my plan is good. But if Poland is already at the point where everything in her is venal and corrupt to the roots, then in vain does she seek to reform her laws and preserve her liberty; she must give up the idea and bend her neck to the yoke. But let us resume.

Each Deputy Senator who has served three times with approval will pass by right to the third grade, the highest in the State, and its badge will be conferred on him by the King when the Diet is appointed. This badge will be a medal of blue steel, similar to the previous ones, and will bear this inscription: Custos legum [guardian of the laws]. Those who have received it will wear it for all the rest of their lives, however high they may rise, and even on the throne if they happen to ascend it.

The Palatines and Grand Castellans will be drawn only from this body of Guardians of the Laws, in the same way that the latter were from the Citizens-Elect, namely by choice of the Diet. And since these Palatines occupy the Republic’s most eminent positions and occupy them for life, in order to prevent their spirit of emulation from slumbering in posts where they no longer see anything above them but the Throne, access to this will be open to them, albeit in a way that again allows it to be attained only through public approval and by dint of virtue.

Before proceeding further, let us note that the career I give citizens to follow in order gradually to reach the head of the Republic appears sufficiently well adapted to the measures of human life for those holding the reins of Government, though they have passed the ardour of youth, to be still at a vigorous age; for them still, after fifteen or twenty years of trial constantly in the public eye, to have a sufficiently large number of years left them to allow the fatherland to enjoy their talents, experience and virtues, and to allow themselves to enjoy in the foremost positions of the State the respect and the honours they will have well deserved. Assuming that a man begins to enter public affairs at twenty, it is possible that at thirty-five he may already be a Palatine; but as it is very hard, and not even desirable, for this gradual advancement to occur so rapidly, this eminent position will scarcely be reached before the age of forty, which in my view is the most suitable age for combining all the qualities to be looked for in a statesman. Let us here add that such an advancement appears as well suited as may be to the needs of government. In the reckoning of probabilities, I estimate that you will have every two years at least fifty new citizens-elect and twenty guardians of the laws: numbers more than adequate to recruit the two parts of the Senate to which these two grades respectively lead. For you can easily see that, although the first rank of the Senate is the most numerous, being for life it will less often have seats to fill than the second, which in my plan is renewed on the occasion of each ordinary Diet.

We have already seen, and will soon see again, that I do not leave idle the supernumerary Elect, pending their entry to the Senate as deputies; in order to avoid leaving the Guardians of the Laws idle either, pending their arrival there as Palatines or Castellans, it is from their body that I should form the college of educational Administrators that I mentioned above. As President of this college you could appoint the Primate or some other Bishop, while also ruling that no other Ecclesiastic may be admitted to it, be he even Bishop and Senator.

So there you have, I think, a quite well-graduated advancement for the essential and intermediary part of the whole, viz. the nobility and the magistrates. But we still lack the two extremes, viz. the people and the King. Let us begin with the former, of which no account has hitherto been taken, but which must finally count for something if you are seeking to endow Poland with a certain strength and stability. Nothing is of greater delicacy than the operation involved here. For, after all, although everyone feels what a great evil it is for the Republic that the nation should be in a sense enclosed within the equestrian order, while all the rest, Peasants and Burghers, is nothing in either Government or legislation, such is the ancient Constitution. At this moment it would be neither prudent nor possible to change it all at once, but to bring about this change by degrees might be; without any perceptible revolution, to ensure that the most numerous part of the nation is attached by affection to the Fatherland and even to the Government. This will be achieved by two means: the first, a scrupulous observance of justice, whereby the serf and the commoner, never having to fear being unjustly injured by the nobleman, may be cured of the aversion that they must naturally have for him. This requires a great reform in the courts and a particular concern for how the body of lawyers is formed.

The second means, without which the first is nothing, is to open a door for the serfs to acquire liberty and for the Burghers to acquire nobility. If the thing would not actually be practicable, you should at least envisage it as a possibility. But you can do more, it seems to me, and that without running any risk. Here, for example, is a means that appears to me to lead in this way to the proposed end.

Every two years, in the interval between one Diet and the next, you would choose in each province a suitable time and place where those Elect from the same province who are not yet Deputy Senators would assemble, under the presidency of a Custos legum who is not yet a Senator for life, in a censorial or charitable Committee, to which you would invite not all priests, but only those whom you would judge most worthy of this honour. I even think that this preference, constituting a tacit judgement in the people’s eyes, might also inspire a spirit of emulation among the Village Priests, and safeguard a large number of them from the dissolute manners to which they are only too prone.

In this assembly, to which you might also summon old men and notables from every estate, you would engage in scrutinizing plans for establishments useful to the province. You would hear reports from Priests on the state of their parishes and the neighbouring parishes, a report by notables on the condition of farming and of families in their canton. These reports would be carefully checked. Each member of the Committee would add his own observations, and you would keep a faithful register of all this, from which concise summaries would be drawn for the Dietines.

You would examine in detail the needs of overburdened families, the infirm, widows, and orphans, and you would provide for them proportionately from a fund created by the free contributions of the province’s well-to-do. These contributions would be all the less burdensome in that they would become the only charitable charge, seeing that neither beggars nor poor-houses should be tolerated in all Poland. The Priests will doubtless raise a great outcry for the preservation of poor-houses, and that outcry will be merely one more reason to destroy them.

In this same committee, which would never concern itself with punishments or reprimands, but merely with rewards, praise and encouragement, on the basis of good information you would make accurate lists of individuals from every estate whose conduct is worthy of honour and recompense.* These lists would be sent to the Senate and to the King to be consulted at the right moment, so that they may allocate their choices and their preferences well; and it is on the basis of indications from these same assemblies that in schools the free places I mentioned earlier would be given by the Administrators of education.

But the principal and most important business of this committee would be to draw up, on the basis of faithful summaries, and on the basis of the well-verified report of the public’s voice, a register of those Peasants distinguished by good conduct, good cultivation, good manners, care for their families, all the duties of their estate well performed. This register would then be presented to the Dietine, which would choose from it a number fixed by the law to be emancipated, and which would provide by agreed means for the compensation of the Masters, while granting them enjoyment of exemptions, prerogatives and advantages finally made proportionate to the number of their peasants who would have been found worthy of liberty. For you must absolutely ensure that, instead of being burdensome to the master, the serf’s emancipation becomes honourable and advantageous to him. Of course, in order to avoid abuse, these emancipations would not be carried out by the master, but in the Dietines, by judgement, and only up to the number fixed by the law.

When you had successively emancipated a certain number of families in a canton, you could emancipate whole villages, little by little form communes there, allocate them a few estates, a few communal lands as in Switzerland, establish communal officials there, and when you had by degrees brought things to the point of being able without any perceptible revolution to accomplish the operation on a large scale, finally give them back the right that nature gave them to take part in the administration of their country by sending deputies to the Dietines.

All this once done, you would arm all those peasants become free men and Citizens, you would enrol them in regiments, you would drill them, and you would finish by having a truly excellent militia, more than sufficient for the defence of the State.

You might follow a similar method for the ennoblement of a certain number of Burghers, and even without ennobling them you could set certain glittering positions aside for them, which they alone could fill to the exclusion of the nobles. In this you would be imitating the Venetians, who though so jealous of their nobility nonetheless, in addition to other humbler functions, always give the second place in the State, viz. that of Grand Chancellor, to a townsman, without any Patrician ever being able to aspire to it. In this way, opening the door to nobility and honours to the Bourgeoisie, you would attach its affections to the fatherland and maintenance of the constitution. You might also, without ennobling individuals, ennoble certain towns collectively, favouring those where commerce, industry and the arts flourish more, and where municipal administration is consequently best. These ennobled towns could like imperial towns send Deputies to the Diet, and their example would not fail to stimulate in all the rest a lively desire to obtain the same honour.

The Censorial Committees entrusted with this area of charitable work, which to the shame of Kings and peoples has never yet existed anywhere, albeit unelected, would be constituted in the manner best adapted for them to fulfil their functions with zeal and integrity; for their members, as candidates for those Senatorial seats to which their respective grades lead, would take great care to deserve the suffrages of the Diet through public approbation. And this would be a sufficient concern to keep these candidates on tenterhooks and in the public eye during such intervals as might separate their successive elections. Note that this would nevertheless occur without removing them in these intervals from the condition of mere graded Citizens, since this kind of tribunal, so useful and so respectable, never having any function other than beneficial, would be endowed with no power of constraint. So I am not here multiplying magistracies, but making use of the passage from one to another to take advantage by the way of those who must fill them.

On the basis of this plan, graduated in its implementation by a successive advancement that you would be able to hasten, slow down or even halt depending on its success or otherwise, one would advance only by will, guided by experience; one would arouse in all the lower estates a burning desire to contribute to the public weal; one would manage finally to invigorate all parts of Poland, and to bind them together in such a way as to make only a single body, whose vigour and strength would be at least ten times greater than they can be today, and this with the inestimable advantage of having avoided any sharp, sudden change and the danger of revolutions.

You have a fine opportunity to begin this operation in a striking and noble manner that should produce the greatest effect. It is not possible that, amid the misfortunes that Poland has just suffered, the confederates have not received help and signs of affection from some burghers and even from some peasants. Imitate the magnanimity of the Romans, so careful after their republic’s great calamities to shower with tokens of their gratitude those foreigners, those subjects, those slaves and even those very animals who, in their time of disaster, had rendered them any signal service. Oh, that is the fine start I should like, ceremoniously to give nobility to those burghers and the franchise to those peasants, and this with all the pomp and all the panoply needed to make the ceremony dignified, touching and memorable! And do not confine yourselves to that start. The men thus distinguished should always remain the chosen offspring of the fatherland. You must watch over them, protect them, help them, support them, even should they be bad subjects. At all costs you must ensure that they prosper as long as they live, so that through this example placed in the public eye Poland may show all Europe what anyone who dared to help her in her hour of distress should expect of her when she is successful.

There you have some crude idea, simply in the shape of an example, of the way in which you might proceed so that everyone might see before him the road clear to achieving everything; so that everyone by serving the fatherland well may aim gradually at the most honourable ranks; and so that virtue may open all the doors that fortune is fond of closing.

But everything is not yet done, and the part of this plan that remains for me to set forth is indubitably the most awkward and difficult; it presents obstacles to be overcome upon which the prudence and experience of the most consummate political minds have always run aground. However, it seems to me that, assuming that my plan is adopted, by the very simple means that I have to propose, all difficulties are removed, all abuses are prevented, and what seemed to constitute a new obstacle turns into an advantage in its execution.

[XIV] Election of Kings

All these difficulties are reduced to that of giving the State a leader, the choice of whom does not cause disputes and who does not violate liberty. What increases this same difficulty is that the leader must be endowed with the great qualities necessary to anyone who dares to govern free men. Inheriting the Crown prevents disputes, but it brings servitude; election maintains liberty, but before every reign it rocks the state. This alternative is regrettable, but before talking about means of avoiding it, allow me a moment of reflection on the way in which the Poles normally dispose of their Crown.

Firstly, I wonder, why must they give themselves foreign Kings? Thanks to what inexplicable blindness have they thus taken the surest means to enslave their nation, abolish their customs, render themselves the plaything of other courts, and wantonly increase the stormy nature of their interregna? What an injustice towards themselves, what an affront offered to their fatherland, as if, despairing of finding within the latter’s bosom a man worthy of commanding them, they were forced to go and seek one far away. How have they not felt, how have they not seen, that it was just the opposite? Open the annals of your Nation, you will see her illustrious and triumphant only under Polish Kings; you will see her almost always oppressed and humiliated under foreigners. May experience finally come to the aid of reason; see what evils you are causing yourselves, and what benefits you are denying yourselves.

For I wonder anew how it is that the Polish nation, having done so much to make its crown elective, has given no thought to taking advantage of that law to arouse among the members of its administration an emulation of zeal and glory, which alone would have done more for the good of the fatherland than all the other laws together. What a powerful stimulus to great, ambitious minds, that crown intended for the most worthy and placed in full view before the eyes of every citizen capable of meriting public esteem! What virtues, what noble efforts, must the hope of winning its highest prize not arouse in the nation, what a ferment of patriotism in every heart, once people realize that these furnish the only way of obtaining that position which has become the secret object of every individual’s desires, once it depends upon themselves by dint of their merit and their services to approach it ever more closely, and if fortune favours them eventually to reach it entirely. Let us seek the best way of bringing this great and powerful stimulus, hitherto so neglected, into play in the Republic. I shall be told that it is not enough to give the Crown only to Poles, in order to eliminate the difficulties in question. This is what we shall see in a moment, once I have proposed my expedient. This expedient is simple, but it will at first appear to miss the goal I have myself just signalled, when I say that it consists in introducing lottery into the election of Kings. I ask as a favour that you allow me time to explain, or that you simply reread me attentively.

For if you ask: ‘how can it be ensured that a King drawn by lot would have the qualities required to fill that position worthily?’, you are making an objection that I have already answered, since to achieve this it suffices that the King can be drawn only from among the Senators for life. For since these will themselves be drawn from the order of Guardians of the Laws, and will have passed with honour through all the Republic’s grades, the test of their entire life and public approval in all the posts they have filled will be sufficient guarantees of the merits and virtues of each of them.

I nonetheless do not intend that even among the Senators for life, lottery alone would decide who is to be preferred. That would still be to miss in part the great goal which you should set yourselves. Lottery must do something and choice must do a great deal, in order on the one hand to stifle the intrigues and machinations of foreign powers, and on the other to engage all the Palatines through an interest sufficient for them not to relax in their conduct, but to continue serving the fatherland zealously in order to merit being preferred to their rivals.

I confess that the class of these rivals strikes me as rather numerous, if you include the Grand Castellans, almost equal in rank to the Palatines by virtue of the current Constitution. But I do not see what drawback there would be in giving Palatines alone immediate access to the Throne. This would make within the same order a new grade which the Grand Castellans would still have to pass through to become Palatines, hence a further means to keep the Senate dependent upon the legislator. As we have already seen, these Grand Castellans strike me as superfluous in the Constitution. Nevertheless, in order to avoid any great change, let them be left their seat and rank in the Senate, I concur with that. But in the graduation that I am proposing, nothing obliges you to put them on the level of the Palatines; and since nothing prevents it either, you can with no disadvantage opt for the course you think best. I am assuming here that your preferred course will be to open immediate access to the throne to Palatines alone.

Hence, at once after the death of the King, in other words within the shortest time that is both possible and in accordance with the law, the election Diet will be solemnly convoked. The names of all Palatines will be placed in competition, and three of them will be drawn by lot, with all possible precautions against any fraud distorting this procedure. These three names will be read out to the assembly, which at the same sitting and by a majority of votes will choose whichever it prefers, and he will be proclaimed King on that very day.

In this form of election you will find one great disadvantage, I confess: this is that the nation is unable to choose freely from among the number of Palatines the one whom she honours and cherishes most, and whom she judges most worthy of kingship. But this disadvantage is not new in Poland, where we have seen in several elections, and especially in the last, that with no regard for those whom the Nation favoured she was forced to choose someone she would have rejected. As against this advantage that she no longer had and that she sacrifices, what a number of more important ones she gains through this form of election!

Firstly, the effect of the lottery at once stifles the factions and intrigues of foreign Nations, which cannot influence this election, being too uncertain of success to put any great efforts into it, seeing that even fraud would be insufficient in favour of a subject whom the nation can always reject. The very scale of this advantage is such that it ensures Poland’s repose, suffocates venality in the republic, and confers upon election almost all the tranquillity of inheritance.

The same advantage occurs against the very intrigues of the candidates. For who among them will be willing to go to any expense to ensure a preference that does not depend on men at all, and sacrifice his fortune to an event depending upon so many unlucky chances as against a single lucky one. Let us add that those favoured by lot are no longer in time to buy electors, since the election has to take place at the same sitting.
