The free choice of the Nation between three candidates preserves her from the drawbacks of the lot that might hypothetically fall upon an unworthy subject. For, under this hypothesis, the Nation will take care not to choose him; and it is not possible that among thirty-three illustrious men, the elite of the Nation, in which it is incomprehensible that a single unworthy subject should be found, those favoured by lot should all three be unworthy.

Hence, and this observation is of great weight, we join through this form all the advantages of election to those of inheritance.

For in the first place, with the crown not passing from father to son, there will never be a continuity of system to enslave the republic. Secondly, in this form lottery itself is the instrument of an enlightened and voluntary election: it cannot make any choice whatsoever, in the respectable body of the Guardians of the Laws and the Palatines drawn therefrom, that has not already been made by the nation.

But see what emulation this prospect can introduce into the body of the Palatines and Grand Castellans, who with seats for life might relax, thanks to the certainty that these could no longer be taken from them. They can no longer be restrained by fear; but the hope of occupying the throne, which each of them sees so close at hand, is a new goad that keeps them perpetually careful of themselves. They know that the lottery would favour them in vain were they to be rejected in the election, and that the only way of being chosen is to merit it. This advantage is too big and too obvious for insistence upon it to be necessary.

Let us assume for a moment, taking the worst case, that you cannot avoid fraud in the operation of the lottery, and that one of the rivals succeeds in deceiving the vigilance of all the others, so interested in this operation. That fraud would be a misfortune for the excluded candidates; but the effect for the republic would be the same as if the decision of the lottery had been fair. For you would nonetheless have the advantage of election; you would nonetheless forestall the disputes of interregna and the dangers of inheritance; the candidate so seduced by his ambition as to resort to this fraud would nonetheless, apart from that, be a man of merit, capable in the nation’s judgement of wearing the crown with honour; and lastly, even after this fraud, in order to profit by it he would nonetheless depend on the subsequent, formal choice of the Republic.

Through this plan, adopted in its full extent, everything in the State is connected and, from the last individual to the first Palatine, no one sees any way of advancing other than by the path of duty and public approbation. The King alone, once elected, no longer seeing anything but the laws above him, has no other curb to restrain him; and, no longer having need of public approbation, he can safely do without it if his plans so require. I scarcely see any remedy for this other than one that should not even be contemplated. This would be for the Crown in some way to be removable, and for Kings to need confirmation after specific periods. However, once again, this expedient cannot be proposed. Keeping the throne and the State in constant turmoil, it would never leave the administration in a stable enough condition to be able to apply itself solely and fruitfully to the public weal.

There was an ancient custom that has only ever been practised by a single people, but astonishingly its success has tempted no other to imitate it. To be sure, it is scarcely suitable other than for an elective kingdom, albeit invented and practised in a hereditary kingdom. I am speaking about how the Kings of Egypt were judged after death, and about the ruling whereby royal burial and honours were granted or refused them, according to whether they had governed the State well or ill in their lifetime. The indifference of the moderns to all such moral issues, and to everything that can animate souls, will doubtless make them look upon the idea of re-establishing that custom for the kings of Poland as a folly. It is not by Frenchmen, especially philosophers, that I should seek to have it adopted, but I think it can be proposed to Poles. I even venture to suggest that this institution would have great advantages for them, impossible to replace in any other way, and not a single drawback. In the present case, it is clear that, short of some vile soul indifferent to the honour of his memory, it is not possible that the integrity of an inevitable judgement should not impress the King and place a curb upon his passions: more or less strong, I admit, but still capable of restraining them to a certain degree, above all when combined with the interests of his children, whose destiny will be decided by the ruling pronounced upon the father’s memory.

So I should wish that upon the death of every King his body be deposited in a suitable place, until his memory has been pronounced upon; that the court which must decide on it and order his burial be convened as soon as possible; that his life and his reign be strictly examined there; and that, after an inquiry to which any citizen would be admitted to accuse him or defend him, the well-informed trial would be followed by a ruling delivered with all possible solemnity.

As a consequence of this ruling, if it was favourable, the late King would be declared a good and just Prince, his name inscribed with honour in the list of Kings of Poland, his body laid with pomp in their burial place, the epithet ‘Of glorious memory’ added to his name in all public documents and speeches, a dowry awarded to his widow, and his children, proclaimed Princes Royal, would be honoured as long as they lived by all the advantages attached to this title.

If, on the contrary, he was found guilty of injustice, violence and embezzlement, and above all of having infringed public liberty, his memory would be condemned and excoriated, his body denied royal burial would be interred without honours as that of a private individual, his name erased from the public register of kings; and his children, denied the title of Princes Royal and the prerogatives attached to it, would revert to the class of mere citizens, without any distinction of either honour or excoriation.

I should like this judgement to be made with the greatest pomp and circumstance, but if possible to precede the election of his successor, so that the latter’s credit could not influence the verdict, the severity of which he would have an interest in mitigating. I am aware that it would be desirable for there to be more time to reveal many hidden truths and better inform the trial. But if there was any delay after the election, I should fear lest this important act soon become merely an empty ceremony and, as would infallibly happen in a hereditary kingdom, more of a funeral oration for the late King than a just and strict judgement upon his conduct. It is preferable on this occasion to give more to the public voice and lose a few detailed insights, in order to preserve the integrity and the austerity of a judgement that would otherwise become futile.

With respect to the court that would pronounce this verdict, I should like it to be neither the Senate nor the Diet nor any body invested with some authority in government, but an entire order of Citizens that cannot easily be either deceived or corrupted. It strikes me that the Cives electi, better informed and with more experience than the State Servants, and less partisan than the Guardians of the Laws already too close to the throne, would be precisely the intermediary body wherein you would find at once most enlightenment and most integrity: the body most appropriate to deliver only reliable judgements, hence preferable to the other two on this occasion. Even if it should happen that this body was not numerous enough for a judgement of such importance, I should prefer it to be given associates drawn from the State Servants than from the Guardians of the Laws. Lastly, I should wish the court not to be presided over by any man of position, but by a Marshal drawn from his own corps, that would itself elect him, like those of the Diets and the Confederations. For you should avoid any individual interest influencing this action, which may be very impressive or very ridiculous depending on how it is undertaken.

In concluding this topic of the election and judgement of Kings, I must say here that one thing in your customs has struck me as quite shocking, and quite contrary to the spirit of your constitution. This is to see the latter almost overturned and destroyed upon the King’s death, to the point where all courts are suspended and closed, as if the constitution were so dependent on this Prince that the death of the one entailed the destruction of the other. Nay, by Heaven, it should be just the opposite. With the King dead, everything should proceed as if he were still alive. You should scarcely notice that a piece of the machinery is missing, so little is that piece essential to its stability. Fortunately this inconsistency depends on nothing. You have simply to say that it will no longer exist, and nothing more need be changed. But you should not let this strange contradiction survive, for if it is already one in the present constitution, it would be a far larger one still after the reform.

[XV] Conclusion

There you have a sufficient outline of my plan, so I shall stop. Whichever one you may adopt, you should not forget what I said in the Social Contract46 about the state of weakness and anarchy in which a nation finds itself while it is establishing or reforming its constitution. In this moment of disorder and effervescence, it is in no condition to offer any resistance and the least shock is capable of overturning everything. So it is important at all costs to arrange for oneself an interval of calm, during which one can act on oneself and rejuvenate one’s constitution without risk. Although the changes to be made in yours are not fundamental, and do not seem very great, they are enough to dictate this precaution. A certain time is necessarily required for the effect of the best reform to be felt, and for the coherence that should be its fruit to be attained. It is only by assuming that your success will match the courage of the Confederates and the justice of their cause that you can contemplate the undertaking in question. You will never be free so long as a single Russian soldier remains in Poland, and you will always be threatened with losing your freedom so long as Russia meddles in your affairs. But if you manage to force her to deal with you as one power to another, and no longer as protector and protégé, then take advantage of the exhaustion into which the Turkish War47 has cast her to accomplish your business before she can interfere in it. Although I place no reliance upon such external security as may be procured by treaties, this unique circumstance will perhaps force you to shore yourself up as much as possible by such props, if only to know the present disposition of those who will parley with you. But excepting this case, and perhaps at other times some commercial treaties, do not weary yourselves with vain negotiations, do not ruin yourselves by Ambassadors and Ministers at other courts, and do not set any store by alliances and treaties. All that is worthless with the Christian powers. They know no other bonds than those of their interest. When they find that this lies in fulfilling their commitments, they will fulfil them; when they find that it lies in breaking them, they will break them. Just as well not enter into any. If only their interest was always true, knowledge of what they ought to do might let you foresee what they will do. But it is almost never raison d’État that guides them, it is the fleeting interest of a Minister, a daughter, a favourite; it is the motive that no human wisdom could have foreseen which decides them now for, now against their true interests. What may be relied upon, with people who have no fixed system, and who behave only in accordance with random impulses? Nothing is more frivolous than the political theory of Courts: as it has no guaranteed principle, no certain consequence may be drawn from it; and that whole fine doctrine concerning the interests of Princes is a game for children that makes sensible men laugh.

Do not, therefore, rely confidently either upon your allies or upon your neighbours. You have but one upon whom you may count a little. This is the Grand Turk,48 and you must spare no effort to gain his support. Not that his Statecraft is much more reliable than that of the other powers. All in it likewise depends upon some Vizier, Favourite or Harem intrigue. But the Porte’s interest is clear, simple and all-important to her; and with far less knowledge or refinement, more uprightness and good sense generally prevail therein. With her, you have at least this advantage more than with the Christian powers, that she likes to fulfil her commitments, and usually respects treaties. You must endeavour to make one with her for twenty years, as strong and clear as may be. This treaty, so long as another power hides her plans, will be the best and perhaps sole guarantee that you could have. And, in the state in which the present war will probably leave Russia, I estimate that it may be enough for you to undertake your business safely. All the more so because the common interest of the European powers, and especially your other neighbours, is always to leave you as a barrier between them and the Russians; and by dint of changing their follies, they must at least sometimes be wise.

One thing makes me believe that they will generally without jealousy see you working to reform your constitution. This is that your undertaking aims only to reinforce legislation, hence liberty; and that this liberty is viewed in every court as a fad of visionaries, which tends rather to weaken than to strengthen a State. This is why France has always favoured the liberty of the Germanic corpus and of Holland, and that is why today Russia favours the present government of Sweden, obstructing the King’s plans with all her might. All those grand Ministers who think to know men, judging the generality of man by themselves and those around them, are very far from imagining what energy love of fatherland and passion for virtue can give to free souls. However often, deceived by the low opinion they have of republics, they may find there in all their undertakings a resistance they were not expecting, they will never shake off a prejudice based on the contempt that they feel befits them and that underlies their estimation of the human race. Despite the rather striking experience that the Russians have just had in Poland, nothing will make them change their opinion. They will always look upon free men as they should themselves be looked upon, namely as nobodies upon whom two instruments alone have any hold, viz. money and the Knout. Hence, if they see that the Republic of Poland, instead of devoting herself to filling her coffers, swelling her finances and raising plenty of regular troops, is on the contrary thinking of disbanding her army and doing without money, they will think that she is striving to weaken herself. And convinced that in order to conquer her they need only turn up whenever they please, they will leave her to order her affairs at her leisure, inwardly mocking her labours. And it must be conceded that the state of liberty does deny a people offensive strength, and that in following the plan I propose you must renounce all hope of conquest. But in twenty years, your business once done, let the Russians try to invade you, and they will know what soldiers they are, these men of peace who do not know how to attack the homes of others and who have forgotten the price of money, when they are defending their own homes.

Moreover, when you are delivered from these cruel guests, beware of taking any middle course with respect to the King they sought to give you.49 It is necessary either to have his head cut off as he has merited, or else, taking no account of his initial election which is entirely null, to elect him anew, with other Pacta conventa whereby you will make him give up the right to appoint high officials. This second course is not merely the more humane, it is wiser; I even find in it a certain generous pride that will perhaps mortify the Court of Petersburg just as much as if you made another appointment. Poniatowski was no doubt very criminal; perhaps today he is merely unfortunate; at least in the present situation, he seems to me to conduct himself pretty much as he should do, not meddling in anything at all. Of course, he must in his innermost heart wish ardently for the expulsion of his harsh masters. There would perhaps be some patriotic heroism in joining the Confederates to drive those masters out; but it is well known that Poniatowski is no hero. Besides, apart from the fact that he would not be allowed to do it and that he is indubitably held in custody, I frankly declare that, if I were in his place, owing everything to Russia, I would certainly not for anything in the world wish to be capable of that kind of heroism.

I am well aware that this is not the King you will need once your reform is complete; but he is perhaps the one you need in order to accomplish it peacefully. Should he live just another eight or ten years, your machinery having then begun to move, and several Palatinates being already filled by Guardians of the Laws, you will not be afraid of giving him a successor who resembles him. But for my part, I am afraid lest in simply deposing him you may not know what to do with him and may expose yourselves to new conflicts.

Nevertheless, whatever the difficulties from which his free election might deliver you, you should contemplate it only after assuring yourselves of his true attitude, and on the assumption that you still find in him some good sense, some feeling of honour, some love for his country, some knowledge of his true interests, and some desire to pursue them. For at any time, and especially in the wretched situation in which Poland’s misfortunes are going to leave her, there would be nothing more fatal for her than to have a traitor at the head of her Government.

As for the way to embark on the business in question, I cannot appreciate all the subtleties being proposed to you in order to surprise, and as it were deceive, the Nation regarding the changes to be made to her laws. My only advice would be, when you show your plan in its full extent, not to begin its implementation abruptly by filling the republic with malcontents; to leave most officials where they are; to confer posts in line with the new reform only as they once again fall vacant. Never shake the machinery too abruptly. I have no doubt but that a good plan, once adopted, may change the spirit even of those who have taken part in Government under a different one. Not being able to create new citizens all at once, you should begin by taking advantage of the existing ones; and offering a new path for their ambition is the means of disposing them to follow it.

What if, despite the courage and constancy of the Confederates and despite the justice of their cause, fortune and all the powers abandon them and deliver up the fatherland to its oppressors … ? But I do not have the honour to be Polish; and in a situation like the one in which you are, it is not permitted to give one’s advice other than by one’s own example.

I have just fulfilled to the best of my abilities, and please God with as much success as enthusiasm, the task that Count Wielhorski imposed upon me. Perhaps it is all merely a collection of pipe-dreams, but there you have my ideas. It is not my fault if they are so unlike those of other men, and it was not up to me to organize my thoughts in another way. I even confess that whatever singularity may be found in them, for my part I see nothing other than what is well adapted to the human heart, good, and practicable, especially in Poland, since I took care in my views to follow the spirit of that Republic, and to propose only the fewest changes I could to correct its faults. It seems to me that a Government based on such resources must proceed to its true goal as directly, as certainly and for as long as possible; without being unaware, moreover, that all the works of men are imperfect, ephemeral and perishable like them.

I have deliberately omitted many very important topics upon which I did not feel that my knowledge was sufficient to pass judgement properly. I leave that task to men more enlightened and wiser than I. And I put an end to this lengthy hotchpotch by making my apologies to Count Wielhorski for having taken up his time with it for so long. Although I think differently from other men, I do not flatter myself that I am wiser than they, nor that there is anything in my musings that might be really useful to his fatherland. But my wishes for her prosperity are too sincere, too pure, too disinterested for pride in contributing to it to add anything to my ardour. May she triumph over her enemies, become and remain peaceful, happy and free, set a great example to the universe, and, benefiting from the patriotic labours of Count Wielhorski, find and form in her bosom many Citizens resembling him!

chapters.title: Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings
chapters.text:
Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

Notes

OF THE SOCIAL CONTRACT

Prefatory Note

1.  the abbé de Saint-Pierre: Charles-Irénée Castel, abbé de Saint-Pierre (1658–1743) was the author of a project for perpetual peace and a number of other works on public affairs and international relations.

Title-page

1.  foederis aequas / Dicamus leges: Aeneid, Book XI, line 321: ‘Let us declare fair terms of compact’.

BOOK I

1.  taking men as they are: Here Rousseau echoes a passage from Spinoza’s Political Treatise.

2.  any legitimate and reliable rule of administration: Rousseau’s reference to ‘administration’ here can mislead. His real focus is on the fundamental principles of the constitutional order.

3.  Man was born free … chains: Rousseau’s account of humankind’s natural freedom and its replacement by various forms of servitude and dependence is given in his Discourse on the Origins of Inequality Among Men.

4.  only through convention: Here, Rousseau recapitulates arguments put by John Locke in his Second Treatise of Government; see, for example, §55 of that work.

5.  Grotius: Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was the author of De Jure Belli ac Pacis, one of the founding texts for international law.

6.  also the view of Hobbes: In fact, Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679) argued for the natural equality of human beings in Leviathan (1651) as part of his argument for unlimited sovereignty. Rousseau often seeks to exaggerate the distance between Hobbes’s views and his own.

7.  Philo’s account: ‘The Embassy to Gaius’ was a report made by Philo Judaeus on the embassy he led from the Jews of Alexandria to the Emperor Gaius Caligula, which Rousseau probably read in a 1687 French edition of works by Flavius Josephus in which it was included.

8.  Ulysses’ companions loved their brutish condition: Ulysses, Latin name for Odysseus, a legendary Greek king of Ithaca and the hero of Homer’s Odyssey, in a celebrated episode of which he visits the island of Circe, who changes half his crew into swine.

9.  Force made the first slaves: Rousseau’s rejection of the idea of natural aristocracy and subordination here stands in contrast to his claims that women are naturally subordinate to men in Book V of Emile.

10.  emperor Noah … Saturn’s children: The biblical figure of Noah had three sons, who were generally interpreted in medieval Christianity as ancestors of the populations of the three known continents, Japheth: Europe, Shem: Asia, and Ham: Africa. According to the Romans, Saturn (Chronos in Greek mythology) was a god, the son of Uranus. He was credited with six children, of whom three – Jupiter, Pluto and Neptune – ruled respectively over the sky, the underworld and the sea (while Vesta, Ceres and Juno were patrons of the home, fertility and women).

11.  in Cyclops’ cave: Cyclops was in Greek and Roman mythology a member of a primordial race of giants, each with a single eye in the middle of his forehead.

12.  the Peace of God: The so-called Peace of God (supplemented in AD 1040 by the ‘Truce of God’) was a broad reform movement initiated by the Church in late tenth- and early eleventh-century France, its aim not merely to protect ecclesiastical property from devastation and the population at large from the ravages of castellans, but beyond that to regulate internecine violence more generally in feudal society. King (St) Louis IX (1226–70) built upon these to limit (albeit not suppress) private wars between barons by imposing a forty-day moratorium before they might be launched, and by abolishing duels as an element of the judicial system.

13.  Cato the Elder … Popilius: Marcus Porcius Cato, 234–149 BC,statesman, general, agriculturist and writer, is taken here by Rousseau as a model of the traditional Roman virtues of respect for discipline and order. His son was likewise called Marcus Porcius Cato (as was his better-known great-grandson Cato the Younger). The Popilius in question was Gaius Popilius Laenas, consul in 172 bc and again in 158. The story here is taken from Cicero’s De Officiis. The reference to the siege of Clusium (c.391 BC) involves a discreditable episode in which Roman treachery led the besieging Gauls to abandon the siege and march instead on Rome itself.

14.  For any States … differing nature: Rousseau is here summarizing the argument of his Principles of the Right of War, contained in this volume but unpublished in his own lifetime.

15.  The primitive state can no longer subsist … way of being: The theory of human development gestured at here is the one sketched in his Discourse on the Origins of Inequality Among Men.

16.  a corporate and collective body: The French phrase Rousseau uses here is ‘corps moral et collectif’, which poses formidable translation difficulties. The most direct translation, ‘moral’, has the misleading connotation of ‘ethical’, whereas what Rousseau intends is that the entity has a special sort of personhood, akin in some ways to legal personality. ‘Artificial’ would probably be too Hobbesian in its associations.

17.  formerly given the name of City: Rousseau’s reference here is probably to Jean Bodin (1530–96) and his Six Books of the Commonwealth (1576).

18.  M. d’Alembert … ‘Geneva’: D’Alembert’s essay on ‘Geneva’ appeared in the Encyclopédie, vol. 7 (1757).

19.  Now the Sovereign: Rousseau’s subject, both in this paragraph, and the two which immediately follow, is the classical problem of who should judge the matter of a breach in the social contract, given that there is no common superior for individuals and the sovereign to appeal to.

20.  guarantees him against all personal dependence: Rousseau makes the connection between freedom and not being dependent on the particular will of another person explicit in the Eighth of the Letters Written from the Mountains; see p. 185–6.

21.  below that from which he emerged: This is another tacit reference to the argument of the Discourse on Inequality. Rousseau believed that the psychological changes that accompany the development of the human race were overwhelmingly likely to result in oppression, alienation and a damaging dependence of individuals on the wills and desires of others, but that they also make possible human rationality and morality.

22.  moral liberty: Although Rousseau here presents ‘moral liberty’ as an afterthought, obedience to oneself is central to the problem of reconciling liberty and authority that he sets himself in Book I, Chapter 6.

23.  When Nuñez Balboa … Princes of the world: Vasco Núñez de Balboa (c.1475–1519) established the first mainland Spanish colony in the Americas in 1510, and in 1513 was the first Spaniard to cross the isthmus of Panama and reach the Pacific Ocean, which he named the Mar del Sur, or South Sea.

BOOK II

1.  at most it is a decree: Here Rousseau makes an essential distinction, which he returns to in Book II, Chapter 6 below. Law is always what the sovereign decides upon as a matter of its general will: it comes from all the citizens and applies to them all. Particular acts of administration are always applications of such laws rather than being laws themselves.

2.  sometimes they separate them: It may appear to a modern reader as if Rousseau is here rejecting a doctrine of the separation of powers. That is not what this passage is about. Rather, he is arguing against the idea that sovereignty can be understood as a list of different functions rather than as the exercise of the general will by the whole people.

3.  the first book of Grotius: The reference is to De Jure Belli ac Pacis (see Book I, note 5 above).

4.  You always will your own good … see it: Cf. Plato, Protagoras 345e and Gorgias 466d, where Socrates argues that all actions aim at the good of the person who acts and that the pursuit of aims that are not actually beneficial to the agent is explained by defects in knowledge.

5.  Numa, and Servius: Numa Pompilius (753–673 BC) was the legendary second king of Rome, succeeding Romulus. He was credited with establishing many of the early institutions of monarchical Rome, and with reforming the calendar. Servius Tullius was the legendary sixth king of Rome, reigning 578–535 BC. Gaining the throne without election by the Senate, he enjoyed popular support and introduced numerous reforms (including an expanded franchise and the city’s first true coinage). He also increased the territory of Rome.

6.  If, when a properly informed people … astray: Some modern writers have seen in the last two paragraphs of this chapter an anticipation by Rousseau of the jury theorem devised by the Marquis de Condorcet (1743–94). However, the evidence for any direct influence of Rousseau on Condorcet is weak. See B. Grofman and S. L. Feld, ‘Rousseau’s General Will, a Condorcetian Perspective’, American Political Science Review 82 (1988), pp. 567–76.

7.  a justice emanating from reason alone: Rousseau here distances himself from Charles-Louis de Secondat, baron de Montesquieu’s opening paragraph in his The Spirit of Laws (1748).

8.  the civil or kingly man: The reference is to Plato’s dialogue Politikos, ‘The Statesman’.

9.  the Decemvirs: A commission of ten men or decemvirate was appointed in 452 BC to draw up a code of administration for Rome, with all other magistracies being temporarily suspended; a code of law under ten headings was duly drawn up and passed. A second decemvirate was then appointed in 450, but although two further laws were added – thus completing the Law of the Twelve Tables that was to form the basis of Roman administration for centuries – on this occasion the experiment turned out to be less successful, since the decemvirate became increasingly violent and tyrannical, leading to its enforced resignation under popular pressure in 449 BC and a return of the normal magistracies.

10.  persuade without convincing: Rousseau gives more detail of the kinds of techniques a legislator might use in his unpublished An Essay on the Origin of Languages, ch. 20, and in Considerations on the Government of Poland, chs. 1–2 (below).

11.  to conclude with Warburton: William Warburton (1698–1779), Bishop of Gloucester, was the author of The Alliance between Church and State (1736, French translation 1742) and Divine Legation of Moses (1737 and 1741).

12.  Minos had imposed discipline … vice: Minos was a mythical king of Crete, or according to some scholars two different kings, one ‘good’ and a lawgiver, the other, his grandson, ‘bad’ and the master of the Minotaur, to whom he sacrificed an annual tribute extracted from Athens of seven boys and seven girls.

13.  Such was Sparta … Tyrants: For Lycurgus, see note 6 to the Introduction above. The seven legendary Tarquin rulers supposedly held sway in Rome before the popular uprising that established the Roman Republic in 509 BC. In 1581 the northern provinces of the Netherlands adopted the Act of Abjuration, the declaration of independence in which the provinces officially deposed Philip II of Spain as reigning monarch. In Switzerland, the ‘Old Confederacy’ fought a long struggle for independence in the fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, but it was only at the 1648 Treaty of Westphalia that the country’s independence from the Holy Roman Empire was generally recognized.

14.  Peter had a genius for imitation: The reference is to Peter I ‘the Great’ (1672–1725), who as tsar of Russia carried out a sweeping programme of modernization, inspired by West European models.

15.  Descartes’ vortices: In his 1644 Principles of Philosophy, René Descartes wrote: ‘Whatever was the manner whereby matter was first set in motion, the vortices into which it is divided must now be so disposed that each turns in the direction in which it is easiest for it to continue its movement for, in accordance with the laws of nature, a moving body is easily deflected by meeting another body.’ His theory of vortices became for a time (prior to Newton) the accepted explanation for the regular movement of planets in the solar system.

16.  the Isle of Corsica: For the Corsican struggle for independence from Genoa, and Rousseau’s own involvement with that cause, see the Prefatory Note to his Constitutional Proposal for Corsica on pp. 189–90.

17.  The author of The Spirit of Laws: I.e. Montesquieu. See Book II, note 7 above.

18.  between intermediate terms: As Rousseau makes clear below, the government is the principal one of these ‘intermediate terms’.

BOOK III

1.  even when the Doge is not present: The Doge was the chief magistrate and leader of the Most Serene Republic of Venice from the eighth century AD until the republic’s overthrow by Napoleon Bonaparte in 1797. The office was elective not hereditary, and was normally a lifetime appointment.

2.  a continued proportion: A ‘continued (or continuous) proportion’ in mathematics is one composed of two or more equal ratios, in which the consequent of each preceding ratio is identical to the antecedent of the following one, as in 4:8, 8:16, 16:32; or an ordered set of numbers such that the ratio between any two successive terms is identical, as in 1:3:9:27:81. A ‘mean proportional’ in mathematics differs from an arithmetic mean or ‘average’ in that the numbers are multiplied and then the nth root taken (where n is the count of numbers in the set). The ‘quotient’ (exposant) here results from division of the antecedent by the successive term.

3.  eight Emperors were seen at one time … divided: This doubtless refers to the decade after AD 275 during which eight emperors laid claim to the imperial power, prior to the establishment of Diocletian’s undisputed rule.

4.  a celebrated author: Montesquieu (see Book II, note 7) in his Spirit of Laws, Book III, Chapter 3.

5.  Malo periculosam libertatem quem quietum servitium: ‘I prefer dangerous liberty to tranquil servitude’.

6.  Gerontes: Magistrates in ancient Sparta, who formed the supreme civic authority alongside the kings and ephors.

7.  Archimedes: Archimedes of Syracuse (c.287–c.212 BC) was a Greek mathematician, inventor, astronomer and engineer, credited notably with many achievements in theoretical and applied hydraulics.

8.  Samuel pointed out forcefully to the Hebrews: See I Samuel, chapter 8.

9.  Machiavelli’s Prince is the book of republicans: Niccolò Machiavelli (1469–1527), Florentine writer and political theorist. In addition to The Prince his Discourses on Livy were also influential on Rousseau.

10.   Titus Livius: The great Roman historian Titus Livius (59 BC–AD 17) is more commonly known in English as Livy.

11.  the young Dionysius: Dionysius the Younger, who succeeded his father Dionysius the Elder as tyrant of Syracuse in Sicily in 367 BC, ruling until 357 and again 346–44.

12.  as in Poland: See Considerations on the Government of Poland, ‘Means of Maintaining the Constitution’, p. 266 below, where Rousseau discusses the independence of ministers and high officials in Poland.

13.  this principle established by Montesquieu: Rousseau will have had in mind Book XVII, Chapters 2 and 6 of The Spirit of Laws, and perhaps also a passage from Letter CXXXI of the same author’s Persian Letters.

14.  We are all carnivorous beasts, says Chardin: This passage comes from Jean Chardin, Voyage en Perse (Amsterdam 1735), volume III, pp. 76 and 83–4. Originally published in ten volumes in 1711 as Voyages de monsieur le chevalier Chardin en Perse et autres lieux de l’Orient, the work was translated into English as The Travels of Sir John Chardin in Persia and the Orient.

15.   We should follow … as liberty: The two Latin quotations in this foontnote are from Tacitus’ Agricola, sections 21 and 31 respectively. The ‘bickerings’ to which Rousseau refers were the so-called 1651–3 Fronde of the nobles; the Coadjutor of Paris was the Cardinal de Retz, himself active in the Fronde, whose lively description of the volatile situation in the parliament can be found in his memoirs: see Mémoires, 1, III (Geneva edition of 1777, volume 2, p. 122). The passage quoted from Machiavelli (see Book III, note 9) can be found in the preface to his  The Florentine Histories (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1990), p.7.

16.  The slow formation … confirms it: The Serrar del Consiglio of 1198 was defined by Ruskin in his Stones of Venice as ‘the final and absolute distinction of the nobles from the commonalty and the establishment of the government in their hands to the exclusion alike of the influence of the people on the one side and the authority of the doge on the other’. The Squitinio della libertà veneta (Scrutiny of Venetian Liberty) was an anonymous anti-Venetian pamphlet published in 1612 which sought to establish the sovereignty of the Holy Roman Emperor over the Republic of Venice. Lucius Cornelius Sulla (c.136–78 BC) was a Roman general and statesman who was appointed dictator by the Senate in 82 BC but resigned the office at the end of 81 after a year of virtually absolute power. The first Triumvirate, formed in 59 BC between Gaius Julius Caesar, Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus (Pompey) and Marcus Licinius Crassus, lasted until the death of Crassus in 53. A second Triumvirate was formed in 43 BC following the assassination of Julius Caesar, between Octavian (later known as Augustus), Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Mark Antony; this lasted until 33 BC, when Augustus became sole ruler, emperor in all but name. In AD 14 Augustus died and was succeeded by Tiberius Julius Caesar Augustus (42 BC–AD 37), whose rule marked the formal transition from Republic to Empire.

17.  at the time of the Gracchi: In the late Roman Republic, the Gracchi brothers, Tiberius and Gaius, were plebeian tribunes (respectively 133–131 and 123–121 BC), each of whom sought to limit patrician power and landholding by rallying popular support, leading in each case to their violent deaths. According to Plutarch, Gaius attracted so many supporters from outside the city that there was no room for them to vote in the usual place, so many of them climbed onto the roofs of houses to cast their votes for him.

BOOK IV

1.  Cromwell: Oliver Cromwell (1599–1658) was the most prominent anti-monarchist leader in the English Civil War and was Lord Protector of England 1653–58.

2.  the Duke of Beaufort: François de Vendôme, duc de Beaufort (1616–69), was the illegitimate grandson of Henri IV of France, a prominent leader of the Fronde and opponent of Cardinal Mazarin, later an admiral serving with distinction against Algerian corsairs and Ottomans in the Mediterranean. He was portrayed fictionally in the novels Twenty Years After and The Man in the Iron Mask by Alexandre Dumas.

3.  I would have many reflections … own members: This paragraph is important to the assessment of how democratic Rousseau’s ideal state would be. On the one hand, this suggests that the magistrates exercise significant control over the political agenda; on the other, it is unclear whether Rousseau is merely reporting the natural tendency of governments to seek control – a theme that is an important part both of this text and the Letters Written from the Mountains – or recommending how government should act.

4.  Tacitus observes … each of them had said: See Tacitus, Histories, I, 85. Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian all briefly wore the imperial purple in AD 69, the so-called year of the four emperors.

5.  Barnaboti: Impoverished Venetian nobles in the later years of the Republic, so called after the area round Campo San Barnaba, where they habitually met and lodged.

6.  the abbé de St Pierre proposed … form of Government: In his Discours sur la Polysynodie (1718).

7.  instruments of war: More precisely, performers of martial music.

8.  capite censi: Literally, ‘those counted by head’.

9.  Marius was the first who deigned to enlist them: Gaius Marius (157–86 BC) was a Roman general and statesman, seven times elected Consul, who enacted sweeping military reforms that included allowing the recruitment of landless citizens.

10.  Cicero: Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), Roman statesman and philosopher. See De Legibus, III, I5.

11.  the blood of Agis: Agis IV, King of Sparta 245–241 BC and a would-be reformer, was the first Spartan king to be killed by the ephors (after a mock trial).

12.  Cleomenes: Cleomenes III, King of Sparta 235–222 BC, after Agis’ execution was forced to marry his widow, Agiatis; when he himself ascended to the throne, he sought to follow Agis’ reforming example; however, despite eliminating the ephors who had killed Agis, he himself was eventually defeated and committed suicide.

13.  Pompey: Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus (106–48 BC) was a military and political leader of the Roman Republic, allied to Julius Caesar in the first Triumvirate, but contending with him for power after the death of the third triumvir Crassus in 53 BC; he was defeated by Caesar at the battle of Pharsalus and later assassinated in Egypt, where he had taken refuge.

14.  the Catiline affair: Lucius Sergius Catilina (108–62 BC) was a Roman politician, implicated (on the first occasion perhaps unjustly) in two conspiracies to overthrow the Republic, in 65 and 63 BC.

15.  the Lacedaemonians: Sparta was generally referred to in ancient Greek times as Lacedaemon, or Lacedaemonia.

16.  from another Island: Chios, in French Chio, pronounced indistinguishably from the vulgar slang word chiots (chiottes) ‘jakes’, ‘shithouse’.

17.  Moloch, Saturn and Chronos … Baal of the Phoenicians: Moloch was the name of an ancient Semitic god, particularly venerated by the Phoenicians, to whom human sacrifices were made. For Saturn and Chronos, see Book I, note 10 above. Baal was an ancient Semitic title (lord) given to various local deities, patrons of individual cities, and used in the Hebrew Bible as synonymous with ‘false god’.

18.  the sect of Ali: Mohammed’s cousin and son-in-law Ali, whom the adherents of Shia Islam hold to have been the Prophet’s true successor.

19.  Bayle and Warburton: Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), French philosopher and author of the Historical and Critical Dictionary (1695); for Warburton see Book II, note 11 above.

20.  sacer esto[d]: ‘Be accursed!’: traditional Roman formula pronounced when delivering someone up to execution and the wrath of the gods.

21.  contrary to the social spirit: Rousseau here reproduces, almost unchanged, the opinions of Machiavelli in the Discourses (II.2).

22.  Fabius’ soldiers: Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus (known as Cunctator, the Delayer, c.280–203 BC) was a Roman politician and general, whose advocacy of attritional warfare was important in Rome’s eventual victory over Carthage in the Second Punic War.

23.  And if anyone … lied before the laws: Rousseau’s rather bloodthirsty opinion here contradicts his stance in other writings such as Julie, where he writes that, if he were a judge in a system where atheists faced the death penalty, he would begin by condemning to death those who denounce their fellow citizens as such (Oeuvres Complètes, vol. 2, p. 589n).

24.  The dogmas of the civil Religion: The only laws that Rousseau specifically prescribes for his ideal state. They therefore form an unusual exception, since it is for the sovereign people and not for some philosopher to decide on the content of the laws.

GENEVA MS

1.  the independent man whom the wise man stifles: The same person as the ‘violent interlocutor’ to whom Diderot responds in his article on ‘Natural Right’ for the Encyclopédie. Diderot replies to this figure by referring him to an abstract general will of the human race; Rousseau’s reply here expresses scepticism about the motivational power of such abstract ideas before rejecting them in favour of particular societies and institutions with their own general will and the capacity to reshape the psychology of individuals.

2.  Justinian: Justinian (AD 483–565), often known as Justinian the Great, ruled as Byzantine emperor from 527 to 565. His reign saw an ambitious attempt to restore the Roman Empire, whose western half had long been effectively defunct. His generals, most notably Belisarius, defeated Vandals and Ostrogoths, and brought large territories in Italy, south-east Europe, Iberia and North Africa back under imperial control. He oversaw a flowering of Byzantine culture, and above all initiated the systematic rewriting of Roman law, the Corpus Juris Civilis, which still forms the basis of civil law in many countries to this day.

3.  Hostis enim … dicimus: ‘For, among our ancestors. he whom we now call foreign was called an enemy’ (De Officiis (On Duties), I, xii, 37).

4.  Hobbes’s error … effect: Rousseau here reproduces an argument against Hobbes that features prominently in the Discourse on Inequality.

PRINCIPLES OF THE RIGHT OF WAR

1.  the right of nations: In other words, international law.

2.  Peace of God: See Of the Social Contract, Book I, note 12, above.

3.  Saint Louis: See Of the Social Contract, Book I, note 12, above.

4.  Minos and the Athenians … emperors of Mexico … kings of Guinea: Minos was a legendary king of Knossos in Crete, who figures in ancient Attic literature and myth (e.g. the story of Theseus) as having exacted from Athens a yearly tribute of seven youths and seven maidens to be sacrificed to the Minotaur. The emperors of Mexico referred to here must be the pre-Hispanic Aztec rulers. Guinea here means the whole of western and equatorial Africa south of the Sahara prior to the establishment of European colonial rule.

5.  Let us leave to the Tarentines … the same policy at Syracuse: In 209 BC, during the Second Punic War of the Roman Republic against Carthage, Quintus Fabius Maximus (see Of the Social Contract, Book IV, note 22, above) recaptured Tarentum (today‘s Taranto) from forces siding with the Carthaginian general Hannibal. During the same war, in 212 BC, Marcus Claudius Marcellus took Syracuse for Rome (Archimedes dying during the subsequent sack of the city) and carried off numerous artworks to adorn Rome.

6.  The only hardship that Cyrus imposed … not to be related: Cyrus the Great, founder of the Persian Empire, conquered Lydia and its capital Sardis in about 546 BC. According to Herodotus (I, 155), he was persuaded by the former Lydian ruler Croesus, who was his prisoner, to respond to a subsequent revolt by the Lydians not, as he had at first planned, by enslaving them, but rather by turning their minds to a life of peace and luxury. Aristodemus (born 550 BC), nicknamed Malakos (the Tender), ruled Cumae, a Greek colony north-west of present-day Naples. According to Dionysius of Halicarnassus, he rose to power with popular support, defeated an Etruscan coalition in 524 BC, but became a ruthless tyrant and was assassinated. Plutarch tells the story of how he compelled young men to dress effeminately and young girls to dress in masculine garb, and how he was brought down by the hand of Xenocrite, a girl whom he had taken against her will.

7.  Aristotle says … declare war upon them: Aristotle reported on this custom in ‘Fragment 538’, included in the third volume of the Bekker edition of his works, edited by Valentin Rose; his account was referred to in Plutarch‘s Life of Lycurgus, 28, 7.

LETTERS WRITTEN FROM THE MOUNTAINS

1.  both books were condemned: For a fuller account of the events in Geneva surrounding the suppression of Of the Social Contract, see Richard Fralin, Rousseau and Representation (New York: Columbia, 1977), ch. 8, which this note draws upon.

2.  the land of dreams: The utopian works referred to here alongside Plato’s Republic are Sir Thomas More’s Utopia and Histoire des Sévarambes by Denis Vairasse d’Allais.

3.  The unfortunate Sidney: Algernon Sidney was an English republican soldier, diplomat and theorist, executed in 1683 for his part in the Rye House Plot to kill Charles II and his brother, the future James II. At his trial for treason, the draft of his Discourses concerning Government, discovered among his papers on his arrest, was taken in lieu of a second witness for the prosecution. The work was published posthumously in 1698, and translated into French in 1702.

4.  Althusius in Germany: The German Calvinist jurist Johannes Althusius (1563–1638) published his Politica methodice digesta in 1603, in which he notably insisted upon the indivisible and inalienable nature of sovereignty, and developed an early version of federalism based on his espousal of the Dutch Revolt.

5.  Liberty consists … your own: Here Rousseau clearly commits himself to an understanding of freedom or liberty as non-subjection to the particular will of others. In other places, such as the famous ‘forced to be free’ passage in Of the Social Contract, he relies on this understanding but does not formulate it as explicitly as he does here.

6.  like Otho: Marcus Salvius Otho was Roman emperor for three months in AD 69. According to Tacitus in Histories, I, 36: ‘Nec deerat Otho protendens manus adorare volgum, jacere oscula, et omnia serviliter pro dominatione’ (‘Otho did not fail to play his part; he stretched out his arms, and bowed to the crowd, and kissed his hands, and altogether acted the slave, to make himself the master’).

CONSTITUTIONAL PROPOSAL FOR CORSICA

1.  the Barbary pirates: Berber pirates, otherwise known as corsairs, operating out of such North African ports as Tunis, Tripoli and Algiers, ravaged shipping especially in the Western Mediterranean from the sixteenth to the nineteenth centuries, capturing hundreds of vessels and perhaps one million mainly Christian slaves for the Islamic (notably Ottoman) market.

2.  each form of government … one form of government or another: On this point, see Of the Social Contract, Book III, Chapter 8, above.

3.  the report drawn up at Vescovado in 1764: The reference is to Count Matthieu de Buttafoco’s ‘Memoria sopra la Costituzione Politica da stabilire nel Regno di Corsica’, presented to the Corsican assembly held at Vescovado in May 1764, but not in fact considered by this body.

4.  pievi: A pieve (plural pievi) was originally a medieval ecclesiastical unit in Italy and in Corsica, roughly equivalent to a parish. Through Pisan administrative reforms in the eleventh century, the pievi of Corsica were established as the basic administrative units on the island, intermediate between communes and provinces. In Rousseau’s day, they were the principal administrative units, rendered here as ‘communes’. The boundaries of the sixtytwo pievi correspond exactly to those of today’s cantons.

5.  Aix-la-Chapelle remonstrance … their nobility: In 1748 the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle at the end of the War of Austrian Succession placed Corsica back under Genoese jurisdiction, despite remonstrations by Corsican patriots arguing that Genoese rule was intolerable to them, and complaining in particular because the Corsican nobility did not enjoy the same privileges as that of Genoa.

6.  the Popes had vested the island of Corsica: The Papacy played a major role in Corsica from the late eleventh century, and annexed the island to the Holy See in 1217, in an ultimately vain attempt to end the rival claims of Genoa and Pisa, cities which, later joined by Aragon, were to contend for mastery over it, and for Papal backing, for the next three centuries.

7.  wholly free: As opposed to the island’s actual condition of semifreedom, with its main ports still in Genoese hands.

8.  terra di commune: Communal land established in the early eleventh century, by a movement aimed at curbing feudal anarchy comparable to the Peace of God movement in Languedoc. In the course of the fourteenth century the entire north-east of the island (between Calvi, Bastia and Solenzara) was freed from feudal obligations; henceforth twelve autonomous communes, each with its own assembly headed by a Podestat, would band together as terra di commune, with the land either leased to individual peasants or left open for flocks. This effectively put an end to the wars between rival barons and petty lords in the north of the island, although the south remained wild.

9.  between the two main parts: Corsica is roughly divided by a mountain range running from south-east to north-west. The area closer to the Italian peninsula, comprising six provinces with forty-one pievi, is known as ‘di quà dai monti’ or ‘this side of the mountains’; the area facing across the Mediterranean to the Iberian peninsula, with three provinces containing twenty-one pievi, is known as ‘di là dai monti’ or ‘beyond the mountains’.

10.  Diodorus says: Diodorus of Sicily was a Greek historian writing in the first century BC, author of a monumental ‘Universal history from the origins of the world up to Caesar’, from which Rousseau takes this description.

11.  you are no longer surprised … against this heroic nation: The three attacks on Switzerland alluded to are presumably those of Austria in the fourteenth century, Burgundy in the fifteenth and the Holy Roman Empire under Maximilian I in the sixteenth.

12.  when a French minister frowns: The reference here is to the duc de Choiseul, principal minister of Louis XV, whom Rousseau blamed for intervening with the authorities of Berne and so causing his expulsion from Switzerland, as he recounts in Confessions, Book XII. He compares this with the time, prior to the Perpetual Peace signed with the Swiss in 1515 by François I, when France feared Swiss depredations.

13.  The wretched Corsicans … the favour of being disarmed: The Genoese raised considerable revenue in Corsica from the sale of permits to bear arms, and also from the sale of safe-conducts to persons guilty of murder. Confronted by an alarming rise in blood crimes, and by public indignation in Corsica, they eventually decided to forbid the bearing of arms. But in order to make up for the consequent loss of revenue, they imposed a new tax indiscriminately on the entire population. Not only did these measures do nothing to lessen the number of murders; they also proved so unpopular that they were a direct cause of the 1729 uprising.

14.  the collection of land taxes: The taille was a feudal direct tax on land; in France by the late fifteenth century it had become a purely royal prerogative, and it continued to be levied until the 1789 Revolution.

15.  the project of an equal population: Rousseau advances the idea that a territory should be evenly populated in Of the Social Contract, Book III, Chapter 13 above.

16.  the pistoles in France: The French name for the Spanish gold coin known in English as a ‘doubloon’, i.e. the double escudo. The louis d’or introduced by Louis XIII in 1640, upon which pre-revolutionary French coinage was based, was initially its equivalent.

17.  Masters of Rivers and Forests: The Grand maître des eaux et forêts was an important officer in feudal France, charged with protecting the royal domain especially in respect of hunting, fishing and wood-gathering rights. From the late sixteenth century on, the office was progressively subdivided, so that the maître des eaux et forêts became an essential official of local administration.

18.  capitation: Capitation or poll-tax was the main form of direct taxation in pre-revolutionary France, with amounts to be paid by head varying according to class.

19.   vectigal: Term used in ancient Rome for all the state’s revenues, but at the height of Roman power the bulk of these did indeed derive from external tribute.

20.  The acquisition … too much or too little: According to the Old Testament story (Genesis 47: 20–31), Joseph was sold by his brothers into slavery in Egypt, but rose to be the Pharaoh’s vizier after interpreting his dream. Following his advice, Egypt stored up goods during seven years of abundance in order to survive the seven years of famine that would follow. Towards the end of the seven lean years, however, even Egypt began to run short, so Joseph obliged its inhabitants – with exception made for the priestly caste – to sell all their property to the Pharaoh in return for seed, so that it became state property. Since they would henceforth be farming on state land, they would have to pay one-fifth of their produce to the Pharaoh.

21.  forced labour: The corvée is a form of unpaid labour imposed by force, as for instance in pre-revolutionary France.

22.  no publicans in the State: Publicans in the ancient world were public contractors, and notably – e.g. in Rome – tax collectors.

23.  Hôtel-Dieu in Paris … Lyons: Hôtel-Dieu, or ‘hostel of God’, was the old term for the principal hospital in French towns, that of Paris dating from 660 and that of Lyons from 1478.

24.  stealing from his creditors: The modern reader, accustomed to fiat currency, may find this passage puzzling since governments intent on fleecing their creditors now inflate away debt in a manner that reduces the value of the currency. However, in earlier times, such as Rousseau’s, currency purportedly derived its value fr0m its metallic content (often gold). Governments could therefore debase the coinage either by stamping a higher face value on coins of constant metallic content (the practice Rousseau refers to here) or by adulterating the metal or by clipping the coin

25.  Gazetteers: Journalists.

26.  the Catos: Members of a distinguished Plebeian family in ancient Rome, notably the statesmen Marcus Porcius Cato (234–149 BC) and his great-grandson Marcus Porcius Cato Uticensis (95–46 BC), both noted for their strict republican morality.

27.  Le prerogative che goderanno le sudette famiglie: The opening words of a quotation from Buttafoco’s report (see note 3 above), expressing support for an idea with which Rousseau strongly disagreed, namely that the privileges of the Corsican nobility should be restored.

CONSIDERATIONS ON THE GOVERNMENT OF POLAND

1.  Count Wielhorski’s description … government: The document Rousseau refers to has not been identified.

2.  end of the Social Contract: The reference is to the chapter on civil religion.

3.  there to take lessons in corruption: Rousseau had condemned the modern theatre for its corrupting effects on republican virtue in his Letter to d’Alembert.

4.  A proof of this … live in the memory: The Bar Confederation of 1768: an association of nobles determined to preserve Polish independence.

5.  black sauce: Spartan ‘black broth’ was a stew made from pork, salt, vinegar and blood; according to Plutarch the older inhabitants of Sparta were devoted to it, but it did not meet with favour elsewhere. The individual referred to is Brasidas.

6.  to be another Croesus: Croesus (596–c.547 BC) was king of Lydia in Asia Minor until his defeat by the Persians, proverbial for his wealth.

7.  what that much praised Tsar did: A reference to Tsar Peter I the Great, who obliged his court to adopt Western (especially French) apparel and customs.

8.  the Magnates: In reference to the Middle Ages, the term ‘magnate’ is widely used for major territorial landowners. Specifically in the Kingdom of Poland, and later in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, the magnates were a distinct social class of wealthy and influential nobility.

9.  duc d’Epernon … duc de Sully: Jean Louis de Nogaret, duc d’Epernon (1554–1642), was a Catholic nobleman who made a brilliant military career under Henri III; out of favour under Henri IV, he took part in various plots culminating in the latter’s assassination, after which he returned to public life and was involved in the persecution of Huguenots. Maximilien de Béthune, duc de Sully (1564–1640) was a prominent Huguenot nobleman, principal adviser to Henri IV from the latter’s accession in 1589 until his assassination in 1610, but obliged to withdraw from the court in 1611.

10.  ‘moot State’: By analogy with ‘moot courts’, ‘moot assemblies’, etc.

11.  three States combined in one: Greater Poland, Lesser Poland and Lithuania being three parts of the whole.

12.  the Dietines: The assemblies of each Palatinate.

13.  the legislator: Rousseau’s reference to the legislator here is confusing, and matters are not helped by the subsequent references in this chapter. He may be referring to the sovereign people who legislate rather than to a figure like the Legislator of Of the Social Contract, Book II, Chapter 7.

14.  the pacta conventa: Articles of agreement: a pledge made by each Polish king to uphold the constitution.

15.  in Of the Social Contract: See Of the Social Contract, Book III, Chapter 18.

16.  in his Polysynodie: See Of the Social Contract, Book IV, note 6, above.

17.  his authority: Again, this may not be a reference to a figure such as the Legislator of Of the Social Contract.

18.  liberum veto: A device that allowed any member of the assembly to bring a session to an end and nullify anything approved there by declaring ‘I do not allow’.

19.  where I advance it: Of the Social Contract, Book III, Chapters 12–13.

20.  The Legislator corporately: The reference to ‘the Legislator corporately’ strengthens the notion that this is a reference to the sovereign people, especially given the language so strongly reminiscent of the opening paragraph of Of the Social Contract, Book II, Chapter 3.

21.  the comitia: For the Roman comitia, see Of the Social Contract, Book IV, Chapter 4.

22.  Rugi: The Polish word rugi can be translated as ‘eviction’ or ‘exclusion’.

23.  Radom’s commissaries … the Tribunal: The dicastery of Radom was a kind of fiscal court scrutinizing accounts, made up of senators designated by the Diet and commissaries elected by the Dietines, abolished by the Diet in 1764 and replaced by a commission of the exchequer. The Tribunal was a supreme court of appeal held alternately at Piotrków and Lublin.

24.  Laudum: The confirmation sworn by officials in each Palatinate that a particular candidate had been duly elected.

25.  this Wilkes is a mere troublemaker: The reference is to John Wilkes (1725–97), the English radical journalist and politician, who in 1769 was elected to Parliament and disqualified three times, formally on the grounds that he had been an outlaw at the time of his election, but more substantially on the grounds of his unacceptability to King George III and the Court.

26.  Venice’s Golden Book: The Libro d’Oro or Golden Book was the formal register of nobles in the Republic of Venice.

27.  in every Grod: The Grod was the registry attached to every local administration.

28.  Now the law … balanced by their multiplicity: These remarks recall Rousseau’s discussion in Of the Social Contract, Book II, Chapter 3 of the difference between the general will and the will of all.

29.  the Palatines of Polock and Witebsk … the Starost of Samogitie: The Palatines of Polock and Witebsk, and the Starost (Elder) of Samogitie, whose status was equivalent to that of a Palatine, were appointed by the King and sat in the Senate; but their appointment went through a two-stage process of election by ‘popular’ assembly and then by the Dietine.

30.  I have discussed most carefully in the Social Contract: See Of the Social Contract, Book IV, Chapter 2.

31.  the Archbishop of Gniezno: The Roman Catholic Archbishop of Gniezno is traditionally Primate of the Polish Church.

32.  Denmark … England … Sweden: In 1770 the Danish royal doctor, Johann Friedrich Struensee (1737–72), who had become the Queen of Denmark’s lover, insinuated himself into a position of supreme power within the state, which he used to promote various Enlightenment reforms. He alienated both the nobility and the Danish people and was arrested and executed in 1772. Ironically, given the remarks here, Struensee was an admirer of Rousseau. In England, the radical John Wilkes (see note 25) was repeatedly disbarred and re-elected to Parliament in 1769. In Sweden, following half a century of parliamentary domination, King Gustav III (1746–92) came to the throne in 1771, and in 1772 led a coup d’état, with French support, that established him as an ‘enlightened despot’.

33.  the imperial capitulations: In 1519 the Imperial Diet and Grand Electors imposed ‘capitulations’ on the German Emperor in return for their recognition of the hereditary principle, and new guarantees were given in 1711 when Charles VI inherited the Habsburg domains and was elected Emperor.

34.  unanimity was required: See Rousseau’s assertion in Of the Social Contract, Book IV, Chapter 2 that the social pact is the only law which requires unanimity.

35.  the Pseudo-Diet of 1768: The last extraordinary Diet of Warsaw, convened under Russian pressure in October 1767, prorogued in March 1768, which listed a number of fundamental laws and constitutional provisions. Those referred to here were the first, that the republic of Poland was composed of three orders, the King, the Senate and the Equestrian Order; the fifth, that the election of kings must be unanimous and excluded heredity of the Crown; the ninth, confirming the indissoluble unity of the Crown and the Grand Duchy; and the eleventh, guaranteeing the equality and the prerogatives of the szlachta, body politic of the nation.

36.  men of the sword and men of the gown: In France, the noblesse d’épée referred to the traditional nobility rooted in medieval feudalism, while noblesse de robe – attained through the occupation of a range of public functions – was formalized in 1600; in European parlance it subsequently came to refer more generally to members of the legal professions and public servants.

37.  entails or Majorats: Majorat is the right of succession to property according to age (primogeniture). A majorat (fidéicommis) would be inherited by the eldest son, or if there was no son by the nearest male relative. The institution was designed to prevent the division of wealthy estates between many family members. In the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, majorat was known as ordynacja. Introduced in the late sixteenth century by King Stefan Batory, it assisted the creation of major magnate fortunes such as that of the Radziwills, and survived until the Communist period following the Second World War.

38.  the Bailiffs of the Canton of Berne: Berne was ruled by a Grand Council, whose members were known as Bailiffs (a term, widespread in Europe, that had lost its original meaning of royal steward and come merely to designate an important civic official). Rousseau’s earlier good opinion of the administration of Berne had given way to the harsh judgements expressed here, following his two expulsions from the canton.

39.  a people of Capuchins: Order of Friars Minor Capuchin, founded in 1520, originally as a reform movement within the Franciscans and aiming to return the latter to the poverty recommended by St Francis. Known for their austere way of life, often as hermits, they took their name from the cappuccio or hood that they wore.

40.  the infallible and natural effect: Rousseau sets out this criterion in Of the Social Contract, Book II, Chapter 9.

41.  Hôtel-Dieu: See Constitutional Proposal for Corsica, note 24, above.

42.  capitation: See Constitutional Proposal for Corsica, note 19, above.

43.  the Maréchal de Vauban and the abbé de Saint-Pierre: Sébastien Le Prestre, Marquis de Vauban (1633–1707), the great military theorist and engineer, also wrote widely on economic issues, including notably in his Projet d’une dixme royale (1707), which called for the imposition of a single 10 per cent tax on all agricultural output (payable in kind) and on income from trade and manufactures, with no exemptions. For Saint-Pierre, see Of the Social Contract, Prefatory Note, note 1, above.

44.  Antony and Crassus easily entered the territory of the Parthians: Marcus Licinius Crassus (115–53 BC) was a Roman politician and general, proverbially wealthy, and a member of the first Triumvirate (see Of the Social Contract, Book III, note 15, above). Given the governorship of Syria, he invaded the territory of the Parthian empire (in present-day Iran) in 53 BC, but was defeated and killed. Mark Antony (Marcus Antonius, 83–30 BC) was a Roman politician and general, a close supporter and ally of Julius Caesar, who following the latter’s assassination became a member of the second Triumvirate. He was involved in sporadic warfare against the Parthians between 41 and 33 BC, sometimes successfully, at other times leading to defeat on Parthian territory, notably in 37 BC.

45.  Themistocles: Themistocles (c.524–459 BC) was an Athenian politician and general, pre-eminent following the battle of Marathon and playing a vital role in the establishment of Athenian naval power and the defeat of the Persians at Salamis. He was widely viewed by later generations as the symbol of ancient Greek statesmanship.

46.  what I said in the Social Contract: See Of the Social Contract, Book II, Chapter 10.

47.  the Turkish war: The Russo–Turkish War of 1768–74 eventually turned into a decisive Russian victory, which brought southern Ukraine, northern Caucasus and the Crimea under Russian rule. In it Turkey was allied with the Polish Confederation of Bar, while Russia was allied with Great Britain.

48.  The Grand Turk: In eighteenth-century Europe, the Ottoman Sultan was commonly referred to as the Grand Turk, and his administration, headed by the Grand Vizier, as the Sublime Porte, or simply Porte, from the gate to the Divan at which the Vizier would receive diplomatic visitors.

49.  the King they sought to give you: Stanisław August Poniatowski (1732–98), a lover of Catherine the Great, was elected King of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1764, following a Russian-backed coup d’état. He supported Russian suppression of the Confederation of Bar in 1768–72, and was briefly taken prisoner by Confederate sympathizers in 1771. Although he did protest against the first partition of the Commonwealth in 1772, he was powerless to do anything about it. He remains a very controversial figure in Polish history.

chapters.title: Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings
chapters.text:
Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

Chronology

1707 Following acute conflict between the Genevan bourgeoisie and the ruling oligarchy, the leader of the democratic party, Pierre Fatio, is executed.

1712 Jean-Jacques Rousseau born on 28 June in Geneva; his mother Suzanne dies on 7 July.

1715 Death of Louis XIV of France.

1722 Rousseau’s father flees from Geneva. Rousseau is sent to live with the Lambercier family outside the city.

1724 Rousseau is apprenticed to an engraver in Geneva.

1728 Rousseau runs away and meets Mme de Warens at Annecy. She sends him to Turin, where he converts to Roman Catholicism.

1729 Rousseau returns to Annecy to live with Mme de Warens.

1738 Following further civil strife in Geneva, the Act of Mediation establishes a new constitution.

1740 Rousseau becomes a tutor to the de Mably family in Lyon. Frederick the Great comes to power in Prussia.

1742 Rousseau moves to Paris and unsuccessfully proposes a numerically based system of musical notation.

1743–4 Serves as secretary to the French Ambassador in Venice.

1744 Rousseau meets with Diderot and is inducted into French Enlightenment circles.

1745 He begins his lifelong relationship with Thérèse Levasseur.

1748 Montesquieu publishes The Spirit of Laws.

1749 On his way to visit the imprisoned Diderot, Rousseau experiences an epiphany on reading of an essay competition set by the Academy of Dijon.

1750 The Discourse on the Sciences and the Arts wins the prize from the Dijon Academy and Rousseau enjoys widespread fame.

1751 The first volume of the Encyclopédie, edited by Diderot and d’Alembert, appears.

1752 Rousseau’s opera Le Devin du Village enjoys success.

1754 Rousseau visits Geneva and reconverts to Protestantism in order to regain his citizenship.

1755 Rousseau publishes the Discourse on the Origin of Inequality and, as an entry in the Encyclopédie, the Discourse on Political Economy. The Lisbon earthquake. Pasquale Paoli proclaims Corsica a republic, independent of Genoa.

1756 Beginning of the Seven Years War.

1758 The Letter to d’Alembert on the Theatre signals Rousseau’s breach with the mainstream of the French Enlightenment.

1761 Publication of Julie, or the New Héloïse.

1762 Publication of the Social Contract and Emile. Condemnation in Paris and Geneva. Facing arrest, Rousseau flees to Môtiers in Switzerland. Catherine the Great comes to power in Russia.

1763 Rousseau renounces his Genevan citizenship. Treaty of Paris ends the Seven Years War.

1764 With Letters Written from the Mountains, Rousseau intervenes in the political debate in Geneva.

1766 At the invitation of David Hume, Rousseau travels to England, where he settles at Wootton in Staffordshire and begins work on the Confessions. Quarrels with Hume and becomes mentally unstable.

1767 Rousseau returns to France under an assumed name.

1768 Confederation of Bar forms to defend Polish independence against Russia.

1768-9 Genoa transfers its nominal sovereignty over Corsica to France. France invades Corsica and ends the Corsican Republic.

1770 Rousseau returns to Paris.

1772 First partition of Poland.

1776 Rousseau composes his final work, The Reveries of the Solitary Walker. American Declaration of Independence. Adam Smith publishes The Wealth of Nations.

1778 Rousseau dies on 2 July, aged sixty-six.

1789 Fall of the Bastille, the French Revolution begins.

1794 The French revolutionaries transfer Rousseau’s remains to the Panthéon in Paris.

1798 Geneva annexed by France.

1815 Geneva becomes a canton of Switzerland.

Of the Social Contract and Other Political Writings

He just wanted a decent book to read ...

Not too much to ask, is it? It was in 1935 when Allen Lane, Managing Director of Bodley Head Publishers, stood on a platform at Exeter railway station looking for something good to read on his journey back to London. His choice was limited to popular magazines and poor-quality paperbacks – the same choice faced every day by the vast majority of readers, few of whom could afford hardbacks. Lane’s disappointment and subsequent anger at the range of books generally available led him to found a company – and change the world.

We believed in the existence in this country of a vast reading public for intelligent books at a low price, and staked everything on it’

Sir Allen Lane, 1902–1970, founder of Penguin Books

The quality paperback had arrived – and not just in bookshops. Lane was adamant that his Penguins should appear in chain stores and tobacconists, and should cost no more than a packet of cigarettes.

Reading habits (and cigarette prices) have changed since 1935, but Penguin still believes in publishing the best books for everybody to enjoy.We still believe that good design costs no more than bad design, and we still believe that quality books published passionately and responsibly make the world a better place.

So wherever you see the little bird – whether it’s on a piece of prize-winning literary fiction or a celebrity autobiography, political tour de force or historical masterpiece, a serial-killer thriller, reference book, world classic or a piece of pure escapism – you can bet that it represents the very best that the genre has to offer.

Whatever you like to read – trust Penguin.
